en: The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.
Oṃ. Homage to the Blessed One, the Noble Perfection of Wisdom.
Chapter One: The Practice of the Knowledge of All Aspects.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain together with a great community of monks, numbering twelve hundred and fifty— all of whom were arhats, whose taints were exhausted, who were free from afflictions, who had attained mastery over themselves, whose minds were well-liberated, whose wisdom was well-liberated, who were noble ones, well-bred, great elephants, who had accomplished their task, completed what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, and whose fetters of existence were utterly destroyed.
with minds perfectly liberated through right knowledge, having attained the supreme perfection of mastery over all mental states— with the exception of one individual, namely the Venerable Ānanda.

Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the venerable elder Subhūti: "May it be inspired in you, Subhūti, concerning the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas— how the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas,
should set out in the perfection of wisdom."

Then, this thought occurred to the venerable Śāriputra: "Will this venerable elder Subhūti teach the perfection of wisdom to the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, by means of the empowerment of his own power of wisdom and eloquence, and by the support of his own power of wisdom and eloquence, or rather through the majestic power of the Buddha?"

Then, indeed, the venerable Subhūti, through the power of the Buddha, having perceived with his own mind this very reflection in the mind of the venerable Śāriputra, said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "Whatever, venerable Śāriputra,
the disciples of the Blessed One speak, teach, instruct, utter, reveal, or fully elucidate,"
All of that should be understood as the personal effort (*puruṣakāra*) of the Tathāgata.
For what reason? Because it is the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata [that constitutes it].
Training in that teaching of the Dharma, they realize and uphold that very nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Having realized and upheld that nature of phenomena, whatever they speak and whatever they teach, [is all in accordance with it].
Whatever they teach, whatever they utter, whatever— (Vaidya 3)
They illuminate;
whatever they illuminate, all that is not in contradiction with the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

Venerable Śāriputra, this is indeed the natural outflow of the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma, that these sons of good family, while instructing, do not contradict that true nature of phenomena with [their own] understanding of the true nature of phenomena.

Then, indeed, the venerable Subhūti, through the power of the Buddha, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "As the Blessed One has said— 'May it occur to you, Subhūti, concerning the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, how the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, might set forth in the perfection of wisdom'— "
"Blessed One, regarding that which is called 'bodhisattva,
bodhisattva,' of what dharma, Blessed One, is this a designation, namely 'bodhisattva'? Blessed One, I do not perceive that dharma which is called 'bodhisattva'."
Furthermore, O Blessed One, I do not perceive that phenomenon which is called "perfection of wisdom.

Thus, O Blessed One, not finding, not apprehending, and not perceiving either a bodhisattva or the qualities of a bodhisattva, and likewise not finding, not apprehending, and not perceiving the perfection of wisdom, which bodhisattva shall I instruct and admonish in which perfection of wisdom?

Moreover, Blessed One, if, when this is thus spoken, taught, and explained, the mind of a bodhisattva does not shrink back, does not sink down, does not despair, and does not fall into despondency; if his mind does not turn away, and does not become discouraged;
He does not tremble, he is not terrified, and he does not fall into fear;
this very Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is to be instructed in the perfection of wisdom.
This indeed should be understood as the perfection of wisdom of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
This is the instruction in the perfection of wisdom;
if he abides thus, this indeed is his instruction and admonition.
Furthermore, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom and cultivating the perfection of wisdom should train in such a way that, while training,
he does not even conceive pride on account of that thought of awakening.
Why is that?
For it is thus: that mind is no-mind;
the nature of the mind is luminous clarity.
Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: "Venerable Subhūti, does that mind which is 'non-mind' exist?
When this was said, the venerable Subhūti said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "Venerable Śāriputra, in that state of non-mind, does existence or non-existence exist, or is it perceived?"
Śāriputra said: "Certainly not, venerable Subhūti.

Subhūti said: "If, venerable Śāriputra, in that state of non-mindfulness (acittatā) neither existence nor non-existence is found or perceived, is it then appropriate for you, venerable Śāriputra, to make such an inquiry as to say: 'Does that mind which is non-mind exist?'"
When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: "But what, venerable Subhūti, is this state of no-mind?
Subhūti replied: "Venerable Śāriputra, the state of no-mind is unchanging and non-conceptual."
Then the venerable Śāriputra gave his approval to the venerable Subhūti, saying: "Excellent, excellent, venerable Subhūti!
Just as you have been designated by the Blessed One as the foremost of those who dwell in the state of non-contention (araṇā), so do you speak.
And for this reason, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should be examined as one who is irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
And it should be known that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is never separated from the perfection of wisdom.
Even by one who wishes to train in the stage of a śrāvaka, this very perfection of wisdom must be heard, taken up, retained, recited, mastered, and promulgated.
One should train right here in this perfection of wisdom and apply oneself to its practice.

Even one who desires to train in the stage of a Pratyekabuddha must hear, take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and propagate this very perfection of wisdom; they should train right here in this perfection of wisdom and apply themselves to its practice.
One who wishes to train even in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* must likewise hear, take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and propagate this very *prajñāpāramitā*.
In this very *prajñāpāramitā*, one endowed with skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*) should apply oneself to the full realization of all the qualities of a bodhisattva.
Why is that?
For it is precisely here in this Perfection of Wisdom that all the qualities of a bodhisattva have been taught in detail,
wherein a bodhisattva mahāsattva must train and apply himself with diligence.
Even one who desires to train for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment should hear, take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and propagate this very Perfection of Wisdom.
In this very Perfection of Wisdom, one endowed with skill in means should apply oneself to the complete realization of all the qualities of a Buddha.
Why is that?
Because it is in this very Perfection of Wisdom that all the qualities of a Buddha are taught in detail.
In this, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train and apply himself to yoga.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, as for me, I do not know, do not apprehend, and do not perceive even this very name 'bodhisattva';
I also do not know, do not apprehend, and do not perceive the perfection of wisdom.
Thus, Blessed One, not finding, not apprehending, and not perceiving even this very name 'bodhisattva'..."
Not finding, not apprehending, and not perceiving even the perfection of wisdom, which bodhisattva shall I instruct and admonish in which perfection of wisdom?
O Blessed One, this itself would be a cause for remorse.
Since I do not find, do not perceive, and do not observe any such entity, how could I perform the accounting of income and expenditure by means of a mere name, namely "bodhisattva"?
Furthermore, Blessed One, even that name is neither established nor unestablished, neither fixed nor unfixed.
Why is that?
Because that name does not exist,
thus that name is neither established nor unestablished, neither fixed nor unfixed. If,
when this profound perfection of wisdom is being spoken, taught, and explained, the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not sink down or become despondent...
He does not despair, he does not fall into despondency; his mind does not turn away,
nor does it become broken.
He is not afraid, he is not terrified, and he does not fall into terror.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is resolved with resolute intention and is never separated from the perfection of wisdom should be known as established on the irreversible bodhisattva stage.
He is well-established by way of non-abiding.
Furthermore, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom and cultivating the perfection of wisdom should not abide in form, nor in feeling, nor in perception,
nor in mental formations.
One should not abide in consciousness.
Why is that?
Because if one abides in form, [one does not abide in the perfection of wisdom].
If one courses in the formative activity of form,
one does not course in the perfection of wisdom;
likewise, if one [courses] in feeling, perception, or volitional formations.
If he abides in consciousness,
he courses in the formative activity of consciousness;
he does not course in the perfection of wisdom.
For what reason?
Because one who courses in volitional formation does not grasp the perfection of wisdom,
nor does one apply oneself to the yoga of the perfection of wisdom.
Nor does he fulfill the perfection of wisdom;
not fulfilling the perfection of wisdom,
while grasping that which is ungraspable in omniscience, he will not go forth to it.
For what reason?
Because form is not grasped in the perfection of wisdom;
likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
For consciousness is not grasped in the perfection of wisdom;
and that which is the non-grasping of form is not form.
In the same way, that which is the non-appropriation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
that is not consciousness.
That perfection of wisdom, too, is ungrasped.
Thus indeed should a bodhisattva mahāsattva course in this perfection of wisdom.
And this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s samādhi called "ungrasping at all dharmas," which is vast, preeminent, immeasurable, fixed, and uncommon.
Even that omniscience is not grasped by all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
for it is not to be grasped by way of signs;
if it were to be grasped by way of signs, [it would not be omniscience].
And Śreṇika the wanderer would not have found faith here;
for there, Śreṇika the wanderer, having resolved upon the knowledge of the Omniscient One, entered as a follower by faith through partial knowledge. Having entered, he did not grasp at form.
In this way, one does not grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
nor does one perceive that knowledge through the pleasure and joy associated with them.
One does not perceive that knowledge of form internally;
one does not perceive that knowledge of form externally;
one does not perceive that knowledge of form both internally and externally.
Nor does he perceive that knowledge as being elsewhere than form;
likewise, he does not perceive that knowledge internally within feeling, perception, or mental formations;
nor does he perceive that knowledge internally within consciousness.
One does not perceive that knowledge of consciousness externally;
one does not perceive that knowledge of consciousness both internally and externally;
nor does one perceive that knowledge apart from consciousness.
In this sequence of words, the wandering mendicant Śreṇika was resolved;
he, being a follower by faith in all respects, having taken the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as his authority regarding the knowledge of the Omniscient One, was thus resolved.
Therefore, no dharma whatsoever was grasped by him.
Nor is there any dharma whatsoever that has been apprehended, which one could either grasp or relinquish;
he does not even conceive of nirvana.

"Blessed One, this too should be known as the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva: that which does not grasp at form; likewise, that which does not grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."

Nor does he attain final nirvana in the interval, as long as the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence of a Tathāgata, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are not yet fulfilled.
Therefore, Blessed One, this too should be understood as the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom and cultivating the perfection of wisdom should investigate in this way and contemplate in this way:
"What is this perfection of wisdom?
To whom does this perfection of wisdom belong?"
Is it that the dharma which does not exist and is not apprehended is the perfection of wisdom?

If, while examining in this way and reflecting in this way, one is not cowed, does not shrink back, does not despair, and does not fall into despondency, [then one is practicing the perfection of wisdom].
His mind does not turn away, nor does it become dejected; he is not startled, nor terrified, nor does he fall into a state of panic.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as not separated from the perfection of wisdom.

Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: "For what reason, venerable Subhūti, should it be understood that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not separated from the perfection of wisdom,
when form itself is separated from the intrinsic nature of form,
and likewise when feeling, perception, and mental formations themselves [are separated from their respective intrinsic natures]?"
When consciousness itself is devoid of the intrinsic nature of consciousness,
when the perfection of wisdom itself is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom,
and when omniscience itself is devoid of the intrinsic nature of omniscience.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "It is so, venerable Śāriputra; it is even so.
Form itself, venerable Śāriputra, is devoid of the intrinsic nature of form.
Likewise, feeling itself, perception itself, and mental formations themselves [are devoid of their respective intrinsic natures]."
Venerable Śāriputra, consciousness itself is devoid of the intrinsic nature of consciousness;
venerable Śāriputra, the perfection of wisdom itself is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom;
venerable Śāriputra, omniscience itself is devoid of the intrinsic nature of omniscience.
The perfection of wisdom is devoid even of the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom;
the characteristic is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the characteristic;
and the characterized object is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the characterized object.
Even by way of the characteristic of intrinsic nature, intrinsic nature is devoid [of itself].
When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: "Furthermore, venerable Subhūti, will that bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this emerge into omniscience?
The venerable Subhūti replied: "So it is, venerable Śāriputra; so it is."
Any bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this will go forth to omniscience.
Why is that?
For all phenomena, O Venerable Śāriputra, are indeed unborn and indeed unproduced.
As a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices in this way, O Venerable Śāriputra, omniscience draws near.
To the extent that omniscience draws near, [so does he draw near].
In that very way, for the sake of maturing sentient beings, there occurs the purification of body and mind, the purification of the marks [of a great man], and the purification of the buddha-field;
and one comes to meet with the Buddhas.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in this manner within the perfection of wisdom draws near to omniscience.
Furthermore, the venerable Subhūti addressed the bodhisattva mahāsattva as follows: "If he courses in form, he courses in a sign;
if he courses in the sign of form, [he courses in a sign]."
One courses in a sign;
if one courses with the thought that "form is a sign," one courses in a sign.
If he courses in the arising of form,
he courses in a sign; if he courses in the cessation of form, he courses in a sign.
He courses in a sign;
if he courses in the destruction of form,
he courses in a sign.
If one practices with the thought that "form is empty," one practices in signs; if one practices with the thought "I am practicing," one practices in signs.
He courses in a sign;
he courses with the thought "I am a bodhisattva," and thus he courses in a sign.

If he thinks, "I am a bodhisattva," he is indeed practicing in apprehension. Likewise, if he practices in feeling, perception, volitional formations, or if he practices in consciousness, [he is practicing in apprehension].
He courses in a sign; if he courses in the sign of consciousness, he courses in a sign;
if he courses with the thought "consciousness is a sign," he courses in a sign.
He courses in a sign;
if he courses in the arising of consciousness,
he courses in a sign.
If one courses in the cessation of consciousness,
one courses in a sign; if one courses in the destruction of consciousness, one courses in a sign.
He courses in a sign.
If he courses with the thought that "consciousness is empty," he courses in a sign.
If one practices thinking "I am practicing," one practices with signs; if one practices thinking "I am a bodhisattva," one practices with signs.
He courses in signs;
for he who thinks "I am a bodhisattva" courses in apprehension indeed. But if it should further occur to him: "He who courses in this way..."
To say that "he courses in the perfection of wisdom" or "he cultivates the perfection of wisdom"—
he courses in a mere sign.
This bodhisattva should be known as one who is unskilled in means.
Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: "But how, venerable Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing, course in the perfection of wisdom?
When this was said, the venerable Subhūti said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "If, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not course in form, nor does he course in the sign of form..."
One does not course in the notion that form is a sign;
one does not course in the arising of form, nor in the cessation of form.
He practices, but he does not practice for the destruction of form;
he does not practice with the thought "form is empty"; he does not practice with the thought "I am practicing."
He does not course with the thought, "I am a bodhisattva. Likewise, if he does not course in feeling, nor in perception, nor in mental formations,
nor if he does not course in consciousness, [then he courses in the perfection of wisdom].
He does not course in the sign of consciousness,
nor does he course [thinking] "consciousness is a sign," nor does he course in the arising of consciousness.
He does not course in the cessation of consciousness, he does not course in the destruction of consciousness, nor does he course with the thought that "consciousness is empty."
He does not practice with the thought, "I am practicing," nor does he practice with the thought, "I am a bodhisattva. Furthermore, it does not occur to him: "He who practices in this way..."
"He practices the perfection of wisdom; he cultivates the perfection of wisdom.
Practicing in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom.
For while walking, he does not conceive "I am walking," nor does he conceive "I am not walking," nor does he conceive "I both walk and do not walk."
He does not approach the thought, "I am practicing," nor "I am not practicing";
he does not approach the thought, "I shall practice," nor "I shall not practice."
He does not approach the thought, "I shall practice," nor "I shall not practice";
he does not even approach the thought, "I neither shall practice nor shall I not practice.
For what reason does he not approach these?
For all dharmas are indeed unapproached and unappropriated.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s samādhi named "Non-appropriation of All Dharmas"; it is vast, preeminent, immeasurable, fixed, and uncommon to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Dwelling by means of this very samādhi, the bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Through the power of the Buddha, the Venerable Elder Subhūti spoke thus: "Lord, this bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells in this samādhi has been predicted for unexcelled [enlightenment] by previous Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas;
yet he does not even perceive that samādhi."
And by that concentration, he does not conceive: "I am concentrated," "I shall enter into concentration," or "I am entering into concentration."
"I have entered into meditative absorption"—
in this way, for him, nothing whatsoever exists in any way whatsoever.

When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: "By means of which concentration, venerable Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell so that he is prophesied by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?"
"Is that concentration possible to demonstrate?
Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, venerable Śāriputra. For what reason?"
For that noble son does not know, nor does he perceive, even that samādhi.
The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Venerable Subhūti, do you say that he does not know and does not perceive?"
The Venerable Subhūti said: "I say, Venerable Śāriputra, that he neither knows nor perceives.
For what reason does he neither know nor perceive?
Because that samādhi does not exist, he neither knows nor perceives that samādhi."
Then the Blessed One gave his approval to the venerable Subhūti: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!
It is so, Subhūti, it is so. It is just as you have been inspired to speak through the power of the Tathāgata."
"You teach by the empowerment of the Tathāgata;
and in this manner, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train herein. For what reason?"
Training in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom.
Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, when training in this way, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in the perfection of wisdom?
When this was said, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, when training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom."
When this had been said, the Venerable Śāriputra said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, in what dharma does he train?
When this had been said, the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, he does not train in any dharma at all. Why is that?"
“Indeed, Śāriputra, those dharmas do not exist in the way that unlearned, ordinary worldlings are attached to them.
The Venerable Śāriputra said, “In what way, then, O Blessed One, do they exist?
The Blessed One replied, “Śāriputra, in the very way that they do not exist.”
They exist in such a way that they do not exist;
therefore, they are called "ignorance.
Unlearned, foolish ordinary people are attached to them.
By them, all phenomena—which do not exist—have been conceptualized. Having conceptualized them, they are attached to the two extremes; thus they neither know nor see those phenomena.
Therefore, they conceptualize all phenomena as existing when they do not exist.

Having conceptualized, they adhere to two extremes; having adhered, based on that cause and relying upon apprehension, they conceptualize past phenomena, they conceptualize future phenomena, and they conceptualize present phenomena.
Having conceptualized, they are attached to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
By them, all dharmas—which do not exist—have been imagined. While imagining those non-existent dharmas, they neither know nor see the path as it truly is.
Not knowing and not seeing the path as it truly is, they do not emerge from the triple world.
They do not realize the limit of reality;
therefore, they receive the designation "fools.
They do not have faith in the true Dharma.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not, indeed, adhere to any dharma whatsoever.
When this had been said, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this way train in omniscience?
The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this way does not even train in omniscience.
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this way trains in all dharmas."
Training in this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in omniscience, draws near to omniscience, and will emerge into omniscience.

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if someone were to ask thus: 'Will this illusory person train in omniscience, will he draw near to omniscience, and will he set out toward omniscience?'"
"Blessed One, when he asks such a question, how should it be explained?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "In that case, Subhūti, I shall question you regarding this matter; answer as you see fit."
"Explain it thus.
"Very well, Blessed One," the venerable Subhūti replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this: "What do you think, Subhūti? Is that illusion something other [than the Tathāgata]?"
That form is one thing, that illusion is another, and that feeling is another.
That perception is one thing, those volitional formations are another;
that illusion is yet another.
"Is that consciousness something other than that?
Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
For, Blessed One, that illusion is not one thing and that form another."
Form itself, Blessed One, is illusion; illusion itself is form.
For, Blessed One, that illusion is not one thing and that feeling another.
That perception is one thing, and those volitional formations are another;
O Blessed One, feeling, perception, and volitional formations themselves are an illusion.
Illusion itself is feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Blessed One, that illusion is not one thing and consciousness another;
consciousness itself, Blessed One, is illusion.
Consciousness itself is indeed illusion.

The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti, is this designation, this appellation, this conceptualization, this conventional usage regarding these five aggregates of clinging—that is to say, 'bodhisattva'?
When this was said, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata."
Therefore, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in the perfection of wisdom should train for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment as if he were an illusory person.
Why is that?
Because, Blessed One, those very five aggregates of clinging are to be understood as an illusory person.
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, form has been declared by the Blessed One to be like an illusion;
and that which is form consists of the six sense-faculties and those five aggregates.
For thus, Blessed One, feeling, perception, and mental formations have been said to be like an illusion;
for thus, Blessed One, consciousness has been described by the Blessed One as being like an illusion.
And that which is consciousness is the six sense faculties, which are those five aggregates.
“Blessed One, let it not be that the bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have newly set out in the vehicle will, upon hearing this teaching, be terrified, become terrified, or fall into terror.

The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, if the bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have newly set out in the vehicle fall into the hands of evil friends, they will be terrified, become terrified, and fall into terror.”
Moreover, Subhūti, if bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have newly set out in the vehicle come into the hands of spiritual friends,
they will not be afraid, they will not be terrified, and they will not fall into terror.
When this had been said, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, who, moreover, are to be known as the good friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Blessed One replied: "Those who instruct and admonish him in the perfections;
those who point out to him the works of Māra."
In this way, the faults of Māra are to be understood: "These are the faults of Māra. In this way, the deeds of Māra are to be understood: "These are the deeds of Māra.
Having understood them, you must avoid them.
"Subhūti, these should be known as the spiritual friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is armored with the great armor, who has set out in the Great Vehicle, and who has mounted the Great Vehicle.

When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One: "Regarding what the Blessed One has thus said: 'Subhūti, these [are the spiritual friends] of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is armored with the great armor, who has set out in the Great Vehicle, and who has mounted the Great Vehicle'..."
"Virtuous friends are to be known.
And as for what is called a "bodhisattva mahāsattva," O Blessed One—
therein, O Blessed One, what is the meaning of the term "bodhisattva"?
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, the term 'bodhisattva' is a term for a non-entity.
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the state of non-attachment toward all phenomena."
"Subhūti, it is because of the realization of all dharmas that a bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in the state of non-attachment.
Yet, Subhūti, it is for the sake of awakening (*bodhi*) that one is called a 'bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti said: "As for what the Blessed One has thus said—that one is a 'bodhisattva mahāsattva'—"
"For what reason, Blessed One, is a bodhisattva called a 'mahāsattva'?
The Blessed One replied: "Because he will bring about leadership over a great mass of beings, a great multitude of beings; for that reason, a bodhisattva is called a 'mahāsattva'."

Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, it occurs to me as well for what reason a Bodhisattva is called a ‘Mahāsattva. The Blessed One said: “Let it occur to you, Śāriputra, whenever you deem it the right time. The venerable Śāriputra said: “It is because of the great view of self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-force, and the view of a person...”
For the sake of abandoning views such as the view of existence, the view of non-existence, the view of annihilationism, the view of eternalism, and the view of a self-identity—
he will teach the Dharma for the abandonment of these and other such views;
for that reason, he is called a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it occurs to me as well for what reason a bodhisattva is called a 'mahāsattva'.
The Blessed One said: "Let it occur to you, Subhūti, whenever you deem it the right time.
Subhūti said: "Blessed One, one is called a 'bodhisattva mahāsattva'..."

Furthermore, Blessed One, even regarding that bodhicitta— the mind of omniscience, the untainted mind, the peerless mind, the mind equal to the unequaled, the mind not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—
one is unattached and uninvolved even in that mind. Why is that?
For that mind of omniscience is untainted and unconditioned; and even with respect to that mind of omniscience which is untainted and unconditioned, he is unattached and unconditioned.
In that sense, he is reckoned as a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: "For what reason, venerable Subhūti, is one unattached and uninvolved even with that mind?
Subhūti replied: "Because it is non-mind, venerable Śāriputra, one is unattached and uninvolved even with that mind."
Śāriputra said: "But, venerable Subhūti, does that mind which is 'no-mind' exist?
Subhūti replied: "But, venerable Śāriputra, in that state of no-mind, does existence or non-existence exist or is it perceived?
Śāriputra said: "Certainly not, venerable Subhūti."

Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāriputra, if in that state of non-mindfulness (acittatā) neither existence nor non-existence is found or perceived, then how, Venerable Śāriputra, can you say: 'Does that mind exist which is a non-mind'?
Śāriputra said: "Excellent, excellent, Venerable Subhūti!"
Just as you have indeed been designated by the Blessed One as the foremost among those who dwell in the state of non-conflict, so do you speak.

Then the venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, regarding that which is called 'mahāsattva, mahāsattva,' that being is one who has donned the great armor; that being is one who has set out upon the Great Vehicle and has mounted the Great Vehicle."
Therefore, that great being comes to be reckoned as a "mahāsattva" (great being).

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, regarding that which is called 'one girded with the great armor,' 'one girded for the Great Vehicle'—to what extent, Blessed One, is a bodhisattva mahāsattva one who is girded with the great armor?
The Blessed One replied: "In this regard, Subhūti, it occurs to a bodhisattva mahāsattva: 'I must lead immeasurable sentient beings to final nirvāṇa.'"
"I must lead incalculable sentient beings to final nirvana," yet there are no such beings by whom they are to be led to final nirvana;
nevertheless, he leads that many sentient beings to final nirvana.
And there is no such being who has entered final nirvāṇa, nor anyone by whom another has been led to enter final nirvāṇa.
For what reason?
Subhūti, this is the true nature of phenomena, based upon the illusory nature of phenomena.
"Subhūti, it is just as if a skilled magician, or a magician’s apprentice, were to conjure up a great multitude of people at a crossroads of four great roads;
and having conjured them, he were then to make that very great multitude of people disappear.
What do you think, Subhūti, would anyone there have been killed, or dead, or destroyed, or made to disappear?"
Subhūti said, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "In just this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva brings immeasurable and incalculable beings to final nirvāṇa."
And there is no such being who has attained parinirvāṇa, nor anyone by whom another has been caused to attain parinirvāṇa.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this teaching being thus expounded, does not tremble, does not become terrified, and does not fall into fear,
then by this much he should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has donned the great armor.

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, as I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken, it should be known, Blessed One, that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is indeed one who is armed with the armor of non-armor.
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Subhūti; so it is."
Indeed, this bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as one who is armored with the armor of the unarmored.
Why is that?
Subhūti, for omniscience is uncreated, unmodified, and unconditioned.
Those beings for whose sake this armor has been donned are also uncreated, unmodified, and unconditioned.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata. For what reason?"
For in this way, Blessed One, form is neither bound nor liberated;
likewise are feeling, perception, and mental formations.
For in this way, Blessed One, consciousness is neither bound nor liberated.
“O Blessed One, even the suchness of form is neither bound nor liberated;
likewise, the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, the suchness of formations,
and even the suchness of consciousness, O Blessed One, are neither bound nor liberated.”

Then the venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: "Venerable Subhūti, do you say that form is neither bound nor liberated? Likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, venerable Subhūti, do you say they are neither bound nor liberated?"
"Venerable Subhūti, you say that even the suchness of form is neither bound nor liberated;
likewise, you say that the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, the suchness of formations, and even the suchness of consciousness, Venerable Subhūti, are neither bound nor liberated."
Now, Venerable Subhūti, what is that form which you say is form that is neither bound nor liberated?
Likewise, what is that feeling, and what is that perception?
"What are those formations?
And what, Venerable Subhūti, is that consciousness which you say is neither bound nor liberated?
And what, Venerable Subhūti, is that suchness of form which you say is the suchness of form that is also neither bound nor liberated?"
"In this way, what is that suchness of feeling, that suchness of perception, that suchness of mental formations?
And what, venerable Subhūti, is that suchness of consciousness of which you say that even the suchness of consciousness is neither bound nor liberated?
When this was said, the venerable Subhūti spoke thus to the venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra: "Venerable Pūrṇa, that which is the form of an illusory person is neither bound nor liberated."
In the same way, whatever is the feeling of an illusory person, whatever is the perception of an illusory person, and whatever are the mental formations of an illusory person—
Venerable Pūrṇa, that which is the consciousness of an illusory person is neither bound nor liberated.
Venerable Pūrṇa, that which is the suchness of form of an illusory person is neither bound nor liberated.
Likewise, that which is the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, and the suchness of mental formations of an illusory person [are neither bound nor liberated].
Venerable Pūrṇa, that which is the suchness of consciousness of an illusory person is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is that?
Because it is non-existent, it is neither bound nor liberated.
Because they are secluded, they are neither bound nor liberated; because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
This is the great armor of the bodhisattva mahāsattva who has donned the great armor, set out upon the Great Vehicle, and mounted the Great Vehicle—an armor that is no armor.
When this had been said, the venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra remained silent.

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "In this way, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having donned the great armor, becomes one who has set out in the Great Vehicle and has mounted upon the Great Vehicle.
And what is that Great Vehicle?"
How, moreover, is one who has set out upon it to be known?
From where will that Great Vehicle depart? Or by what means has that Great Vehicle set out?
"Where will that Great Vehicle abide? Or who will set forth by means of this Great Vehicle?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, 'Great Vehicle' is a designation for immeasurability."
"Subhūti, it is 'immeasurable' because it is measureless.
Furthermore, Subhūti, as to what you asked: 'How is one who has set out in that [vehicle] to be known?
Or from where will that Great Vehicle depart?'"
By what has that Great Vehicle set out?
Where will that Great Vehicle abide? Or who will depart by means of this Great Vehicle?
Having set out by means of the perfections,
he will depart from the triple world;
he has set out toward that which is the objective support.
The bodhisattva mahāsattva will abide in omniscience and will set forth;
yet, moreover, he will not set forth from anywhere at all.
It has not set out by means of anything; it will not abide anywhere;
rather, it will abide in omniscience through the yoga of non-abiding.
Nor has anyone departed by means of that Great Vehicle, nor will anyone depart, nor does anyone depart.
Why is that?
Because whoever might depart—
And that by which one would go forth—
both these factors do not exist and are not apprehended.
Since all phenomena are thus non-existent, what phenomenon will go forth by means of what phenomenon?
For in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes one who is armored with the Great Vehicle, set out upon the Great Vehicle, and mounted upon the Great Vehicle.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it is called the 'Great Vehicle, the Great Vehicle.
That Great Vehicle will set forth surpassing the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, because of its equality with space and its extreme vastness.
Just as in space there is room for immeasurable and incalculable beings,"
In the same way, Blessed One, there is room in this vehicle for immeasurable and incalculable beings.
By this method, Blessed One, this is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas;
its arrival is not seen at all.
Neither its departure is seen, nor does its staying exist;
in this same way, Blessed One, no prior limit of this Great Vehicle is apprehended.
Neither the future limit nor the middle is perceived; therefore,
Blessed One, that vehicle is equal.
Therefore, the Great Vehicle is called the "Great Vehicle.
Then the Blessed One gave his approval to the venerable Subhūti: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!
It is so, Subhūti; it is just so."
Thus is this Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas;
having trained in it, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas have attained, will attain, and are attaining omniscience.

Then the venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, this Elder Subhūti, having been requested for the sake of the perfection of wisdom, thinks that he should teach the Mahāyāna.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, I have not spoken of the Mahāyāna by departing from the perfection of wisdom."
The Blessed One said: "Not so, Subhūti.
Subhūti, you are teaching the Mahāyāna in accordance with the perfection of wisdom.
When this was said, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "It is through the power of the Buddha, Blessed One."
Furthermore, Blessed One, a bodhisattva is not apprehended from the past limit,
a bodhisattva is not apprehended from the future limit, and a bodhisattva is not apprehended from the middle.
For what reason does he not approach it?
Because the boundlessness of form should be understood as the boundlessness of the bodhisattva;
and so too for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Indeed, through the boundlessness of consciousness, the boundlessness of the bodhisattva is to be understood.
One does not approach the notion that "form is the bodhisattva";
this too does not exist and is not apprehended.
In the same way, one does not approach the idea that "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the bodhisattva";
this too does not exist and is not apprehended.
Thus, O Blessed One, not perceiving any bodhisattva-dharma whatsoever in every way and in all respects, I do not, O Blessed One, perceive that dharma for which this name exists, namely "bodhisattva.
I do not perceive nor do I apprehend even the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

I do not perceive omniscience, nor do I apprehend it. Therefore, O Blessed One, since I do not apprehend or perceive that dharma in any way, in any manner, or in any respect whatsoever, what dharma shall I instruct, by means of what dharma, and in what dharma shall I teach?
"Buddha," O Blessed One, is a mere name; "Bodhisattva," O Blessed One, is a mere name;
"Perfection of Wisdom," O Blessed One, is a mere name.
And that designation is unproduced.
Just as, O Blessed One, "self, self" is spoken of,
yet, O Blessed One, the self is absolutely unproduced.
Thus, for all phenomena that lack intrinsic nature, what is that form which is ungraspable and unproduced?
What are those feelings, perceptions, and mental formations?
And what is that consciousness which is ungraspable and unproduced?
Thus, that which is the absence of intrinsic nature in all these phenomena is their non-origination;
and that which is the non-origination of all phenomena, those are not phenomena.
So then, shall I instruct and admonish [the Bodhisattva] in a perfection of wisdom that is non-origination by means of non-origination?
For, Blessed One, apart from non-origination, neither all dharmas, nor Buddha-dharmas, nor Bodhisattva-dharmas are apprehended, nor anyone who would course toward enlightenment.

Blessed One, if, when this is thus spoken, thus taught, and thus instructed, the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not shrink back, does not sink down, does not despair, and does not fall into despondency;
if his mind does not turn away, does not become discouraged, and does not tremble, does not fear, and does not fall into terror,
then it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the perfection of wisdom; this bodhisattva mahāsattva examines the perfection of wisdom;
this bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the perfection of wisdom."
For what reason? Because,
Blessed One, at the time when a bodhisattva mahāsattva thoroughly examines these phenomena within the perfection of wisdom, at that time he does not approach form.
He does not approach form;
he does not perceive the arising of form, nor does he perceive the cessation of form.
In this way, one does not approach feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations;
one does not approach consciousness, nor does one go toward consciousness.
He does not perceive the arising of consciousness, nor does he perceive the cessation of consciousness.
Why is that?
For indeed, that which is the non-arising of form is not that form;
that which is the non-perishing of form is not that form.
Thus, non-arising and form are non-dual; this is an indivisible unity.
Thus, the imperishable and form— these are non-dual and cannot be divided.
Furthermore, that which is called "form" is merely a designation applied to this non-duality.
In the same way, it is so for feeling, perception, and mental formations; likewise,
that which is the non-arising of consciousness is not that consciousness,
and that which is the non-perishing of consciousness is not that consciousness.
Thus, non-arising and consciousness are non-dual; this is an indivisible unity.
Thus, the imperishable and consciousness are non-dual; this is an indivisible unity.
Furthermore, that which is called "consciousness"—
This calculation was made by means of non-duality.
Thus, Blessed One, when one examines all phenomena in all their aspects within the perfection of wisdom, at that time one does not approach form,
nor does one arrive at form.
He does not perceive the arising of form,
nor does he perceive the cessation of form;
likewise, he does not [perceive the arising or cessation] of feeling, perception, or mental formations.
He does not approach consciousness,
he does not go toward consciousness,
and he does not perceive the arising of consciousness.
One does not perceive the cessation of consciousness.
Why is that?
Because that which is the non-arising of form is not that form.
That which is the non-perishing of form is not that form;
thus, non-arising and form are non-dual, this being an indivisible unity;
thus, the non-perishing and form are non-dual, this being an indivisible unity.
Furthermore, as for this which is called "form," this is merely a designation made for that which is non-dual.
It is the same for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
For indeed, that which is the non-arising of consciousness is not that consciousness;
that which is the non-perishing of consciousness is not that consciousness.
Thus, non-arising and consciousness are non-dual; this is an indivisible unity.
Thus, the inexhaustible and consciousness are non-dual, without division.
Furthermore, as for this which is called "consciousness," this is merely a designation applied to the non-dual.
Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: "In that case, as I understand the meaning of what the venerable Subhūti has said, a bodhisattva is also non-arising.
And if, venerable Subhūti, a bodhisattva is also non-arising, why does a bodhisattva practice the conduct of difficult deeds?"
"Or rather, would he be willing to undergo those sufferings for the sake of sentient beings?

When this was said, the venerable Subhūti said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "Venerable Śāriputra, I do not wish for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to practice a course of difficult deeds, nor does that bodhisattva mahāsattva [wish to do so]."
Whoever practices with the perception of difficulty—
why is that? For,
venerable Śāriputra, it is not possible to accomplish the welfare of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings after having generated the perception of difficulty.
Rather, having formed the very perception of happiness,

and having formed the perception of mother, the perception of father, the perception of son, and the perception of daughter toward all sentient beings— toward both women and men— the bodhisattva mahāsattva, having formed these perceptions, practices the conduct of a bodhisattva.

Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should produce toward all sentient beings the perception of them as mother, the perception of them as father, the perception of them as son, and the perception of them as daughter, even up to the perception of them as oneself.

Just as one’s own self is to be liberated from all sufferings in every way, entirely, and in all respects, so too all sentient beings are to be liberated from all sufferings in every way, entirely, and in all respects.
And thus, one should conceive this thought toward all sentient beings: "I must not abandon these all sentient beings;
I must liberate these all sentient beings from the immeasurable mass of suffering.
And I must not give rise to a single thought of malice toward them, even if I were to be cut into pieces a hundred times over."
For in this way a bodhisattva mahāsattva should generate the thought: "If he dwells with such a mind,
he will practice without the perception of difficulty,
and he will dwell without the perception of difficulty."

Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should generate this thought: "Just as in every way, in all respects, and in every manner, a self does not exist and is not apprehended, so too, in every way, in all respects, and in every manner, all phenomena do not exist and are not apprehended.
In this way, one should generate such a perception regarding all internal and external phenomena.
If he practices with such a mind,
he will not practice with the perception of difficulty,
nor will he dwell with the perception of difficulty.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, as to what you have said— that a bodhisattva is non-arising—
so it is, Venerable Śāriputra, so it is;
a bodhisattva is non-arising.
Śāriputra asked: "Furthermore, venerable Subhūti, is it only the bodhisattva who is non-arising, or are the qualities of a bodhisattva also non-arising?
Subhūti replied: "Venerable Śāriputra, even the qualities of a bodhisattva are non-arising. Śāriputra asked: "Furthermore, venerable Subhūti, are only the qualities of a bodhisattva non-arising..."
"Or is even omniscience non-arising?
Subhūti said, "O venerable Śāriputra, even omniscience is non-arising. He asked, "But what then, venerable Subhūti..."
"Is omniscience itself non-arising, or are the dharmas of omniscience also non-arising?
He replied, "Venerable Śāriputra, even the dharmas of omniscience are non-arising."
He asked: "Venerable Subhūti, are only the dharmas of omniscience non-arising, or is even the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) non-arising?
He replied: "Venerable Śāriputra, even the ordinary person is non-arising."
He asked: "Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, is it only the ordinary person who is non-arising, or are even the dharmas of the ordinary person non-arising?
He replied: "Venerable Śāriputra, even the dharmas of the ordinary person are non-arising."
When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: "Venerable Subhūti, if even a bodhisattva is non-arising,
if even the qualities of a bodhisattva are non-arising,
and if even omniscience is non-arising..."
The qualities of omniscience are non-arising,
the ordinary person is non-arising,
and even the qualities of an ordinary person are non-arising.
"Venerable Subhūti, surely all-knowledge is already attained by a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva without effort?
When this was said, the venerable Subhūti said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "Venerable Śāriputra, I do not desire the attainment of an unarisen dharma, nor its clear realization."
Nor is an unarisen attainment attained by means of an unarisen dharma.
He asked: "But, Venerable Subhūti, is an unarisen attainment attained by means of an unarisen dharma, or rather, is an unarisen attainment attained by means of an arisen dharma?"
He asked: "Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, is a non-arisen dharma arisen, or is a non-arisen dharma simply non-arisen?
He replied: "Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, is arising itself the non-arising of a dharma?"
"Or is the dharma non-arising, or is it arising?
He replied, "Venerable Śāriputra, it does not occur to me to speak of the dharma as 'arising' or the dharma as 'non-arising'.
[Śāriputra] said, "Venerable Subhūti, does it not also occur to you to speak of 'non-arising'?"
He said: "Venerable Śāriputra, non-arising itself is discourse;
venerable Śāriputra, non-arising itself appears;
venerable Śāriputra, non-arising itself is eloquence."
In the same way, venerable Śāriputra, it appears to me quite clearly.
When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: "The venerable Subhūti should be established as the foremost among those who discourse on the Dharma.
Why is that?
Because in whatever way the elder, the venerable Subhūti, is questioned,"
From that very state it emerges,
yet it does not deviate from the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
nor does it contradict that nature of phenomena.

When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra: "This, venerable Śāriputra, is the nature of things (dharmatā) regarding the Blessed One’s disciples who have no fixed reliance:
from whatever they are questioned, from that very point they emerge."
And they do not contradict the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), nor do they deviate from the nature of phenomena. Why is that?
"Just as it is because all phenomena are indeed non-reliant.
When this was said, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: "Excellent, excellent, venerable Subhūti!
What is this perfection of non-reliance upon all phenomena for the sake of bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas?"

Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāriputra, the perfection of wisdom itself is universal for all vehicles; and because it does not rely upon any phenomena, it is the perfection that does not rely upon any phenomena.
Thus, when this profound perfection of wisdom is being spoken, taught, and explained in this way, if the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not [become discouraged],"
There is no state of doubt, there is no state of hesitation,
and there is no alteration of the mind.
"It should be understood that this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells by means of this dwelling in the perfection of wisdom and is not devoid of this mental attention.

Then, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: "In what way, venerable Subhūti, is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells by means of the dwelling in the perfection of wisdom not devoid of mental attention?"
For if, venerable Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not separated from mental attention,
then he is separated from dwelling in the perfection of wisdom.
And if, venerable Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not separated from dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, [then he is not separated from mental attention].
In this way, he becomes separated from mental engagement.
And if, venerable Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not separated from mental engagement,
then he is indeed not separated from dwelling in the perfection of wisdom.
This being so, all sentient beings will also never be separated from the dwelling in the perfection of wisdom.
Why is that?
Because all sentient beings also dwell without being separated from mental attention.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "Excellent, excellent, venerable Śāriputra!
Nevertheless, I shall reprove you.
Yet, the very meaning has been grasped by the venerable Śāriputra through his use of words that express reality."
For what reason?

Venerable Śāriputra, because sentient beings lack intrinsic nature, one should know that mental attention lacks intrinsic nature; Venerable Śāriputra, because sentient beings do not exist as real entities, one should know that mental attention does not exist as a real entity.
Venerable Śāriputra, through the solitude of sentient beings, the solitude of mental attention should be understood.
Venerable Śāriputra, through the inconceivability of sentient beings, the inconceivability of mental attention should be understood.
Venerable Śāriputra, through the non-awakening of sentient beings, the non-awakening of mental attention should be understood.
Venerable Śāriputra, through the realization of the meaning of sentient beings as it truly is, one should understand the realization of the meaning of mental attention as it truly is.
Venerable Śāriputra, by means of such mental attention as this, I desire that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should dwell in this dwelling.
In the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom, the first chapter, titled "The Practice of the Knowledge of All Aspects."
(Vaidya 17) Chapter Two: Śakra.
Now at that time, Śakra, the lord of the gods, was present and seated in that very assembly together with forty thousand sons of the gods belonging to the Trāyastriṃśa host.
Together with him were the four world-protectors, along with twenty thousand sons of the gods belonging to the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm;
and Brahmā Sahāpati also, together with ten thousand sons of the gods belonging to the Brahmakāyika realm.
And five thousand sons of the gods from the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa) were also assembled and seated in that very assembly.

Furthermore, whatever radiance belonged to those gods, born of the maturation of their own karma, all of it was eclipsed by the power of the Buddha, the majesty of the Buddha, and the empowerment of the Buddha.

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the venerable Subhūti the Elder: "Noble Subhūti, these many thousands of sons of the gods have assembled and are seated here in this assembly, desiring to hear the perfection of wisdom from the noble Subhūti, and seeking his instruction, advice, and exhortation for the sake of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas."
Therefore, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide in the perfection of wisdom, how should they train, and how should they apply themselves to yoga?
The Elder Subhūti said: "In that case, Kauśika, through the power of the Buddha, the majesty of the Buddha, and the empowerment of the Buddha, I shall instruct you.
Those sons of the gods who have not yet resolved their minds toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment should now resolve their minds upon it."
But those who have entered into the fixed course of rightness are no longer capable of generating the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Why is that?
For they have set a boundary against the stream of saṃsāra;
indeed, they are incapable of wandering again and again in saṃsāra or of generating the mind directed toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Nevertheless, I nonetheless rejoice in them as well.
Even if they were to generate thoughts directed toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
I would not create an obstacle to their roots of virtue;
for one should aspire to the most distinguished dharmas from among those that are already distinguished.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Subhūti: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!
It is indeed excellent of you, Subhūti, that you provide encouragement to the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas."
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, we must be grateful to the Blessed One, not ungrateful.
Why is that?

Because, O Blessed One, for our sake, while formerly practicing the holy life for the sake of awakening as a bodhisattva, the Blessed One [served] in the presence of the former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones."
While he was thus [practicing], the Blessed One, while practicing there under the guidance and instruction of those disciples regarding the perfections, produced unsurpassed knowledge.
In this way, Blessed One, we too must assist and attend upon the bodhisattva mahāsattvas; we must fully assist and fully attend upon them.
Why is that?

For by us also, Blessed One, have the bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, been assisted and surrounded; they have been fully assisted and fully surrounded so that they quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then the venerable Subhūti addressed Śakra, the lord of the gods: "In that case, Kauśika, listen and attend closely and well;
I shall speak to you of how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should stand in the perfection of wisdom."
Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who abides in emptiness should abide in the perfection of wisdom.
Therefore, Kauśika,
that bodhisattva mahāsattva must be one who has donned the great armor.
One should not abide in form;
one should not abide in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
One should not abide in the eye;
one should not abide in forms;
one should not abide in eye-consciousness.
One should not abide in eye-contact;
one should not abide in the feeling born of eye-contact.
Likewise, one should not abide in the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
It is not in sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects; nor in auditory consciousness, up to and including mental consciousness.
One should not abide in mental contact, nor in the feeling born of mental contact;
one should not abide in the earth element.
not in the water element, not in the fire element,
not in the wind element, and not in the space element;

One should not abide in the element of consciousness; one should not abide in the applications of mindfulness; nor in the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, or the factors of enlightenment.
One should not abide in the factors of the path;
one should not abide in the fruit of stream-entry;
nor in the fruit of once-returning.
One should not abide in the fruit of non-returning, nor in arhatship;
one should not abide in the state of a pratyekabuddha.
One should not abide in Buddhahood;
thus, one should not abide thinking, "This is form," nor "This is feeling."
Regarding "perception," "formative factors," and "consciousness"—
one should not abide in the thought that these are such.
Thus, one should not abide in the thought "this is the eye," up to and including "feeling born of mind-contact"; likewise,
one should not abide in the thought "this is the earth element."
One should not abide in the thought, "as far as the element of consciousness";
one should not abide in the thought, "these are the applications of mindfulness";
and one should not abide in the thought, "these are the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment."
Thus, one should not abide in the thought, "These are the factors of the path";
nor should one abide in the thought, "This is the fruit of stream-entry," nor in the thought, "This is the fruit of once-returning."
One should not abide in the thought, "This is the fruit of non-returning," nor in "This is arhatship"; likewise, one should not abide in the thought, "This is the state of a pratyekabuddha."
Thus, one should not abide in the thought "this is Buddhahood";
one should not abide in the thought that form is permanent or impermanent;
and likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
One should not abide in the thought that consciousness is permanent or impermanent;
one should not abide in the thought that form is pleasure or pain;
and the same applies to feeling, perception, and mental formations.
One should not abide in the thought that consciousness is pleasure or pain;
one should not abide in the thought that form is empty or not empty.
The same applies to feeling, perception, and mental formations.
One should not abide in the thought that consciousness is empty or non-empty; one should not abide in the thought that form is self or non-self;
and the same applies to feeling, perception, and mental formations.
One should not abide in the notion that consciousness is the self or not the self; one should not abide in the notion that form is beautiful or ugly;
and the same applies to feeling, perception, and mental formations.
One should not dwell on the thought that consciousness is pure or impure;
nor should one dwell on whether form is empty or is perceived.
The same applies to feeling, perception, and mental formations.
One should not abide in the thought that "consciousness is empty" or "is perceived.
One should not abide in the thought that "the fruit of stream-entry is characterized by the unconditioned.
Likewise, one should not abide in the thought that "the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship are characterized by the unconditioned."
One should not abide in the thought that "the state of a Pratyekabuddha is characterized by the unconditioned.
One should not abide in the thought that "a Stream-enterer is worthy of offerings.
One should not abide in the thought that "Stream-enterers have seven births at most as the limit of existence."
One should not stand on the notion that "the once-returner is worthy of offerings.

One should not stand on the notion that "because the once-returner has not yet reached final completion, he will come to this world once more and make an end of suffering. One should not stand on the notion that "the non-returner is worthy of offerings. One should not stand on the notion that "the non-returner, without returning to this world, will attain parinirvāṇa right there."
One should not stand on the notion that "the Arhat is worthy of offerings.
One should not stand on the notion that "the Arhat will attain final nirvana right here in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
One should not stand on the notion that "the Pratyekabuddha is worthy of offerings."
One should not stand on the notion that a Pratyekabuddha, having transcended the stage of a Śrāvaka but not yet reached the stage of a Buddha, will enter parinirvāṇa.
One should not stand on the notion that a Buddha is a worthy recipient of offerings.
A Buddha has transcended...
Having transcended the stage of ordinary beings, having transcended the stage of the śrāvakas, and having transcended the stage of the pratyekabuddhas;

having accomplished the welfare of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings; having brought to final nirvāṇa immeasurable and incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings; and having established immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings in the certainty of attaining the state of a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or a perfectly enlightened buddha.

"Having stood upon the Buddha-ground and performed the deeds of a Buddha, he will enter final nirvana through the Buddha-parinirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder"— even regarding this, he should not abide.

Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the venerable Śāriputra: "If the Buddha, having transcended the stage of ordinary worldlings, having transcended the stage of disciples, and having transcended the stage of solitary buddhas, having accomplished the welfare of immeasurable and incalculable beings,
and having brought to final nirvana immeasurable and incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of beings, [having done so] for immeasurable and incalculable [beings]..."

Having established sentient beings in the state of being destined for the level of a Śrāvaka, a Pratyekabuddha, or a Samyaksaṃbuddha, and having remained on the stage of a Buddha and performed the deeds of a Buddha, he will enter final nirvana through the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder—
even with regard to this, he should not dwell.
"How, then, should one abide by this, and how should one train?
Then, indeed, the venerable Subhūti, through the power of the Buddha, perceived with his own mind the reflection in the mind of the venerable Śāriputra.
He said this to the Venerable Śāriputra: "What do you think, Venerable Śāriputra, where does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha abide?
The Venerable Śāriputra replied: "Nowhere at all, Venerable Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha abide."
For what reason?
Because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has a mind that is non-abiding;
he does not abide in the conditioned realm, nor does he abide in the unconditioned realm, yet he has not emerged from them either.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "In this very way, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should stand and should train:
'Just as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is not stationed anywhere, nor unstationed, nor fixed, nor unfixed, so shall I stand'—in this manner he should train."
"Just as is the state of a Tathāgata, so shall I abide; thus shall I train;
just as is the state of a Tathāgata, so shall I abide."
"I shall train thus:
I shall abide in that manner in which the Tathāgata abides," by means of the yoga of non-abiding; in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide and in this way should he train.
For training in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling of the perfection of wisdom and is never separated from this mental attention.

Then, indeed, it occurred to some of the sons of the gods in that assembly: "Those things which are the speech of yakṣas, the cries of yakṣas, the words of yakṣas, the mantras of yakṣas, and the utterances of yakṣas—when they are spoken, they are understood.
But this which the elder Subhūti speaks, utters, teaches, and instructs—is not understood."

Then, indeed, the venerable Subhūti, through the power of the Buddha, perceiving with his own mind this very reflection in the minds of those sons of the gods, addressed those sons of the gods: "It is not known, it is not known, O sons of the gods!
For indeed, nothing at all is indicated here."
Nothing at all is heard here.
Then, indeed, it occurred again to those sons of the gods: "Ah, this noble Subhūti will clarify [this matter]! Ah, this noble Subhūti will clarify it!
Yet, the noble Subhūti enters further and further into the distance.
"Ārya Subhūti enters, teaches, and speaks that which is subtler than the subtle and deeper than the deep.
Then, indeed, the venerable Subhūti, through the power of the Buddha, again perceiving with his own mind the reflection in the minds of those very sons of gods, addressed those sons of gods: [Vaidya]

"Therefore, O sons of gods, whoever desires to attain the fruit of stream-entry, or desires to abide in the fruit of stream-entry, he cannot do so without having attained this patience... [and so on] ...whoever desires to attain the fruit of once-returning,"
One who desires to abide in the fruit of once-returning;
one who desires to attain the fruit of non-returning and desires to abide in the fruit of non-returning; and one who desires to attain arhatship and desires to abide in arhatship.
Whoever desires to attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha and desires to abide in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, they cannot do so without having attained this patience (kṣānti).
Whoever desires to attain unexcelled perfect enlightenment and desires to abide in unexcelled perfect enlightenment, [they too cannot do so without having attained this patience].
Without having attained this patience, he... [cannot realize it].
Then, once again, this thought occurred to those sons of the gods: "What kind of persons should be sought out as listeners to the Dharma from this noble Subhūti?

Then the venerable Subhūti, through the power of the Buddha, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the minds of those sons of the gods, addressed those sons of the gods: "O sons of the gods, listeners to my Dharma should be sought out as being like illusions and magical emanations."
For what reason?
Because they will neither hear it nor realize it directly.
Then those sons of the gods said this to the venerable Subhūti: "But, noble Subhūti, are those beings like an illusion, or are they not an illusion?
When this was said, the venerable Subhūti said this to those sons of the gods: "Those beings, sons of the gods, are like an illusion;
those beings, sons of the gods, are like a dream."
For thus, illusion and sentient beings are non-dual, this being an indivisible unity;
likewise, dreams and sentient beings are non-dual, this being an indivisible unity.
Furthermore, O sons of the gods, all phenomena are like illusions and like dreams.
Even the stream-enterer is like an illusion, like a dream;
even the fruit of stream-entry is like an illusion, like a dream. Likewise, even the once-returner and the fruit of once-returning are [like an illusion and a dream].
The non-returner as well as the fruit of non-returning,
the arhat as well as arhatship,
and even the pratyekabuddha are like an illusion, like a dream.
Even the state of a pratyekabuddha is like an illusion, like a dream;
even a perfectly awakened buddha (samyaksaṃbuddha) is like an illusion, like a dream;
even the state of perfect awakening is like an illusion, like a dream.
Then the sons of the gods said this to the venerable Subhūti: "Noble Subhūti, do you say that even a perfectly awakened Buddha (samyaksaṃbuddha) is like an illusion and like a dream?
Do you say that even perfect awakening itself is like an illusion and like a dream?
Subhūti replied: "Sons of the gods, I say that even nirvāṇa is like an illusion and like a dream."
"What other dharma, then?
Those sons of the gods said, "Noble Subhūti, do you say that even *nirvāṇa* is like an illusion and like a dream?
The Venerable Subhūti replied, "Sons of the gods, if there were any dharma whatsoever more distinguished than even *nirvāṇa*, [I would say it too was like an illusion and like a dream]."
I would say that even this is like an illusion and like a dream.
For, O sons of the gods, illusion and nirvāṇa are non-dual; they are not divided into two.
For, a dream and nirvāṇa are non-dual; they are not divided into two.
Then indeed, the venerable Śāriputra, the venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, and the venerable Mahākauṣṭhila—
The venerable Mahākātyāyana, the venerable Mahākāśyapa,
and other great śrāvakas, together with many thousands of bodhisattvas, addressed the venerable elder Subhūti.
[Śāriputra said: "Venerable Subhūti, who will be those who accept this Perfection of Wisdom when it is being taught in this manner?
Then the venerable Ānanda said this to those elders: "Venerable sirs, those should be known as irreversible Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas."
Either individuals endowed with right view,
or Arhats whose outflows are exhausted, will be those who accept this Perfection of Wisdom when it is thus being taught.
Then the Venerable Subhūti, the Elder, said this to those elders: "Venerable ones, when this perfection of wisdom is being taught in this manner, there will be no one at all who accepts it.
Why is that?
Because herein not a single dharma is indicated."
No dharma whatsoever is illuminated, nor is any dharma designated;
just as no dharma at all is indicated here.
No dharma whatsoever is illuminated, nor is any dharma whatsoever designated;
likewise, when this perfection of wisdom is thus taught, there will be no one at all to receive it.

Then, it occurred to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "In order to honor this Dharma-discourse being spoken by the noble Subhūti, what if I were to manifest flowers and scatter them over the noble Subhūti?
Then, at that moment, Śakra, the lord of the gods, manifested flowers and scattered them over the venerable Subhūti.

Then, indeed, it occurred to the Venerable Subhūti, the Elder, in order to address Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Certainly, these flowers which have been scattered by Śakra, the lord of the gods, have never before been seen by me circulating among the Trāyastriṃśa gods."
These flowers are emanated;
these flowers have not grown from trees, shrubs, or creepers,
but were scattered by Śakra, the lord of the gods.

"These flowers are mind-made. Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the mind of the venerable Subhūti, said this to the venerable Subhūti: "These flowers, noble Subhūti, are unproduced."
For what reason?
Because there are no flowers whatsoever produced from the mind,
nor are there any produced from trees, shrubs, or creepers.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Kauśika, as for what you have said— that these flowers are unproduced,
that they are not produced from the mind,
nor are they produced from trees, shrubs, or creepers."
"Kauśika, that which is unproduced is not a flower.
Then, it occurred to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "How profound is the wisdom of this noble Subhūti!
Yet he explains even that designation of words."
And he does not contradict that [teaching],
he clarifies it, and he teaches that very same thing.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the venerable Subhūti: "So it is, noble Subhūti; so it is.
And in this way a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train here, just as the noble Subhūti instructs.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "So it is, Kauśika; so it is."
In this way, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train here; training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train for the fruit of stream-entry,
nor for the fruit of once-returning.
He does not train for the fruit of non-returning, nor does he train for the state of an arhat, nor does he train for the state of a pratyekabuddha.
One does not train for the state of Buddhahood;
he who does not train in these stages trains for Buddhahood or for omniscience.
Whoever trains for Buddhahood or for omniscience trains in the immeasurable and incalculable qualities of a Buddha;
whoever trains in the immeasurable and incalculable qualities of a Buddha [trains in omniscience].
