He does not train for the increase of form, nor for its diminution;
likewise, he does not [train] for feeling, perception, or mental formations.
He does not train for the increase of consciousness, nor for its decrease;
he who does not train for the increase of form, nor for its decrease.
In the same way, it is not for the increase of feeling, nor of perception, nor of mental formations;
he who does not train for the increase of consciousness nor for its diminution,
does not train for the grasping of form nor for its relinquishing.
In this way, he does not train for the sake of grasping feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations;
he does not train for the sake of grasping consciousness, nor for its relinquishment.
Nor does one train for the sake of grasping any dharma, nor does one train for its arising or its disappearance;
he who does not train for the sake of grasping any dharma—
He trains neither for the sake of production nor for the sake of disappearance;
he does not even train for the sake of grasping omniscience, training neither for the sake of production nor for the sake of disappearance.
Training in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in omniscience and will emerge into omniscience.

Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: "Venerable Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not train for the sake of grasping any dharma, nor trains for its arising or its disappearance,
he does not even train for the sake of grasping omniscience."
He trains neither for the sake of arising nor for the sake of disappearance.
Training in this way, Venerable Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in omniscience and will emerge into omniscience.
The Venerable Subhūti said: "So it is, Venerable Śāriputra; so it is.
Venerable Śāriputra, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not train for the sake of grasping any dharma, nor trains for its arising, nor for its disappearance—"
He does not train for the sake of grasping even omniscience; he does not train for its arising or its disappearance.
He does not train for the sake of grasping even all the qualities of a Buddha.
He trains neither for the sake of arising nor for the sake of disappearance.
And thus, Venerable Śāriputra, training in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in omniscience and shall go forth toward omniscience.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "Noble Śāriputra, from where should a bodhisattva mahāsattva seek the perfection of wisdom?
Śāriputra replied: "Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should seek the perfection of wisdom from the discourse of the venerable Subhūti.
When this was said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "Noble Śāriputra, whose power is this to be recognized?"
"By whose empowerment is this to be understood, that the noble Subhūti speaks the perfection of wisdom?
The venerable Śāriputra said: "Kauśika, it should be understood that this is the power of the Tathāgata;
it should be understood that this is the empowerment of the Tathāgata, that the venerable Subhūti speaks the perfection of wisdom."

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Kauśika, as for what you say—'Whose power is this to be known? Whose accomplishment is this to be known, that the noble Subhūti speaks the perfection of wisdom?'—Kauśika, it should be known that this is the power of the Tathāgata."
It should be understood that this is the empowerment of the Tathāgata by which I speak this perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika, as to what you have said— "From where should the perfection of wisdom be sought by a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"—
the perfection of wisdom, Kauśika, should not be sought from form, nor should it be sought elsewhere than from form.
Thus, they are not to be sought in feeling, nor in perception, nor in mental formations, nor in consciousness;
nor are they to be sought apart from consciousness.
For what reason?
For thus it is: form is not the perfection of wisdom, nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than in form;
likewise, feeling, perception, and mental formations are not [the perfection of wisdom].
Consciousness is not the perfection of wisdom,
nor is the perfection of wisdom elsewhere than consciousness.

When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the venerable Subhūti: "O Noble Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is a great perfection; O Noble Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is an immeasurable perfection; O Noble One, this perfection of wisdom is an infinite perfection."
"Subhūti, it is this very perfection of wisdom.
Noble Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is an infinite perfection.
The Elder Subhūti said: "So it is, Kauśika; so it is."
This, Kauśika, is the great perfection, namely, the perfection of wisdom;
this, Kauśika, is the immeasurable perfection, namely, the perfection of wisdom;
this, Kauśika, is the limitless perfection, namely, the perfection of wisdom.
This perfection, Kauśika, is infinite, namely, the perfection of wisdom.
For what reason?
Because of the greatness of form, Kauśika, this is a great perfection, namely, the perfection of wisdom.
In the same way, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness [are great].
Because of the greatness of consciousness, Kauśika, this is a "great perfection," namely, the perfection of wisdom.
Because of the immeasurability of form, Kauśika, this is an "immeasurable perfection," namely, the perfection of wisdom.

In the same way, Kauśika, because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are immeasurable, this perfection of wisdom— that is, the *prajñāpāramitā*— is an immeasurable perfection. Because form is unlimited, Kauśika, this perfection of wisdom— that is, the *prajñāpāramitā*— is an unlimited perfection.
In the same way, Kauśika, because feeling, perception, mental formations,

and consciousness are immeasurable, this perfection of wisdom— that is, the *prajñāpāramitā*— is an immeasurable perfection. Because form is infinite, Kauśika, this perfection of wisdom— that is, the *prajñāpāramitā*— is an infinite perfection.

In the same way, Kauśika, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are infinite; because consciousness is infinite, this perfection—namely, the perfection of wisdom—is an infinite perfection.
Thus, Kauśika, one does not become attached to the idea that it is a "great perfection."
Thus, one does not become attached to the idea that "this is the perfection of the immeasurable," "this is the perfection of the limitless," or "this is the perfection of the infinite."
Therefore, Kauśika, this is a great perfection; this is an immeasurable perfection; this is an infinite perfection.
This perfection of wisdom is indeed an infinite perfection.
"Kauśika, because its objective referents are infinite, this perfection is infinite—namely, the perfection of wisdom.
Because sentient beings are infinite, Kauśika, this perfection is infinite—namely, the perfection of wisdom.
But how, Kauśika, is this perfection of wisdom infinite because its objective referents are infinite?"
For, Kauśika, since no beginning, middle, or end of all phenomena is apprehended, therefore, Kauśika, this perfection of wisdom is an infinite perfection; that is to say, the perfection of wisdom.
By this method, Kauśika, through the infinity of its objective referent, this perfection of wisdom is an infinite perfection; that is to say, the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika, because all dharmas are infinite and boundless,
and neither their end, nor their middle, nor their conclusion can be apprehended, therefore, Kauśika, this perfection of wisdom is an infinite perfection.
For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, neither an end, nor a middle, nor a conclusion of form (rūpa) is apprehended;
and likewise for feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), and mental formations (saṃskāra).
For, Kauśika, neither the end, nor the middle, nor the conclusion of consciousness is apprehended.
By this method also, Kauśika, through the infinity of its objective support, this perfection is infinite; that is to say, the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a sentient being is infinite and boundless.
Why is that?
Because neither an end, nor a middle, nor a conclusion of a sentient being can be apprehended.
Therefore, Kauśika, because beings are infinite, this perfection is infinite—namely, the perfection of wisdom.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said to the venerable Subhūti: "How is it, venerable Subhūti, that because beings are infinite, this perfection is infinite—namely, the perfection of wisdom?

The Elder Subhūti replied: "It is not, Kauśika, by means of calculation or by the multiplicity of calculation that this perfection is infinite because beings are infinite—namely, the perfection of wisdom."
Śakra said: "In that case, Noble Subhūti, how is it that through the infinity of beings, this perfection of wisdom—that is, the *prajñāpāramitā*—is infinite?
The Elder Subhūti replied: "What do you think, Kauśika, of what dharma is this a designation, namely 'being,' 'being'?"
Śakra said: "Noble Subhūti, this term 'sentient being, sentient being' is neither a designation for a dharma nor a designation for a non-dharma. This name is adventitiously applied;
this name is applied without any real basis."

"This designation 'sentient being,' namely 'sentient being,' is an unappropriated designation superimposed; it is a non-referential designation superimposed. The Elder Subhūti said: "What do you think, Kauśika, has any indication of a sentient being been made here?"
Śakra said: "Certainly not, noble Subhūti.
Subhūti said: "Kauśika, where no indication of a sentient being has been made at all, what 'infinitude of beings' could there be?"

If, Kauśika, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, speaking with an infinite resonance and a profound sound the words "sentient being,
sentient being," would there, in that case, be any sentient being who has arisen, will arise, or is currently arising?
"Has it ceased, will it cease, or is it ceasing?
Śakra replied, "Certainly not, Noble Subhūti. And why is that?"

"Because a sentient being is primordially pure and primordially purified," Subhūti said, "By this method also, Kauśika, through the infinitude of sentient beings, this perfection is infinite— namely, the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Kauśika, by the infinitude of sentient beings, the infinitude of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood."
Then indeed, the gods together with Indra, together with Brahmā, together with Prajāpati, and all the hosts of men and women, uttered this inspired utterance three times: "O, the Dharma!
O, the Dharma! O, the true nature of the Dharma!"
The manifestation of the Tathāgata is indicated, taught, revealed, and elucidated here by the noble Elder Subhūti through his well-spoken words.
O Blessed One, from this day forward, we shall regard as a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva anyone who is not separated from this perfection of wisdom.
And furthermore, whichever bodhisattva mahāsattva shall dwell by means of this dwelling in the perfection of wisdom.
Then the Blessed One addressed those hosts of gods, including Indra, Brahmā, and Prajāpati, along with the multitudes of men and women: "It is so, O sons of gods; it is even so.

Sons of gods, when I was in the presence of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, in the royal capital of Dīpavatī, standing in the middle of a crossroads, I was not separated from this perfection of wisdom."

Then I was prophesied by the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding my attainment of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment: "Young man, in a future time, after incalculable eons, you shall become a Tathāgata named Śākyamuni, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed."
"The Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Then those sons of the gods said this to the Blessed One: "It is marvelous, Blessed One;
it is most marvelous, Sugata!"
To this extent, this perfection of wisdom is the bringer and the sustainer of omniscience for the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas.
The second chapter, titled "Śakra," in the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom.
(Vaidya 25) Chapter Three: The Merit of Honoring the Stūpa of the Perfection that Upholds Immeasurable Qualities.
Then, the Blessed One [addressed] those sons of the gods who had gathered and were seated there in the assembly.

Having perceived those monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who had assembled and were seated, and having perceived those sons of gods who had assembled and were seated, as well as all those four assemblies who had assembled and were seated—

Having established as witnesses the sons of the gods of the desire realm, the sons of the gods of the form realm, the sons of the gods of the Brahma-realm, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Parīttāśubha gods, and the Akaniṣṭha gods,
he addressed the sons of the gods of the desire realm headed by Śakra, the king of gods, and the sons of the gods of the Brahma-realm headed by Mahābrahmā,
and the Ābhāsvara gods: "O sons of the gods, whichever son of good family..."
Whether it be a son of good family or a daughter of good family who shall take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and propagate this Perfection of Wisdom,

neither Māra nor the deities belonging to Māra’s host— who look for a vulnerability and seek a vulnerability— shall find an opportunity to harm them. Nor shall humans or non-humans— who look for a vulnerability and seek a vulnerability— find an opportunity to harm that son or daughter of good family.
Furthermore, that son of good family or daughter of good family shall not meet their end through the failure to avoid dangerous circumstances.

Furthermore, sons of the gods, those sons of the gods who have set out for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, but by whom this perfection of wisdom has not been taken up, nor maintained, nor recited, nor mastered, nor promulgated—
they will think that they should approach that son of good family or daughter of good family.

And from that son of good family or daughter of good family who takes up, bears in mind, recites, masters, and sets forth this Perfection of Wisdom, others shall hear it; having heard it, they shall take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, and set it forth.
Furthermore, O sons of the gods, for that son of good family or daughter of good family who takes up this Perfection of Wisdom...
Whether he is upholding, reciting, mastering, or propagating it— whether he has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree,

or to an empty dwelling, or to an open space, or is on a path, or on a bypath, or in a wilderness, or on the great ocean; wherever he may approach, or whether he is walking back and forth, or standing still.
Or for one who is sitting, or for one who has fallen ill, there will be fear,
or there will be paralysis,
or it will arise.

Then the four great kings said this to the Blessed One: "It is wonderful, Blessed One, that when a son of good family or a daughter of good family takes up, bears in mind, recites, masters, and propagates this perfection of wisdom, they discipline beings in the three vehicles,
yet they do not give rise to the notion of a 'being'."

"Blessed One, we shall provide protection, shelter, and defense for that son of good family or daughter of good family who will take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and propagate this perfection of wisdom."

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: "I too, Blessed One, will provide protection, shelter, and defense for that son of good family or daughter of good family who shall take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and propagate this perfection of wisdom."

Brahmā Sahāpati, together with the sons of the gods belonging to the Brahma-kāyika realm, said this to the Blessed One: "I too, Blessed One, shall provide protection, shelter, and defense for that son of good family or daughter of good family who shall take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and propagate this perfection of wisdom."
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: "It is marvelous, Blessed One,

that a son of good family or a daughter of good family who takes up, bears in mind, recites, masters, and propagates this perfection of wisdom obtains and acquires these very qualities pertaining to the present life."
"Furthermore, Blessed One, when the perfection of wisdom is taken up, are all six perfections thereby taken up?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "So it is, Kauśika, so it is.
When the perfection of wisdom, Kauśika, is taken up, all six perfections are taken up."

Furthermore, Kauśika, when the perfection of wisdom is taken up, maintained, recited, mastered, and set in motion, that son of good family or daughter of good family acquires qualities pertaining to the present life.
Listen, Kauśika, to all of them.
"Pay close and careful attention;
I shall speak to you.
"So be it, Blessed One," Śakra, lord of the gods, replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this: "In that regard, Kauśika, those who think my Dharma should be contested, should be disputed, or should be opposed— "
The disputes, quarrels, and conflicts that arise again and again among those who desire to engage in strife, to dispute, and to oppose will once more disappear and not remain.
The intentions of those who wish to quarrel with them, to dispute with them, or to oppose them shall not reach fulfillment.
Why is that?
For it is thus, Kauśika: when a son of good family or a daughter of good family shall take up this perfection of wisdom...
Whoever shall uphold, recite, master, propagate, teach, explain, expound, and study it—
for such a person, those disputes as they arise one after another will once again disappear and shall not remain.

The intentions of those who wish to quarrel with them, who wish to dispute with them, or who wish to oppose them will not reach fulfillment. Furthermore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family who takes up, bears in mind, recites, masters, propagates, teaches, explains, indicates, and studies this Perfection of Wisdom acquires this very quality pertaining to the present life.
Kauśika, it is just as if there were a medicinal herb called Maghī that pacifies all poisons.

Suppose a venomous serpent, hungry and seeking food, were searching for prey and should see some living creature. That venomous serpent would pursue and follow that creature by its scent, desiring to devour it for the sake of food.
Then that creature would approach where that medicinal herb named Madhī is located;
having approached it, it would stand there.
Then, by the mere scent of that herb, the venomous snake would turn back.
For what reason?
Because the medicinal quality of that herb is such that it overcomes the poison of that venomous serpent;
for so powerful is that herb.
In the same way, Kauśika, whatever noble son or noble daughter shall take up, bear in mind, recite, master, propagate, teach, explain, expound, and study this perfection of wisdom—
Kauśika, regarding those various disputes, quarrels, and conflicts that may arise for them as they occur, [they shall be pacified].

By the splendor, power, and strength of the perfection of wisdom, through the empowerment of the perfection of wisdom, they will quickly cease from that very point, be pacified, and disappear; they will not increase.
From wherever they may arise, right there they shall be extinguished and disappear.
They will not increase, nor will they remain stable.
Why is that?
For the perfection of wisdom is the pacifier of everything from passion up to the grasping at nirvāṇa.
It shall not increase [evil].
Furthermore, the four great kings,
Śakra the lord of the gods, Brahmā Sahāpati, and all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as well as the Bodhisattvas, will provide protection, defense, and guardianship for it.

That son of good family or daughter of good family who shall take up this perfection of wisdom, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, propagate it, teach it, explain it, proclaim it, and study it, will have acquired these qualities pertaining to the present life.

Furthermore, Kauśika, any son of good family or daughter of good family who shall take up this perfection of wisdom, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, propagate it, teach it, explain it, proclaim it, and study it,
will become one whose words are authoritative.
He will be gentle in speech, measured in speech,
and not diffuse in speech.
And he will not be overcome by anger,
nor will he be overcome by pride.
Why is that?
For it is thus that the perfection of wisdom tames him, the perfection of wisdom transforms him, and he does not increase his anger.
He does not increase pride;
he does not harbor resentment, nor does he harbor ill will.
He does not harbor a latent tendency (*anuśaya*).
As this son of good family or daughter of good family practices in this way, mindfulness and loving-kindness (*maitrī*) arise in him.
It occurs to him: "If I were to give rise to malice (*vyāpāda*),..."
"Therefore, my sense-faculties will be impaired and the complexion of my face will be scorched;
and it would be improper for me, who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment," [to act thus].
In that regard, desiring to train himself,
he quickly regains mindfulness, thinking: "May I not fall under the power of anger."

“Furthermore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family who will take up, bear in mind, recite, master, propagate, teach, explain, proclaim, and study this perfection of wisdom, also acquires these qualities pertaining to the present life.

When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, Blessed One, how this perfection of wisdom stands as a means for the taming and the non-inflation of bodhisattvas!”
of the great beings (mahāsattvas).

The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family shall take up this perfection of wisdom, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, propagate it, teach it, explain it, proclaim it, and study it..."

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, while thus taking up, bearing, reciting, mastering, propagating, teaching, explaining, indicating, and studying this Perfection of Wisdom, should find themselves engaged in battle and mounted at the head of the army;

Whether he is entering battle, has already entered it, is advancing through it, is in the midst of the fray, standing, or sitting— Kauśika, it is impossible and there is no occasion for this to happen that such a son of good family or daughter of good family, while attending to, taking up, retaining, or reciting this perfection of wisdom, [should suffer harm].
Or for one who is mastering, propagating, teaching, explaining, instructing, or reciting it, there might be an obstacle to life;
he might meet with an obstacle to life through the assault of others.
This is impossible.
Furthermore, Kauśika, if someone were to throw a weapon, a staff, a clod of earth, or anything else at him there,
it would not fall upon his body.
For what reason?
Kauśika, this is a great lore, namely the perfection of wisdom;
Kauśika, this is an immeasurable lore, namely the perfection of wisdom.
"Kauśika, this knowledge, namely the perfection of wisdom, is immeasurable.
Kauśika, this knowledge, namely the perfection of wisdom, is unsurpassed. Kauśika, this knowledge, namely the perfection of wisdom, is peerless."
This knowledge, Kauśika, namely the perfection of wisdom, is unequaled.
For what reason? Because here, Kauśika—
A son of good family or a daughter of good family who is training in this knowledge does not intend harm for themselves,
does not intend harm for others, and does not intend harm for both.
For here, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this knowledge will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and will attain the knowledge of omniscience.
Having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he will survey the minds of all sentient beings.
For what reason? Because, Kauśika, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this vidyā, there is nothing whatsoever that would not be attained, or not known, or not realized.
Therefore, it is called the "knowledge of the omniscient one.

Furthermore, Kauśika, this son of good family or daughter of good family who will take up, bear in mind, recite, master, propagate, teach, explain, expound, and study this *prajñāpāramitā* will have acquired a merit pertaining to the present life.
Furthermore, Kauśika, wherever this Prajñāpāramitā— even if only having been written out and made into a book— is set up with worship as its precursor, yet is not honored,
nor taken up, nor retained;
It will not be recited,
it will not be mastered, and it will not be propagated.
It will not be taught, it will not be instructed, and it will not be expounded.
It will not be studied;

and in that regard, Kauśika, neither humans nor non-humans seeking an opportunity or searching for an opening against beings there shall find such an opportunity, except as a result of the ripening of past karma.
This, Kauśika, is another quality pertaining to the present life that this son of good family or daughter of good family acquires.

Furthermore, Kauśika, it is just as if there were humans or non-humans— down to those belonging to the animal realm— who have gone to the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), or to its vicinity, or into its interior, or to the foot of the tree of awakening (bodhivṛkṣa).
As long as they cannot be harmed, killed, or possessed by humans or non-humans— except for the ripening of past karma— for what reason?
Because therein the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present have awakened, will awaken, and are awakening.

Those who cultivate and proclaim fearlessness, non-enmity, and lack of terror for all sentient beings— in the same way, Kauśika, wherever a son of good family or a daughter of good family shall take up, bear in mind, recite, master, propagate, teach, explain, expound, and study this perfection of wisdom, [there they will provide such protection].
For in that place, Kauśika, beings cannot be harmed, killed, or possessed by humans or non-humans, except as a result of the ripening of their own past karma.
Why is that?

For by this very perfection of wisdom, Kauśika, that spot of earth will be made a shrine for beings, worthy of being saluted, honored, worshipped, revered, venerated, and respected; it will become a protection, a refuge, a shelter, and a final resort for those beings who have approached it.
This, Kauśika, is another quality pertaining to the present life that a son of good family or a daughter of good family acquires.

When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to write down this perfection of wisdom, make it into a book, and honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate it with divine flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, bells, and flags, and with rows of lamps all around, and with many kinds of offerings;..."
And whoever, after the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one has passed into parinirvāṇa, should establish the relics in stupas, take them up, and preserve them,
and should likewise honor them with divine flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, bells, and flags;
and who would honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate them on all sides with garlands of lamps and various kinds of offerings—
of these two, whether a son of good family or a daughter of good family, which one would generate the greater merit?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "In that case, Kauśika, I shall question you on this very matter; you should answer as you see fit."

"What do you think, Kauśika? Regarding this embodiment of omniscience that has been manifested by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—training in which practice did the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, attain and fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and omniscience?
When this was said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: "It was precisely here, Blessed One, in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), that the Blessed One [attained it]."
"By training in this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, attained and fully awakened to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and omniscience.
The Blessed One said: "Therefore, Kauśika, it is not by the acquisition of this physical body that a Tathāgata comes to be designated as a 'Tathāgata'."
But when omniscience has been attained, the Tathāgata comes to be designated as "Tathāgata.
O Kauśika, this omniscience of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is born from the perfection of wisdom.
Moreover, Kauśika, this acquisition of the physical body of the Tathāgata, being born from the perfection of wisdom and skill in means, serves as the basis for the knowledge of omniscience.
For, depending upon this basis, there is the manifestation of the knowledge of omniscience,
and there is the manifestation of the Buddha-body.
The manifestation of the body of Dharma occurs, and the manifestation of the body of the Saṅgha occurs.
Thus, this acquisition of the physical body has the knowledge of omniscience as its cause, because it serves as the basis for the knowledge of omniscience for all sentient beings.
He becomes like a shrine, worthy of being saluted, honored, revered, respected, worshipped, adored, and venerated.
And thus, even after I have passed into final nirvāṇa, there will be worship of these relics.
Therefore, Kauśika, whatever son of good family or daughter of good family should write down this perfection of wisdom, or having made it into a book, should establish it;

And one should honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate this [perfection] with divine flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, bells, and flags;
Kauśika, it is this very [act] that would produce far more merit for those two, whether sons of good family or daughters of good family.
For what reason?
For, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family will have performed worship of the knowledge of the All-Knowing One—

any son of good family or daughter of good family who, while this Perfection of Wisdom is being written out or exists in the form of a book, should perform various acts of respect, reverence, honor, worship, adoration, veneration, and worship toward it.
This person alone would produce much more merit than that.
Why is that?
For, Kauśika, by him an offering will have been made to the knowledge of the All-Knowing One.
Whoever shall perform an offering to the Perfection of Wisdom.

When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, those humans of Jambudvīpa who will not write down this perfection of wisdom, nor take it up, nor bear it in mind,
nor recite it, nor master it, nor set it in motion, nor teach it, nor explain it, nor proclaim it, nor study it— "

And they will not honor this Perfection of Wisdom with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, bells, and flags, nor with rows of lamps all around, nor with various kinds of worship.
They will not hold it in high regard, they will not honor it,
and they will not worship it.
They will not honor it, nor will they revere it;
why is this, Blessed One? Will they not know that such worship as this, performed toward the perfection of wisdom, has been declared by the Blessed One to be of great benefit?

Lord, will they not know that the worship of the perfection of wisdom has been performed, as it has been said by the Blessed One to have such great benefits, such great fruits, and such a great maturation?
Will they not perceive it, or rather, will they know it and understand it?
"Will they experience [the results], yet will they not, moreover, have faith?

When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "What do you think, Kauśika? How many among the humans of Jambudvīpa are endowed with verified clarity regarding the Buddha?"
“Those who are endowed with verified clarity regarding the Dharma, and those who are endowed with verified clarity regarding the Saṅgha?
When this was said, Śakra, lord of the gods, addressed the Blessed One as follows: “Blessed One, those people of Jambudvīpa who are endowed with verified clarity regarding the Buddha are few.”
Those who are endowed with verified clarity regarding the Dharma, and those who are endowed with verified clarity regarding the Saṅgha.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "So it is, Kauśika; so it is."

Few are those humans of Jambudvīpa who are endowed with verified clarity regarding the Buddha, who are endowed with verified clarity regarding the Dharma, and who are endowed with verified clarity regarding the Saṅgha.
Among them, Kauśika, those who attain the fruit of stream-entry are few; even fewer than they are those who attain the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of non-returning.
Even fewer than those few attain arhatship;
even fewer than those few realize pratyekabodhi;
and even fewer than those few generate the resolve for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Even among those few, fewer still are those who, having generated the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, cause that generation of the mind to increase.
Even among those few, fewer still are those who, having generated the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and having increased it, dwell with aroused vigor.
Even among those few, fewer still are those who apply themselves to the yoga of the perfection of wisdom.
Even fewer than those are they who practice the perfection of wisdom;
even fewer than those are they who, practicing the perfection of wisdom with diligence, abide on the irreversible stage of a bodhisattva;
even fewer than those are they who, practicing the perfection of wisdom with diligence, will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Even fewer than those are they who, practicing and striving in the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Those, Kauśika, are the bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, having stood upon the irreversible bodhisattva stage, fully awaken to unsurpassed,
perfect enlightenment and [teach] other sons of good family and daughters of good family who are endowed with resolute intention.
And they teach and instruct the Perfection of Wisdom to those who are training and striving in the Perfection of Wisdom;
and they take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, set it in motion, explain it, demonstrate it, point it out, and study it.
And they honor this very Perfection of Wisdom with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, flags, and with rows of lamps all around.
And with many kinds of offerings, they honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate [them].
Furthermore, Kauśika, there truly exist immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings.
Those who generate the mind of awakening,
having generated the mind of awakening, they cultivate the mind of awakening; having cultivated the mind of awakening, they course toward enlightenment.

Furthermore, Kauśika, although those immeasurable and incalculable beings practice for the sake of awakening, it may be that only one or two among them abide in the irreversible stage of a bodhisattva.
For what reason is that?

For, Kauśika, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is difficult to realize for those who are of inferior vigor, who are indolent, who are of inferior nature, who have inferior minds, who have inferior perceptions, who have inferior resolute intentions, and who have inferior wisdom. Therefore, Kauśika, a son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to quickly awaken to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment should easily and repeatedly hear, take up, bear in mind, and recite this very perfection of wisdom.
It should be mastered, set in motion, taught, explained, recited, studied, and inquired about.
Why is that?
Because he will know this: "In this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was trained while formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva."
We too must train in this,
thinking, "This is our Teacher.
Whether the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is present, Kauśika, or has entered parinirvāṇa, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas must rely solely upon the perfection of wisdom.

Therefore, Kauśika, if some son of good family or daughter of good family, for the sake of honoring the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one who has passed into parinirvāṇa, were to have ten million stupas made, consisting of the seven precious jewels and containing the relics of the Tathāgata;
and having had them made, were to honor them throughout their entire life with divine flowers, divine incenses, divine perfumes, and divine...
With divine garlands, divine ointments, divine powders, divine garments, divine parasols,
divine banners, divine bells,
and divine pennants.
And all around with garlands of lamps of many kinds.

and were to honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate them with divine offerings—what do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One."
"Much, Sugata.

The Blessed One said: "Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family produces much more merit who, having faith in this perfection of wisdom, conceiving it, and being resolved upon it, with a serene mind [dedicates it] to awakening."

Having generated the thought [of awakening], one should listen with resolute intention, take it up, retain it, recite it, master it, set it in motion, teach it, instruct it, explain it, direct it, study it,
and reveal it in detail to others, and elucidate its meaning.
One should examine it with the mind and, according to one's superior wisdom, engage in a thorough investigation of it;

at the very least, having committed it to a book, one should preserve and maintain it for the sake of ensuring that the True Dharma endures for a long time, so that the guidance of the Buddhas may not be cut off.
"May there be no disappearance of the True Dharma;
may favor and assistance be rendered to the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, so that there shall be no deficiency in the Guide.
And one should honor, revere, esteem, worship, adore, and venerate this Perfection of Wisdom with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and bells.
And one should worship it with garlands of lamps all around and with various kinds of offerings;
for this reason, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family produces far more merit than the former.
Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone this Jambūdvīpa being filled with stūpas made of the seven precious jewels containing the relics of the Tathāgata;

if, Kauśika, as many beings as there are in a world-system of four great continents were each to have a single stūpa made of the seven precious jewels containing the relics of the Tathāgata constructed for them,

And for as long as life lasts, one should honor him with divine flowers, divine incenses, divine perfumes, divine garlands, divine powders, divine garments, divine parasols, divine banners, divine bells,
and on all sides with divine rows of lamps,
and with many kinds of divine offerings.
With offerings, one should honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate them.
What do you think, Kauśika, would all those beings generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said: "Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family generates far more merit than that."

Whoever, having full faith in this perfection of wisdom, accepting it, being convinced of it, with a serene mind, having generated the thought of awakening, should listen to it with resolute intention, take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, set it in motion,
teach it, explain it, point it out, and study it;
And one should reveal it in detail to others, explain its meaning,
and examine it with the mind.
And with whatever superior wisdom one may possess, one should apply thorough investigation here;
at the very least, having committed it to a book, one should preserve and establish it for the sake of the long endurance of the True Dharma— so that the guidance of the Buddhas may not be severed,
and so that the True Dharma may not disappear.
And he will have rendered assistance to the bodhisattvas by means of the non-deficiency of the Guide.

Furthermore, one should honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate this Perfection of Wisdom with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, flags, and with rows of lamps all around.
And one should worship with many kinds of offerings;
then, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family produces far more merit on that account.
Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone all the sentient beings in a world-system of four great continents.
Kauśika, suppose all the beings in a thousand-fold world system with a crest,
and each single being among them were to have a stūpa constructed for the Tathāgata’s relic-casket made of the seven precious gems;

And for as long as life lasts, one should honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate him with divine flowers, divine incenses, divine perfumes, divine garlands, divine ointments, divine powders, divine garments, divine parasols, divine banners, divine bells, and with rows of lamps all around, and with manifold kinds of offerings.
"What do you think, Kauśika, would all those beings generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata."

The Blessed One said: "Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family produces a far greater merit who, having faith in this *prajñāpāramitā*, accepting it, and being resolved upon it, with a serene mind, having generated the thought of awakening, listens to it, takes it up, bears it in mind, recites it, masters it, sets it forth, teaches it, instructs it, explains it, and studies it with a resolute intention."
And one should reveal it in detail to others, explain its meaning,
and examine it with the mind.
And with superior wisdom, one should apply thorough investigation here;

at the very least, having committed it to a book, one should preserve and establish it for the sake of the long endurance of the true Dharma— so that there may be no severance of the Buddha’s guidance, and no disappearance of the true Dharma.
Thus, a favor will have been bestowed upon the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, through the non-deficiency of the Guide.

And one should honor, revere, esteem, worship, adore, and venerate this Perfection of Wisdom with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, and with rows of lamps all around.
And one should honor them with many kinds of worship;
for this reason, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family produces much more merit than that.
Furthermore, let alone all the beings in a thousandfold world system of the crest, Kauśika.

Kauśika, suppose all the sentient beings in the second-order intermediate thousandfold world-system were each to have a stūpa built for them, made of the seven precious jewels and containing the relics of a Tathāgata,
and were each to honor it with divine [offerings] for as long as they live.
With divine flowers, divine incenses, divine perfumes, divine garlands, divine ointments, divine powders, divine parasols, divine banners, divine bells, and all around with divine rows of lamps,
and with many kinds of divine [offerings].
With offerings,
one should honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate them.
What do you think, Kauśika, would all those beings generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said: "Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family produces far more merit than that."

Whoever, having full faith in this perfection of wisdom, having conviction in it, having resolved upon it with a serene mind, and having generated the thought of awakening, should listen to it with a resolute intention, take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, set it forth, teach it, explain it, point it out, study it, and reveal it in detail to others;
One should explain its meaning,
examine it with the mind,
and apply thorough investigation here with superior wisdom.

Even by making it into a book, one should preserve and store it for the sake of the long endurance of the true Dharma— so that there may be no severance of the Buddha’s guidance, so that the true Dharma does not disappear,
and so that a benefit will be conferred upon the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, through the non-deficiency of the guidance.
And one should honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate this Perfection of Wisdom with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells,
and rows of lamps all around,
and worship it with many kinds of offerings.
Therefore, Kauśika, this son of good family or daughter of good family produces far more merit on that account.
Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone all the beings in a second-order intermediate world-system;
as for all the beings, Kauśika, in a third-order great trichiliocosm world-system—
Suppose each one of those beings were to have a single stūpa made, consisting of the seven precious gems and containing the relics of a Tathāgata,

and were to honor it for as long as they live with divine flowers, divine incenses, divine perfumes, divine garlands, divine powders, divine garments, divine parasols, divine banners, divine bells, and divine...
And if one were to honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate [the Tathāgata] with garlands of divine lamps all around and with various kinds of divine offerings—
what do you think, Kauśika, would all those beings generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said: "Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family produces far more merit than this."

Whoever, having faith in this perfection of wisdom, accepting it, and being resolved upon it with a serene mind, having generated the thought of awakening, should listen to it with a resolute intention, take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, set it in motion, teach it, instruct it, explain it, study it, and reveal it in detail to others;
One should explain its meaning,
examine it with the mind,
and engage in thorough investigation of it with superior wisdom.
Even by making it into a book, one should preserve and store it for the sake of the long endurance of the True Dharma— so that there may be no severance of the Buddha’s guidance,
so that the True Dharma may not disappear,
and so that a benefit will be conferred upon the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, through the non-deficiency of the guidance.
And one should honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate this Perfection of Wisdom with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments,
powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, bells, and flags, as well as with rows of lamps all around and with manifold kinds of worship.
Kauśika, this son of good family or daughter of good family would, on that account, generate far more merit than that.
Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone all the beings in a triple-thousand great thousandfold world system,
were each one of those beings to have a stūpa made for them, consisting of the seven precious jewels and containing the relics of a Tathāgata.

And for as long as life lasts, one should honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate him with divine flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, bells, and flags, as well as with rows of lamps all around and with many kinds of offerings;
and furthermore, Kauśika, whatever beings there may be in the triple-thousand great-thousand world system—

Furthermore, if all those beings were to obtain a human existence simultaneously, without one preceding another— taking this as a conceptual possibility— and if each single being were to have a stūpa built for them, made of the seven precious jewels and containing the relics of a Tathāgata,
and each single being were to have all those stūpas built;

Having had them made and having installed them, for an eon or the remainder of an eon, one should worship them with all kinds of musical instruments, all songs, all dances, and all types of cymbals and percussion; with divine flowers, all incenses, all perfumes, all garlands, all ointments, all powders, and all garments; and with divine parasols, banners, bells, and flags.
And on all sides with garlands of lamps,
and with all kinds of divine and human offerings, they would honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate them;
and by such meritorious action as this, all those beings, having established those immeasurable and incalculable stūpas, would cause such worship to be performed.
"What do you think, Kauśika, would all those beings produce much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata."

The Blessed One said: "Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family produces far more merit who, having faith in this Perfection of Wisdom, accepting it, and being devoted to it with a serene mind, having generated the thought of awakening, listens to it with a resolute intention, takes it up, bears it in mind, recites it, masters it, sets it in motion, teaches it, instructs it, explains it, and studies it."
And he should reveal it in detail to others, explain its meaning,
and examine it with the mind.
And with whatever superior wisdom one may possess, one should apply oneself to a thorough investigation of this;

at the very least, having committed it to a book, one should preserve and establish it for the sake of the long endurance of the True Dharma— lest the guidance of the Buddhas be cut off, lest the True Dharma disappear.
Thus, a favor will have been bestowed upon the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, through the non-deficiency of the Guide.

And one should honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate this Prajñāpāramitā with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, bells, and with rows of lamps all around.
And one should worship with many kinds of offerings;
for this reason, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family generates far more merit than the former.
Thus addressed, Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
For, Blessed One, by one who honors, reveres, respects, worships, adores, and venerates the perfection of wisdom..."

A son of good family or a daughter of good family has, by this means, ultimately honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, adored, and venerated the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present, throughout all world-systems known by the Buddha-gnosis.
Furthermore, O Blessed One, let alone all the sentient beings in a triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system by this method;

Furthermore, O Blessed One, suppose all the sentient beings in as many triple-thousand great thousandfold world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges were each to have a single stūpa made of the seven precious gems, containing the relics of a Tathāgata,
and suppose each individual being were to cause all those stūpas to be constructed.

Having had them made and having installed them, for an eon or the remainder of an eon, one should honor them with all kinds of musical instruments, all songs, all dances, and all types of cymbals and percussion; with divine flowers, incenses, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, and garments; and with divine parasols, banners, bells, and flags.
And if one were to honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate [the stupa] on all sides with garlands of lamps and all kinds of divine and human offerings,
O Blessed One, this son of good family or daughter of good family would generate far more merit than those [other] beings.

Whoever, having full faith in this perfection of wisdom, accepting it, and being devoted to it with a serene mind, having generated the thought of awakening, should listen to it with a resolute intention, take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, set it forth, teach it, explain it, point it out, study it, and reveal it in detail to others;
One should explain its meaning,
examine it with the mind,
and apply thorough investigation here with superior wisdom.

At the very least, having even committed it to a book, one should preserve and establish it for the sake of the long endurance of the true Dharma— so that there may be no severance of the Buddha’s guidance, nor the disappearance of the true Dharma;
and so that a benefit will be conferred upon the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, through the non-deficiency of this guidance.
And one should honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate this Perfection of Wisdom with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells,
and rows of lamps all around,
and worship it with many kinds of offerings.
Then the Blessed One said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "So it is, Kauśika; so it is.
On that account, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family produces much more merit.
On that account, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family produces immeasurable and much more merit."
Kauśika, on that basis, that son of good family or daughter of good family produces much more merit—indeed, incalculable merit;
Kauśika, on that basis, that son of good family or daughter of good family produces much more merit—indeed, inconceivable merit;
Kauśika, on that basis, that son of good family or daughter of good family produces much more merit—indeed, incomparable merit.
Kauśika, on that account, that son of good family or daughter of good family produces immeasurable and far more abundant merit.
Why is that?
For, Kauśika, the omniscience of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas is born from the perfection of wisdom;
and the worship of the relics of the Tathāgatas is born from that omniscience.
Therefore, Kauśika, whatever son of good family or daughter of good family, having faith in this perfection of wisdom, accepting it, and being resolved upon it...

With a serene mind, having generated the aspiration for awakening, one should listen with resolute intention, take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, propagate it, teach it, instruct it, explain it, study it,
and reveal it in detail to others.
One should explain its meaning,
examine it with the mind,
and apply thorough investigation here with superior wisdom.

Even by committing it to a book, one should preserve and establish it for the sake of the long endurance of the true Dharma— lest there be a severance of the Buddha’s guidance, lest the true Dharma disappear—
and so that a benefit will be conferred upon the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, through the non-deficiency of the guidance.

And one should honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate this Perfection of Wisdom with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, bells, and flags, and with rows of lamps all around,
and worship it with many kinds of offerings.

Kauśika, compared to this accumulation of merit, that previous accumulation of merit resulting from the construction of the stūpa made of the seven precious gems— containing the relic of the Tathāgata— does not approach even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part,
nor even a hundred-thousandth part.
Even a ten-millionth part, even a hundred-ten-millionth part, even a thousand-ten-millionth part.
It does not approach even a hundred-thousandth part, nor even a ten-million-billionth part;
it does not admit of any calculation, fraction, reckoning, comparison, likeness, resemblance, or even a point of analogy.

Then, indeed, those forty thousand sons of the gods who had assembled together with Śakra, the lord of the gods, in that very assembly, said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Take up, O noble sir, the perfection of wisdom!
The perfection of wisdom, O noble sir, must be taken up."
The Perfection of Wisdom, friends, should be upheld;
the Perfection of Wisdom, friends, should be recited;
the Perfection of Wisdom, friends, should be mastered.
The Perfection of Wisdom, friend, should be set in motion;
the Perfection of Wisdom, friend, should be taught;
the Perfection of Wisdom, friend, should be explained.
“Venerable sir, the Perfection of Wisdom should be recited;
venerable sir, the Perfection of Wisdom should be studied.
Then the Blessed One addressed Śakra, the lord of the gods: “Kauśika, you must take up the Perfection of Wisdom.”
Kauśika, you should uphold the perfection of wisdom; Kauśika, you should recite the perfection of wisdom;
Kauśika, you should master the perfection of wisdom.
Set forth the perfection of wisdom, Kauśika! Teach the perfection of wisdom, Kauśika! Instruct in the perfection of wisdom, Kauśika!
Pointing out the Perfection of Wisdom, O Kauśika;
recite the Perfection of Wisdom, O Kauśika.
For what reason?
For when, Kauśika, such thoughts arise among the asuras— “We shall fight the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven,” or “We shall wage war against the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa”—
then you, Kauśika, should bring this perfection of wisdom to mind.
Through their own recitation,
those practices of the asuras will once again disappear.
When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the Blessed One as follows: “O Blessed One, this is a great spell, namely the perfection of wisdom.
O Blessed One, this is an immeasurable spell, namely the perfection of wisdom. O Blessed One, this is an infinite spell, namely the perfection of wisdom.”
Knowledge, that is to say, the perfection of wisdom;
this, O Blessed One, is the unsurpassed knowledge, namely the perfection of wisdom;
this, O Blessed One, is the peerless knowledge, namely the perfection of wisdom.
“Blessed One, this knowledge, namely the perfection of wisdom, is unequaled.
Blessed One, this knowledge, namely the perfection of wisdom, is equal to the unequaled.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods: “So it is, Kauśika; so it is.”
This, Kauśika, is the great spell, namely the perfection of wisdom;
this, Kauśika, is the immeasurable spell, namely the perfection of wisdom;
this, Kauśika, is the boundless spell, namely the perfection of wisdom.
This, Kauśika, is the unsurpassed lore, namely the perfection of wisdom;
this, Kauśika, is the peerless lore, namely the perfection of wisdom;
this, Kauśika, is the incomparable lore, namely the perfection of wisdom.
Kauśika, this knowledge, namely the perfection of wisdom, is unequaled.
For what reason?
It is because, having relied upon this knowledge, Kauśika, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened ones of the past fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Namely, the perfection of wisdom.

Moreover, Kauśika, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who will appear in the future time and will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment— [they too shall do so by relying on this].

They too, Kauśika, having relied upon this very same lore, will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment— namely, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). And whatever Buddhas, Blessed Ones, Kauśika, are currently awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in the immeasurable and incalculable three-thousand great thousandfold world-systems,
they too, Kauśika, having relied upon this very same lore, awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment— namely, the perfection of wisdom.
I too, Kauśika, having relied upon this very same knowledge, have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment— namely, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
It is by relying upon this very same knowledge, Kauśika, that the ten paths of wholesome action are manifested in the world,
and the four meditative concentrations associated with the factors of enlightenment are manifested in the world.
The four immeasurables associated with the factors of enlightenment are manifested in the world;
the four formless attainments embraced by the factors of enlightenment are manifested in the world;
and the six supernormal powers associated with the factors of enlightenment are manifested in the world.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are manifested in the world;
in brief, eighty-four thousand aggregates of dharma are manifested in the world;
and the Buddha-knowledge, the self-existent knowledge, and the inconceivable knowledge are manifested in the world.
It is by relying on this very spell, Kauśika— that is to say, the perfection of wisdom—

even when, Kauśika, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not appear in the world, at that time too, Kauśika, those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who are endowed with skill in means through the outflow of the perfection of wisdom as previously heard, [will act].

Those beings as well, Kauśika, out of compassion for sentient beings and motivated by compassion, having come to this world, cause the ten paths of wholesome action to flourish in the world; they cause the four meditative absorptions, though dissociated from the factors of enlightenment, to flourish in the world; and they cause the four immeasurables, though dissociated from the factors of enlightenment, to flourish in the world.
They promote in the world the four formless attainments, which are dissociated from the factors of enlightenment;
they promote in the world the five superknowledges, which are dissociated from the factors of enlightenment.
It is just as if, Kauśika, depending upon the orb of the moon, all medicinal herbs and stars illuminate according to their respective strength and power.
Just as the stars illuminate according to their respective strength and position,
even so, Kauśika, after the passing away of the Tathāgata,

Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, when the True Dharma has disappeared and there is no arising of other Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, whatever practice of the Dharma there may be— whether it be a practice of equanimity or a practice of non-equanimity.
Whatever wholesome conduct is known and manifested in the world, all that is born from the Bodhisattva, manifested by the Bodhisattva, and set in motion by the Bodhisattva’s skill in means.
And that skill in means of the bodhisattvas should be understood as being born from the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Kauśika, for those sons of good family or daughters of good family who take up, bear in mind, recite, master, propagate, teach, explain, point out, study, write down, attend to, and reflect upon this perfection of wisdom, many qualities pertaining to the present life are to be expected as a result thereof.

When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, with what qualities pertaining to the present life will those sons of good family and daughters of good family be endowed?
The Blessed One replied: "Kauśika, those sons of good family or daughters of good family shall not meet their end through the avoidance of untimely dangers."
They will not die by poison, they will not die by weapons,
and they will not die by fire.
They will not die by water, they will not die by a staff,
nor will they die by violence.

Furthermore, whatever calamities may arise for them— whether from kings, princes, royal ministers, or royal high officials— shall vanish again and again as they bring this Perfection of Wisdom to mind or recite it.
And as they repeatedly bring this Perfection of Wisdom to mind or recite it, those who might approach them seeking an opportunity to harm shall find no such opening.
Kings, princes, royal ministers, or royal high officials seeking an opportunity for harm shall not find such an opportunity, precisely because they are protected by the perfection of wisdom.
And when those kings, princes, or royal ministers approach [him],...
Or there may be a desire among the king’s high ministers to converse with you, a desire to address you, and they will consider that you should be greeted by them in return.
For what reason?

Because, Kauśika, this perfection of wisdom is present toward all sentient beings through the application of loving-kindness and a mind of loving-kindness, and through the application of compassion and a mind of compassion.
Therefore, Kauśika, even those who have entered the midst of a wilderness infested with predatory beasts and reptiles—

Kauśika, whether they be humans or non-humans who look for a weakness or seek an opportunity against those sons or daughters of good family, they shall not find such an opportunity, except in the case of the ripening of past karma.
Then, at that time, a hundred wandering mendicants of other sects, intending to find fault [with the Buddha], approached the place where the Blessed One was.

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, seeing those wandering mendicants of other sects approaching from afar and observing their thoughts, reflected thus: "These wandering mendicants of other sects have indeed come with the intention of finding fault."
They approached the place where the Blessed One was.
[He thought: "Suppose I were to recollect, study, and set into motion, through mindfulness, that portion of this Perfection of Wisdom which I have received from the presence of the Blessed One."
"May these followers of other sects and wandering mendicants not approach the Blessed One,
so that there may be no interruption while this perfection of wisdom is being spoken.
Then, Śakra, the lord of the gods, [took up] as much of this portion of the perfection of wisdom as he had received from the presence of the Blessed One.
To that same extent, he attended with mindfulness, recited,
and set it forth.
Then those wandering mendicants of other sects, having circumambulated the Blessed One from a distance even further away, departed by that very same gate and by that very same path.
Then, this thought occurred to the venerable Śāriputra:

"What is the reason why these wandering mendicants of other sects, having circumambulated the Blessed One from a distance even further away, have departed by that very same gate and by that very same path?"
Then the Blessed One, having known with his own mind this very reflection in the mind of the venerable Śāriputra,

said to the venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, Śakra, the lord of the gods, having observed the minds of those wandering mendicants of other sects who intended to find fault, [upheld] this perfection of wisdom through mindfulness."
It has been attended to, studied,
and set in motion for the purpose of turning back those other sectarian wanderers who desire to dispute, desire to argue, and desire to oppose it,
so that while this Perfection of Wisdom is being spoken, these other sectarian wanderers may not approach.
"May they not create an obstacle while the Perfection of Wisdom is being spoken.
And I have granted permission to Śakra, the lord of the gods.
For what reason?
Śāriputra, I do not perceive even a single pure quality in any of those wanderers of other sects.
Śāriputra, they all approached with the intention of finding fault, their minds full of hostility, desiring only to attack.

Then, indeed, this thought occurred to Māra, the Evil One: "These four assemblies of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, have gathered and are seated together, face-to-face with the Tathāgata; and these sons of the gods from the realm of desire and the realm of form are also present.
Surely, here the Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, will receive their predictions regarding unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
"What if I were to approach him in order to cause him to lose his sight?
Then Māra the Evil One, having conjured up an army of four divisions, approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Then it occurred to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Ah, this is surely Māra the Evil One who, having conjured up an army of four divisions, approaches the place where the Blessed One is."
And as for this array of the fourfold army,
it is not the array of King Bimbisāra’s fourfold army, nor is it the array of King Prasenajit’s fourfold army.
Neither is this the array of the fourfold army of the Śākyas, nor is it the array of the fourfold army of the Licchavis; rather, it has been conjured by Māra, the Evil One.
For a long time, Māra the Evil One has followed the Blessed One, seeking an opening and searching for an opportunity to harm him, with the intention of harassing sentient beings.
Therefore, let me now, through mindfulness, bring this very Perfection of Wisdom to mind, recite it, and set it forth.
Then indeed Śakra, the lord of the gods, recalled this very perfection of wisdom, brought it to mind, recited it, and set it forth.
And in whatever measure Śakra, the lord of the gods, recalled this perfection of wisdom, brought it to mind, recited it, and set it forth,
in that same measure Māra, the evil one, turned back again by that very same path.

Then, indeed, the sons of the gods belonging to the Trāyastriṃśa realm, having miraculously created divine māndārava flowers, while situated in the sky in the midst of the air, scattered them toward the Blessed One;
they showered those divine māndārava flowers upon the Blessed One and uttered this exclamation: "Ah! After a long time, indeed, this Perfection of Wisdom has returned to the humans of Jambudvīpa!"
Again, taking divine *māndārava* flowers, they scattered and strewed them over where the Blessed One was,
and spoke thus: "Blessed One, whatever beings shall speak of and cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*, [they shall all attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment]."
They will practice the perfection of wisdom;
neither Māra nor the deities belonging to Māra’s host will find an opportunity to harm them.
Blessed One, those beings do not possess inferior roots of merit.
Those who hear this perfection of wisdom and, having heard it, take it up will be endowed with [these qualities].
Those beings, O Blessed One, who shall uphold, recite, master, propagate,
teach, explain, proclaim, and study [this],
will have performed services for previous Victors.
For those to whom this Perfection of Wisdom shall come within the range of hearing—
how much more so for those who will take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, propagate it, teach it, explain it, expound it, and study it,
and who will train themselves in accordance with suchness!
They will practice for the sake of suchness;
they will apply themselves to yoga for the sake of suchness;
those beings, O Blessed One, will have attended upon the Tathāgatas.
For what reason? Because omniscience is to be sought from this very source, namely, the perfection of wisdom. Just as, Blessed One, whatever jewels there may be, whatever great jewels there may be—
All those [jewels] are produced by the great ocean;
all those are to be sought from the great ocean.
In the same way, Blessed One, the great jewel of omniscience of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas is to be sought from the great ocean of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "So it is, Kauśika, so it is!
From this very source has arisen the great jewel of the omniscience of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; that is to say, from the great ocean of the perfection of wisdom."

Then the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, you do not speak in praise of the perfection of generosity, nor do you proclaim its name; nor [do you do so] for the perfection of ethical discipline."
He does not praise the perfection of patience,
nor the perfection of vigor;
O Blessed One, he does not speak in praise of the perfection of meditative concentration.
He does not proclaim the names of others;
rather, the Blessed One speaks only the praise of the single perfection of wisdom and proclaims its name alone.
The Blessed One said: "It is so, Ānanda, it is so.
It is of the perfection of wisdom alone, Ānanda, that I speak the praise and proclaim the name, and not of the other perfections."
For what reason?
Because, Ānanda, the perfection of wisdom is the precursor of the five perfections.
What do you think, Ānanda, does a gift that has not been dedicated toward omniscience receive the designation "perfection of giving"?
The Venerable Ānanda said, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "What do you think, Ānanda? Is morality untransformed, is patience untransformed, is vigor untransformed, and is meditative concentration untransformed?
What do you think, Ānanda? Does wisdom that is untransformed receive the name 'perfection of wisdom' (prajñāpāramitā) in relation to omniscience?"
Ānanda said, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "What do you think, Ānanda? Is that wisdom inconceivable which dedicates the roots of virtue by means of their dedication toward omniscience?
Ānanda said, "It is so, Blessed One."
"So it is, Sugata!
That wisdom, Blessed One, is inconceivable;
that wisdom, Blessed One, is supremely inconceivable."

When one dedicates the roots of virtue through the dedication toward omniscience, the Blessed One said: "Therefore, Ānanda, because of its supremacy, that [wisdom] receives the name 'perfection' (pāramitā), by which the roots of virtue dedicated toward omniscience receive the name 'perfections.
Therefore, Ānanda, because the roots of virtue are dedicated toward omniscience, the perfection of wisdom is the precursor, the leader, and the guide of the five perfections."
By this yoga, Ānanda, the five perfections are included within the perfection of wisdom alone; indeed, "perfection of wisdom" is a designation for the fulfillment of all six perfections.
Therefore, Ānanda, when the perfection of wisdom is proclaimed, all six perfections are proclaimed.
It is just as, Ānanda, seeds scattered upon the great earth grow when they obtain the necessary conditions.
And the great earth is the foundation for those seeds;
established upon the great earth, those seeds grow.
In the same way, Ānanda, the five perfections, when embraced by the perfection of wisdom, are established in omniscience.
The five perfections grow only when they are established in the perfection of wisdom;
and because they are embraced by the perfection of wisdom, they receive the name "perfection.
Therefore, Ānanda, the perfection of wisdom alone is the precursor, the leader, and the guide of the five perfections.
Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has not yet fully described all the qualities of the perfection of wisdom—

those qualities which a son of good family or a daughter of good family acquires by taking up, bearing in mind, reciting, mastering, setting in motion, teaching, explaining, indicating, and studying the perfection of wisdom."
"For indeed, that portion of this Perfection of Wisdom which I have received from the presence of the Blessed One has been set in motion by me.
The Blessed One said, "Excellent, excellent, Kauśika!"

Furthermore, Kauśika, these qualities will not belong to him alone who shall take up, bear in mind, recite, master, propagate, teach, explain, and expound this perfection of wisdom. But also, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family who, having written down this perfection of wisdom and made it into a book, shall bear it in mind and preserve it for the sake of the long endurance of the true Dharma— [for them too these qualities shall exist].
"May there be no severance of the Buddha's guidance, may there be no disappearance of the True Dharma;
and may a favor be bestowed upon the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, so that they shall not lack the guidance."
And he will honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate this Perfection of Wisdom with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, bells, and flags,
and with rows of lamps all around.
And he will honor it with many kinds of worship;
Kauśika, I declare that this son of good family or daughter of good family shall also possess these qualities pertaining to the present life.

When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: "I too, Blessed One, shall provide protection, shelter, and defense for that son of good family or daughter of good family who, having written down this perfection of wisdom and made it into a book, shall preserve and maintain it for the sake of the long endurance of the true Dharma— so that the lineage of the Buddhas may not be cut off, and so that the true Dharma may not disappear."
Furthermore, a favor will have been bestowed upon the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, by means of the non-deficiency of the Guide.
And they will honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate this Perfection of Wisdom with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, and flags.
He will worship it with garlands of lamps all around and with many kinds of offerings;
how much more so for one who will write down this Perfection of Wisdom, take it up, bear it in mind, and recite it?

He will master it, set it in motion, teach it, instruct in it, explain it, recite it, honor it, revere it, respect it, worship it, adore it, and venerate it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, and with rows of lamps all around.
And he will worship with many kinds of offerings.
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, Kauśika!
Furthermore, Kauśika, many hundreds of sons of gods and many thousands of sons of gods will approach that son of good family or daughter of good family who recites this Perfection of Wisdom."
Many hundreds of thousands of sons of gods will approach to hear the Dharma.
And those sons of gods, while listening to the Dharma, will think that they must provide eloquence for that Dharma-preacher;
even when that Dharma-preacher has no desire to speak, [they will do so].
Even then, those sons of the gods will consider it their duty to provide him with eloquence out of that very same reverence for the Dharma,
so that that son of good family or daughter of good family will have the desire to speak.
