Kauśika, this son of good family or daughter of good family also acquires this quality pertaining to the present life.
Whoever shall take up this Perfection of Wisdom, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, propagate it, teach it, explain it, proclaim it, and study it.

Furthermore, Kauśika, when that son of good family or daughter of good family speaks this perfection of wisdom in the presence of the four assemblies, their mind will not be cowed by the thought: "Lest someone should question me with the intention of finding fault."
For what reason?
Because the perfection of wisdom provides him with protection, defense, and guardianship;
moreover, one who dwells in the perfection of wisdom does not perceive even those who would find fault.
One who dwells in the perfection of wisdom does not perceive even those who would find fault, nor does he perceive one who might be found fault with,
nor does he perceive that perfection of wisdom itself.
In this way, for a son of good family or a daughter of good family who is embraced by the perfection of wisdom, there will be no further questioning by anyone; and they shall not tremble,
nor shall they be terrified.

He shall not fall into terror. Furthermore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family who will take up, bear in mind, recite, master, propagate, teach, explain, proclaim, and study this perfection of wisdom, acquires these very qualities pertaining to the present life.

Furthermore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family will be beloved by their parents, friends, ministers, kinsmen, blood relatives, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, as well as by those who wish them well; and they will be competent and capable of refuting, in accordance with the Dharma, whatever opposing disputants may arise.
Furthermore, when questioned by others, he will be capable of answering those questions.

Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family who shall take up, bear in mind, recite, master, propagate, teach, explain, and expound this perfection of wisdom also acquires these qualities pertaining to the present life.
He will study [it].

Furthermore, Kauśika, wherever a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having written down this Perfection of Wisdom and made it into a book, shall set it up preceded by worship and pay homage to it— there, Kauśika, whichever sons of the gods among the Cāturmahārājakāyika deities have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they too will think that they must go there.

They too, having come there, will behold this Prajñāpāramitā written in a book, and they will salute it, pay homage to it, take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, set it in motion, teach it, explain it, proclaim it, and study it. Having beheld, saluted, and paid homage to it, and having taken it up, recited it, mastered it, set it in motion, taught it, explained it, and proclaimed it— (Vaidya 43)
They will think that they must once again proceed with their private recitation.
Likewise, Kauśika, whatever sons of the gods among the Trāyastriṃśa deities have set out for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
they too will think that they must go there.

They too, having come there, will behold this Perfection of Wisdom written in a book; they will pay homage to it, bow down to it, take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, set it forth, teach it, explain it, proclaim it, and study it.
Having beheld, paid homage to, bowed down to, taken up, borne in mind, recited, mastered, set forth, taught, explained, proclaimed, and studied it, they will think that they should depart once again.
Furthermore, Kauśika, whichever sons of the gods among the Yāma deities have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening,
they too will think that they must go there; having arrived there, they too will behold this Perfection of Wisdom written in a book, pay homage to it, prostrate before it, and take it up.

"Kauśika, those among the sons of the gods in the Tuṣita heaven who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening— whosoever they may be— they will think that after having looked upon, saluted, honored, taken up, retained, recited, mastered, promulgated, taught, explained, expounded, and studied [this teaching], they should then depart."
They too will think that they must go there; having arrived there,

they too will behold this Perfection of Wisdom written in a book, and they will pay homage to it, bow down to it, take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, set it in motion, teach it, instruct in it, explain it, and study it.
Having beheld, saluted, honored, taken up, retained, recited, mastered, set in motion, taught, instructed, pointed out, and studied it, they will think that they must depart once more;
and even those sons of the gods among the Nirmāṇarati deities, Kauśika, who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
they too will think that they must come there.

They too, having come there, will behold this Perfection of Wisdom written in a book; they will pay homage to it, bow down to it, take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, set it forth, teach it, explain it, proclaim it, and study it.
Having beheld, paid homage to, bowed down to, taken up, borne in mind, recited, mastered, set forth, taught, explained, proclaimed, and studied it, they will think that they should depart once again.
Kauśika, whatever sons of the gods among the Paranirmitavaśavartin deities have set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,
they too will think that they must go there; having arrived there, they too will behold this Perfection of Wisdom written in a book, and they will honor and pay homage to it.
They will take it up, preserve it, recite it, master it, propagate it, teach it, explain it, proclaim it, and study it.

Having looked upon it, having paid homage, having prostrated, having taken it up, having preserved it, having recited it, having mastered it, having propagated it, having taught it, having explained it, having proclaimed it, and having studied it, they will think that they should then depart once again.

In the same way, Kauśika, whatever sons of the gods among the deities of the realm of form (rūpāvacara), and as many as there are sons of the gods belonging to the Brahma-body (brahmakāyika) in the Brahma-world who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment— they too will think that they must come there. Having come there, they too will behold this Perfection of Wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) contained in a book, and they will pay homage to it and revere it.
They will take it up, preserve it, recite it, master it, propagate it, teach it, explain it, declare it, and study it.

Having looked upon it, having paid homage, having bowed down, having taken it up, having preserved it, having recited it, having mastered it, having propagated it, having taught it, having explained it, having declared it, and having studied it, they will think that they should then depart once more.
O Kauśika, let it not occur to you that they are only the Brahmakāyika gods;
for as it is with the Brahmakāyikas, so it is also with whoever among the gods of the Brahma-purohitas, O Kauśika.
The sons of the gods... [and so forth]...

likewise, Kauśika, whoever among the Mahābrahmas, Parīttābhas, Apramāṇābhas, Ābhāsvaras, Parīttaśubhas, Apramāṇaśubhas, Śubhakṛtsnas, Anabhrakas, Puṇyaprasavas, Bṛhatphalas, Asaṃjñisattvas, Avṛhas, or Atapas;
In the Sudṛśa and Sudarśana [heavens],
Kauśika, whatever sons of the gods there may be among the Akaniṣṭha gods who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,
they too will think that they must go there.

They too, having come there, will behold this Perfection of Wisdom written in a book; they will pay homage to it, bow down to it, take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, set it forth, teach it, explain it, proclaim it, and study it.
Having beheld, paid homage to, bowed down to, taken up, borne in mind, recited, mastered, set forth, taught, explained, proclaimed, and studied it, they will think that they should depart once again.

And thus, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family should resolve: "Whatever gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans there may be in the immeasurable and incalculable world-systems in the ten directions,"
May they behold, revere, pay homage to, take up, bear in mind, master, set in motion, teach, instruct, explain, and recite the Perfection of Wisdom from this book.
Having beheld, revered, paid homage to, taken up, borne in mind, recited, mastered, set in motion, and taught [it],...
"Having taught, having pointed out, and having recited [this], let them return once more to their own abodes, thinking: 'May this very gift of Dharma be given to them.

Do not let it occur to you, Kauśika, that only those sons of the gods belonging to the desire realm and the form realm in this very world-system of four great continents who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment will think they must go there."
Kauśika, you should not view it in that way.

Rather, Kauśika, as many sons of the gods belonging to the desire realm and the form realm as there are in the triple-thousand great-thousand world system who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening—
they too will think that they must go there.

They too, having come there, will behold this Perfection of Wisdom written in a book; they will pay homage to it, bow down to it, take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, set it in motion, teach it, explain it, proclaim it, and study it.

Having beheld, paid homage to, bowed down to, taken up, borne in mind, recited, mastered, set in motion, taught, explained, proclaimed, and studied it, they will think that they should depart once again.
Furthermore, Kauśika, the house, dwelling, or palace of that son of good family or daughter of good family will be well-protected;
and no one at all shall cause them harm, except as a result of the ripening of past karma.
This too, Kauśika, is a quality pertaining to the present life that that son of good family or daughter of good family will acquire.
For indeed, it is to this place that gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans of such great majesty will think they must come.

When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the Blessed One: "But how, Blessed One, should that son of good family or daughter of good family know: 'Here, gods, or nāgas, or yakṣas, or gandharvas, or asuras, or garuḍas, or kinnaras, or mahoragas, or humans, or non-humans, are coming to this perfection of wisdom'?"

"To hear it, to see it, to worship it, to pay homage to it, to take it up, to bear it in mind, to recite it, to master it, to set it in motion, to teach it, to instruct in it, to explain it, and to study it?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family perceives therein a sublime radiance..."
That son of good family or daughter of good family should reach the conclusion that a deva, nāga, yakṣa, gandharva, asura, garuḍa, kinnara, mahoraga, human, or non-human has approached him here.
Furthermore, Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family should there smell a non-human fragrance never smelled before,
and having smelled that fragrance, that son of good family or daughter of good family should conclude:
"A deva, or a nāga, or a yakṣa, or a gandharva, or an asura, or a garuḍa, or a kinnara, or a mahoraga is here."
Whether it be a human or a non-human who has come, or one who has approached.
Furthermore, Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family should smell there a non-human fragrance never smelled before,
and having smelled that fragrance, that son of good family or daughter of good family should conclude:
"A god, or a nāga, or a yakṣa, or a gandharva, or an asura, or a garuḍa, or a kinnara, or a mahoraga, or a human, or a non-human has come here."
Regarding the phrase "having approached":
furthermore, Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family shall be of pure conduct and of clean conduct, [they will approach].
Because of his pure conduct and his clean behavior, those gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans will think that they ought to come;
and whichever gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans shall have arrived there, [they will be honored].
Because of his pure conduct and his clean behavior, they will become uplifted, joyful, and filled with gladness and happiness.
Furthermore, those deities of little power who may be dwelling there will think that they must depart from that place.
For what reason?
Because it is from the very splendor, majesty, and dignity of those most powerful gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans [that it arises].
And those deities of little power, being unable to endure it, will think that they must depart from there.

Furthermore, Kauśika, to the extent that those gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans of great power frequently approach, to that same extent that son of good family or daughter of good family will become full of serene faith.
Furthermore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family will also acquire this quality pertaining to the present life.
Moreover, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family must not engage in any impure or unclean conduct in the vicinity of that place where the guidance of the Dharma is situated,
out of a sense of profound reverence for it.
Furthermore, Kauśika, neither physical fatigue nor mental fatigue shall arise for that son of good family or daughter of good family;
he shall lie down in comfort and shall proceed in comfort.
And while asleep, he will not see evil dreams;
and even when seeing, he will see only Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas,
and he will see only stūpas.
He will see only bodhisattvas and will see only the disciples of the Tathāgata;
and hearing sounds, he will hear only the sounds of the perfections.
He will see only the factors conducive to enlightenment;
he will see only the trees of enlightenment; and within them, he will see only the Tathāgatas, the Arhats.
He will see the perfectly awakened Buddhas as they attain full awakening;

he will see those who have already attained awakening turning the wheel of Dharma; and he will see many bodhisattvas reciting this very perfection of wisdom, delighting in the communal chanting of the perfection of wisdom, [saying]: "In this way, omniscience is to be grasped."
"In this way, a buddha-field is to be purified," thus he teaches skillful means;
and he will hear the sublime sound of the perfect enlightenment of the Blessed Buddhas, [saying]: "In such a direction, in such a place..."

In that direction, in such-and-such a world-system, there is a certain Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named so-and-so, [accompanied] by many hundreds of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, many thousands of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, many hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas,
many koṭis of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, many hundreds of koṭis of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, and many thousands of koṭis of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.

Surrounded and honored by many hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, and many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, he teaches the Dharma.
Furthermore, Kauśika, whichever son of good family or daughter of good family shall see such dreams as these, [will attain great merit].
He will sleep in peace, he will awaken in peace,
and with his body infused with vitality, he will experience well-being.
He will experience [the result] very quickly,
and his mental continuum will not arise with excessive greed for food; moreover,
his perception of food becomes mild.
Just as, Kauśika, for a monk practicing yoga who has emerged from meditative concentration, there is no strong craving for food because his mind is saturated with mental attention (*manasikāra*),
and his perception of food becomes faint;
even so, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family will have no strong craving for food.
And his perception of food will become slight.
Why is that?

It is because, Kauśika, it is thus for that son of good family or daughter of good family who is devoted to the practice of the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; for in this way, non-human beings [will not approach] his body.
They will think that vigor must be summoned;
furthermore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family acquires these qualities pertaining to the present life.

Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having written down this perfection of wisdom and made it into a book, were to set it out preceded by worship and honor it, but did not take it up, nor bear it in mind, nor recite it, nor master it, nor set it in motion, nor teach it, nor explain it, nor point it out, nor study it;
Therefore, Kauśika, this son of good family or daughter of good family produces far more merit than that—

namely, the son of good family or daughter of good family who, having faith in this *prajñāpāramitā*, having conviction in it, and having resolute belief in it, with a serene mind, having generated the thought of awakening, listens to it, takes it up, bears it in mind, recites it, masters it, sets it forth, teaches it, instructs it, explains it, and studies it with a profound intention (*adhyāśaya*).
And one should reveal it in detail to others, explain its meaning,
and examine it with the mind.
And with whatever superior wisdom one may possess, one should apply thorough investigation here;
at the very least, having committed it to a book, one should preserve and maintain it for the sake of the long endurance of the True Dharma— so that there be no severance of the Buddha’s guidance,
and no disappearance of the True Dharma.
"Thus, a favor will have been bestowed upon the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, through the non-deficiency of the Guide.

One should honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate this Perfection of Wisdom; one should worship it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, and with rows of lamps all around, and with manifold kinds of offerings."
Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family generates far more merit on that account.

For this reason, Kauśika, a son of good family or daughter of good family who wishes to acquire these distinguished qualities pertaining to the present life should have faith in this very perfection of wisdom.
It should be accepted, it should be enjoyed; with a serene mind, having generated the thought of awakening, one should listen to it with reverence and with a resolute intention,
and it should be taken up, retained, recited, mastered, promulgated, taught, explained, pointed out, and studied.
And it should be proclaimed in detail to others, explained according to its meaning,
and examined with the mind.
And with superior wisdom, one should apply thorough investigation here;
at the very least, having committed it to a book, it should be kept and honored for the sake of the long endurance of the true Dharma— so that the guidance of the Buddhas may not be cut off,
and so that the true Dharma may not disappear.
"Thus, a benefit will be conferred upon the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, through the non-deficiency of the Guide.
I shall share this with those sons of good family and daughters of good family who seek it,
so that for myself and for other virtuous beings, there shall be no deficiency in the Great Eye of the Buddha’s Guide."
And she should always be treated with respect, revered, honored, worshipped, adored, and venerated with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells,
and rows of lamps all around,
and she should be worshipped with many kinds of offerings.
In the Noble Eight Thousand Line Prajñāpāramitā, this is the third chapter, titled "The Merit of Upholding the Immeasurable Qualities and the Veneration of the Stūpa."
(Vaidya 48) Chapter Four: The Proclamation of Qualities.

Furthermore, the Blessed One addressed Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Kauśika, suppose this Jambudvīpa of yours, filled to the very top and brimming over, were given to you as a gift consisting of the relics of the Tathāgata."
And if this Perfection of Wisdom were written down and offered, and one were then invited to choose between these two portions thus set out, which portion, Kauśika, would you take?
Śakra said: "If, Blessed One, this Jambudvīpa were filled to the very top with the relics of the Tathāgata and offered to me,"

And if this Perfection of Wisdom were written down and presented to me, and I were then offered a choice between these two portions thus set out, O Blessed One, I would choose this very Perfection of Wisdom.
Why is that?
It is just as if one were to show reverence for the guidance of the Tathāgata;
for this is indeed the body of the Tathāgatas in its ultimate sense.
Why is that?
For this has been said by the Blessed One: "The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are the Dharma-body.
Monks, do not indeed regard this body as a 'satkāya' (a perishable collection).
Monks, you shall see me through the perfection of the Dharma-body."
And this body of the Tathāgata is to be seen as being manifested from the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), namely, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, O Blessed One, it is not that I lack respect for those relics of the Tathāgata;
indeed, O Blessed One, I have great respect for those relics of the Tathāgata.
Moreover, Blessed One, it is because the relics of the Tathāgatas are born from this perfection of wisdom that they receive worship.
Therefore, Blessed One, by worshipping this very perfection of wisdom, a complete worship of those relics of the Tathāgatas is also performed.
Why is that?
Because the relics of the Tathāgata are born from the perfection of wisdom.
It is just as if, Blessed One, when I am seated upon my own divine throne in the Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods, at that time the sons of the gods come to attend upon me.
At whatever time I am not seated,
at that time the sons of the gods, out of reverence for me, pay homage to my seat, circumambulate it, and then depart once more.
For what reason is this?

"For indeed, it is said that Śakra, the lord of the gods, having sat upon this very seat, teaches the Dharma to the Trāyastriṃśa gods. In the same way, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is the cause and condition for the great majesty [of the Tathāgata]; it is the bringer of omniscience to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha."
Furthermore, the relics of the Tathāgata serve as the physical basis for omniscience;
however, they do not function as its conditions,
nor do they function as its causes for the arising of that knowledge.
In the same way, Blessed One, worship performed toward the bodies of the Tathāgatas has as its cause the wisdom of the Omniscient One.
Therefore, Blessed One, if these two portions were set before me, I would choose this very Perfection of Wisdom, Blessed One.
It is not that I lack respect for those bodies of the Tathāgatas, Blessed One.
"O Blessed One, I have indeed great reverence for those relics of the Tathāgata.
Nevertheless, O Blessed One, it is because they have been permeated by the perfection of wisdom that those relics of the Tathāgata receive worship.
Furthermore, O Blessed One, let alone this Jambūdvīpa filled to the brim with the relics of the Tathāgata."
Let alone a world-system of four great continents filled to the brim with the relics of the Tathāgata;
let alone a thousandfold world-system filled to the brim with the relics of the Tathāgata;
let alone, O Blessed One, a second-order intermediate world-system filled to the brim with the relics of the Tathāgata.

Blessed One, suppose this very trichiliocosm, filled to the brim with the relics of the Tathāgata and bound together like a topknot, were divided into two portions and set aside; and suppose this Perfection of Wisdom were written down and set aside as the second portion.
"If one were offered a choice between these two portions thus set aside, saying, 'Take whichever of these two portions you prefer,' then,
O Blessed One, I would take this very Perfection of Wisdom. Indeed, [I would not take the other]."
Furthermore, Blessed One, it is not that I lack respect for those relics of the Tathāgata;
indeed, Blessed One, I have great respect for those relics of the Tathāgata.
Nevertheless, Blessed One, it is because those relics of the Tathāgata have been permeated by the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) that they receive worship.
For the relics of the Tathāgata are the basis for the knowledge of the omniscient one;
and that knowledge of the omniscient one, too, is born from the perfection of wisdom.
Therefore, Blessed One, if these two portions were set before me, I would choose this very perfection of wisdom, Blessed One.
"Furthermore, Blessed One, it is certainly not that I lack respect for those relics of the Tathāgata;
indeed, Blessed One, I have great respect for those relics of the Tathāgata.

However, Blessed One, it is because they have been born from this perfection of wisdom that those relics of the Tathāgata receive worship—that is to say, because they have been thoroughly permeated by the perfection of wisdom."
It is just as if, Blessed One, there were an invaluable jewel endowed with such qualities as these:
namely, wherever it might be placed,
there neither humans nor non-humans would find an opportunity to gain entry.
Wherever there may be a man or a woman possessed by a non-human spirit, as soon as that jewel-gem is introduced there, that non-human spirit shall depart from them.
Even for one afflicted by wind-disorders, if that jewel-gem were placed upon their body while it is being blown [by the wind], [it would provide relief].
One should restrain that wind of his, not allow it to increase, and cause it to subside.
Even when the body is being burned by bile, it should be established [in mindfulness];
that bile of his would then be restrained and not allowed to increase.
One should pacify it;
even when the body is seized by phlegm and afflicted on all sides, it should be applied,
and it will subdue that phlegm as well.
One should not increase it, but should pacify it;
even for one suffering from a disease caused by the combination of all three humors, it should be applied to the body.
He would suppress even that combined disease,
not increase it,
but bring it to pacification.
It would also produce illumination even on a night of blinding darkness;
and even when heat is present, whatever spot of earth it is placed upon,
that spot of earth would become cool.
Even when cold prevails, whichever region of the earth it might be placed upon, that region of the earth would become warm;
and in whichever region of the earth venomous serpents might roam, [it would become free of them].
Likewise, even other small creatures might be held or placed upon that spot of earth.
Those venomous serpents and those small creatures would also depart from there.
Blessed One, if a woman or a man were bitten by a venomous serpent, that jewel should be shown to him.
By the mere sight of that jewel-gem, that poison would be neutralized and vanish.
Blessed One, that jewel-gem would be endowed with these and other such qualities.
Furthermore, Blessed One, for anyone who might have a cataract, blindness, eye disease, or a film on the eyes, [that jewel would cure it].
And if that precious jewel were placed in their eyes, by the mere act of placing it, those defects of the eyes would be utterly destroyed and pacified.
Blessed One, that precious jewel would be endowed with such qualities as these and others.
And wherever it might be placed in water,
it would make even that water one color with its own color;
if it were wrapped in a white cloth and cast into the water, [it would make the water white].
That water would turn white. Likewise,

if that jewel were wrapped or tied with a cloth of blue, yellow, red, madder-red, or any other kind of cloth among various types, and then thrown into the water, [the water would take on the color of that cloth].

By means of each respective dye for cloth, that water would take on the corresponding natural color; it would also clarify whatever turbidity that water might have. Blessed One, that jewel-gem would be endowed with such qualities as these.

Then the venerable Ānanda said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Furthermore, Kauśika, do those jewel-gems exist only in the world of the gods, or do those jewel-gems also exist among the humans of Jambudvīpa?"
Śakra said: "Noble Ānanda, those precious jewels exist among the gods;
however, humans of Jambudvīpa also possess precious jewels.
But those are heavy, few, limited, and deficient in qualities."
They are not endowed with such qualities;
they do not approach even a hundredth part, nor even a thousandth part, of those divine mani-jewels.
even a hundred-thousandth part,
even a ten-millionth part, even a hundred-ten-millionth part,
They do not approach even a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-koṭī-niyuta part.
They do not admit of, nor do they approach, even a number, a fraction, a calculation, a comparison, a likeness, a resemblance, or a subtle analogy;
for those [blessings] which exist among the gods are indeed slight, whereas these are perfected in every aspect of virtue.
And in whatever casket that precious jewel has been placed or deposited,
even after that precious jewel has been removed from the casket, that casket remains truly desirable;
by virtue of the qualities of that precious jewel, a supreme longing for that casket arises in them.
In the same way, Blessed One, these are the qualities of the perfection of wisdom and of the knowledge of the omniscient one,

by which even after the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has entered final nirvāṇa, those relics of the Tathāgata receive worship— these relics of the Tathāgata being [the embodiments] of the knowledge of the omniscient one.
And just as, Blessed One, the teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in all world-systems is worthy of worship because it is born from the perfection of wisdom;
Thus, the Dharma-preacher’s teaching of the Dharma is worthy of worship because it is born from the perfection of wisdom.

And just as, Blessed One, a king’s officer is worthy of worship by a great multitude of people and is fearless from any quarter due to the majesty of the king, so too that Dharma-preacher is worthy of worship by a great multitude of people and is fearless from any quarter due to the majesty of the Dharma-body.
And just as the teaching of the Dharma and the preachers of the Dharma receive worship,
so too do those relics of the Tathāgata receive worship.
Therefore, Blessed One, let alone a trichiliocosm great thousandfold world system filled to the brim and bound together with the relics of the Tathāgata;
Furthermore, Blessed One, suppose all those world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges were filled to the brim with the relics of the Tathāgatas and set aside as one portion,
and this Perfection of Wisdom were written down and set aside as a second portion.
In that case, Blessed One, if someone were to offer me a choice between one of these two portions, saying, "Of these two portions set before you, take whichever portion you prefer," then,
Blessed One, of those two portions set before me, I would choose this very one: namely, the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Blessed One, it is not that I lack reverence for those relics of the Tathāgata; indeed, Blessed One, I have great reverence for those relics of the Tathāgata.
Nevertheless, Blessed One, omniscience is permeated by the perfection of wisdom.
And the worship of the relics of the Tathāgatas arises from omniscience.
Therefore, Blessed One, when the perfection of wisdom is worshipped, the worship of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present, has been performed.

Furthermore, Blessed One, a son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to see by way of the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who currently abide, remain, and maintain themselves in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems, should practice the perfection of wisdom and apply themselves to the yoga of the perfection of wisdom.
The perfection of wisdom should be cultivated.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "So it is, Kauśika, so it is!

Those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, Kauśika, who appeared in the past time and fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment—they too, Kauśika, having relied upon this very perfection of wisdom, fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
Moreover, Kauśika, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who will appear in the future time—
they too, Kauśika, will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment by relying on this very perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Kauśika, those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who at present reside, stay, and maintain themselves in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems— [they too do so by relying on this very perfection of wisdom].
Those Buddhas, O Kauśika, those Blessed Ones, too, having relied upon this very perfection of wisdom, fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

I too, O Kauśika, who am now the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly and completely enlightened one, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by relying upon this very perfection of wisdom.
When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the Blessed One: "This is a great perfection, Blessed One—namely, the perfection of wisdom.
For, Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, correctly knows and correctly perceives the mental activities of all sentient beings.
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Kauśika; so it is."
For in this way, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva has practiced the perfection of wisdom for a long time;
therefore, through that practice of the perfection of wisdom, he correctly understands and clearly perceives the mental activities of all sentient beings.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice only in the perfection of wisdom and not in the other perfections?
The Blessed One replied: "Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in all six perfections.
Nevertheless, Kauśika, it is the perfection of wisdom alone that is the precursor here for a bodhisattva mahāsattva when he gives a gift."
Whether one is guarding ethical discipline,
accomplishing patience, or exerting diligence;

Whether a bodhisattva mahāsattva is entering into meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) or discerning phenomena (*dharmas*), it is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) alone that is the precursor in these matters.

Furthermore, Kauśika, there is no distinction among these six perfections when they are embraced by skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), dedicated through the perfection of wisdom, and dedicated toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

And no difference is perceived. It is just as if, Kauśika, in Jambudvīpa there were various trees— of various colors, various shapes, various leaves, various flowers, various fruits, and endowed with various heights and circumferences— and yet, among those trees, no distinction or difference is discernible in their shadow.

Moreover, just as "shadow" receives the designation "shadow," even so, Kauśika, among these six perfections when they are embraced by skillful means, dedicated to omniscience, and dedicated to the perfection of wisdom, no distinction or difference is perceived.
When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is endowed with great qualities;
Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is endowed with immeasurable qualities;
Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is endowed with boundless qualities."
The fourth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of Qualities," in the Noble Eight Thousand Verse Perfection of Wisdom.
(Vaidya 52) Chapter Five: The Exposition of Merit.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, whichever son of good family or daughter of good family..."

Or, having faith in this perfection of wisdom, accepting it, and being resolved upon it with a serene mind, one should generate the thought of awakening and, out of high resolve, listen to it, take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, set it in motion, teach it, instruct in it,
explain it, direct it, study it, and reveal it in detail to others.
One should explain its meaning,
examine it with the mind,
and apply thorough investigation here with superior wisdom.
Even by making it into a book, one should preserve and store it for the sake of the long endurance of the true Dharma— so that there may be no severance of the Buddha’s guidance,
so that the true Dharma may not disappear,
and so that a benefit will be conferred upon the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, through the non-deficiency of the guidance.
Having heard this exposition, one thinks: "Oh, how truly of great purpose is this perfection of wisdom! How truly of great benefit! How truly of great fruit!"
"Indeed, this perfection of wisdom has such great maturation;
indeed, this perfection of wisdom is endowed with such manifold qualities;
this perfection of wisdom must not be abandoned by me."
One should have faith, thinking: "My perfection of wisdom must be protected; my perfection of wisdom must be guarded; for this perfection of wisdom is exceedingly difficult to obtain."

Or suppose someone else, having honored this very *prajñāpāramitā*— revering, respecting, esteeming, worshiping, adoring, and venerating it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells,
and rows of lamps all around, and with many kinds of offerings— were to give it, present it, bestow it, and relinquish it to another noble son or noble daughter who is seeking and desiring it.

"Even if it were merely committed to a book, Blessed One, which of those two—whether the son of good family or the daughter of good family—would generate the greater merit: the one who has the intention to relinquish [the teaching], or the one who does not have the intention to relinquish it?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "In that case, Kauśika, I shall question you on this very point."
Please explain this as you see fit.

What do you think, Kauśika: if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having honored the body of the Tathāgata after his parinirvāṇa, should attend to it, preserve it, honor it, revere it, respect it, worship it, adore it, and venerate it by their own hand?

Or if another son of good family or daughter of good family were to personally honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate the relics of the Tathāgata, and were to extensively proclaim them to others, give them away, and distribute them, thinking, "May there be widespread worship," out of compassion for sentient beings; [the latter would generate more merit].
Of those two, which son of good family or daughter of good family would produce more merit:
the one who themselves makes offerings and extensively proclaims, gives, and distributes it to others;
or the one who themselves alone makes offerings privately?

Śakra said: "Blessed One, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were themselves to honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate the body of the Tathāgata, and furthermore were to extensively proclaim it to others, give it away, and distribute it, thinking, 'May this worship become widespread,' out of compassion for sentient beings—
of these two, the son or daughter of good family, the latter generates far more merit."
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Kauśika, so it is!

So it is, Kauśika: if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having written down this perfection of wisdom and made it into a book, should take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, set it forth, teach it, explain it, point it out, study it, and should give it, hand it over, bestow it, and relinquish it—even if only as a book—to another son of good family or daughter of good family who seeks it and desires it; [then their merit would be great]."

Kauśika, between these two— the son of good family or daughter of good family who acts for the benefit of others, and the son of good family or daughter of good family whose intention is renunciation— it is the latter who, on that account, generates far more merit.

Furthermore, Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to go wherever there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who have become fit vessels for this perfection of wisdom, and were to give this perfection of wisdom to them and share it with them,
he or she, Kauśika, would generate much more merit than that son or daughter of good family.
Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to exhort all the beings in Jambudvīpa and establish them in the ten paths of wholesome action.
What do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Śakra replied: "Much, Blessed One."
"Much, Sugata," [Kauśika replied].

The Blessed One said: "Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much more merit, who, having even made this Perfection of Wisdom into a book, places their faith in it and causes others to place their faith in it."
Accepting with conviction, he accepts; resolving with faith, he resolves;

with a serene mind, he offers it to one with a serene mind; endowed with resolute intention, he offers it to one endowed with resolute intention; having generated the mind set on awakening, he offers it with resolute intention to the Bodhisattva who has likewise generated the mind set on awakening.

One should accomplish even the mere writing or reading of it with tireless diligence— one should zealously cause another to grasp it, demonstrate it, encourage its adoption, inspire them, and gladden them;
one should lead them by means of speech, discipline them,
and fully illuminate its meaning for them.
In this way he will purify his mind and make it free from doubt,
and he will say to him: "Come, son of good family, train yourself in this very path of the bodhisattvas."
For by training in this, practicing it, and exerting yourself in it, you will very quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And having awakened, you will lead the immeasurable realm of beings to the unsurpassed destruction of the substrates of existence—that is, to the realization of the limit of reality.
Kausika, this son of good family or daughter of good family, through their intention of renunciation, would generate much more merit than that previous son of good family or daughter of good family.
Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone all the beings in Jambudvīpa;

by this same method, Kauśika, if some son of good family or daughter of good family were to encourage and establish even all those beings in the world-system of four great continents in the ten paths of wholesome action.

Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone all the beings in a world-system of four great continents; by this same method, Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to exhort and establish even all those beings in a thousandfold minor world-system in the ten paths of wholesome action.
Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone all the beings in a thousandfold world-system of the Cūḍika type;

by this same method, Kauśika, if some son of good family or daughter of good family were to encourage and establish even all those beings in a second-order intermediate thousandfold world-system in the ten paths of wholesome action.
Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone all the beings in a second-order intermediate thousandfold world system;

by this same method, Kauśika, if some son of good family or daughter of good family were to exhort and establish even all those beings in a third-order great trichiliocosm in the ten paths of wholesome action.
Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone all the beings in a single trichiliocosm;
by this same method, Kauśika, as many beings as there are in as many trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges—

If some son of good family or daughter of good family were to encourage all those beings and establish them in the ten paths of wholesome action, what do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One."
Much, Sugata.

The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would indeed produce much more merit who, having even made this Perfection of Wisdom into a book, places their faith in it and has faith in it, and conceives conviction in it and has conviction in it."
Resolving with conviction, he becomes resolved;

with a clear mind, he offers his clear mind; endowed with high resolve, he offers his high resolve to a Bodhisattva who has likewise generated the mind of enlightenment and is endowed with high resolve, and with that high resolve, he should accomplish even the mere writing or reciting [of this teaching] without weariness.
Being diligent, he should cause him to grasp it, demonstrate it, encourage its adoption, inspire him, and gladden him;
he shall lead him by means of speech,
and discipline him.
He will reveal its meaning to him,
and in this way he will purify his mind and make it free from doubt.
And he will say this to him: "Come, son of good family, train in this very path of the bodhisattvas!
For by training, practicing, and striving in this, you will very quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And having awakened, you will lead immeasurable realms of beings to the supreme destruction of the substrates of existence."
That is to say, in the manifestation of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Kausika, this son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much more merit through the intention of renunciation than that previous son of good family or daughter of good family.
Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings in Jambūdvīpa in the four dhyānas.
What do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata."

The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would indeed generate much more merit who, having even made this Perfection of Wisdom into a book, places their faith in it, has faith in it; accepts it, accepts it; and resolves upon it, resolves upon it."

With a serene mind, one should give with a sincere intention to a Bodhisattva who possesses a serene mind and is endowed with high resolve, and who has already generated the mind set on awakening; one should accomplish this by means of writing or reciting it, without weariness, out of a sincere intention.
Being diligent, he should cause him to grasp it, demonstrate it, encourage its adoption, inspire him, and gladden him;
he shall lead him by means of speech and discipline him.
He will fully illuminate its meaning for him,
and in this way he will purify his mind and make it free from doubt.
And he will say this to him: "Come, son of good family, train in this very path of the bodhisattvas!
For by training, practicing, and striving in this, you will very quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And having awakened, you will lead immeasurable realms of beings to the unsurpassed destruction of the substrata of existence."
Namely, in the manifestation of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone all the beings in Jambudvīpa;
by this same method, Kauśika, even those beings who are in the world-system of four great continents—
If some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all of them as well in the four dhyānas—
let alone, Kauśika, all the beings in a world-system of four great continents,
by this same method, even those beings, Kauśika, who are in a thousandfold small-world system (sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu)—
Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all those beings in the four dhyānas;
let alone all the beings in a thousandfold world system of the Cūlikā type.

In this same manner, Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all those beings who exist in the second-order intermediate thousandfold world-system in the four meditative absorptions (dhyāna).
Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone all the beings in the second-order intermediate thousandfold world-system.

In this same manner, Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all those beings who exist in the triple-thousand great-thousand world-system in the four dhyānas.
Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone all the beings in the triple-thousand great-thousand world-system;

In this manner, Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all those beings who exist in as many triple-thousand great-thousand world systems as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā in the four dhyānas.
What do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata."
The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would indeed produce much more merit who,
having at least placed this Perfection of Wisdom in the form of a book, places full faith in it and has full faith, and conceives conviction in it and has conviction."
Resolving with conviction, he resolves;

with a clear mind, he offers his clear mind; endowed with resolute intention, he offers his resolute intention to a Bodhisattva who has likewise resolved with conviction, possesses a clear mind, and is endowed with resolute intention—having generated the mind set on enlightenment, he should, with resolute intention, accomplish for that Bodhisattva who has already generated the mind of enlightenment even the mere writing or reciting, without weariness.
Being diligent, he should cause him to grasp it, demonstrate it, incite him toward it, inspire him, and gladden him;
he shall lead him with his speech,
discipline him, and encourage him.
He will fully reveal its meaning to him,
and in this way he will purify his mind and render it free from doubt.
And he will say this to him: "Come, son of good family, train in this very path of the bodhisattvas!

For by training, practicing, and striving in this, you will very quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. And having awakened, you will lead immeasurable realms of beings to the unsurpassed destruction of the substrata—that is, to the realization of the limit of reality."

Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings in Jambudvīpa, as many as there are, in the four immeasurables; in this way, the same should be applied by way of analogy.
Just as it is with the four immeasurables, so it is with the four formless attainments and the five supernormal powers.

"Up to the point that one might establish them in all the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
What do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata."

The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would produce much more merit who, having even made this Perfection of Wisdom into a book, should have faith in it, have faith; should find conviction in it, find conviction; should have resolve toward it, have resolve."

With a serene mind toward one with a serene mind, endowed with resolute intention toward one endowed with resolute intention, having generated the thought of awakening toward a bodhisattva who has generated the thought of awakening, he will— with resolute intention and without weariness— accomplish even the writing or the recitation;
being diligent, he will cause that person to grasp it.
He will demonstrate it, incite others toward it, inspire them, and gladden them; he will lead them by means of speech, discipline them, and encourage them; [he will explain] its meaning.
He will reveal this to him,
and he will thus purify his mind and make it free from doubt.
And he will say this to him: "Come, son of good family, train yourself in this very path of the bodhisattvas.

For by training, practicing, and striving in this, you will very quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. And having awakened, you will lead immeasurable realms of beings to the unsurpassed destruction of the substrata—that is, to the realization of the limit of reality."

"What do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata."

with a clear mind, he offers his clear mind; endowed with resolute intention, he offers his resolute intention to a Bodhisattva who has likewise generated the thought of awakening and is endowed with resolute intention; and with such resolute intention, he shall accomplish the task—even down to writing or reciting it—without ever becoming weary.

That is to say, it is in the manifestation of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).

Furthermore, Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to write down this Perfection of Wisdom, recite it themselves, and having written it down, give it to others as previously described—
Kauśika, without effort, they would generate much more merit than that previous son or daughter of good family.

Furthermore, Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, being skilled in the meaning, should recite this Perfection of Wisdom, and having written it down, should give it to others as before, and should teach and elucidate it together with its meaning and its phrasing;
Without effort, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would produce much more merit.
Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, should this perfection of wisdom also be taught?

When this was said, the Blessed One said this to Śakra, lord of the gods: "Kauśika, this perfection of wisdom should indeed be taught to a son of good family or a daughter of good family who does not understand it.
And why is that?"
"For indeed, Kauśika, in a future time, a counterfeit of the perfection of wisdom will arise.

Therein, a son of good family or a daughter of good family who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment might be ruined if, failing to recognize it, they hear that counterfeit of the perfection of wisdom.

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: 'How, Blessed One, is the counterfeit of the perfection of wisdom to be known in a future time? How is it taught that "this is the counterfeit of the perfection of wisdom"? "

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Kauśika, in a future time there will be certain monks who have not cultivated the body, have not cultivated ethical discipline, have not cultivated the mind, and have not cultivated wisdom; they will be like sheep or the mute, devoid of wisdom.
Claiming, 'We shall teach the perfection of wisdom,' they will instead teach a counterfeit of it."
And how, Kauśika, will they teach a counterfeit of the perfection of wisdom?
They will teach that "the destruction of form is the impermanence of form," and likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
They will teach that the destruction of consciousness is the impermanence of consciousness;
and they will teach thus: "Whoever investigates in this way will course in the perfection of wisdom."
This, Kauśika, should be known as a counterfeit of the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika, the impermanence of form is not to be viewed as the destruction of form;
and the same applies to feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Furthermore, Kauśika, the impermanence of consciousness should not be viewed as the destruction of consciousness.
If one views it in this way,
one is practicing a counterfeit perfection of wisdom.
Therefore, Kausika, a son of good family or a daughter of good family should teach the meaning of the perfection of wisdom.

This person would produce even more merit than that.
Why is that?
Because, Kauśika, it is from this that arhatship is manifested.
And in this way, it will increase his enthusiasm: "For in whatever measure, noble son, you train in the perfection of wisdom,
in that same measure you will gradually become a recipient of the Buddha-dharmas and will draw near to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
For here, training yourself in this training, practicing and striving, you will realize the fruit of stream-entry; you will realize the fruit of once-returning;
you will realize the fruit of non-returning.
You will manifest the state of an Arhat; you will manifest the state of a Pratyekabuddha;
you will manifest the state of a Samyaksambuddha. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings in Jambudvīpa, as many as there are, in the state of a pratyekabuddha.
What do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family produce much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.

The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would indeed generate much more merit than that, who [would uphold] this perfection of wisdom, at the very least, even as a book."
Having done so, they have faith and continue to have faith; they are convinced and continue to be convinced; they resolve and continue to resolve.
With a serene mind, one should give with a serene mind;

endowed with high resolve, one should give with high resolve to a Bodhisattva who is endowed with high resolve and has generated the thought of awakening, having generated that thought of awakening themselves;
and one should accomplish this through tirelessness, even down to the writing or the reciting of it.
Being diligent, he will cause others to grasp this,
will demonstrate it, will inspire them to take it up, will encourage them, and will gladden them.
He will lead him by means of speech, discipline him, and encourage him; he will fully reveal its meaning to him,
and in this way, he will purify his mind.
He will act without doubt and will speak to him thus: "Come, son of good family, train in this very path of the bodhisattvas!
For by training, practicing, and striving in this, you will very quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

And having attained full awakening, you will lead the immeasurable realm of sentient beings to the unsurpassed destruction of the substrata—that is, to the realization of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
And you should speak these words: "O son of good family, may you become a recipient of these very same dharmas, namely those associated with the perfection of wisdom.
This alone would produce much more merit than that.
For what reason?
Because from this, Kauśika, the state of a pratyekabuddha is manifested.
And thus he will increase his enthusiasm: "In whatever way, O son of good family, you shall train in the perfection of wisdom..."
In that very way, you will gradually become a recipient of the qualities of a Buddha and will draw near to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
For by training, practicing, and striving in this discipline, you will swiftly realize the fruit of stream-entry.
You will manifest the fruit of once-returning,
you will manifest the fruit of non-returning,
and you will manifest arhatship.
"He will manifest the state of a Pratyekabuddha; he will manifest the state of a Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone the accumulation of merit from establishing all the beings of Jambudvīpa in the state of a Pratyekabuddha.

Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings as numerous as there are in a world-system of four great continents in the state of a pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone the accumulation of merit from establishing all the beings in a world-system of four great continents in the state of a pratyekabuddha.

Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings, however many there may be, in a thousandfold world-system of the crest (cūlikā) in the state of a pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone the accumulation of merit from establishing all the beings in a thousandfold world-system of the crest in the state of a pratyekabuddha.

Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings as numerous as there are in the second-order intermediate thousandfold world-system in the state of a pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone the accumulation of merit from establishing all the beings in the second-order intermediate thousandfold world-system in the state of a pratyekabuddha.

Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings whatsoever in this triple-thousand great-thousand world-system in the state of a pratyekabuddha.
But let alone, Kauśika, the accumulation of merit from establishing all beings in the triple-thousand great-thousand world-system in the state of a pratyekabuddha.

Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all those beings as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in world-systems as great as the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-systems in the state of a pratyekabuddha.
What do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata."

The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would indeed produce much more merit who, having even made this Perfection of Wisdom into a book, places their faith in it and has faith in it, and conceives confidence in it and has confidence in it."
Resolving with resolve,
one should give with a serene mind to one whose mind is serene,
and being endowed with high resolve, one should give with high resolve to a bodhisattva who has generated the thought of awakening and to whom the thought of awakening has been generated.
To the extent that he will accomplish even the mere writing or reciting without weariness, being intent upon it, he will cause others to grasp it,
will demonstrate it, will encourage its adoption, will inspire them, and will gladden them.
He will lead him by means of speech, discipline him, and encourage him; he will clearly reveal its meaning to him,
and in this way, he will purify his mind.

He will act without doubt and will say this to him: "Come, son of good family, train in this very path of the bodhisattvas; for by training, practicing, and striving in this, you will very quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

And having attained full awakening, you will lead the immeasurable realm of sentient beings to the unsurpassed destruction of the substrata—that is, to the realization of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
And you should speak these words: "O son of good family, may you become a recipient of these very same dharmas, namely those associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
This alone would produce far more merit than that.
For what reason?
Because from this, Kauśika, the state of a pratyekabuddha is manifested.
And in this way you shall increase his enthusiasm: "In whatever measure, noble son, you train in the perfection of wisdom..."
In that very way, you will gradually become a recipient of the Buddha-dharmas and will draw near to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
For by training, practicing, and striving in this instruction, you will manifest the fruit of stream-entry.
You will manifest the fruit of once-returning,
you will manifest the fruit of non-returning,
and you will manifest arhatship.
"You shall manifest the state of perfect enlightenment."

Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose there were as many beings in Jambudvīpa as there exist, and some son of good family or daughter of good family were to cause them all to generate the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; and then, Kauśika, another son of good family or daughter of good family, having caused all of them to generate the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, were to write down this Perfection of Wisdom for them—
Or, Kauśika, if some son of good family or daughter of good family were to write down this perfection of wisdom and present it to an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva,
[thinking] that he will train in this very perfection of wisdom;
He will enter into yoga;
by cultivating the perfection of wisdom right here, having attained growth, increase, and vastness, he will fulfill the qualities of a Buddha.
This person would therefore generate much more merit than that aforementioned son of good family or daughter of good family.
For what reason?
Because it is certain that he, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, will bring an end to the suffering of sentient beings.
Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone the accumulation of merit by all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa who have generated the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Kauśika, suppose there were as many beings as there are in a world-system of four great continents,

and some son of good family or daughter of good family were to generate the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment for all of them. Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone the accumulation of merit from generating the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment for all the beings in a world-system of four great continents;
Kauśika, suppose there were as many beings as there are in a thousand-fold world system consisting of minor chiliocosms,

and some son of good family or daughter of good family were to generate the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment for all of them. Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone the accumulation of merit from generating the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment for all the beings in a thousand-fold world system consisting of minor chiliocosms.
Kauśika, suppose there were as many beings as there are in the second-order intermediate thousandfold world-system,

and some son of good family or daughter of good family were to cause all of them to generate the mind directed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone the accumulation of merit from causing all those beings in the second-order intermediate thousandfold world-system to generate the mind directed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Kauśika, suppose there were as many beings as there are in the triple-thousand great-thousand world system; and suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to cause all of them to resolve their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone the accumulation of merit by all the beings in a triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system who have resolved their minds upon unexcelled perfect enlightenment;

even if, Kauśika, some son of good family or daughter of good family were to resolve their minds upon unexcelled perfect enlightenment for as many beings as there are in as many triple-thousand great thousandfold world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges— [the latter would be greater].

Furthermore, Kauśika, if some other son of good family or daughter of good family, having generated the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment for all of them, were to write down this perfection of wisdom and give it to them; or, Kauśika,
if a son of good family or daughter of good family were to write down this perfection of wisdom and give it to an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva— [the latter would produce greater merit].
One should offer it;
herein, in this very Perfection of Wisdom, he will train and apply himself to yoga.
In this way, this perfection of wisdom will, to a greater degree, reach cultivation, increase, growth, expansion, and fulfillment.
Kausika, that person would generate much more merit than that aforementioned son of good family or daughter of good family.
Why is that?
"It is certain that he, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, will bring an end to the suffering of sentient beings."
Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose there were as many beings in Jambudvīpa as there actually are,
and they were all irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

If some son of good family or daughter of good family were to write down this Perfection of Wisdom in a book and give it, and present it, to those who have set out for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;

And if some son of good family or daughter of good family were to write down this Perfection of Wisdom in a book and give it to them, and present it to them, and instruct them in its meaning and its phrasing—
what do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One;
much, Sugata. Even the number of that mass of merit, Blessed One, is not easy to calculate."
Blessed One, it is not easy to calculate, nor to compare, nor to illustrate by analogy, nor to approximate, nor even to find a basis for comparison for that mass of merit.
The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would indeed produce much more merit who,

having written out this perfection of wisdom in a book, should give it to those irreversible bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas who desire to more swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
He should present it to them and teach it with both its meaning and its phrasing;

furthermore, he should instruct and exhort them here in this perfection of wisdom. Moreover, Kauśika, let alone presenting this perfection of wisdom to all the beings in Jambudvīpa who are irreversible.
Kauśika, suppose all the beings as numerous as there are in a world-system of four great continents were themselves non-retrogressive regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening;
even to them, some son of good family or daughter of good family might write down this perfection of wisdom in a book and give it, or offer it.
One should teach it with both its meaning and its phrasing.

Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone the accumulation of merit from presenting this perfection of wisdom to all the beings who are irreversible [from enlightenment] in a world-system of four great continents;
as for all the beings, Kauśika, in a thousandfold world-system of the small chiliocosm—
They all would become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
And among them, if some son of good family or daughter of good family were to write down this perfection of wisdom in a book, give it, and present it to them;
One should teach it with both its substance and its phrasing.
Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone the accumulation of merit from presenting this perfection of wisdom to all the beings who are irreversible in a thousandfold world-system of the minor chiliocosm;
as for all the beings, Kauśika, who exist in a second-order intermediate world-system of two thousand worlds—
They all would become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

And among them, some son of good family or daughter of good family might write down this perfection of wisdom in a book, give it, and present it, and explain it together with its meaning and its phrasing.

Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone the accumulation of merit from presenting this perfection of wisdom to all the beings who are irreversible [from awakening] in a second-order intermediate world system;

as for all the beings, Kauśika, who exist in a third-order great trichiliocosm world system, were they all to become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening— [the merit from that would not equal the former].

Even compared to those, some son of good family or daughter of good family might write down this Perfection of Wisdom in a book, give it, and present it; they would teach it with its meaning and its phrasing.

Furthermore, Kauśika, let alone the accumulation of merit from presenting this Perfection of Wisdom to all the beings in a triple-thousand great thousandfold world system who are irreversible [from enlightenment].

Kauśika, suppose there were as many beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the Ganges— each being a trichiliocosm— and all of them were irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; yet,
some son of good family or daughter of good family were to write down this perfection of wisdom in a book and give it to them, or present it to them.
One should teach it with both its meaning and its phrasing.
What do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: Much, Blessed One.
"Much, Sugata! Lord, it is not easy to calculate that mass of merit;
nor, Lord, is it easy to count it, nor to illustrate it by analogy, nor to provide a comparison, nor even to find a point of reference for that mass of merit."
The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would indeed produce much more merit who,

having written this Perfection of Wisdom in a book, should give it and present it to those irreversible Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who desire to more swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
He should teach it with its meaning and its phrasing, and here he should instruct and admonish them in this perfection of wisdom.
Then, Kauśika, suppose another bodhisattva mahāsattva were to arise.
He would say: "I shall more swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment than these.

Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family who instructs and advises such a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva of swifter higher knowledge in the perfection of wisdom would generate much greater merit than that previous son of good family or daughter of good family.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, in whatever measure a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws near to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, in that same measure he should be exhorted and instructed in the perfection of wisdom; being thus exhorted and instructed in the perfection of wisdom, he draws near to suchness."

As he draws near to suchness, whatever robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick he enjoys from those [who provide them], he makes those services rendered by them bear great fruit and great benefit;
therefore, he generates much greater merit.
For what reason?
Because it is thus, Blessed One, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws near to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Excellent, excellent, Kauśika! It is well that you give encouragement to those persons who belong to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, and that you favor and protect them.
And it is thus, Kauśika, that you should act: an noble disciple who desires to bring benefit to all sentient beings [should do so]."
He increases the enthusiasm of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; he favors them and attends to them, thinking, "This is what must be done.
For what reason?
For it is from this that the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is born.
Indeed, if bodhisattva mahāsattvas were not to generate this thought of enlightenment,
these bodhisattva mahāsattvas would not train for the sake of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
If they did not train in the six perfections,
then by not training, they would not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. However,
because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas do indeed train in these six perfections, which constitute the Bodhisattva training, [they do so attain it].
Therefore, they generate this bodhicitta;
therefore, they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
In the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom, this is the fifth chapter, titled "The Enumeration of Merit."
(Vaidya 69) Chapter Six: The Dedication of Rejoicing.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the venerable Elder Subhūti:
Furthermore, noble Subhūti, as for the basis of meritorious action consisting of the rejoicing and dedication of a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
and as for the basis of meritorious action consisting of giving and the basis of meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline belonging to all sentient beings—
The basis of meritorious action consisting of cultivation—
this very basis of meritorious action of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, accompanied by rejoicing and dedication, is declared to be the foremost and is declared to be the most excellent.
It is called the eldest; it is called the best; it is called the most excellent.
It is described as sublime; it is described as supreme;
it is described as unsurpassed.
It is declared to be unsurpassed; it is declared to be unequaled;
it is declared to be equal to the unequaled.

When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti, long-lived, spoke thus to the elder Maitreya, the bodhisattva mahāsattva: "Furthermore, Maitreya, as for this bodhisattva mahāsattva who, by means of a cognition that reaches everywhere, in all ways, and in every respect throughout the worlds of the ten directions—
in immeasurable and immeasurable, incalculable and incalculable, limitless and limitless, inconceivable and inconceivable, and infinite and boundless [worlds]..."
