In the past, throughout the triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems, in each direction and within each individual triple-thousand great thousandfold world system, there were Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas— those who had cut off the path— who, being immeasurable, incalculable, innumerable, limitless, inconceivable, infinite, and boundless, had entered final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder.

[They were] those for whom the path was cut off, whose guide to the existence of conceptual proliferation was severed, who had exhausted their tears, who had crushed the thorns, who had laid down their burden, who had attained their own goal, whose fetters of existence were completely worn away, whose minds were well-liberated through right knowledge,
and who had reached the supreme perfection of mastery over all states of mind— from the first production of the thought [of awakening] until [the attainment of] unsurpassed [enlightenment].
From the time they fully awakened to perfect enlightenment until they passed away into the realm of nirvana without remainder, and for as long as their true Dharma has not disappeared—

in this interval, whatever aggregate of morality, aggregate of concentration, aggregate of wisdom, aggregate of liberation, and aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation those Blessed Buddhas possessed;
And those roots of merit associated with the six perfections,
those roots of merit associated with the perfection of the qualities of a Buddha, and those roots of merit associated with the perfections of the powers and the grounds of self-confidence;

Likewise, there are roots of merit associated with the perfection of supernormal knowledges, associated with the perfection of thorough understanding, associated with the perfection of aspiration, and associated with the attainment of the knowledge of omniscience;
as well as that which is the desire for the welfare [of others] and that which is great loving-kindness.
And that which is great compassion,
and those immeasurable and incalculable qualities of a Buddha, and that which is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—
And that which is the bliss of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening;
and that which is the perfection of sovereignty over all phenomena;
and that which is the immeasurable, unconquerable, and all-conquering supreme accomplishment of supernatural power—
And that which is the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge of things as they truly are— unobstructed, unattached, unimpeded, unequaled, incomparable, peerless, and immeasurable;
that which is the power of the Buddha’s knowledge,
the foremost among powers, and the vision of the Buddha’s knowledge.
And that which is the perfection of the ten powers;
and that realization which is fulfilled by the supreme happiness of the four grounds of self-confidence;
and that realization of the Dharma through the actualization of the ultimate truth of all phenomena.
And that which is the turning of the wheel of Dharma, the raising of the torch of Dharma, and the beating of the drum of Dharma;
the blowing of the conch of Dharma, the sounding of the conch of Dharma,
and the striking with the sword of Dharma;
The raining down of the rain of Dharma,
the performance of the sacrifice of Dharma,
and the satisfying of all sentient beings through the gift of Dharma.
The offering of the gift of Dharma; and those who therein, through the teachings of the Dharma— whether in the teachings of the Buddhas, the teachings of the Pratyekabuddhas,
or the teachings of the Śrāvakas— have been disciplined, trained, resolved, and established, being destined for supreme enlightenment.
And whatever roots of merit belong to all of them,

and whatever roots of merit belong to those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have been prophesied by those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, for unexcelled perfect enlightenment, and which are associated with the six perfections; [all these he dedicates].

And whatever roots of merit belong to all those persons who have been prophesied for the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, as well as the basis of meritorious action consisting of giving belonging to those persons who belong to the vehicle of the śrāvakas—
The basis of meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline,
the basis of meritorious action consisting of cultivation,
and those untainted roots of goodness belonging to those in training.
And those roots of merit that are beyond training and free from outflows,
as well as the roots of merit in the Dharma planted there by ordinary persons,
and those of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and their fourfold assembly— namely, the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—
And that basis of meritorious action consisting of giving,
the basis of meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline,
and the basis of meritorious action consisting of cultivation.

And by those gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, or humans and non-humans who, while those Blessed Buddhas were teaching the Dharma there, planted roots of merit; and by those beings,
even those belonging to the animal realm, who also planted roots of merit while those Blessed Buddhas were entering final nirvāṇa.

And by those who have planted roots of merit even toward those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who have passed into parinirvāṇa there—having relied upon the Buddha, the Blessed One; having relied upon the Dharma; having relied upon the Saṅgha; and having relied upon those individuals worthy of veneration—as well as all the roots of merit belonging to them all: having gathered together, condensed, and weighed all those roots of merit without exception, without remainder, and without omission, one should rejoice with the supreme rejoicing.
With the most excellent, the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the sublime, the highest, the unsurpassed, the peerless, the incomparable, and the matchless rejoicing, one should rejoice.

Having thus rejoiced, one should utter these words: "I dedicate this basis of meritorious action associated with rejoicing toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment—may it become a bringer of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
In that regard, by means of which things, which objects, and by means of which aspects a person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle might rejoice, and with which he might produce that thought—
would those things, or those objects, or those aspects be apprehended in the same way as he forms them into signs?
When this had been said, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya said this to the Venerable Subhūti the Elder:
"Venerable Subhūti, those things, those objective supports, or those aspects are not perceived in the way that one forms a mental sign of them."

When this had been said, the Venerable Subhūti, the Elder, addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya as follows: "If he were to take as an object that non-existent thing, that non-existent focal point, and were to conceptualize it as a sign, how could there not be for him a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view?
For what reason? Because it is thus."

For even passion arises by conceptualizing and imagining a non-existent object as permanent in what is impermanent, as pleasure in what is suffering, as self in what is not-self, and as beautiful in what is foul;
it is a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view.
Nevertheless, just as the object is, just as the focal point is, and just as the mental aspect is, so is awakening, so is the mind.
In this way, all phenomena and all realms are so. And if awakening is as the thing, as the objective support, and as the mental aspect,
then by means of which things, which objective supports, and which mental aspects does one dedicate which mind toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening?
"What is the basis of meritorious action associated with rejoicing, and where does one dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya said this to the Venerable Subhūti the Elder:
"Noble Subhūti, this should not be spoken before, nor should it be taught to, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has newly set out in the vehicle."
For what reason?
For even that which may be his mere measure of faith, mere measure of affection, mere measure of serene confidence, and mere measure of reverence—
all that would vanish from him.
Noble Subhūti, this should be spoken and taught in the presence of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva,
or of any being who is a mahāsattva supported by a spiritual friend;
such a one will not be cowed, will not shrink back, will not despair, and will not fall into despondency.
He will not turn his mind away,
he will not break his back [in retreat],
and he will not be afraid, nor terrified, nor fall into a state of terror.
And in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should dedicate the basis of meritorious action accompanied by rejoicing toward omniscience.

Then the Venerable Subhūti the Elder said this to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya: "Maitreya, that mind by which one rejoices and that which one dedicates—this mind has perished, ceased, vanished, and changed.
Which, then, is that mind by which one dedicates for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Or what is that mental basis of meritorious action accompanied by rejoicing which one dedicates toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?
Or how is it possible for a mind to dedicate a mind, given that there is no meeting of two minds, and the intrinsic nature of that mind cannot be dedicated?

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the venerable Subhūti the Elder: "Noble Subhūti, let it not be that bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have newly set out in the vehicle, upon hearing this teaching, will be terrified, tremble, or fall into a state of terror."
"And how, noble Subhūti, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva dedicate that basis of meritorious action associated with rejoicing toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?
And how, by one who grasps the basis of meritorious action associated with rejoicing and dedicates the mind associated with rejoicing, is that mind associated with rejoicing well-grasped?
Then the venerable elder Subhūti, addressing the bodhisattva mahāsattva Maitreya—beginning with Maitreya—said:

Having empowered the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, he addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya: "In this regard, Maitreya, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva [should reflect upon] those past Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who have cut off the path [of rebirth],
cut off the tracks [of craving], severed the conduit to the proliferation of existence, whose tears are dried up, who have crushed the thorns, laid down their burdens, and attained their own goal."
Of those whose fetters of existence were completely exhausted, whose minds were well-liberated through right knowledge, and who had attained the supreme perfection of mastery over all mental states—

of the immeasurable and incalculable Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in each of the ten directions and in every single great trichiliocosm world-system throughout the immeasurable and incalculable great trichiliocosm world-systems.
From the time those Buddhas first generated the thought of awakening, until they fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,

and until they passed away into the realm of nirvana without remainder, and as long as their true dharma has not vanished— in this interval, whatever roots of merit belonging to those Blessed Buddhas were associated with the perfections, [all that should be dedicated].
Whatever accumulation of merit and accumulation of roots of goodness those Buddhas, those Blessed Ones, have;

whatever aggregate of ethical discipline, aggregate of concentration, aggregate of wisdom, aggregate of liberation, and aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation those Buddhas, those Blessed Ones, possess; and whatever benevolence they have—
That which is great loving-kindness,
that which is great compassion, and those immeasurable and incalculable qualities of a Buddha—
And whatever Dharma has been taught by those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones;
and whoever have trained in that Dharma, have gained conviction in it, and are established in it;
and whatever roots of merit belong to them—

And those roots of merit associated with the six perfections belonging to those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have been predicted by those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, for unsurpassed perfect enlightenment;
and those persons belonging to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas who have been predicted for pratyekabodhi;

And whatever roots of goodness they possess, as well as the roots of goodness consisting of giving, the roots of goodness consisting of ethical discipline, and the roots of goodness consisting of cultivation belonging to persons of the Śrāvaka vehicle,
and those untainted roots of goodness belonging to those in training—
And those roots of merit which are beyond training and untainted,
and those roots of merit planted by ordinary persons in that Dharma,
and by whomsoever— whether gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans— that Dharma was heard;
And having heard it, roots of merit were planted;
and by those beings, even those who had fallen into the animal realm, that Dharma was heard, and having heard it, roots of merit were planted.
And whatever roots of merit have been planted by those while those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, were entering final nirvana or had already entered final nirvana— one should,
having gathered all those roots of merit together from all of them, having rolled them into one mass, having weighed them, and having left nothing out, rejoice in them without exception.
Having rejoiced, one dedicates the basis of meritorious action associated with that rejoicing toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is thus dedicating, how is it that there is no perversion of perception, no perversion of mind, and no perversion of view?

When this was said, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Maitreya spoke thus to the venerable elder Subhūti: "Venerable Subhūti, if the bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of the very same mind with which he dedicates..."
He does not form the perception of "mind" regarding that mind.
In this way, the basis of meritorious action accompanied by rejoicing is dedicated by the bodhisattva mahāsattva toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
such that he does not perceive that mind as "this is that mind."
In this way, for the bodhisattva mahāsattva, there is no perversion of perception, no perversion of mind, and no perversion of view.

However, if by means of whatever mind he performs that dedication, he perceives that mind, thinking, "This is that mind," and thus becomes one who has a perception of mind; [then he falls into error].
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva undergoes a perversion of perception, a perversion of thought, and a perversion of view. However,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that very mind with which he performs the dedication in such a manner, [he does not fall into these perversions].
He attends in this way;
as that mind is being attended to, he perceives it as "exhausted, exhausted," and he perceives it as "ceased, departed, and transformed."
And that which has been exhausted cannot be dedicated;
as for the mind by which one dedicates, its true nature (dharmatā) is likewise the same.
The very same dharmic nature belongs to those dharmas by which one dedicates,
as well as to those dharmas into which one dedicates.
The true nature of those phenomena is also that very same dharmatā;
if one dedicates in this way,
one dedicates correctly.
He does not dedicate falsely;
and in this manner, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should perform dedication.

Furthermore, noble Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should train] regarding the future Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— those whose path has been cut off, whose tracks have been cut off, whose proliferation of the pathways to existence has been severed— who are immeasurable and incalculable, from the moment they first generated the thought of awakening until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, just as [he has trained] regarding the past [Buddhas].

And for as long as they shall pass into final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder, and for as long as the true dharma does not disappear— in this interval, whatever roots of merit associated with the perfections belong to those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, [may they all be dedicated to the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment].

And whatever aggregate of ethical discipline, aggregate of concentration, aggregate of wisdom, aggregate of liberation, and aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation those Blessed Buddhas possess,
as well as their desire for the welfare [of others] and their great loving-kindness—
And that which is great compassion,
and those immeasurable and incalculable qualities of a Buddha, and those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who will teach the Dharma—

And those who will train in that Dharma, who will have faith in it, and who will be established in it— the roots of merit belonging to them, and the roots of merit belonging to those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas whom the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, will prophesy for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and their roots of merit associated with the six perfections— [all these he transforms into the cause of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment].

And those roots of merit belonging to those persons who belong to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas whom those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, will prophesy for pratyekabodhi; and those roots of merit belonging to persons of the śrāvaka vehicle, whether consisting of giving, consisting of ethical discipline, or consisting of cultivation.
And those untainted roots of goodness belonging to those in training,
and those untainted roots of goodness belonging to those beyond training,
and whatever roots of goodness ordinary persons shall plant in that Dharma—
And those gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans who shall plant roots of merit,
and even those beings belonging to the animal realm who shall hear that Dharma and, having heard it, plant roots of merit—

And whatever sentient beings shall plant roots of merit while those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are passing into parinirvāṇa or have already passed into parinirvāṇa— one should, having gathered together, collected, weighed, and taken all those roots of merit of them all without exception, rejoice in them without remainder.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having rejoiced, dedicates the basis of meritorious action associated with that rejoicing toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,

how is it that for him there is no perversion of perception, no perversion of mind, and no perversion of view? If the bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of the very same mind with which he dedicates, [perceives it as such]...
He does not form the perception of "mind" regarding that mind;
in this way, the basis of meritorious action accompanied by rejoicing is dedicated by the bodhisattva mahāsattva toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Just as he does not perceive that mind as "this is the mind," [so it is dedicated].
In this way, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, there is no perversion of perception, no perversion of mind, and no perversion of view.
However, if with whatever mind one performs that dedication, one perceives that very mind—thinking, "This is that mind"—then he becomes one who has a perception of mind.
In this way, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, there occurs a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view.
If, however, a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that very mind with which he dedicates in this way, and attends to it in this way,
then while that mind is being attended to, he perceives it as "exhausted, exhausted," and he perceives it as "ceased, departed, and transformed."
And that which has been exhausted cannot be transformed;
as for the mind by which one transforms, its true nature (dharmatā) is also exactly the same.
The same dharmic nature belongs to those dharmas by which one dedicates,
as well as to those dharmas in which one dedicates.
The true nature of those phenomena is also that very same dharmatā;
if one dedicates in this way,
one dedicates correctly.
He does not dedicate falsely;
and in this manner should a bodhisattva mahāsattva perform dedication.

Furthermore, noble Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should train] with regard to the present Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— who have cut off the path, cut off the tracks, and severed the conduit to the proliferation of existence; who, being immeasurable and incalculable, are currently staying, remaining, and maintaining themselves in immeasurable and incalculable trichiliocosm great thousandfold world systems— beginning from their first production of the thought of awakening.
And as long as they do not fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
and as long as they do not pass into final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder; and as long as the true Dharma does not disappear—
In the meantime, whatever roots of merit associated with the perfections belonged to those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones;

and whatever aggregate of ethical discipline, aggregate of concentration, aggregate of wisdom, aggregate of liberation, and aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation belonged to those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; and whatever benevolence [they possessed];
And that which is great loving-kindness, and that which is great compassion,
and those immeasurable and incalculable qualities of a Buddha—
And whatever Dharma those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach; and whoever trains in that Dharma, has faith in it, and is established in it;
and whatever roots of merit belong to them—
And those roots of merit associated with the six perfections belonging to those bodhisattva mahāsattvas whom those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, prophesy for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
and those persons belonging to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas whom those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, prophesy for pratyekabodhi.

And whatever roots of merit they possess, as well as the roots of merit consisting of giving, the roots of merit consisting of ethical discipline, and the roots of merit consisting of cultivation belonging to persons of the Śrāvaka vehicle,
and whatever untainted roots of merit belong to those in training—
And those roots of merit which are beyond training and untainted,
and those roots of merit which ordinary persons plant in that Dharma,
and those gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans who hear that Dharma—
And having heard it, they plant roots of merit;
and even those beings who have gone into the animal realm, when they hear that Dharma, having heard it, plant roots of merit.

And whatever roots of virtue they plant while those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are passing into parinirvāṇa or have already passed into parinirvāṇa— all those roots of virtue of all of them, having gathered them together from one side, having rolled them into a single mass, having weighed them, and leaving nothing out, they should be rejoiced in without remainder.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having rejoiced, dedicates the basis of meritorious action associated with that rejoicing toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, how is it that for him there is no perversion of perception, no perversion of mind, and no perversion of view? If the bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of whatever mind he dedicates [the merit],...
He does not form the perception of "mind" regarding that mind.
In this way, the basis of meritorious action accompanied by rejoicing is dedicated by the bodhisattva mahāsattva toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment— just as that mind does not perceive itself,
thinking, "This is that mind."

In this way, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, there is no perversion of perception, no perversion of mind, and no perversion of view. However, if with whatever mind he performs that dedication, he perceives that mind, thinking, "This is that mind," and thus becomes one who has the perception of a mind—
then for that bodhisattva mahāsattva, there is a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva dedicates that very mind which he is dedicating,

he perceives that mind in this way and attends to it in this way: as that mind is being attended to, he perceives it as "exhausted, exhausted," and he perceives it as "ceased, departed, and transformed."
That which has been exhausted cannot be transformed;
and as for the mind by which one transforms,
that mind also possesses that very same nature.
Even those phenomena by which one dedicates [merit],
their true nature is that very same dharmatā.
Even those phenomena into which [the merit] is dedicated possess that very same nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
If one dedicates in this manner, [it is a true dedication].
One dedicates correctly and does not dedicate falsely;
in this manner, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should perform dedication.

Furthermore, noble Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should train] regarding the past, future, and present Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— who have cut off the path, who have cut off the tracks, who have cut off the conduit to the proliferation of existence, who are immeasurable and incalculable—
from the first production of the thought of awakening until they have fully awakened, will fully awaken, or will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
They attain full awakening;

and as long as they have entered final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder, or will enter it, or are entering it; and as long as the true Dharma has not disappeared, will not disappear, or is not disappearing.
In the meantime, whatever roots of merit those Blessed Buddhas possessed in connection with the six perfections,

and whatever aggregate of ethical discipline, aggregate of concentration, aggregate of wisdom, aggregate of liberation, and aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation those Blessed Buddhas possessed, as well as their benevolence—
That which is great loving-kindness,
that which is great compassion, and those immeasurable and incalculable qualities of a Buddha—
And by those Blessed Buddhas through whom the Dharma has been taught, will be taught, and is being taught;
and those who have trained, will train, and are training in that Dharma;
and those who have had faith, will have faith, and are having faith in it.
Those who have stood, will stand, and are currently standing—
whatever roots of merit belong to all of them,
and those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have been, will be, or are being prophesied by those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
And whatever roots of virtue belong to all of them,

and whatever roots of virtue belong to those persons belonging to the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas who have been predicted, will be predicted, or are being predicted for Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment— all these roots of virtue of all of them;
And whatever roots of merit consisting of giving, roots of merit consisting of ethical discipline, and roots of merit consisting of cultivation belonging to persons of the Śrāvaka vehicle;
and whatever untainted roots of merit belonging to those in training (śaikṣa), and whatever untainted roots of merit belonging to those beyond training (aśaikṣa);
And by those ordinary persons who have planted, will plant, or are planting roots of merit in that Dharma;
and by those gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, or humans and non-humans, by whom that Dharma has been heard, will be heard, or is being heard,
and having heard it, they have planted, will plant, or are planting roots of merit.
And by those beings, even those belonging to the animal realm, who have heard, will hear, or are hearing that Dharma,

and having heard it, have planted, will plant, or are planting roots of merit; and by those beings who, when those Blessed Buddhas had entered parinirvāṇa, were entering parinirvāṇa, or were entering parinirvāṇa, have planted, will plant, or are planting roots of merit.
And having gathered together, collected, weighed, and taken all those roots of merit of all of them without exception, one should rejoice with the foremost rejoicing;

one should rejoice with the most excellent, the eldest, the best, the preeminent, the sublime, the supreme, the unsurpassed, the incomparable, the peerless, the unequaled, and the matchless rejoicing.

Having thus rejoiced, he should utter the words: "I dedicate this basis of meritorious action associated with rejoicing toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; may it become a bringer of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
How is it that for that bodhisattva mahāsattva there is no perversion of perception, no perversion of mind, and no perversion of view?
If, while dedicating, one attends to the fact that "those dharmas have been exhausted, ceased, departed, and transformed,
and that dharma into which they are dedicated is inexhaustible," then it is thus dedicated to unexcelled,
perfect enlightenment.
If, however, he investigates in this way: "A dharma does not dedicate a dharma," even so it becomes dedicated to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
In this way, O Venerable Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who dedicates in such a manner, there is no perversion of perception, no perversion of mind, and no perversion of view.
Why is that?
Because he does not become attached to that dedication.
Furthermore, if he perceives thus: "mind does not know mind," [then he is dedicating correctly].
"Even the thought that 'one dharma does not know another dharma' is dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
this is the unexcelled dedication of the bodhisattva mahāsattva."
If, however, a bodhisattva perceives that formation of merit, he does not dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is that?
For he becomes attached to that dedication.
However, if it occurs to him: "That formation of merit is also secluded and peaceful;
even that basis of meritorious action associated with rejoicing is likewise secluded and peaceful," he then dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

If he does not even perceive that "all conditioned phenomena are peaceful and secluded," then this is the perfection of wisdom of that bodhisattva mahāsattva; for that root of merit belonging to those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones who have passed into parinirvāṇa, is of exactly the same nature as that dedication.
It is just as that dedication is, so too is that root of merit.
That by which it is dedicated is also of that same kind, that same characteristic, that same class, and that same intrinsic nature.
If one perceives it in this way,
one does not dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
For what reason?
Because the Buddha-Bhagavāns do not authorize dedication by means of signs (*nimitta*).
That which is past is exhausted, ceased, vanished, and transformed.
That which is future has not yet been reached;
the stability of the present is not apprehended;
and that which is not apprehended is neither a sign nor an object.
If he thus forms a mental sign,
yet does not attend to it or dedicate it toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment;

or if, due to a deficiency of mindfulness, he does not form a mental sign, does not attend to it, or does not bring it to mind— either because of that deficiency of mindfulness or because of a lack of comprehension— then [he fails].
Even so, one does not dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Yet, one attends to that sign without making it into a sign.
In this way, that root of merit is dedicated by the bodhisattva mahāsattva toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus should the bodhisattva mahāsattva train in this matter; this should be understood as the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skill in means, by which skill in means he dedicates the root of merit.
He is close to omniscience.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in skillful means here should repeatedly hear, take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and propagate this very perfection of wisdom.
It should be taught, explained, recited, studied, and questioned about.
Why is that?
For indeed, without relying upon the perfection of wisdom, it is not possible for one who has not heard [the Dharma] to enter into the practice of the dedication of the perfection of wisdom.

In this regard, whoever should say, "It is possible to dedicate that basis of meritorious action toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment without having relied upon the perfection of wisdom," he should be told,
"Do not speak thus.
Why is that?
For those personal existences have ceased;
for those conditioned phenomena have ceased; they are stilled, secluded, devoid of anything to be apprehended.

Moreover, that person, having made a sign and having conceptualized, perceives what is not as it truly is as being as it truly is; they would dedicate their roots of virtue toward non-apprehension while [still] apprehending.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not approve of such roots of virtue dedicated toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is that?
For this indeed constitutes his great non-apprehension: that he takes even the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as a sign and conceptualizes it.
One perceives nirvāṇa by way of its formal characteristics;
however, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not say that the dedication of merit performed by one who possesses the perception of an object of perception brings about great benefit.
Why is that?
For this ripening is indeed poisonous and thorny;
it is just as if there were a choice meal that was poisonous,
which, despite being desirable in its color, fragrance, taste, and texture, [would still be harmful].
Moreover, because it is poisonous, it must be avoided by the wise and not used for consumption;
yet a person of a foolish nature, one of poor wisdom, would think that very thing should be consumed.
As he consumes that food, which is pleasant in its color, fragrance, taste, texture, and flavor, yet results in a painful ripening upon digestion,
he may consequently meet with death or suffer a pain equal to death.

In the same way, noble Subhūti, some here, having grasped it wrongly, perceived it wrongly, and recited it wrongly, not knowing the meaning of what was well-spoken and failing to comprehend the meaning as it truly is,

will instruct and advise thus: "Come, son of good family, [emulate] the aggregate of morality, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present."
And as for those disciples who, among those past, future, and present Buddhas, Blessed Ones, have planted, will plant, or are planting roots of merit—

throughout this interval, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the time when their True Dharma has not vanished, will not vanish, and does not vanish— of those Buddhas, Blessed Ones...
Of the Blessed Ones who have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, up until those who have entered final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder;

and of those roots of merit planted, to be planted, and being planted by those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, for those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas who have been, will be, and are being prophesied for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

And those persons belonging to the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas who have been predicted, will be predicted, or are being predicted for Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, and whatever roots of virtue they have planted, will plant, or are planting;
and those persons belonging to the vehicle of the Śrāvakas who have been predicted, will be predicted, or are being predicted for Śrāvaka-enlightenment.
And whatever roots of goodness they have planted, will plant, or are planting,

as well as those of ordinary beings in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems— consolidating, aggregating, and weighing all those roots of goodness of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present in all world-systems, into one;

Having rejoiced without exception and having rejoiced completely, one dedicates the basis of meritorious action associated with that rejoicing toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. In this way, if that dedication is performed by way of signs (*nimitta*), it proceeds toward toxicity,
just like that very food which contains poison.
There is no dedication for one who possesses the perception of apprehension.
Why is that?
Because apprehension is poisonous.
Therefore, a person belonging to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas should not train in this way.
How, then, should they train?
How should they take hold of the roots of goodness of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present?
And how is it that what has been grasped becomes well-grasped? And how should it be dedicated?
And how is it that what has been dedicated becomes well-dedicated toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?

In this regard, that son of good family or daughter of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, not wishing to misrepresent the Tathāgata, should rejoice in all those roots of merit and dedicate them in such a way that those Tathāgatas,

Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones know and see with their Buddha-knowledge and Buddha-eye what kind of root of merit it is, what its category, what its nature, what its essence, and what its characteristics.
"In whatever manner that dharma-nature exists, in that same manner I rejoice in that root of merit;

and in whatever manner those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones authorize that root of merit being dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, in that same manner I dedicate it."
Rejoicing in this way and dedicating [the merit] in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva remains without fault;
that root of goodness becomes correctly rejoiced in and dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones,
and he does not misrepresent those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones.

And thus his transformation becomes poisonless, a great transformation, a transformation of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), complete and perfectly fulfilled, as he transforms with high resolve (*adhyāśaya*) and resolute faith (*adhimukti*).
Furthermore, a son of good family or a daughter of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle should transform in this way:
whatever morality, whatever concentration, whatever wisdom, whatever liberation, and whatever knowledge and vision of liberation there may be—just as these are unattached (*aparyāpanna*).
It is not included in the desire realm, not included in the form realm, nor included in the formless realm; it is neither past, nor future, nor present.
Why is that?
Because it is not included within the three times or the three realms.
In the same way, the transformation is also unattached;
and even the dharma into which that transformation is transformed—
that dharma, too, is unattached.

If he resolves in this way and dedicates in this manner, for that bodhisattva mahāsattva, the dedication becomes undestroyed, unconfined, poisonless, a great dedication, a dedication to the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu),
fulfilled, and perfectly fulfilled.
If he then dedicates it, settles upon it, or makes it into a sign,
he dedicates it falsely. In that regard, this dedication of a bodhisattva mahāsattva—

"By means of this dedication of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), just as the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, know and just as they authorize that root of virtue to be dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, so does it become well-dedicated;
in that manner I dedicate it"— this is the correct dedication.
And when dedicated in this way, it becomes well-dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then the Blessed One gave his approval to the venerable Subhūti: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!
You are performing the work of the Teacher, Subhūti, in that you teach the Dharma to the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas."
For what reason?
Subhūti, this dedication which is the dedication to the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is the dedication of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Within this very reality (*dharmatā*), just as the Buddha Bhagavāns know and see— that root of merit being of such a kind, of such a class, of such a nature, of such a character, and existing by such a reality—
I rejoice accordingly.
"And just as they authorize it, so do I dedicate it.
In this regard, there is the mass of merit, and there are those sentient beings in the world systems of the triple-thousand great thousandfold worlds, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā.

If some son of good family or daughter of good family were to encourage and establish all of them in the ten paths of wholesome action, the accumulation of merit resulting from that would be surpassed by this very mass of merit of the bodhisattva mahāsattva born from the transformation of the dharma-realm; it is declared to be superior to that.
He is called the most excellent, he is called the eldest, he is called the best.
It is called excellent, it is called sublime, it is called supreme.
It is called the unsurpassed; it is called the peerless; it is called the incomparable.
He is called "the Unequaled.

Furthermore, Subhūti, let alone the accumulation of merit from establishing all sentient beings in the ten paths of wholesome action within world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in trichiliocosms.
Subhūti, suppose all the beings in as many triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges were each to become attainers of the four dhyānas;
and whatever accumulation of merit there might be from them—
Therefore, this very mass of merit associated with the dedication of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is declared to be the foremost, declared to be the most excellent, and declared to be the preeminent.
It is called excellent, it is called preeminent, it is called sublime.
It is called supreme,
it is called unsurpassed, it is called peerless.
He is called the Unequaled;
he is called the One Equal to the Unequaled.

Furthermore, Subhūti, let alone the accumulation of merit arising from the accomplishment of the four dhyānas by all sentient beings in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in a triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system.
Subhūti, suppose all the beings in as many triple-thousand great thousandfold world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges were each to become attainers of the four immeasurables.

Furthermore, Subhūti, let alone the accumulation of merit by all those beings in as many triple-thousand great thousandfold world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges who have attained the four immeasurables;
Subhūti, suppose all the sentient beings in as many triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges were each to attain the four formless attainments.

Furthermore, Subhūti, let alone the accumulation of merit by all those sentient beings who have attained the four formless attainments in as many triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges.
Subhūti, suppose all the beings in as many triple-thousand great thousandfold world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges were to become possessors of the five superknowledges.

Furthermore, Subhūti, let alone the accumulation of merit from all those beings possessing the five superknowledges in as many triple-thousand great thousandfold world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges.
Subhūti, suppose there were stream-enterers in as many triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges.

Furthermore, Subhūti, let alone the accumulation of merit of all those beings who are stream-enterers in as many triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges;
Subhūti, consider those beings who exist in as many triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges.
They would all become once-returners.

Furthermore, Subhūti, let alone the accumulation of merit of all those beings who are once-returners in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in trichiliocosm great thousandfold world-systems;
as many beings as there are, Subhūti, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in trichiliocosm great thousandfold world-systems—
They would all become non-returners (*anāgāmin*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, let alone the accumulation of merit by all the beings in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges within these great trichiliocosms;
suppose, Subhūti, that as many beings as there are in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges within these great trichiliocosms were all to become arhats.
Furthermore, Subhūti, let alone the mass of merit of all the arhats in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in these three-thousandfold great thousandfold world systems;

suppose, Subhūti, that all those beings in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in these three-thousandfold great thousandfold world systems were each to become a pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, Subhūti, let alone the mass of merit of all the pratyekabuddhas among all the sentient beings in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in trichiliocosms;
suppose, Subhūti, that all those sentient beings in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in trichiliocosms were to set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Suppose there were all those beings in each and every one of other world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges,

and a single bodhisattva were to attend upon them all with robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick, providing every comfort and necessity for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges.
With all modes of dwelling in pleasant contact,
they might give that gift while perceiving it through the notion of objective apprehension (*upalambha-saṃjñin*).
In this manner, having conceived each of those sentient beings as a single individual, and each of those bodhisattvas as a single individual—

Suppose a bodhisattva were to attend upon [the Buddhas] for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, providing them with robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
with all articles of comfort,
and with every mode of pleasant dwelling, he would honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate them.
In this manner, one would give a gift to each and every one of all those bodhisattvas by this method; in this way, all of them together would give gifts.
What do you think, Subhūti, would those bodhisattvas generate much merit on that account?
Subhūti said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
It is immeasurable, Blessed One."
"It is immeasurable, Sugata.

Blessed One, it is not easy to express even a number for that mass of merit; nor, Blessed One, is it easy to calculate it, to compare it, to provide an analogy for it, to find its proportion, or to reach its limit."
If, Blessed One, that mass of merit were material, it would not fit even within trichiliocosm world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Venerable Subhūti the Elder: "So it is, Subhūti, so it is.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a person belonging to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, being embraced by skill in means and the perfection of wisdom, should dedicate that root of merit toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of this dedication of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu),"
He generates merit.

Subhūti, compared to this mass of merit born from the dedication to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), that previous accumulation of merit consisting of giving by Bodhisattvas who perceive objects through the notion of apprehension does not approach even a hundredth part.

It does not approach even a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-ten-millionth part, nor a thousand-ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-koṭī-niyuta-part; it does not admit of any calculation,
fraction, reckoning, comparison, analogy, resemblance, or even a remote comparison.
For what reason?
Because for those former bodhisattvas who possessed the notion of apprehension, even though they gave very much in gift, it was reckoned as "very much."

Then indeed, twenty thousand sons of the gods from the retinue of the Four Great Kings, with palms joined in reverence, paid homage to the Blessed One and said this to him: "O Blessed One, great is this dedication of roots of merit toward omniscience by Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, who are embraced by skillful means and the perfection of wisdom."
For indeed, he surpasses the entire accumulation of merit consisting of giving belonging to those apprehending Bodhisattvas.

Then, hundreds of thousands of sons of the gods from the Trāyastriṃśa realm scattered and showered the Blessed One with rains of divine flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, and powders, as well as with rains of divine jewels and rains of divine garments.
With divine parasols, divine banners, divine bells, and divine flags, and with rows of divine lamps on all sides, as well as with various kinds of divine offerings, they honored, revered, esteemed,
worshipped, adored, and venerated the Blessed One.

They played divine musical instruments and spoke these words: "O Blessed One, how great indeed is this dedication of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva— this dedication of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu-pariṇāma)—
for it surpasses the entire mass of merit consisting of giving produced by those Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas who perceive objects as real."
Just as it is because this great transformation is embraced by skill in means and the perfection of wisdom,
so too did sons of the gods come from other assemblies of gods to the Blessed One with the highest honor, the highest reverence, the highest respect, and the highest worship.
Having honored, revered, esteemed, worshiped, venerated, and paid homage with the highest worship and the highest respect,
they uttered this very sound and caused this proclamation to be heard.
In this way, it should be expanded by ellipsis:
the Yāmas, Tuṣitas, Nirmāṇaratis, Paranirmitavaśavartins, Brahmakāyikas, Brahmapurohitas,
Brahmapārṣadyas, Mahābrahmans, Parīttābhas, Apramāṇābhas, Ābhāsvaras, Parīttaśubhas, Apramāṇaśubhas, and Śubhakṛtsnas.

The Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Asaṃjñisattva, Abṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha gods likewise joined their palms in reverence and, bowing to the Blessed One, said this: "It is marvelous, Blessed One, how far this perfection of wisdom and skill in means of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, who are embraced by them,
surpasses even that mass of merit accumulated over a long night by those bodhisattvas who possess the notion of apprehension, however vast and extensively acquired it may be."

Then the Blessed One, having addressed those sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host, spoke to all those sons of the gods: "Moreover, O sons of the gods, let alone all the beings in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
For those who give gifts for the sake of attaining perfect enlightenment, the accumulation of merit is by this method;

and likewise, O sons of the gods, all those beings in other and other world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in each of the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-systems, they too, having made a vow for unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, have generated the mind set on awakening.

Suppose each individual bodhisattva were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, bestowing upon all sentient beings in various other world-systems— each as vast as a great trichiliocosm— as many robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, medicinal requisites for the sick, and all articles of comfort and every pleasant mode of dwelling as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges.

In this way, let all of them— even those who give gifts while perceiving [objects] as real— give gifts; and by this method, calculating each one of all those beings, and each one of all those bodhisattvas,

until all those bodhisattvas remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, providing all those beings with robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
They would serve them with all provisions for happiness and all modes of dwelling in comfort;
yet they would give that gift while perceiving it through the notion of objective apprehension (*upalambha-saṃjñin*).
And as for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is embraced by the perfection of wisdom and skill in means (*prajñāpāramitopāyakauśalya-parigṛhīta*) regarding the past, future, and present...

The aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; and the roots of goodness planted, to be planted, and being planted by those persons belonging to the vehicles of the Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas, as well as by whatever other beings there may be.
Having gathered all that together, condensed it into one mass, weighed it, and left nothing remaining— without exception— he rejoices with the foremost rejoicing;

he rejoices with the most excellent, the eldest, the best, the preeminent, the sublime, the supreme, the unsurpassed, the peerless, the ever-higher, the incomparable, the unequaled, the matchless, and the inconceivable rejoicing.

Having rejoiced, he dedicates the basis of meritorious action associated with that rejoicing toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, thinking: "May it become a bringer of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Compared to this basis of meritorious action associated with rejoicing and dedication, even the former accumulation of merit by those bodhisattvas who perceive objects does not approach even a hundredth part.

It does not approach even a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-ten-millionth part, nor a thousand-ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-billionth part; it does not admit of any calculation, nor any fraction, nor any comparison.
It does not admit of calculation, nor comparison, nor analogy, nor resemblance, nor even a fraction thereof.
Why is that?
Because all those bodhisattvas give gifts while perceiving them as objective entities.

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Regarding that which the Blessed One has thus spoken: concerning all the roots of merit—past, future, and present—of all the Buddhas, Blessed Ones, of their assemblies of Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas, and of all sentient beings, past, future, and present; having gathered all that together and condensed it into one mass..."
Having weighed it and considered it without exception, he rejoices with an exhaustive rejoicing;

he rejoices with the foremost, the best, the eldest, the excellent, the most excellent, the sublime, the supreme, the unsurpassed, the peerless, the ever-higher, the incomparable, the unequaled, the matchless, and the inconceivable rejoicing. Thus he rejoices.
"In that regard, Blessed One, to what extent does there come to be supreme rejoicing?

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "If, Subhūti, a person belonging to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas does not grasp at, does not conceive of, does not apprehend, does not conceptualize, and does not falsely discriminate past, future, or present [dharmas]..."
He does not see them, nor does he perceive them; rather, he examines these phenomena in this way: all phenomena are constructed by conceptualization;
they are unborn, unarisen, without coming, and without going.
In this, no dharma has arisen, nor will any dharma arise, nor is any dharma arising;
no dharma has ceased, nor will any dharma cease, nor is any dharma ceasing.
Having thus examined these dharmas, he rejoices in accordance with the true nature (*dharmatā*) of these dharmas.
Having rejoiced, he likewise dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
To this extent, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s rejoicing becomes supreme.

Compared to this dedication of roots of virtue, Subhūti, the mass of merit consisting of that gift of those former bodhisattvas—who possessed the notion of apprehension and held the view of apprehension—is not even a hundredth part.
It does not approach even a fraction [of it],

nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-ten-millionth part, nor a thousand-ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-billionth part.
It does not admit of being compared even by number, nor by a fraction, nor by calculation, nor by analogy, nor by likeness, nor by resemblance, nor by a subtle comparison.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a person belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who wishes to rejoice in the generosity, morality, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom of all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present, should rejoice in this way.
As is liberation, so is generosity; as is liberation, so is ethical discipline;
as is liberation, so is patience.
As is liberation, so is vigor; as is liberation, so is meditative concentration;
as is liberation, so is wisdom.
As is liberation, so is the knowledge and vision of liberation;
as is liberation, so is rejoicing;
as is liberation, so is the basis of meritorious action associated with rejoicing.
As is liberation, so is the dedication;
as is liberation, so are the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the Pratyekabuddhas;
as is liberation, so are their Śrāvakas who have attained final nirvāṇa.
Just as liberation is, so are those phenomena that have passed away and ceased;
just as liberation is, so are those phenomena that are yet to come and have not arisen;
just as liberation is, so are those phenomena that are now present and currently occurring.
As is liberation, so were those past Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and their disciples;
as is liberation, so will those future Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and their disciples be;
as is liberation, so are those present Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and their disciples.
Those who now abide, dwell, and maintain themselves in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems—
just as liberation is, so are the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present.
Such is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of these phenomena, which are unbound, unliberated, and unattached.
I rejoice in that with unsurpassed rejoicing.

Having rejoiced, I dedicate the basis of meritorious action associated with that rejoicing toward unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, by means of the yoga of non-dedication, because there is no transmigration and no destruction.
To this extent, Subhūti, there is the supreme rejoicing of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, let alone those other beings in each and every world-system of three thousand great thousand worlds, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; let alone those others in each and every world-system of three thousand great thousand worlds, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges...

Suppose that in all world-systems, every single sentient being, having generated the mind set on enlightenment, were each to become a bodhisattva and remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, bestowing gifts upon each and every other bodhisattva while perceiving them as real objects— serving them with robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, medicinal requisites for the sick, and all articles of comfort, providing them with all pleasant conditions and dwelling in all forms of physical ease.
In this manner, even if all those beings were to attend upon all [others] and give gifts while perceiving them as objective entities;

and, Subhūti, if all the beings in as many triple-thousand great thousandfold world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges were to set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

Having set out for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, suppose they were to observe the precepts for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, maintaining good conduct of body, speech, and mind while perceiving them as objective entities;
by this method, all those bodhisattvas— each individual bodhisattva [observing] for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges...

Suppose one were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, maintaining the good conduct of body, the good conduct of speech, and the good conduct of mind while perceiving them through the notion of objective apprehension (*upalambha-saṃjñin*), having undertaken and abiding in ethical discipline (*śīla*).
By this same method, suppose all those bodhisattvas were likewise to undertake and abide in ethical discipline while perceiving it through the notion of objective apprehension.

And whichever bodhisattva mahāsattva, embraced by skill in means and the perfection of wisdom, [perceives] the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present;
and the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of those pratyekabuddhas; and those of the śrāvakas—

Having gathered together, condensed, totaled, and weighed without exception all the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, as well as all the roots of goodness of all sentient beings— past, future, and present— he rejoices with the supreme rejoicing.

With the most excellent, the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the refined, the supreme, the unsurpassed, the peerless, the ever-higher, the incomparable, the unequaled, the matchless, the inconceivable rejoicing, he rejoices. Having rejoiced, he dedicates the basis of meritorious action associated with that rejoicing toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti, compared to this basis of meritorious action accompanied by rejoicing, that former accumulation of merit consisting of morality by those bodhisattvas who apprehend objects does not approach even a hundredth part,

nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-ten-millionth part, nor a thousand-ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-billionth part.
It does not bear comparison even by way of number, fraction, calculation, likeness, analogy, resemblance, or proximity.
Why is that?
Because those bodhisattvas practice having undertaken ethical discipline while perceiving it as a substantial entity.
Furthermore, Subhūti, let alone all the beings in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in trichiliocosms who have set out for unsurpassed,

perfect enlightenment; and having set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, who for eons as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā maintain good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind, and observe morality while perceiving through the notion of objective apprehension— Subhūti, as for those beings in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in trichiliocosms...
May they all be established in unsurpassed,
perfect enlightenment. Having set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, may they remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges,

and while remaining in each of those various world-systems of three thousand great thousand worlds— each numbering as many as the grains of sand in the river Ganges— may every single one of those bodhisattvas be reviled, struck, and insulted by everyone.
Suppose all those [beings], perceiving things as objective entities, were to dwell having undertaken patience;
and while all those bodhisattvas were thus dwelling having undertaken patience,
by this same method each single bodhisattva were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā.

Suppose that for eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, in various other world-systems each as vast as a great trichiliocosm and as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, they were being reviled, struck, and abused by everyone, yet they maintained patience while perceiving a real object.
Suppose all of them likewise, being reviled, struck, and abused by everyone, maintained patience while perceiving a real object.

And whichever bodhisattva mahāsattva, embraced by this perfection of wisdom and by skill in means, [perceives] the aggregate of morality, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present; and those aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of those pratyekabuddhas— of them...

And having gathered together, condensed, and weighed all the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to the disciples, as well as all the roots of merit of all sentient beings— past, future, and present— without exception, he rejoices with the supreme rejoicing.

With the most excellent, the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the sublime, the highest, the unsurpassed, the peerless, the ever-increasing, the incomparable, the unequaled, the matchless, the inconceivable rejoicing, he rejoices. Having rejoiced, he dedicates the basis of meritorious action associated with that rejoicing toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti, compared to this basis of meritorious action accompanied by rejoicing, that former accumulation of merit associated with the patience of those bodhisattvas who perceived [phenomena] does not approach even a hundredth part; it does not approach a thousandth part,

nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-ten-millionth part, nor a thousand-ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-billionth part.

It does not approach even a fraction, nor a number, nor a part, nor a calculation, nor a comparison, nor a likeness, nor a resemblance, nor even a remote comparison; it does not bear comparison at all.
Why is that?
For those bodhisattvas abide having undertaken patience while perceiving through the notion of objective apprehension.

Furthermore, Subhūti, let alone all the sentient beings in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in trichiliocosms equal to the sands of the river Ganges who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment— having set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, [let alone] others and yet others in other world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in trichiliocosms...

Subhūti, suppose there were beings in as many great trichiliocosm world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, and they were all being reviled, struck, and abused, yet— while still perceiving objective referents— they maintained and practiced patience for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges. [Compared to those,] those who...

Suppose all of them were to set out for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; and having set out for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, they were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges,

standing upon walking-frames for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, never becoming despondent or overcome, yet perceiving through the notion of objective apprehension (*upalambha-saṃjñin*).

They would abide having undertaken diligence; and whatever bodhisattva mahāsattva, sustained by the perfection of wisdom and skill in means, [dedicates] the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present, as well as those of...

He gathers together, condenses, totals, and weighs without exception all the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to the Pratyekabuddhas and their Śrāvakas, as well as all the formative roots of merit— past, future, and present— of all sentient beings; having thus condensed them into one mass, he rejoices in them entirely and without remainder.
With the foremost rejoicing, with the most excellent,

the best, the choicest, the preeminent, the sublime, the supreme, the unsurpassed, the peerless, the ever-higher, the incomparable, the unequaled, the matchless, and the inconceivable rejoicing, he rejoices.
Having rejoiced, one dedicates the basis of meritorious action associated with that rejoicing toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Subhūti, this basis of meritorious action associated with rejoicing does not even approach a hundredth part of the previous accumulation of merit consisting of vigor belonging to those bodhisattvas who perceive objects.

It does not approach even a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-ten-millionth part, nor a thousand-ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-koṭī-niyuta-ten-millionth part; it does not admit of any calculation,
fraction, reckoning, comparison, likeness, resemblance, or even a subtle analogy.
For what reason?
Because all those bodhisattvas, perceiving things as objective referents (*upalambha-saṃjñin*), persist in undertaking their vigor.
Furthermore, Subhūti, let alone all the sentient beings in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in trichiliocosms who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;

Having set out for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, they remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, standing on walking-frames for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, never becoming despondent and remaining unconquered by sloth and torpor; yet, perceiving objects through the notion of apprehension, they continue to exert themselves with applied vigor.
Subhūti, suppose all those beings in as many triple-thousand great thousandfold world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges were to set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;

and having so set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, they were to enter the four dhyānas with the perception of non-apprehension for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges.

And that bodhisattva mahāsattva who is embraced by this perfection of wisdom and by skill in means [takes hold of] the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present,
as well as the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of those Pratyekabuddhas.

He gathers together, collects, weighs, and— without exception— rejoices with the supreme rejoicing in all the aggregates of the disciples’ morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, as well as in all the formative roots of merit of all sentient beings belonging to the past, future, and present.

With the most excellent, the eldest, the best, the preeminent, the refined, the supreme, the unsurpassed, the peerless, the ever-increasing, the incomparable, the unequaled, the matchless, and the inconceivable rejoicing, he rejoices. Having rejoiced, he dedicates the basis of meritorious action associated with that rejoicing toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti, compared to this basis of meritorious action accompanied by rejoicing, that former accumulation of merit consisting of the four dhyānas of those bodhisattvas who apprehend objective referents does not approach even a hundredth part; it does not approach a thousandth part,

nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-ten-millionth part, nor a thousand-ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-billionth part.
It does not approach even a fraction of it; it does not admit of being reckoned as a number, a fraction, a calculation, a comparison, a likeness, a resemblance, or even a subtle analogy.
Why is that?
For those bodhisattvas enter into the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) while perceiving them as objective referents.
The sixth chapter, titled "Rejoicing and Dedication," in the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom.
(Vaidya 86) Chapter Seven: On the Hells.
Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is the accomplishment of the knowledge of the omniscient one."
“O Bhagavat, omniscience is the perfection of wisdom.
The Bhagavat said: “So it is, Śāriputra; so it is, just as you say.”
Śāriputra said: “O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is illuminating.
O Blessed One, I pay homage to the perfection of wisdom. O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is worthy of homage.”
“O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is unstained;
O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is unsullied by the entire world;
O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is the maker of light.”
O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom dispels the cataracts of all the three realms.
O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom removes the darkness of all afflictions and views.
O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is that which is to be relied upon.
“O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is the foremost of the factors conducive to enlightenment.
O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom brings security.
O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom provides light for sentient beings who are blind.”
"Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom eliminates all fears and calamities and brings light.
Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom, having acquired the five eyes, shows the path to all sentient beings. Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is the eye."
O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom dispels the darkness and gloom of delusion.
O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom does not produce any phenomena.
O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom leads those beings who have set out upon wrong paths back onto the path.
“O Blessed One, omniscience itself is the perfection of wisdom.
Because it has abandoned the connection with the latencies of all afflictive and cognitive obscurations, O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is the non-arising of all phenomena;
O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is the non-ceasing of all phenomena.”
"Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is unarisen and unceasing.
Blessed One, based on the emptiness of its own characteristic, the perfection of wisdom is the mother of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas.
Blessed One, because it bestows the jewels of all the buddha-qualities, the perfection of wisdom brings about the ten powers."
"Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is invincible.
Blessed One, because it produces the four grounds of self-confidence, the perfection of wisdom is the protector of those beings who are without a protector.
Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is the antidote to saṃsāra."
“Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom reveals the intrinsic nature of all phenomena by virtue of their non-abidingness.

Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is that which fully turns the wheel of Dharma in its three revolutions and twelve aspects. Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva stand in the perfection of wisdom?”
"How, O Blessed One, should the perfection of wisdom be brought to mind?
How, O Blessed One, should the perfection of wisdom be paid homage?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, [one should do so] as one does toward the Teacher."
In that same way, one should abide in the perfection of wisdom.
Śāriputra, the perfection of wisdom should be attended to in the very same manner as the Teacher.
Śāriputra, the perfection of wisdom should be paid homage to in the very same manner as the Teacher.
Then, this thought occurred to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Whence, alas, has this question of the noble Śāriputra arisen?
What is the cause, alas, of this question having arisen for the noble Śāriputra?
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "From whence has this question of the noble Śāriputra arisen?"
"What indeed is the cause for this question that has arisen to the noble Śāriputra?

When this was said, the venerable Śāriputra said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is embraced by the perfection of wisdom and skill in means, when dedicating the basis of meritorious action associated with rejoicing toward omniscience, [surpasses] those..."

Whatever accumulation of merit consisting of generosity, and whatever accumulation of merit consisting of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, and meditative concentration, belonging to those former bodhisattvas who were characterized by apprehension;
"It surpasses all that," he said.
"It is for this reason that this question of mine has arisen.
Furthermore, Kauśika, it is indeed the perfection of wisdom alone that precedes the five perfections for the sake of entering the path to omniscience."
Kauśika, it is just as if there were a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand people born blind who, lacking a guide, would be incapable of entering upon the path,
