It is just as if, Blessed One, a man were to emerge from a wilderness or forest tract extending for a hundred yojanas, or two hundred, or three hundred, or four hundred, or five hundred, or even a thousand yojanas; having emerged, he would see signs of an inhabited place, such as cowherds or shepherds, boundary markers, or the presence of groves and forests.
Furthermore, there are other signs by which a village, a city, or a market town might be indicated.
Upon seeing those preliminary signs, it occurs to him: "Since these preliminary signs are seen, [a village or city must be near]."
Likewise, thinking, "A village, city, or market town is near to me," he becomes one who has attained consolation; no further mental preoccupation with thieves arises for him.

In the same way, Blessed One, when this profound perfection of wisdom approaches a bodhisattva mahāsattva, it should be known by him, Blessed One: "I am close to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; before long, I shall receive the prophecy of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
Nor should he be startled, nor terrified, nor afraid of the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha.
Why is that?
Because these preliminary signs are seen in him, namely, that he obtains this profound Prajñāpāramitā for the purpose of seeing, worshipping, attending upon, and hearing it.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra: "So it is, Śāriputra; so it is.
Let this matter occur to you again, Śāriputra, for it is through the power of the Buddha that you have spoken and will speak thus."
When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, it is just as if, for example, some man here were desirous of seeing the great ocean;
he would go toward the great ocean in order to see it.
And in whatever manner he goes toward the great ocean to see it..."
In the same way, if he should see a tree or the sign of a tree, or a mountain or the sign of a mountain,
by that he should know: "The great ocean is still far from here."
If he should again see a tree or the sign of a tree, or a mountain or the sign of a mountain, by that he should know: "The great ocean is near from here.
For what reason?
For the great ocean slopes gradually downward;
within the great ocean there is no tree or sign of a tree, nor any mountain or sign of a mountain.
Even though he does not see the great ocean directly with his eyes, [he knows it exists].
And yet again, he reaches the conclusion: "I am close to the great ocean;
the great ocean is no longer far from here.

In the same way, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva hearing this profound perfection of wisdom should understand: "Although I have not [yet been] by those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones..."
I have been prophesied face-to-face,
and yet again, I am close to receiving the prophecy of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
For what reason is that?
For it is thus that one obtains this profound *prajñāpāramitā* for the purpose of seeing, worshipping, attending upon, and hearing it.
Lord, it is just as when spring has arrived and the withered leaves have fallen from various trees, and various new shoots appear.
When the shoots have appeared, the people of Jambudvīpa become joyful, seeing those preliminary signs in the forests, knowing that before long the forest flowers and fruits will come forth.
For what reason?
Because these preliminary signs are seen in the tree trunks.
In the same way, Blessed One, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva obtains this profound perfection of wisdom for the purpose of seeing, venerating, attending upon, and hearing it,
This profound *prajñāpāramitā* attends to him;
then that bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as one whose roots of merit are fully ripened, for this profound *prajñāpāramitā* has been brought to him by those very same former roots of merit.
In that regard, there are deities who have seen previous Buddhas.

They become overjoyed, filled with gladness and happiness, thinking: "These very same preliminary signs occurred for the former Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, when they were to receive the prophecy of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Ah! Before long, this Bodhisattva, this Mahāsattva, will surely receive the prophecy of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
It is just as if, Blessed One, there were a woman who was pregnant, heavy with child.
When her body feels constricted,
or when excessive physical fatigue arises,
she does not have the habit of walking.
She eats little; she has little sloth and torpor; and she speaks little.
She is weak in strength,
she is full of painful sensations,
and she dwells for the most part weeping.
Nor does she become inclined toward cohabitation.

When, through that former improper mental attention which was practiced, cultivated, developed, and frequently repeated, she experiences such bodily sensations as these, then, O Blessed One, it should be known: "Just as her preliminary signs are now appearing."
"Just as one might think, 'Ah, before long this woman will give birth,' even so,
Blessed One, when this profound perfection of wisdom comes to a bodhisattva mahāsattva for the purpose of seeing, worshipping, attending upon, and hearing it,
and when his mind delights in this perfection of wisdom as he hears it,"
And when it arises through the pursuit of the goal,
then, O Blessed One, it should be known that this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva will before long receive the prophecy of his attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra: “Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!
This too, Śāriputra, has occurred to you through the power of the Buddha.

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: “It is marvelous, Blessed One, how well these bodhisattva mahāsattvas have been taken hold of, well protected, and well entrusted by the Tathāgata, the Arhat...”
The Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, said: "For it is thus, Subhūti, that those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, have set out for the welfare of many people,
for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, and for the sake, the welfare, and the happiness of the great mass of beings, both gods and humans."
Out of compassion, being compassionate, they desire to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
and having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they desire to teach the unsurpassed Dharma.
Subhūti said: "In this regard, Blessed One, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, how does the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom reach fulfillment?
The Blessed One replied: "If, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive the increase of form, he practices the perfection of wisdom."
In this way, when one does not perceive the increase of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness,
one courses in the perfection of wisdom.
One does not perceive the diminution of form;
one courses in the perfection of wisdom.
Likewise, one does not [perceive the diminution] of feeling, perception, or mental formations.
He does not perceive the diminution of consciousness;
he courses in the perfection of wisdom and does not perceive any phenomenon.
One practices in the perfection of wisdom;
one does not even perceive a non-dharma,
for thus one practices in the perfection of wisdom.
In this way, his cultivation of the perfection of wisdom reaches fulfillment.
Subhūti said: "This which is being taught, Blessed One, is inconceivable.
The Blessed One said: "For form, Subhūti, is inconceivable;
likewise are feeling, perception, and mental formations."
For consciousness, Subhūti, is inconceivable;
when one does not even perceive that "form is inconceivable," Subhūti,
one courses in the perfection of wisdom.
In the same way, Subhūti, when one does not even perceive that feeling, mental formations, and consciousness are inconceivable,
one courses in the perfection of wisdom.
Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, who will have faith in such a profound perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, whichever bodhisattva mahāsattva has practiced the perfection of wisdom will have faith in this perfection of wisdom."
The Venerable Śāriputra said: "How, Blessed One, will a bodhisattva mahāsattva be one who has practiced? How does he obtain the designation 'one who has practiced'?
The Blessed One replied: "In this regard, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not conceptualize the powers."
He does not conceptualize the grounds of self-confidence;
he does not conceptualize the Buddha-qualities;
nor does he conceptualize omniscience.
For what reason?
Śāriputra, the powers are indeed inconceivable,
and the grounds of self-confidence are also inconceivable.
The qualities of a Buddha are inconceivable, omniscience is inconceivable,
and all phenomena are also inconceivable.
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices in this way does not course in anything at all.
He courses in the perfection of wisdom;
thus he is called "one who has coursed," and he receives the designation "one who has coursed."
Then the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is profound.
O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is a heap of jewels.
O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is a heap of purity, by virtue of the purity of space."

"It would be a marvel, Blessed One, if many obstacles were to arise for those sons of good family and daughters of good family who take up, bear in mind, recite, master, propagate, teach, explain, point out, study, and write down this Perfection of Wisdom."
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "So it is, Subhūti; so it is.
Subhūti, there are many obstacles for those sons of good family who take up, bear in mind, recite, master, propagate, teach, explain, point out, study, and write down this perfection of wisdom."
And it will be so for the daughters of good family.
For what reason?

For it is thus, Subhūti: Māra, the Evil One, will exert himself to create obstacles for those sons of good family and daughters of good family who take up, bear in mind, recite, master, propagate, teach, explain, point out, study, and write down this perfection of wisdom.
In that regard, if it were to be written quickly— whether in one month, two months, or three months—
it certainly ought to be written.
Even if it were to be written after a year or even longer than that, it still must be written.
Nevertheless, Subhūti, that son of good family or daughter of good family must indeed write down this Perfection of Wisdom.
Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, it happens thus: many obstacles arise for great jewels.

When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows: "In this regard, Blessed One, while this perfection of wisdom is being taken up, maintained, recited, mastered, set in motion, taught, explained, pointed out, studied, and written down, Māra, the Evil One, will exert himself in many ways."
And he will exert himself in acts of obstruction.

The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Subhūti, although Māra, the Evil One, may exert himself in acts of obstruction while this perfection of wisdom is being taken up, maintained, recited, mastered, and set in motion..."
While it is being taught, instructed, pointed out, recited, and written down, nevertheless,
one will not be able to create an obstacle for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who maintains his commitments flawlessly.

Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, when noble sons and noble daughters take up, bear in mind, recite, master, propagate, teach, explain, point out, study, and write down this perfection of wisdom, Māra the Evil One will exert himself to create obstacles."

In that case, Blessed One, how will sons of good family and daughters of good family at this time take up, bear in mind, recite, master, propagate, teach, explain, proclaim, study, and write down this perfection of wisdom?

And by whose power, Blessed One, will those sons of good family and daughters of good family take up, bear in mind, recite, master, propagate, teach, explain, proclaim, study, and write down this perfection of wisdom?

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, it is through the power of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, that those sons of good family and daughters of good family will take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and propagate this perfection of wisdom."
They will teach, instruct, recite, study, and write it down;
they will train for the sake of suchness and practice for the sake of suchness.
They will apply themselves to yoga for the sake of suchness.
Why is that?
Śāriputra, for this is the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who reside, remain, and maintain themselves in those immeasurable and incalculable world-systems,
will attend to and uphold this Perfection of Wisdom as it is being spoken, taken up, retained, recited, mastered, set in motion, taught, explained, and pointed out.
Whether it is being recited or written down—

those sons of good family and daughters of good family who shall take up this Perfection of Wisdom, bear it in mind, read it, master it, propagate it, teach it, explain it, proclaim it, and recite it;
They will train for the sake of suchness,
they will practice for the sake of suchness,
and they will apply themselves to yoga for the sake of suchness.
And those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, will attend to them and take them under their protection.
For it is not possible, Śāriputra, to create an obstacle for those sons of good family or daughters of good family who are attended to by the Buddhas and taken under the protection of the Buddhas.

When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, even those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who shall hear this profound perfection of wisdom, and who shall take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, set it forth, teach it, explain it, proclaim it, study it, and write it down— "
They will train for the sake of suchness,
they will practice for the sake of suchness,
and they will apply themselves to yoga for the sake of suchness.

All of them, O Blessed One, through the power of the Buddha, the empowerment of the Buddha, and the protection of the Buddha, shall hear this perfection of wisdom, and they shall take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, set it in motion, teach it, explain it, proclaim it, study it, and write it down.
And they will train for the sake of suchness,
they will practice for the sake of suchness,
and they will apply themselves to yoga for the sake of suchness.
And they will accomplish it in this way.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra: "So it is, Śāriputra; so it is.

All those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, Śāriputra, will hear, take up, bear in mind, and recite this profound perfection of wisdom through the power of the Buddha, through the sustaining grace of the Buddha, and through the protection of the Buddha."
They will master it, they will set it in motion, they will teach it, they will instruct in it, they will explain it, they will recite it, and they will write it down;
they will train for the sake of suchness,
and they will practice for the sake of suchness.
Śāriputra, those who apply themselves to yoga for the sake of suchness are known by the Tathāgata;
Śāriputra, they are sustained by the Tathāgata.

Śāriputra, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who will hear, take up, and retain this perfection of wisdom have been seen by the Tathāgata; Śāriputra, they have been beheld by the Tathāgata with his Buddha-eye.
They will read it, master it, propagate it, teach it, instruct in it, explain it, recite it, write it down,
and they will train themselves for the sake of suchness.
They will practice for the sake of suchness,
they will apply themselves to yoga for the sake of suchness,
having heard it, taken it up, retained it, recited it, mastered it, set it in motion, taught it, instructed in it, pointed it out, and studied it.

Having written it down, training for the sake of suchness, practicing for the sake of suchness, and applying themselves to yoga for the sake of suchness, they will draw near to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
they will abide for the sake of suchness for the sake of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Moreover, Śāriputra, those who, having written down this perfection of wisdom, shall preserve it, recite it, master it, teach it, explain it, proclaim it, study it, and write it down,
yet do not train for the sake of suchness,
nor practice for the sake of suchness—
And they will not apply themselves to the yoga of suchness;

training neither for suchness, practicing neither for suchness, nor applying themselves to the yoga of suchness, they will not abide in suchness regarding unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Śāriputra, those too are known by the Tathāgata.
They too are sustained by the Tathāgata;
they too are seen by the Tathāgata; they too are beheld by the Tathāgata with the Buddha-eye.
Śāriputra, even for them, that exertion and effort will be of great purpose, great benefit, great fruit, and great maturation.
Why is that?
Because the perfection of wisdom, which is connected with the ultimate truth, has appeared for the sake of all sentient beings so that they may penetrate all phenomena as they truly are.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, after the passing of the Tathāgata, these sūtras associated with the six perfections will circulate in the southern region; from the southern region they will again circulate in Vartanī; and from Vartanī they will circulate in the northern region.

Śāriputra, when this Dharma-Vinaya has reached its ninth stage of decline, at the time of the disappearance of the True Dharma, those sons of good family and daughters of good family who will take up,
bear in mind, recite, master, propagate, teach, explain, proclaim, and study this Perfection of Wisdom have been taken into account by the Tathāgata for that time.
Even those who, having written it down, shall preserve it even in the form of a book—
Śāriputra, they are known by the Tathāgata;
Śāriputra, they are sustained by the Tathāgata.
They have been seen by the Tathāgata, Śāriputra; they have been beheld by the Tathāgata with his Buddha-eye.
Śāriputra said: "Lord, will this very Prajñāpāramitā, so profound as this, be widely propagated in the future time, in the final age, in the northern direction, in the northern region?

The Blessed One said: "Śāriputra, those who, having heard this profound Prajñāpāramitā there in the northern direction, in the northern region, shall apply themselves to yoga in this Prajñāpāramitā—they will cause it to be widely propagated."

Śāriputra, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who shall hear, write down, take up, bear in mind, recite, master, set in motion, teach, explain, and proclaim this perfection of wisdom, and who shall train themselves in accordance with suchness, should be known as having set out on the journey long ago.
They will practice for the sake of suchness;
they will apply themselves to yoga for the sake of suchness.

Śāriputra said: "Blessed One, how many will those bodhisattva mahāsattvas be in the northern direction, in the northern quarter— will they be many or few— who will hear this profound perfection of wisdom, write it down, take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, set it forth, and teach it?"
They will teach it, they will recite it, they will study it,
they will train for the sake of suchness,
and they will practice for the sake of suchness.
"Will they apply themselves to the yoga for suchness?
The Blessed One said: "Śāriputra, there will be many, very many bodhisattva mahāsattvas in the northern region, in the north, in the northern quarter.
And although, Śāriputra, they are many,"

Even among those many, only a few will be those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who shall hear this profound perfection of wisdom, write it down, take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, propagate it,
teach it, explain it, proclaim it, and study it.
They will train for suchness, they will practice for suchness, and they will apply themselves to yoga for suchness.
And when the Perfection of Wisdom is being taught, they will not shrink back, nor will they shrink away; they will not be despondent, nor will they fall into despair;
they will not turn their minds away.
They will not have their backs broken;
they will not be afraid, they will not be terrified, and they will not fall into terror.
It should be known that those bodhisattva mahāsattvas have long since set out upon the Great Vehicle.
Those former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones were followed by them; they were questioned, interrogated, and cross-examined.
And those former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones were honored by those sons of good family, daughters of good family, and persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle.
And they will be those who act with complete fulfillment regarding the precepts,
and they will accomplish the welfare of many people,
namely, by means of this very unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
For what reason?
Because it was by me alone that these discourses associated with omniscience were delivered for those sons and daughters of good family.
Even when they have passed away from that birth, these very same activities associated with omniscience and associated with the perfection of wisdom will continue to manifest for them;
they will carry on this very discourse and they will rejoice in this very discourse.
That is to say, with reference to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
they will be well-established and concentrated in this perfection of wisdom;
even by Māra, they cannot be divided.
How much less so by other beings,
whether by their own will or by means of mantras?
For what reason?
Just as it is because their resolve for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment is so firm,
those sons of good family and daughters of good family, having heard this perfection of wisdom, will attain a sublime joy, gladness, and serene confidence;
and they will plant roots of merit for many people, namely, for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
For what reason?
Because those sons of good family and daughters of good family have spoken these words in my presence:
"There are many hundreds of beings, many thousands of beings, many hundreds of thousands of beings, and many hundreds of millions of beings."

We shall establish, demonstrate, inspire, encourage, gladden, and empower many thousands of koṭis of living beings, many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of living beings, and many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of living beings, as they practice the conduct of a bodhisattva, for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
"We shall establish them;
we shall make them irreversible.
For what reason?
Śāriputra, I have indeed rejoiced in those sons of good family and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who,

having observed my mind with their own minds, have spoken these words: "While practicing for the sake of awakening, we [will lead] many hundreds of beings, many thousands of beings, many hundreds of thousands of beings, many hundreds of millions of beings, many billions of beings [to liberation]."

We shall establish many hundreds of thousands of millions of beings, many hundreds of thousands of billions of millions of beings, in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; we shall demonstrate it to them, incite them toward it, inspire them, gladden them, and empower them.
"We shall establish them in full enlightenment;
we shall make them irreversible.
And thus those sons of good family and daughters of good family will possess noble resolve.
They will consider that they must also take up other Buddha-fields where Tathāgatas,

Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are present and will teach the Dharma; there, in the presence of those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, they will once again hear this profound Prajñāpāramitā in detail.

In those buddha-fields as well, they will establish, inspire, and guide toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment many hundreds of beings, many thousands of beings, many hundreds of thousands of beings, many hundreds of millions of beings, many billions of beings, many trillions of beings, and many hundreds of quadrillions of beings.

They will cause them to take up [the practice], they will inspire them, they will gladden them, they will empower them, they will establish them in perfect enlightenment, and they will make them irreversible.

When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One as follows: "It is marvelous, Blessed One, how there is nothing whatsoever among past, future, and present phenomena that has not been seen, heard, known, or understood by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
There is no dharma whatsoever that is not known, and no conduct of sentient beings whatsoever that is not understood,

for indeed, even the conduct of future bodhisattva-mahāsattvas— those who desire awakening, who are endowed with high resolve, and who have initiated vigor— is already known. Those who, at that time, will take up and uphold this profound perfection of wisdom;
They will read, master, propagate, teach, explain, recite, and write them down;
and those who, at that time, for the sake of all sentient beings and for the purpose of these six perfections, shall apply themselves with diligence and seek and search for them.
They will search for them;
and among those sons of good family and daughters of good family who are thus seeking and searching, some bodhisattvas who are searching will find them, while others will not find them.
"Some will obtain this profound *prajñāpāramitā* even without seeking it.
What, Blessed One, is the reason for this?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra: "So it is, Śāriputra; so it is."
There is nothing whatsoever—among the phenomena of the past, future, or present—that is unseen, unheard, unknown, or unperceived by the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, at that time and on that occasion, some bodhisattvas who seek, search for, and investigate will indeed find this perfection of wisdom;
yet other bodhisattvas, without seeking, searching for, or investigating, will also find it.
For what reason?
Because these bodhisattva mahāsattvas have sought and investigated this perfection of wisdom from the very beginning without laying down their burden;
by that very same former desire for roots of virtue, even though they do not seek, do not investigate, and do not search for this perfection of wisdom now, they will obtain it.
Furthermore, whatever other sūtras there may be that proclaim this very Perfection of Wisdom, those too will themselves come to them, accrue to them, and lead toward them.
For what reason?

It is thus, Śāriputra, that it happens: a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, without laying down the burden, seeks and searches for this perfection of wisdom, will obtain this perfection of wisdom even after passing through another birth and even after passing through another lifetime.
Furthermore, other sūtras associated with the perfection of wisdom will come to him of their own accord.
They will be reborn and they will approach [the Buddha].

When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, will only these sūtras associated with the six perfections arise and be presented to those sons of good family and daughters of good family, and no others?
The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, there will also be other sūtras that are profound, exceedingly profound."
These [qualities] will also arise spontaneously for those sons of good family and daughters of good family, and they will be presented to them spontaneously.
For what reason?
Because it is thus, Śāriputra, regarding those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who [are established] in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
They will send them forth, show them, encourage them, inspire them, gladden them, and manifest them;
they will establish them in perfect enlightenment and make them irreversible.

And they will themselves train therein; Śāriputra, even when they have passed away from that birth, these most profound discourses connected with non-apprehension, connected with emptiness, and connected with the six perfections will arise spontaneously and present themselves to them of their own accord.
The tenth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of the Qualities of the Dhāraṇīs," in the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.
(Vaidya 115) Chapter Eleven: The Chapter on the Deeds of Māra.
Then the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, these qualities of those sons of good family and daughters of good family have been proclaimed by the Blessed One."
“Furthermore, Lord, will some obstacles arise for them?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: “Subhūti, many deeds of Māra, which act as obstacles, will arise for them.
Subhūti said: “Of what kind, Lord, will those many deeds of Māra that act as obstacles arise for them?”
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, for those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who are speaking the perfection of wisdom, their eloquence will arise only after a long time.
Subhūti, this should be known as the first work of Māra.
Furthermore, even that eloquence, as it is being produced, will be distracted."
This also, Subhūti, should be known as the work of Māra:
they will write [the sūtra] while yawning, laughing, and mocking.
This also, Subhūti, should be known as the work of Māra.
Those with distracted minds will master it;
Subhūti, this too should be known as the work of Māra.
They will write it down while possessing mutual consciousness [of one another].
Subhūti, this too should be known as the work of Māra:
they will not attain mindfulness.
Subhūti, this too should be known as the work of Māra.
They will write it while mocking one another;
Subhūti, this too should be known as the work of Māra.
They will write it while deriding one another.
This too, Subhūti, should be known as the work of Māra:
they will write with distracted eyes.
This too, Subhūti, should be known as the work of Māra.
As they write to one another, there will be a lack of harmony;
Subhūti, this too should be known as the work of Māra.
Thinking, "We find no firm footing nor any taste here," they will rise from their seats and depart.
Subhūti, this too should be known as the work of Māra:
they will rise from their seats and depart with minds lacking faith, thinking, "We have not been prophesied here in the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, this too should be known as the work of Māra.
"Neither the name of our village, nor our city, nor our town where we were born has been mentioned here;
neither our own name or clan has been taken up here, nor the name or clan of our mother and father."
Nor will they think, "This is not the family from which we were born," and thus they will consider that the Perfection of Wisdom should not be heard,
and they will consider that they must depart from it.
And to whatever extent they shall turn away, for that many eons they will repeatedly take up cyclic existence through those very same mental impulses,
wherein they must once again apply themselves to yoga.
Why is that? Subhūti, for it is because they do not hear this perfection of wisdom that bodhisattva mahāsattvas fail to emerge in mundane and supramundane dharmas.
Subhūti, this too should be understood as the work of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti, those persons belonging to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas who [reject] this perfection of wisdom, which brings about the knowledge of omniscience—

Subhūti, it should be understood that this too is a work of Māra: that they will think those discourses (*sūtrānta*) which do not bring about the knowledge of an omniscient one (*sarvajña-jñāna*) are the ones to be sought after, having set them aside and abandoned them.

Furthermore, Subhūti, it is as follows: those who do not wish to train in the mundane and supramundane, nor wish to emerge into the mundane and supramundane dharmas, do not train here in this perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Not training in the perfection of wisdom, they do not emerge into mundane or supramundane dharmas.

Thus, those of limited intelligence, having rejected and abandoned the perfection of wisdom—which is the root for the thorough knowledge of mundane and supramundane things as they truly are—will think that the branches should be relied upon.
Subhūti, it is just as if a dog, having cast aside morsels from its master, should think that a mouthful from a servant must be sought.
In the same way, Subhūti, there will be in the future some persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who,
having cast aside this perfection of wisdom— the root of the knowledge of omniscience— will [rely] upon the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, which are like branches, leaves, and chaff.
They will think that they must seek out the essence in old age.
Subhūti, this too should be known as a work of Māra.
Why is that?
For those of small intelligence will not understand that the perfection of wisdom is the bringer of the knowledge of all-knowledge;
they will reject, abandon, and cast aside the perfection of wisdom, and instead [rely on] other sūtras which describe the stage of the śrāvaka or describe the stage of the pratyekabuddha.
They will consider those [teachings] to be even more to be mastered;
such bodhisattvas who have undertaken [the path] should be known as being like branches, leaves, and foliage.
Why is that?
For indeed, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not train in the same way that persons belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas train.
And how, Subhūti, do persons belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas train?
Subhūti, they think thus: "We shall tame only ourselves."
Thinking, "We shall pacify this one self;
we shall bring this one self to final nirvana," they undertake the application of all formative activities of the roots of merit for the sake of the self's taming, tranquility, and final nirvana.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not train in this way;

rather, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in this way: "For the sake of benefiting the entire world, I shall establish myself in suchness, and I shall also establish all sentient beings in suchness."

Thinking, "I shall bring immeasurable realms of sentient beings to final nirvana," all applications of the formative activity of roots of virtue should be undertaken by the bodhisattva mahāsattva in this manner, yet he should not conceive of them as such.
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a certain man, not having seen an elephant, were to search for the color and shape of the elephant;
having found the elephant in the darkness, he would go toward the light to examine it, yet while examining it there, he would think that the footprint of the elephant must be sought.
"Suppose one were to think that the color and shape of an elephant should be grasped from the footprint of an elephant.
What do you think, Subhūti, would such a person be considered wise?
Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it should be understood that those persons belonging to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas are just like this:

being ignorant of this perfection of wisdom and not inquiring about it, they abandon it while desiring to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—those discourses which proclaim the level of the śrāvakas and which proclaim the level of the pratyekabuddhas."
They will think that those [qualities] are to be sought after;
Subhūti, this too should be known as a work of Māra for them.
It is just as if, Subhūti, a man seeking jewels, upon seeing the great ocean, were not to plunge into it.

One should not gaze upon the jewels, nor should one grasp them; such a person would think that for the sake of those jewels, one must search for the water in a cow’s footprint, and would think that one must equate the water in a cow’s footprint with the great ocean.
"What do you think, Subhūti, should that man be considered wise?
Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "In the same way, Subhūti, those persons belonging to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas should be understood as being of such a kind."
Having obtained this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, those who do not plunge into it and do not understand it will reject it;

and they will consider those discourses (*sūtrānta*) which proclaim the stage of the *śrāvaka* and the stage of the *pratyekabuddha*— which teach dwelling with little concern— to be the ones they should seek.
Where the Bodhisattvayāna is not praised,
but only self-taming, tranquility, and parinirvāṇa are taught as "retreat" (pratisaṃlayana), [thinking] "may I attain the fruit of stream-entry,"...
"May I attain the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or arhatship; may I attain solitary enlightenment;
or, in this very life, having liberated the mind from the outflows through non-clinging, may I enter final nirvana."
This is called that which is associated with the levels of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
herein, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should not give rise to such a thought.
Why is that?
For, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have set out in the Mahāyāna are those who have donned the great armor;
they should never give rise to a thought of having few aspirations.
For what reason?
Because those true persons are leaders of the world and performers of the world's welfare.
Therefore, they should at all times, constantly and continuously, train themselves in the six perfections.

Furthermore, Subhūti, those individuals belonging to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas who have not yet ripened their roots of virtue, who possess limited and inferior intelligence, and who have weak resolute intentions—

being ignorant of and failing to understand the discourses associated with the six perfections— they will cast aside this perfection of wisdom and think that those discourses which extol the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are what they should seek.
Subhūti, this too should be known as the work of Māra regarding those persons belonging to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas who are of such a kind.
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a carpenter or a carpenter’s apprentice, desiring to build or construct a palace equal in measure to the Vaijayanta Palace, should wish to create one.
He would search for a mandala equal in size to the celestial palaces of the sun and moon;
while searching, he might see the celestial palaces of the sun and moon,
and he would think that the measurement should be taken from them.
"What do you think, Subhūti? Would one who wishes to build and create a palace the size of the Vaijayanta palace need to take the measure from the celestial mansions of the sun and the moon?
Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "In the same way, Subhūti, there will be in the future some persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle."

Those who, having heard the perfection of wisdom and having obtained the perfection of wisdom, yet neglect the perfection of wisdom and abandon the perfection of wisdom, thinking that omniscience is to be sought through discourses associated with the levels of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—
those discourses which speak thus: "We shall tame this one self alone"— [they are like those who, having obtained a priceless gem, cast it away and seek a counterfeit].
"We shall pacify the one self; we shall cause the one self to attain final nirvana.
Thus, they bring about only the taming, the pacification, and the final nirvana of the self.
They will seek out such sūtras and consider themselves as having trained accordingly.
What do you think, Subhūti, should those bodhisattvas be known as being of a wise nature?
Subhūti said, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, this too should be understood as the work of Māra.
Subhūti, it is just as if some man were desirous of causing a universal monarch (cakravartin) to fall from his position."
He would see a universal monarch (cakravartin);
having seen him, he would grasp the signs [thinking], "Such is a universal monarch in terms of complexion, physical form, majesty, and supernatural power.
Then, seeing a local king (koṭṭarāja), he would grasp the signs of that local king’s complexion, physical form, majesty, and supernatural power, yet he would be unable to [match] them.
Regarding the apprehension of specific qualities, one might say: "Such indeed is that universal monarch (cakravartin) in terms of complexion, physical form, majesty, power, and characteristics.
What do you think, Subhūti—is such a person to be considered wise who would think to equate a universal monarch with a local king?
Subhūti said, "Certainly not, Blessed One.

The Blessed One said, "It is just so, Subhūti. In a future time, there will be certain individuals belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who, having heard this perfection of wisdom and having obtained this perfection of wisdom, will neglect the perfection of wisdom and abandon the perfection of wisdom."
They will think that omniscience is to be sought through discourses associated with the levels of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Subhūti, this too should be known as a deed of Māra for them.
Indeed, Subhūti, I do not say that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should seek omniscience through such discourses associated with the levels of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
I say this:

moreover, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train in that skill in means which has been declared by the Tathāgata in the perfection of wisdom, he will not go forth to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, the realization of a bodhisattva is slow in other sūtras. Therefore, seeing this benefit in the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata, by means of many methods, [praises it].

He demonstrates, exhorts, inspires, gladdens, settles, and establishes the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, in this perfection of wisdom, so that these bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, may become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"What do you think, Subhūti? Would those bodhisattvas appear to be wise who, having obtained and attained the irreversible Great Vehicle, would then abandon it, turn back from it, and think that they should seek the Lesser Vehicle?
Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One."

The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is just as if a hungry man, having obtained food of a hundred flavors—which has a beneficial ripening, a pleasant ripening, which wards off hunger and thirst for the duration of his life—were to set that aside and think that he should seek out sixty-day-old rice. Having obtained that sixty-day-old rice, he would think that he should abandon and discard the food of a hundred flavors and consume that sixty-day-old rice instead."
"What do you think, Subhūti, would that man be considered wise?
Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "In just this way, Subhūti, there will be certain bodhisattvas in a future time,"
Those who, having heard this perfection of wisdom and having obtained the perfection of wisdom, will abandon the perfection of wisdom,
will cast aside the perfection of wisdom, will discard the perfection of wisdom,
and will distance themselves from the perfection of wisdom.

Having abandoned the perfection of wisdom, having cast aside the perfection of wisdom, having discarded the perfection of wisdom, and having distanced themselves from the perfection of wisdom, they will think that the sūtras associated with the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are what should be sought after—
those sūtras which proclaim the level of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
They will think that omniscience is to be sought through them.
What do you think, Subhūti, should those bodhisattvas be known as being of a wise nature?
Subhūti said: "Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, this too should be known as the work of Māra.
Subhūti, it is just as if some man, having obtained a priceless jewel, should think that it ought to be equated with a jewel of little value and little substance.
What do you think, Subhūti, would such a person be considered wise?"
Subhūti said, “Certainly not, Blessed One.

The Blessed One said, “It is just so, Subhūti. In a future time, there will be certain persons belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, having obtained and heard this profound and luminous jewel of the perfection of wisdom, will think that it should be equated with the vehicle of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
They will think that omniscience and skill in means are to be sought on the level of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
What do you think, Subhūti, should those Bodhisattvas be considered wise?
Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, this too should be known as a work of Māra for those bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, Subhūti, while this profound perfection of wisdom is being spoken, taught, explained, recited, mastered, chanted, and even written down, many flashes of inspired eloquence will arise."
Subhūti, whatever causes distraction of the mind— this too should be understood as the work of Māra for those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas.
When this had been said, the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "But, Blessed One, is it possible to write down the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One replied: "Certainly not, Subhūti.
Subhūti, those who, having written the perfection of wisdom in letters and syllables, should think, 'The perfection of wisdom has been written,' [they do not understand it]."
Or if they will adhere to the perfection of wisdom in syllables as "non-existent," or as "without syllables," Subhūti, this too should be known as their work of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti, while this perfection of wisdom is being written out, there will arise mental preoccupations with places;
mental preoccupations with villages, towns, market towns, districts, kingdoms, and royal capitals will arise; and mental preoccupations with parks will arise.
Mental preoccupations with teachers will arise;
mental preoccupations with storytelling will arise; mental preoccupations with thieves will arise.
Mental engagements with encampments will arise;
mental engagements with streets will arise;
mental engagements with palanquins will arise.
Mental attentions of pleasure will arise;
mental attentions of suffering will arise; mental attentions of fear will arise.
Mental attentions toward women will arise; mental attentions toward men will arise; mental attentions toward neuter beings will arise.
Mental engagements involving the alternation between the pleasant and the unpleasant will arise;
mental engagements associated with mother and father will arise;
mental engagements associated with brothers and sisters will arise.

Mental engagements associated with friends, kinsmen, blood relations, and ministers will arise; mental engagements associated with sons and daughters of the subjects will arise; and mental engagements associated with houses, food, and drink will arise.

Mental preoccupations with clothing will arise; mental preoccupations with beds and seats, mental preoccupations with life, mental preoccupations with duties, mental preoccupations with passion, mental preoccupations with hatred,

mental preoccupations with delusion, mental preoccupations with the seasons, mental preoccupations with good times, mental preoccupations with bad times, mental preoccupations with song, and mental preoccupations with instrumental music.

Subhūti, Māra the Evil One will bring forth these and other mental preoccupations in this perfection of wisdom: mental preoccupations with dancing, mental preoccupations with poetry, drama, and history, mental preoccupations with treatises, mental preoccupations with worldly affairs, mental preoccupations with laughter, mental preoccupations with the *lāsya* dance, mental preoccupations with sorrow, mental preoccupations with fatigue, and mental preoccupations with the self.

Whether it is being spoken, taught, instructed, grasped, recited, pointed out, studied, or even written down, he will create obstacles and cause distraction of mind for the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas.
In this regard, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must recognize the works of Māra;
having recognized them, he must avoid them.

Furthermore, Subhūti, there will arise mental engagements with kings, mental engagements with princes, mental engagements with elephants, mental engagements with horses, mental engagements with chariots, and mental engagements with the sight of military outposts.
This too, Subhūti, should be understood as the work of Māra for them.
Furthermore, Subhūti, there will arise mental preoccupations with fire, mental preoccupations with sensual desires, and mental preoccupations with the abundance of wealth and grain.
This too, Subhūti, should be understood as the work of Māra for bodhisattva mahāsattvas.

Furthermore, Subhūti, obstacles will arise for bodhisattvas mahāsattvas regarding their gains, honors, robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick, while they are speaking, teaching, instructing, reciting, or even writing this perfection of wisdom; or there will be mental affliction due to the taste of gain, honor, and praise.
Subhūti, this too should be understood by bodhisattva mahāsattvas as the work of Māra. All these works of Māra must be recognized by them,
and having recognized them, they must be avoided.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are speaking, teaching, instructing, explaining, reciting, or even writing this Perfection of Wisdom, there will be those very profound sūtras associated with the levels of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Then Māra, the Evil One, will approach them in the guise of a monk and will urge them: "Train in this! Write this down! Study this!"
"This is the private recitation;
from this, omniscience will be accomplished.
However, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is skilled in means should not, on account of these, give rise to longing.
For what reason?
Although, Subhūti, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are taught in those sūtras,
skill in means has indeed not been explained therein for the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas.

In that regard, those bodhisattvas who will lack proficiency in the specific knowledge of skillful means (*upāyakauśalyajñānaviśeṣa*) will think that this profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is to be abandoned.
Having abandoned this profound perfection of wisdom, they will think that skillful means is to be sought in discourses (*sūtrānta*) associated with the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Subhūti, this too should be understood by a bodhisattva mahāsattva as the work of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti, there will be a listener who is zealous and desires to take up the perfection of wisdom,
while the teacher of the Dharma will be indolent and does not desire to teach the Dharma.
This too, Subhūti, should be recognized by a bodhisattva mahāsattva as the work of Māra, which is a lack of harmony.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Dharma-preacher may be untiring and desirous of giving the *prajñāpāramitā*,
while the listener of the Dharma may be weary or have many duties.
This too, Subhūti, should be recognized by a bodhisattva mahāsattva as the work of Māra consisting of a lack of harmony.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the listener of the Dharma will be zealous; he will desire to take up the Perfection of Wisdom, to retain it, to recite it, to master it, and to propagate it— even to the extent of desiring to write it down—
and he will be possessed of intelligence, wisdom, and mindfulness.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Dharma-preacher will be sent to another region, or he may be one who understands through brief hints (*uddhaṭṭitajña*) but not through detailed explanations (*vipañcitajña*),
or he may be altogether ignorant; this too, Subhūti, will be a lack of harmony there when the *prajñāpāramitā* is being spoken, taught, instructed, recited, and studied, even to the very end.
While it is being written, Subhūti, this too should be understood by the bodhisattva mahāsattva as the work of Māra consisting of a lack of harmony.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Dharma-preacher may be untiring, knowledgeable, and desirous of giving and reciting this Perfection of Wisdom, yet [the conditions for its practice will not be met].

Furthermore, Subhūti, the listener of the Dharma will have set out for another country; he will be one who does not understand what has been condensed, or one who does not understand what has been elaborated, or one who lacks comprehension.
This too, Subhūti, should be known by a bodhisattva mahāsattva as the work of Māra consisting of a lack of harmony.
Moreover, Subhūti, the preacher of the Dharma will be heavy with worldly goods, heavy with gain, honor, and robes.
Furthermore, Subhūti, those who listen to the Dharma may have few desires, be contented, and live in seclusion, yet they will not wish to give the meaning [of the teaching].
This too, Subhūti, will be a lack of harmony when training in or writing out the *prajñāpāramitā*.
This also, Subhūti, should be recognized by a bodhisattva mahāsattva as the work of Māra.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the listener of the Dharma will be faithful, desiring to hear this perfection of wisdom, desiring to understand its meaning, desiring to give its meaning, and desiring to relinquish its meaning;
yet the preacher of the Dharma will be lacking in faith, or have few desires, or not wish to speak.
For this reason also, Subhūti, it should be understood as the work of Māra that there is a lack of harmony.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the listener of the Dharma may be faithful, desiring to hear and desiring to understand the meaning;
yet, for the Dharma-preacher, those sūtras may not be available or accessible due to obstacles to the Dharma.
For this reason also, Subhūti, the listener of the Dharma will encounter a refusal from the Dharma-preacher before having attained [the teaching].
Subhūti, this too will be a lack of harmony for those who take up, maintain, recite, master, and propagate the *prajñāpāramitā*, even down to those who write it out.
Subhūti, this also should be recognized by a bodhisattva mahāsattva as the work of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti, there will be a time when the Dharma-preacher desires to speak, yet...
And the listener of the Dharma will be lacking the desire to hear it.
Subhūti, this too will be a lack of harmony there for taking up, bearing in mind, reciting, mastering, propagating, or even writing down the Prajñāpāramitā.
This too, Subhūti, should be understood by a bodhisattva mahāsattva as the work of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the listener of the Dharma will be heavy with drowsiness; he will be heavy with physical lethargy.
Endowed with that heaviness of drowsiness and endowed with physical exhaustion, he will not desire to listen,
while the Dharma-preacher will desire to speak.
Subhūti, this too should be understood by a bodhisattva mahāsattva as the work of Māra consisting of a lack of harmony.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Dharma-preacher will be heavy with drowsiness and heavy with physical lethargy.
Possessed of that heaviness of drowsiness and possessed of physical fatigue, he will have no desire to speak.
And the listener of the Dharma will be desirous of hearing it.
Subhūti, this too will be a lack of harmony there for the purpose of writing, reciting, or mastering [the teaching].
Subhūti, this also should be recognized by a bodhisattva mahāsattva as the work of Māra.

Furthermore, Subhūti, while this perfection of wisdom is being written down, spoken, or studied, someone may come there and speak in dispraise of the hells, speak in dispraise of the animal realm, and speak in dispraise of the domain of hungry ghosts.
He will speak dispraise of the hosts of asuras, saying: "The hells are thus painful; the animal realm is thus painful;
the domain of hungry ghosts is thus painful."
Thus are the bodies of the asuras full of suffering; thus are conditioned phenomena full of suffering.
Right here, the end of suffering must be made.
Subhūti, this too should be understood by a bodhisattva mahāsattva as the work of Māra that causes a lack of harmony.

Furthermore, Subhūti, while this perfection of wisdom is being written down, spoken, or practiced, someone might come there and speak in praise of the gods, saying: "The heavens are thus blissful, thus full of happiness;
in this way, the desires of the realm of desire (kāmadhātu) are to be enjoyed."
In this way, the meditations in the realm of form are to be attained;
likewise, the attainments in the formless realm are to be attained.
And all of that, having been examined through wisdom, is entirely the arising of suffering.
For this was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, I do not praise even a duration as brief as the snap of a finger for the production of existence.
For all that is conditioned is impermanent; all that is understood as fearful is suffering; the entire triple world is empty; and all phenomena are without self.
Thus, having understood that everything is non-eternal, impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, the wise should attain the fruit of stream-entry right here."
"The fruit of once-returning and the fruit of non-returning must be attained right here;
may we not again encounter those states of prosperity and adversity which are for the most part suffering."
In that regard, some bodhisattvas will experience a sense of spiritual urgency;
Subhūti, this too should be understood by a bodhisattva mahāsattva as the work of Māra consisting of a lack of harmony.
Furthermore, Subhūti, those monks who are Dharma-preachers will delight in solitude,
while those who listen to the Dharma will value their assemblies.
Those Dharma-preachers will also say: "To those who follow me, I shall give this Perfection of Wisdom;
to those who do not follow me," [I shall not].
"I will not give to them.

In this way, those sons of good family and daughters of good family, out of purpose, desire, and reverence for the Dharma, will follow that Dharma-preacher and will not grant him any opportunity [to refuse].
And that Dharma-preacher will desire some small amount of material goods,
yet they will not wish to give them;
consequently, he will go here and there.
Wherever there will be famine, lack of security, and a threat to life,
those listeners of the Dharma will hear from others: "That region is characterized by famine and lacks security."
And in that region there will be a threat to life.
Then that Dharma-preacher will speak thus to those sons of good family: "Sons of good family, in that region there is the fear of famine.
Sons of good family, will you come? Lest you later feel regret for having entered into the fear of famine."
In this way, that Dharma-preacher will reject them through subtle means;
and they, appearing despondent, will think: "These are signs of refusal, not signs of a desire to give."
Knowing that "this person does not wish to give," they will not comply.
Subhūti, this too will be a lack of harmony when the *prajñāpāramitā* is being written down, studied, taught, explained, recited, or rehearsed.
Subhūti, this also should be recognized by a bodhisattva mahāsattva as the work of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti, there will come a time when the Dharma-preacher sets out toward a place where there is danger from wild beasts, danger from venomous serpents, or danger from non-human beings.
While traveling and dwelling there, he will proceed toward a wilderness of predatory beasts, a wilderness of reptiles, a wilderness of thieves, a wilderness lacking water, or a wilderness of famine.
He will say this to those listeners of the Dharma: "O sons of good family, you should know that in such-and-such a region..."

"There is fear of living beings, fear of wild beasts, fear of carnivorous creatures, the wilderness of reptiles, the wilderness of thieves, the wilderness of water, and the wilderness of famine; it is for these that we have set out.
Know this, noble sons: are you able to experience such sufferings?"
In this way, he will reject them through subtle means;
then they will become disillusioned, and being disillusioned, they will no longer follow him.
Furthermore, they will indeed turn back.
Subhūti, this too will arise as an obstacle to the Perfection of Wisdom while it is being taught, recited, and even written down.
Subhūti, this also should be recognized by a bodhisattva mahāsattva as the work of Māra, namely, the lack of harmony.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the monk who is a Dharma-preacher will become preoccupied with families of friends and families from whom he receives alms.

Because of that preoccupation with families of friends and families from whom he receives alms, he will think that he must constantly visit and look upon those families of friends and families from whom he receives alms.
Due to that constant visiting and his many obligations, he will reject those listeners of the Dharma, saying: "I still have something to look after."
"There is still someone I must visit"—
Subhūti, this too will be a lack of concord when the *prajñāpāramitā* is being written down or mastered.
Subhūti, this also should be recognized by a bodhisattva mahāsattva as the work of Māra.
For in this way, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One will act in various ways and by various means so that no one shall take up this perfection of wisdom,
nor retain it.
he will not cause it to be recited,
he will not master it,
and he will not propagate it;
He will not teach, he will not instruct, he will not recite.
He will not recite it, nor cause it to be written, nor write it himself.
Therefore, Subhūti, whatever obstacles lead to a lack of harmony,
all of those should be understood by a bodhisattva mahāsattva as the deeds of Māra; and having understood them, they should be avoided.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One: "What, O Blessed One, is the reason that Māra, the Evil One, will here exert such great effort,
and will strive by such various means,
so that [he may obstruct] this perfection of wisdom?"
"Will no one take it up, nor retain it, nor recite it, nor master it, nor propagate it, nor teach it, nor explain it, nor expound it, nor study it, nor cause it to be written, nor write it down?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, for the omniscience of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is born from the perfection of wisdom."
The teaching of the Tathāgata is born from omniscience;
the teaching of the Tathāgata gives rise to the abandonment of the afflictions of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings;
and for those whose afflictions have been abandoned, Māra the Evil One finds no opportunity for entry.
Not obtaining it, he becomes afflicted by suffering, dejected, and pierced by the arrow of grief.
Therefore, while the Perfection of Wisdom is being written out or mastered, he applies himself with great exertion and intense urgency.
With that great exertion, he strives in various ways through skillful means.
So that no one might write down or master this perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One will come in the guise of a śramaṇa and sow dissension. He will cause those sons of good family who have newly set out in the vehicle to be alienated, saying: "This is not the Perfection of Wisdom that you, venerable ones, are hearing;
rather, it is according to what has been handed down in my own sūtras and included in my own sūtra-collections."
"This is that perfection of wisdom"—
in this way, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One will sow doubt.
Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One, having come in the guise of a śramaṇa, will create a schism among those who have newly set out in the vehicle.
He will cause doubt regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment to fall upon those bodhisattvas who possess little intelligence, dull intelligence, limited intelligence, who are mentally obscured,
and who are undecided; having fallen into doubt, they will not take up this perfection of wisdom, nor will they retain it, nor will they recite it.

They will not master it, they will not set it in motion, they will not teach it, they will not instruct in it, they will not expound it, they will not recite it, they will not cause it to be written, and they will not write it themselves. Subhūti, this too should be recognized by a bodhisattva mahāsattva as the work of Māra.

Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One, having conjured up monks and approached in the guise of Buddhas, will bring forth this work of Māra: "The bodhisattva who courses in profound dharmas realizes the limit of reality; he becomes a śrāvaka."
That a bodhisattva does not think, "This is a bodhisattva," as this one is—
Subhūti, this too should be understood by a bodhisattva mahāsattva as the work of Māra.

In this way, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One will produce these and many other such deeds of Māra while this Perfection of Wisdom is being written and mastered; these must be recognized by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva,
and having recognized them, they must be avoided.
They should not be consumed;
one should be one who has initiated vigor, and who possesses mindfulness and clear comprehension.
When this had been said, the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
As for those great jewels, Blessed One,"
They are subject to many adversaries.
Why is that?
It is because they are difficult to obtain and of great value.
"For those things, Blessed One, are preeminent;
therefore, they encounter many adversaries.
In the same way, Blessed One, many obstacles will generally arise for this perfection of wisdom."

In that regard, Blessed One, those who become indolent due to the power of obstacles should be known as bodhisattvas possessed by Māra; and, Blessed One, they will be those who have newly set out in the vehicle.
And they, O Blessed One, will be of little intelligence;
they, O Blessed One, will be of dull intelligence;
and they, O Blessed One, will be of limited intelligence.
And, Blessed One, their intellects will be perverted;
their minds will not incline toward the sublime and most sublime dharmas, they who will think that this perfection of wisdom should not be taken up.

They will think that it should not be upheld, nor recited, nor mastered, nor promulgated, nor taught, nor instructed, nor explained, nor studied, nor caused to be written, and ultimately not even written down.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "So it is, Subhūti, so it is.
Subhūti, those bodhisattvas should be known as being under the influence of Māra;
and, Subhūti, those bodhisattvas will be beginners who have newly set out in the vehicle."
And they will be of little intelligence,
they will be of dull intelligence,
and they will be of limited intelligence.
Their intellects will be perverted,
and their minds will not incline toward the most sublime and exalted teachings,
as they will think that this perfection of wisdom is not to be taken up.
They will think that it should not be upheld, nor recited, nor mastered, nor set in motion, nor taught, nor expounded, nor studied, nor caused to be written, and ultimately, not even written down.
Moreover, Subhūti, although these works of Māra will arise, and very many faults of Māra that create obstacles will arise therein,
nevertheless, Subhūti, those who think that this perfection of wisdom should be taken up, retained, and recited—

They will think that it should be mastered, set in motion, taught, recited, studied, written down, and even, at the very least, committed to writing; Subhūti, it should be known that they will think this through the power of the Buddha and through the sustaining grace of the Buddha.
Through the protection of the Buddha, they will take it up, uphold it, recite it, master it, propagate it, teach it, explain it, proclaim it, study it,
have it written down, and even write it themselves. Why is that?
For even Māra, the Evil One, will exert great effort here to create obstacles;
likewise, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, will exert effort for the sake of providing support.
The eleventh chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Deeds of Māra," in the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.
(Vaidya 125) Chapter Twelve: The Manifestation of the World.
Then the Blessed One again addressed the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, it is just as if a woman were to have many sons."
Whether five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, or a thousand—let them all exert themselves for their sick mother, thinking: "How may no obstacle to our mother's life arise?
How may our mother live long?"
"How might our mother's body not perish? How might our mother be long-lived?
How might our mother's name remain undestroyed?"
"How might painful sensations not arise for our mother, nor might there arise in her body any unpleasant or disagreeable state of unease?
For what reason?"
"For by her we were brought forth;
she is the doer of what is difficult for us, the giver of our life, and the one who showed us the world.
Thus those sons would support their mother well with all the requisites for happiness.
They should guard her who has been well-guarded, and cherish her who has been well-cherished— lest some painful sensation or painful contact should arise for her,
whether from the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, or the mind, or from wind, bile, or phlegm.

Or from phlegm, or from a derangement of the humors, or from the bite of a gadfly, or a mosquito, or a reptile, or from humans, or non-humans, or from a sudden calamity, or a portentous event—an undesirable affliction might fall upon his body.

In this way, those sons, having provided for their mother with every kind of comfortable requisite, would cherish her, treat her as their own, and protect her, thinking: "This is our mother, our progenitress."
"She is a doer of what is difficult; she is the giver of our life and the one who reveals the world.
In just this way, Subhūti, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones hold this Perfection of Wisdom in their mind.
Those who write it down, take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, propagate it, teach it, instruct in it, explain it, and study it—

all of them do so through the power, the empowerment, and the mindful attention of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One. And those other Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones who currently reside, stay, and maintain themselves in other world-systems for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, and out of compassion for the world— [they too act through their power].
For the sake of the great body of people,
for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of both gods and humans,
and out of compassion, having taken up compassion for all sentient beings.
They all likewise attend to this perfection of wisdom and apply themselves with zeal, thinking: "How might this perfection of wisdom endure for a long time?
How might the name of this perfection of wisdom not perish?"
"Why is it that Māra, or the deities belonging to Māra’s host, would not create obstacles while this Perfection of Wisdom is being spoken, written, or practiced?
"For this reason, Subhūti, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones cherish, treasure, and protect this Perfection of Wisdom. Why is that?"
For this is the mother, the progenitor of the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the perfectly enlightened ones;
she is the revealer of this omniscience and the one who shows the way to the world. Indeed, Subhūti, it is from her that the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the perfectly enlightened ones are born.
For, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is the mother and the revealer of this knowledge of omniscience of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas;
it is likewise the revealer of this world.
For, Subhūti, the omniscience of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas has been born from this.
Subhūti, whatever Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment in the past, they all did so by relying on this very perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, those Tathāgatas, Arhats [who will appear] in the future time...

The perfectly awakened ones who will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment— they too, all of them, will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by relying on this very perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly awakened ones who currently reside in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems—

They abide, remain, and maintain themselves throughout the worlds of the ten directions for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, welfare, and happiness of the great mass of beings, both gods and humans.

Those compassionate ones, out of compassion, awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; they all, too, having relied upon this very perfection of wisdom, awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti, I too, who am now the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by relying upon this very perfection of wisdom.
In this way, Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is the mother of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas;
in this way, it is the one that reveals this world.

Then the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Regarding what the Blessed One has thus said—that the perfection of wisdom is the revealer of this world to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas—how, Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom the revealer of this world to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas?
And what, Blessed One, is the world that has been described by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, the Tathāgata has declared that the five aggregates are the world.
Which five?
Namely, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
Subhūti, these five aggregates have been designated as "the world" by the Tathāgata.
Subhūti said: "How, Blessed One, have the five aggregates been shown by the *prajñāpāramitā* of the Tathāgatas?
Or what, Blessed One, has been shown by the *prajñāpāramitā*?

When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "They do not break down, they do not crumble—thus, Subhūti, the five aggregates are 'the world' according to the *prajñāpāramitā* of the Tathāgatas."
They have been shown.
For what reason have they been shown as neither breaking nor disintegrating?
Subhūti, it is because the five aggregates have emptiness as their intrinsic nature.
Because it lacks intrinsic nature,
Subhūti, emptiness neither breaks nor disintegrates.
In this way, Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is the revealer of this world for the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Moreover, Subhūti, neither the signless, nor the wishless, nor the unconditioned, nor non-arising, nor non-existence, nor the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is broken or destroyed.
In this way, Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is the revealer of this world to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, that "sentient beings are immeasurable" and "sentient beings are incalculable.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, [understand] that sentient beings are immeasurable?
"How does he understand, as it truly is, that 'sentient beings are incalculable'?
Subhūti, because sentient beings lack intrinsic nature, he understands, as it truly is, that 'sentient beings are immeasurable' and 'sentient beings are incalculable.
It is in this way, Subhūti, that the Tathāgata, relying on this perfection of wisdom, understands, as it truly is, that 'sentient beings are immeasurable' and 'sentient beings are incalculable.'"
Furthermore, Subhūti, those mental activities of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings—
Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows them precisely as the non-existence of sentient beings.

It is in this way, Subhūti, that by relying on the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows the immeasurable and incalculable mental activities of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings as they truly are.
For it is thus, Subhūti, that the perfection of wisdom is the revealer of this world to the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the perfectly enlightened Buddhas.

Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the contracted minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings, [knowing] "contracted minds, contracted minds. And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know, as it truly is, the contracted minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings, [knowing] "contracted minds, contracted minds"?

He understands contraction as contraction from the perspective of exhaustion, and he understands exhaustion as non-exhaustion, in accordance with reality. For in this way, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, in accordance with reality, the contracted minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings as "contracted minds."

Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgatas truly know, as they really are, the distracted minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings, thinking, "These are distracted minds. And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, truly know, as it really is, the distracted minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings, thinking, "These are distracted minds"?
"Subhūti, by way of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), those minds are distracted.
For those minds are without marks; they are neither diminished nor undiminished, and those minds are undistracted—thus he knows them as they truly are.

In this way, Subhūti, the Tathāgatas, relying on this perfection of wisdom, know the distracted minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings as 'distracted minds,' knowing them as they truly are."
He understands.
