Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the immeasurable and inexhaustible minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings, [knowing] "these are immeasurable and inexhaustible minds.

And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, understand the immeasurable and inexhaustible minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings as "immeasurable and inexhaustible minds"?
Subhūti, that mind of the Tathāgata is sustained by his empowerment;
it is unceasing, unarisen, non-abiding, without support, unequaled, immeasurable, and incalculable.
By means of this very [mind], he understands things as they truly are: that because space is immeasurable and inexhaustible, the mind is immeasurable and inexhaustible.

For in this way, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the immeasurable and inexhaustible minds of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings as "immeasurable and inexhaustible minds."
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the defiled minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "defiled minds.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know, as it truly is, the defiled minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "defiled minds"?
Subhūti, those minds are undefiled by defilement; they are without conventional designation.
For in this way, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the defiled minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "defiled minds.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the undefiled minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "undefiled minds."
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know the unafflicted minds of immeasurable beings as they truly are—knowing them as "unafflicted minds"?
Subhūti, those minds are luminous by nature.
It is in this way, Subhūti, that the Tathāgata [knows them].
Relying upon the perfection of wisdom, one understands, as it truly is, that the unafflicted minds of immeasurable sentient beings are unafflicted minds.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the sunken minds of immeasurable sentient beings, [knowing] "sunken minds, sunken minds.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, understand, as it truly is, the sunken minds of immeasurable sentient beings, [knowing] "sunken minds, sunken minds"?
Subhūti, those minds are sunken because they lack any abiding place (*anālaya*).

For in this way, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the sunken minds of immeasurable sentient beings, [knowing] "these are sunken minds, these are sunken minds."
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the agitated minds of immeasurable beings as "agitated minds.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know, as it truly is, the agitated minds of immeasurable beings as "agitated minds"?
Subhūti, those minds are ungraspable, yet they are to be restrained.
For in this way, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the grasping minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "grasping minds.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the defiled minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "defiled minds."
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know the outflowing minds of immeasurable sentient beings as they truly are—knowing them as "outflowing minds"?
Subhūti, those minds are without intrinsic nature and consist of unreal conceptualizations.

It is in this way, Subhūti, that the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, knows the outflowing minds of immeasurable sentient beings as they truly are—knowing them as "outflowing minds."
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the untainted minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "untainted minds.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, understand, as it truly is, the untainted minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "untainted minds"?
Subhūti, those minds have non-existence as their destination; they are effortless.
For in this way, Subhūti, having relied upon this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the uncontaminated minds of immeasurable beings as "uncontaminated minds."
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the minds with attachment of immeasurable sentient beings as "minds with attachment.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know, as it truly is, the minds with attachment of immeasurable sentient beings as "minds with attachment"?
Subhūti, that which is the state of attachment of the mind—
That which is the suchness of the mind is not the state of the mind as it truly is;
that which is the suchness of the mind is not the state of the mind possessed of passion.

For in this way, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the minds with passion of immeasurable sentient beings: "minds with passion are minds with passion."
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the minds free from passion of immeasurable beings as "minds free from passion.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know, as it truly is, the minds free from passion of immeasurable beings as "minds free from passion"?
Subhūti, that which is the departure of the mind is not the state of the mind being possessed by passion; rather,
it is the suchness of the mind that is free from passion.
That is not the mind's state of being with passion.
For in this way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, having relied upon this perfection of wisdom, understands, as it truly is, the minds free from passion of immeasurable beings as "minds free from passion."
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the minds of immeasurable sentient beings that are with hatred as "minds with hatred.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know, as it truly is, the minds of immeasurable sentient beings that are with hatred as "minds with hatred"?
Subhūti, that which is the state of being with hatred in the mind—
That which is the suchness of the mind is not the state of being defiled by faults;
that which is the suchness of the mind is not the state of having faults.
For in this way, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the minds with faults of immeasurable sentient beings as "minds with faults."
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the minds of immeasurable sentient beings that are free from hatred as "minds free from hatred.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know, as it truly is, the minds of immeasurable sentient beings that are free from hatred as "minds free from hatred"?
Subhūti, it is that which is the departure of the mind.
That which is the suchness of a mind free from defilement is not a state of defilement in that mind;
that is not a state of defilement in the mind.
For in this way, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the minds free from hatred of immeasurable sentient beings as "minds free from hatred."
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the deluded minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "deluded minds.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know, as it truly is, the deluded minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "deluded minds"?
Subhūti, that which is the state of delusion of the mind—
That which is the suchness of the mind is not the state of delusion of the mind;
that which is the suchness of the mind is not the state of confusion of the mind.
For in this way, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the deluded minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "deluded minds."
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the minds free from delusion of immeasurable beings as "minds free from delusion.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know, as it truly is, the minds free from delusion of immeasurable beings as "minds free from delusion"?
Subhūti, it is that which is the departure of the mind.
That which is the state of a mind free from delusion as it truly is, is not the deludedness of the mind;
that is not the deludedness of the mind.

For it is thus, Subhūti, that the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, knows as they truly are the minds free from delusion of immeasurable beings, [knowing] "the minds are free from delusion, the minds are free from delusion."
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the non-vast minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "non-vast minds.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know, as it truly is, the non-vast minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "non-vast minds"?
Subhūti, those minds are characterized by the yoga of non-arising; they are included within the sphere of non-arising.
In this way, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the non-vast minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "non-vast minds."
Furthermore, Subhūti, relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the vast minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "vast minds.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, relying on this perfection of wisdom, know, as it truly is, the vast minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "vast minds"?
Subhūti, those minds do not diminish.
Those minds do not increase,
nor do those minds disappear,
precisely because those minds do not disappear.
For it is thus, Subhūti, that the Tathāgata, having relied upon this perfection of wisdom, knows, as it truly is, the vast minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "vast minds."
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the non-magnificent minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "non-magnificent minds.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, understand, as it truly is, the non-magnificent minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "non-magnificent minds"?
Subhūti, those minds have no coming, they have no going, and they are not included within any category.

For in this way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, having relied upon this perfection of wisdom, knows truly, as they really are, the non-magnificent minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "non-magnificent minds.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, having relied upon this perfection of wisdom, knows truly, as they really are, the magnificent minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "magnificent minds."
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know truly as they are the vast minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "vast minds"?
Subhūti, those minds are equal through their sameness; they are equal in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
It is in this way, Subhūti, that the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, knows truly as they are the vast minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "vast minds."
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the immeasurable minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "immeasurable minds.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, understand, as it truly is, the immeasurable minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "immeasurable minds"?
Because they are without support, Subhūti, those minds are immeasurable.
For in this way, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the immeasurable minds of immeasurable beings as "immeasurable minds."
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the visible minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "visible minds.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know, as it truly is, the visible minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "visible minds"?
Subhūti, those minds are views of equality; they have the nature of mind.
For in this way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, knows as it really is the visible minds of immeasurable beings as "visible minds.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, knows as it really is the invisible minds of immeasurable beings as "invisible minds."
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know as it really is the invisible minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "invisible minds"?
Because they are without marks and because they are isolated from objects, Subhūti, that mind is invisible to the three eyes or to all [eyes], having entered into the sphere of non-appearance.
It is in this way, Subhūti, that the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, knows as it really is the invisible minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "invisible minds."
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the obstructed minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "obstructed minds.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, understand, as it truly is, the obstructed minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "obstructed minds"?
Subhūti, those minds are conceptualized where they do not exist.
They are empty and dependent upon objective referents.
For it is thus, Subhūti, that the Tathāgata, relying on this perfection of wisdom, understands as they truly are the obstructed minds of immeasurable beings as "obstructed minds.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, relying on this perfection of wisdom, understands as they truly are the unobstructed minds of immeasurable beings as "unobstructed minds."
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know truly as they are the non-obstructed minds of immeasurable beings as "non-obstructed minds"?
Subhūti, those minds are non-dual; they have arisen from what has not arisen.
It is in this way, Subhūti, that the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, knows truly as they are the non-obstructed minds of immeasurable beings as "non-obstructed minds."
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the surpassable minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "surpassable minds.
And how, Subhūti, does he, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, understand, as it truly is, the surpassable minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "surpassable minds"?
Subhūti, it is the suchness (*yathābhūtatā*) of a surpassable mind.
Therein there is no conceiving.
For in this way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, having relied upon this perfection of wisdom, knows as it truly is the surpassable minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "surpassable minds."
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the unsurpassed minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "unsurpassed minds.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, understand, as it truly is, the unsurpassed minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "unsurpassed minds"?
For even the slightest atom of a mind, Subhūti, is unapprehendable;
therefore, those minds are free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).

In this way, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the unsurpassed minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "unsurpassed minds."
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the unconcentrated minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "unconcentrated minds.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know, as it truly is, the unconcentrated minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "unconcentrated minds"?
It is because, Subhūti, those minds are unequally equal and not brought into concentration.
In this way those minds are unconcentrated.

For in this manner, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, having relied upon this perfection of wisdom, knows as it truly is that the unconcentrated minds of immeasurable sentient beings are "unconcentrated minds."
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the concentrated minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "concentrated minds.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know, as it truly is, the concentrated minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "concentrated minds"?
For those minds, Subhūti, are equally concentrated.
In this way, concentrated minds are equal to space.

For it is thus, Subhūti, that the Tathāgata, having relied upon this perfection of wisdom, understands as they truly are the concentrated minds of immeasurable sentient beings, [knowing] "these are concentrated minds."
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, that the unliberated minds of immeasurable sentient beings are "unliberated minds.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know, as it truly is, that the unliberated minds of immeasurable sentient beings are "unliberated minds"?
Subhūti, those minds are liberated by their own nature; they have non-existence as their own nature.
For in this way, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the unliberated minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "unliberated minds."
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the liberated minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "liberated minds.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know, as it truly is, the liberated minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "liberated minds"?
For, Subhūti, the Tathāgata has not apprehended a mind that is past, nor one that is future.
The present is not apprehended, because the mind does not exist.
In this way, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, that the liberated minds of immeasurable beings are "liberated minds."
Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the invisible minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "invisible minds.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, understand, as it truly is, the invisible minds of immeasurable sentient beings as "invisible minds"?
Subhūti, because it does not exist, that mind is invisible;
because it has not come into being, it is unknowable; and because it is not fully established, it is ungraspable by the eye of wisdom or the divine eye.
How much less so by the fleshly eye?
Because they have not come within the range of perception for anyone.
For in this way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, having relied upon this perfection of wisdom, knows as it truly is that the invisible minds of immeasurable beings are invisible minds.
For it is thus, Subhūti, that the perfection of wisdom is the revealer of this world to the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the perfectly enlightened Buddhas.

Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the opening and closing of the eyes of immeasurable and incalculable other beings and other individuals.

And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, know, as they truly are, the opening and closing of the eyes of immeasurable and incalculable other beings and other individuals?
Subhūti, he understands as it truly is that all those [phenomena], when arising, arise dependent upon form;
likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
He understands as it truly is that all those, when arising, arise dependent upon consciousness.
In this regard, Subhūti, how are those open and closed states based on form known by the Tathāgata?
How are feeling, perception, and mental formations [known]?
And how are those open and closed states based on consciousness known by the Tathāgata?
"The Tathāgata exists after death"—this is a matter pertaining to form.
"The Tathāgata does not exist after death"—this is a matter pertaining to form.
"The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death"—this is a matter pertaining to form.
"That the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death" is a category of form (*rūpagata*).
Likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskārāḥ*).
"The Tathāgata exists after death" is a category of consciousness (*vijñānagata*).
"The Tathāgata does not exist after death"—this is a matter pertaining to consciousness.
"The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death"—this is a matter pertaining to consciousness.
"The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death"—this is a matter pertaining to consciousness.

"The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is delusion"—this pertains to form. "The self and the world are non-eternal; this alone is true, all else is delusion"—this pertains to form.
"The self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal; this alone is true, all else is delusion"—this pertains to form.
"The self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal; this alone is true, all else is delusion"—this pertains to form (*rūpa*).
Likewise for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and mental formations (*saṃskāra*).
"The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is delusion"—this pertains to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
"The self and the world are non-eternal; this alone is true, all else is delusion"—this belongs to the sphere of consciousness.
"The self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal; this alone is true, all else is delusion"—this belongs to the sphere of consciousness.
"The self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal; this alone is true, all else is delusion"—this belongs to the sphere of consciousness.

"The self and the world are finite; this alone is true, all else is delusion"—this pertains to form (*rūpa*). "The self and the world are infinite; this alone is true, all else is delusion"—this pertains to form.
"The self and the world are both finite and infinite; this alone is true, all else is delusion"—this pertains to form.
"The self and the world are neither finite nor infinite—this alone is the truth, all else is delusion"—this pertains to form (*rūpa*).
Likewise for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and mental formations (*saṃskāra*).
"The self and the world are finite—this alone is the truth, all else is delusion"—this pertains to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
"The self and the world are infinite; this alone is true, everything else is delusion"—this belongs to the sphere of consciousness.
"The self and the world are both finite and infinite; this alone is true, everything else is delusion"—this belongs to the sphere of consciousness.
“The self and the world are neither finite nor infinite—this alone is true, all else is delusion”: this belongs to the sphere of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
“The soul is identical with the body—this alone is true, all else is delusion”: this belongs to the sphere of form (*rūpa*).
“The soul is one thing and the body another—this alone is true, all else is delusion”: this belongs to the sphere of form.
In the same way, feeling, perception, and mental formations [are considered].
"The soul is this very body; this alone is the truth, all else is delusion"—this belongs to the sphere of consciousness.
"The soul is one thing and the body is another; this alone is the truth, all else is delusion"—this belongs to the sphere of consciousness.

For in this way, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, has known those winkings and blinkings of countless and incalculable other beings, other persons, which are based upon form;
and so too for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Those openings and closings, being dependent upon consciousness, become cognized.

Furthermore, Subhūti, by relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the opening and closing of the eyes of immeasurable and incalculable other beings and other persons.
Here, Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows form.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata know form?
Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows form in the same way that suchness is.
For in this way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows form; in this way, he knows feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Here, Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows consciousness.
And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata know consciousness?
Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows consciousness in the same way that suchness is.
For it is in this way, Subhūti, that the Tathāgata knows consciousness.

For it is in this way, Subhūti, that the Tathāgata, having relied upon this perfection of wisdom, understands as they truly are the opening and closing of the eyes of immeasurable and incalculable other beings and other persons.
For in this way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata designates suchness by means of the suchness of the Tathāgata, the suchness of the aggregates, and the suchness of opening and closing;
and that which is the suchness of the aggregates, Subhūti, is precisely the suchness of the world as well.
For what reason?
For it has been said by the Tathāgata, Subhūti: "The five aggregates are designated as 'the world'.
Therefore, Subhūti, that which is the suchness of the aggregates—
That is the suchness of the world;
that which is the suchness of the world is the suchness of all phenomena.
That which is the suchness of all phenomena is the suchness of the fruit of stream-entry;
that which is the suchness of the fruit of stream-entry is...
That which is the suchness of the fruit of once-returning is the suchness of the fruit of non-returning.
That which is the suchness of the fruit of once-returning is the suchness of the fruit of non-returning.
That which is the suchness of the fruit of non-returning is the suchness of the fruit of arhatship;
that which is the suchness of the fruit of arhatship is...
That is the suchness of pratyekabuddhahood;
that which is the suchness of pratyekabuddhahood is the suchness of the Tathāgata.
For thus, the suchness of the Tathāgata and the suchness of the aggregates, the suchness of all dharmas, and the suchness of all noble śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—

this is one single suchness, free from manifoldness and non-existence, because it is not manifold, not diverse, inexhaustible, unchanging, non-dual, and without division. In this way, Subhūti, this suchness has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata by means of the perfection of wisdom.
For it is thus, Subhūti, that the perfection of wisdom is the revealer of this world to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
For it is thus, Subhūti, that the Tathāgata reveals the world of this world.

And such is the vision of this world: for it is thus, Subhūti, that the perfection of wisdom is the mother, the progenitor, the bringer-forth of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
For in this way, Subhūti, having fully awakened to suchness, the Tathāgata knows the suchness of the world, he knows its non-falsity, and he knows its non-otherness.
And thus, Subhūti, because the Tathāgata has perfectly awakened to suchness, he is called "Tathāgata."
The Elder Subhūti said: "O Blessed One, suchness is profound.
O Blessed One, it is from this suchness that the awakening of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is manifested and revealed.
Who else here, O Blessed One, would have faith in this, other than an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, or an Arhat whose resolve is fulfilled, or a person endowed with right view?"
"For indeed, Blessed One, these points are supremely profound, having been fully awakened to and proclaimed by the Tathāgata.

When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "So it is, Subhūti, so it is. These points are supremely profound, having been fully awakened to and proclaimed by the Tathāgata."
For in this way, Subhūti, this suchness which has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata is inexhaustible; having fully awakened to it, he has declared it to be inexhaustibly inexhaustible.

Then indeed, the sons of the gods belonging to the realm of desire and the realm of form, headed by Śakra, the lord of the gods, and twenty thousand sons of the gods from the Brahma-realm, approached the Blessed One; having bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they stood to one side.
Standing to one side, those sons of the gods from the realm of desire and the realm of form said this to the Blessed One: "Profound, O Blessed One, are the dharmas that are being revealed."
"How, Blessed One, are the characteristics established here?
The Blessed One said: "O sons of gods, 'emptiness' is how the characteristics are established here;
'signlessness' and 'wishlessness,' O sons of gods, are how the characteristics are established here."

"Non-conditioning," "non-arising," "non-cessation," "non-defilement," "non-purification," "non-existence," "nirvāṇa," "the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu)," and "suchness"— O sons of the gods, these are established here as characteristics.
For what reason?
For these characteristics, O sons of the gods, are indeed non-dependent;
for these characteristics, O sons of the gods, are like space;
these characteristics were not established by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha.
These characteristics are not reckoned as form;
likewise, they are not reckoned as feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
These characteristics do not depend upon form.
They do not rely on feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
These characteristics were not established by gods, nor by nāgas, nor by humans, nor by non-humans.
These characteristics cannot be shaken by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
For what reason?
Because even this world, including its gods, humans, and asuras, is characterized by these very marks;
nor have these marks been established by anyone with their hands.
“O sons of the gods, if someone were to say, ‘This space was established by someone,’ would he, O sons of the gods, be speaking correctly?
When this was said, the sons of the gods belonging to the realm of desire and the realm of form said this to the Blessed One: “No, Blessed One; space was not established by anyone.”
For what reason?
Because space, O Blessed One, is unconditioned; space has not been established by anything.
Then the Blessed One addressed those sons of the gods belonging to the realm of desire and the realm of form: "It is even so, sons of the gods;
whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, these characteristics remain exactly as they are. For what reason?"
For just as these things exist, so have they been fully awakened to and declared by the Tathāgata.
Therefore, O sons of the gods, the Tathāgata is called "Tathāgata."
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, these characteristics which have been perfectly awakened to by the Tathāgata are profound.
And the unimpeded knowledge of the Tathāgatas is indeed the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
For the sake of unimpeded knowledge, the perfection of wisdom is the domain of the Tathāgatas."
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "So it is, Subhūti, so it is.
For in this way, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is the revealer of this world to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
Just as, Subhūti, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones dwell depending upon this Dharma, the perfection of wisdom,"
In the very same way, these phenomena have always remained thus;
they have been perfectly awakened to by the Tathāgatas as being without any fixed location.
Therefore, they dwell relying solely upon the Dharma.
They revere, honor, respect, worship, adore, and venerate the Dharma.

Subhūti, it is because this very perfection of wisdom is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones revere, honor, respect, worship, adore, and venerate the perfection of wisdom.
For what reason?
For it is from this perfection of wisdom, Subhūti, that the omniscience of the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the perfectly enlightened Buddhas, is manifested.
The Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the perfectly enlightened Buddhas are grateful and appreciative.
Indeed, Subhūti, those who would speak correctly should say: "He is grateful; he is appreciative."
For those who speak correctly of that Tathāgata say: "He is grateful and appreciative.
Indeed, Subhūti, by whichever vehicle the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has come, and by whichever path he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment—
The Tathāgata favors and protects that very vehicle and that very path out of gratitude and thankfulness for what has been done.
Subhūti, this is to be seen as the Tathāgata’s gratitude and thankfulness.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata has perfectly awakened to all dharmas as uncreated, uncreated; he has perfectly awakened to them as unaltered, unaltered;
he has perfectly awakened to them as unconditioned, unconditioned.
This too, Subhūti, should be seen as the Tathāgata’s gratitude and thankfulness.
For it is by relying on the perfection of wisdom, Subhūti, that the knowledge of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, has proceeded with respect to all dharmas in this way.
By this method also, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is the revealer of this world to the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the perfectly enlightened Buddhas.

When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, since all dharmas are without a knower and without a seer, how then, Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom the revealer of this world to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas?
When this had been said, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"
That you consider it necessary to question the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, regarding this matter—Subhūti has said thus: "All dharmas are without a knower and without a seer.
It is so, Subhūti; it is even so.
All phenomena are without a knower and without a seer.
Subhūti, how is it that all phenomena are without a knower and without a seer?
Subhūti, it is because all phenomena are empty.
For all dharmas, Subhūti, are indeed non-dependent.
Thus, Subhūti, all dharmas are neither knowers nor seers.
In this way, Subhūti, having relied upon the perfection of wisdom, all these dharmas have been fully awakened to by the Tathāgatas.
In this way, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is the revealer of this world for the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas, because form is not seen;
likewise, it is the revealer because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not seen.
For it is in this manner, Subhūti, that the perfection of wisdom becomes the revealer of this world for the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas.
Subhūti said: "How, O Blessed One, does the non-seeing of form occur?
How [does it occur] for feeling, perception, and mental formations?
How, O Blessed One, does the non-seeing of consciousness occur?"
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, if consciousness does not arise with form as its objective support, in this way there is the non-seeing of form.
It is the same for feeling, perception, and mental formations."
If, Subhūti, consciousness does not arise with consciousness as its object,
in that way there is the non-seeing of consciousness.
And that which, Subhūti, is the non-seeing of form—
And, Subhūti, that which is the non-seeing of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
that itself becomes the seeing of the world.
For it is in this way, Subhūti, that the world is seen by the Tathāgata.
For it is in this way, Subhūti, that the perfection of wisdom is the revealer of this world to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
And how, Subhūti, does the perfection of wisdom reveal the world?
Thus, by saying "the world is empty," he indicates the world;
in this way he makes it known,
and in this way he reveals the world.
Thus, by means of the purity of the world, he indicates the world as being inconceivable, the world as being peaceful, and the world as being secluded.
In this way he designates the world; in this way he reveals it.
The twelfth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the World," in the Noble Eight Thousand Line Prajñāpāramitā.
(Vaidya 138) Chapter Thirteen: The Inconceivable.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is profound.”
"Indeed, Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom has appeared for a great task;
indeed, Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom has appeared for an inconceivable task, an incomparable task, an immeasurable task, an incalculable task, and a task equal to the unequaled.
The Blessed One said, "So it is, Subhūti, so it is."
Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom has appeared for a great task.
Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom has appeared for an inconceivable task, an incomparable task, an immeasurable task, an incalculable task, and a task equal to the unequaled.
And how, Subhūti, has this perfection of wisdom appeared for an inconceivable task?
For, Subhūti, the state of a Tathāgata, the state of a Buddha, the state of a Self-Existent One, and omniscience are indeed inconceivable.
Thus, Subhūti, it is by means of an inconceivable function that this perfection of wisdom is present;
for it is not possible to conceive of this with the mind.
For what reason?
Because neither mind, nor volition, nor any mental factor whatsoever functions here as a phenomenon.
And how, Subhūti, is this perfection of wisdom present through its incomparable activity?
Subhūti, it is not possible to conceive of or to weigh the state of a Tathāgata, the state of a Buddha, the state of a Self-Existent One, or the state of omniscience.
For in this way, Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is present through its incomparable activity.
And how, Subhūti, is this perfection of wisdom present through its immeasurable activity?
For, Subhūti, the state of a Tathāgata, the state of a Buddha, the state of a Self-Existent One, and omniscience are indeed immeasurable.
It is in this way, Subhūti, that this perfection of wisdom is present through its immeasurable function.
And how, Subhūti, is this perfection of wisdom present through its incalculable function?
For, Subhūti, the state of a Tathāgata, the state of a Buddha, the state of a Self-Existent One, and omniscience are indeed incalculable.
It is in this way, Subhūti, that this perfection of wisdom is present by means of an incalculable function.
And how, Subhūti, is this perfection of wisdom present by means of a function that is unequaled and equal?
Subhūti, there is no one equal to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Self-Existent, the All-Knowing; how much less anyone superior?
For it is in this way, Subhūti, that this perfection of wisdom is present through its function of being unequaled and equal.
The Elder Subhūti said: "But, Blessed One, is it only Tathāgatahood that is inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled?
Is it likewise only Buddhahood, only Self-Existent-hood, and only Omniscience that are incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled;
or is form also inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled?"
Is it thus that feeling, perception, mental formations,

and consciousness are also inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled; or rather, are all phenomena also inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled?
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "So it is, Subhūti, so it is.
Form, Subhūti, is also inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled;
and the same is true of feeling, perception, and mental formations."
Consciousness, Subhūti, is also inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.
In the same way, Subhūti, all phenomena are also inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.
Why is that?
For, Subhūti, that which is the true nature (dharmatā) of form—
therein there is no mind, no volition, no mental factors, and no deliberation. It is the same for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
For, Subhūti, that which is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of consciousness—
therein there is no mind, no volition, no mental factors, and no deliberation. For, Subhūti, that which is the true nature of all phenomena...
Therein there is no mind, no volition, no mental factors, and no deliberation.
For in this way, Subhūti, form also is inconceivable and incomparable;
likewise feeling, perception, and formations are also so.
Consciousness, too, is inconceivable and incomparable;
likewise, all phenomena are also inconceivable and incomparable.
Form, too, [is so].
Subhūti, it is immeasurable.
In the same way, feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness, Subhūti, are also immeasurable.
All dharmas, Subhūti, are also immeasurable.
Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, no measure of form is perceived.
In the same way, Subhūti, no measure of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is known;
for indeed, Subhūti, no measure of any phenomena whatsoever is known.
For what reason, Subhūti, is the measure of form not discerned?
For what reason [is the measure] of feeling, perception, and mental formations?
For what reason, Subhūti, is the measure of consciousness not discerned?
For what reason, Subhūti, is the measure of all dharmas not perceived?
For, Subhūti, the measure of form does not exist;
likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
For indeed, Subhūti, there is no measure of consciousness;
for indeed, Subhūti, there is also no measure of all phenomena.
For what reason, Subhūti, is there no measure of form?
Is it the same for feeling, perception, and mental formations?
For what reason, Subhūti, is there no measure of consciousness?
For what reason, Subhūti, is there also no measure of all phenomena?
Subhūti, because all dharmas are immeasurable,
form also, Subhūti, is incalculable;
likewise are feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Consciousness, Subhūti, is also incalculable;
all dharmas, Subhūti, are also incalculable, because they transcend all calculation.
Subhūti, form also is unequaled;
likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness, Subhūti, are also unequaled.
In the same way, Subhūti, all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are also unequally equal, because all phenomena, Subhūti, are equal to space.

What do you think, Subhūti: is there anything that is equal to space, or can it be counted, measured, compared, or is there any mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika*), or phenomena (*dharma*) that is its equal?
Subhūti said: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said: "Just so, Subhūti; by this method, all dharmas are also inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.
And these, Subhūti, are the dharmas of the Tathāgata, which are inconceivable because of the cessation of the mind."
They are incomparable because they have transcended all comparison.
Subhūti, "inconceivable" and "incomparable" are designations for this dharma that pertains to consciousness.

Likewise, Subhūti, "immeasurable," "incalculable," and "unequaled" refer to the Tathāgata’s dharmas; they are immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled because they have reached the cessation of all equality, calculation, and measure.

Because they are equal to space in being incalculable and immeasurable, these dharmas are unequaled and equal, incalculable and immeasurable. Because they are equal to space, these dharmas are indeed incomparable and unconditioned.
Therefore, Subhūti, these dharmas are called "incomparable."
Because space is inconceivable, these phenomena are inconceivable; because space is incomparable, these phenomena are incomparable;
because space is immeasurable, these phenomena are immeasurable.
Because space is incalculable, these dharmas are incalculable;
because space is unequaled in its equality, these dharmas are unequaled in their equality.

Furthermore, while this inconceivability, incomparability, immeasurability, incalculability, and unequaled equality were being taught, the minds of five hundred bhikṣus were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging.
The minds of twenty hundred bhikṣuṇīs were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging; the dust-free and stainless Dharma-eye regarding phenomena was purified for sixty hundred upāsakas;
and the dust-free and stainless Dharma-eye regarding phenomena was purified for thirty hundred upāsikās.
And twenty bodhisattvas attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
They were prophesied by the Blessed One to attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) in this very Fortunate Aeon (*bhadrakalpa*).
As for those laymen (*upāsaka*) and laywomen (*upāsikā*) whose dustless and stainless eye of Dharma (*dharma-cakṣus*) regarding all phenomena was purified—
They too have been prophesied by the Blessed One:
their minds, too, will be liberated from the outflows through non-clinging.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Profound, O Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom!
Indeed, O Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom has appeared for a great task.
When this was said, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti: "So it is, Subhūti; so it is."
Profound, Subhūti, is the perfection of wisdom.
It has appeared, Subhūti, for a great task.
Why is that?
For here, Subhūti, omniscience is fully integrated;
here the stage of the Pratyekabuddhas is fully integrated; and here the stage of all Śrāvakas is fully integrated.
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, there were certain royal duties of an anointed Kṣatriya king who has attained power and prowess over his realm,
as well as certain duties concerning the city and certain duties concerning the countryside.
All of those are attended by ministers;
consequently, the king has little concern, as his burden has been taken away.
In the same way, Subhūti, whatever are the qualities of a Buddha, or the qualities of a Pratyekabuddha, or the qualities of a Śrāvaka—
All of them are conjoined with the perfection of wisdom;
therein, the perfection of wisdom performs its function.
Subhūti, it is by this method that this perfection of wisdom is present for the great task: for the non-appropriation and non-adherence to form.

In the same way, for the sake of non-appropriation and non-attachment to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and for the sake of non-appropriation and non-attachment to the fruit of stream-entry.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom is present for the sake of non-appropriation and non-attachment toward the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship;
for the sake of non-appropriation and non-attachment toward pratyekabuddha-enlightenment;
and for the sake of non-appropriation and non-attachment toward omniscience.
Subhūti said: "How, O Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom established for the sake of non-appropriation and non-attachment to omniscience?
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Do you perceive any state of arhatship wherein one might make appropriation or attachment?
Subhūti said: "Certainly not, O Blessed One."
“Blessed One, I do not perceive any such dharma that I might grasp or adhere to as ‘arhatship.
The Blessed One said, “So it is, Subhūti; so it is.
Even I, Subhūti, do not perceive the state of a Tathāgata.”
Therefore, Subhūti, not perceiving suchness as a Tathāgata, I do not grasp it and I do not adhere to it.
For that reason, Subhūti, even omniscience is without grasping and without adherence.
Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, is even omniscience without grasping and without adherence?"

“Blessed One, let it not be that bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have newly set out in the vehicle and possess only limited roots of merit, upon hearing this teaching, will be startled, terrified, or fall into a state of great fear. Rather, Blessed One, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are endowed with the necessary causes, who have performed services for previous Victors, and who have planted roots of merit over a long period of time—
they, having heard this profound perfection of wisdom, will have faith in it.”
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Subhūti; so it is."
Then indeed, those sons of the gods belonging to the realm of desire and the realm of form said this to the Blessed One: "Profound, O Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom;
it is difficult to see and difficult to realize.
Those beings, O Blessed One, will have performed services under previous Victors and will have planted roots of merit for a long time."
Those who will have faith in this profound *prajñāpāramitā*:

if, O Blessed One, all the beings in the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world-system were to practice on the level of a follower by faith for an eon, or for the remainder of an eon; yet someone here were to find pleasure in and seek even a single day’s patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) toward this profound *prajñāpāramitā*—[the latter would be superior].
“O Blessed One, this alone is superior to those.

When this had been said, the Blessed One addressed those sons of the gods from the desire realm and the form realm: “Sons of the gods, if some son of good family or daughter of good family were to hear this profound perfection of wisdom...”
“O sons of the gods, for him, a more rapid attainment of nirvāṇa is to be expected than for those who practice on the stage of the follower by faith for an eon or the remainder of an eon.
Then the sons of the gods of the desire realm and the form realm said this to the Blessed One: “This is a great perfection, Blessed One, namely, the perfection of wisdom.”

Having spoken thus, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and announced, "We shall depart from the presence of the Blessed One," and then they withdrew. Having gone a short distance, they vanished;
and the sons of the gods belonging to the realm of desire returned to the world of desire.
And the sons of the gods belonging to the realm of form established themselves in the Brahma-world.
The thirteenth chapter, titled "The Inconceivable," in the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom.
(Vaidya 142) Chapter Fourteen: The Chapter on Similes.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, as for that bodhisattva mahāsattva..."

Upon merely hearing this profound perfection of wisdom, he has faith in it; he does not shrink back, does not become despondent, does not hesitate, does not falter, does not doubt, and does not waver,
but rather rejoices in the perfection of wisdom.
"From where, Blessed One, has he passed away, and where has he been reborn?

The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who, upon merely hearing this profound perfection of wisdom, will have faith in it, and will not shrink back, will not be cowed, will not become despondent, and will not be bewildered—"
He will not doubt, he will not hesitate;
he will rejoice in seeing and hearing it,
and he will uphold and cultivate this profound perfection of wisdom.
He will not abandon mental attentions associated with the perfection of wisdom, nor will he turn his mind away from them;
he will generate the desire to take it up, preserve it, recite it, master it, and propagate it.
He will form a continuous connection and follow after the Dharma-preacher, never abandoning him;
just as, Subhūti, a cow with a young calf does not abandon her calf.
In the same way, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who, having heard this profound perfection of wisdom, does not abandon the Dharma-preacher as long as this perfection of wisdom remains with him—
whether residing in his body or in the form of a book—
this bodhisattva mahāsattva, Subhūti, has passed away from among humans and has been reborn again among humans.

Subhūti said: "Could it be, Blessed One, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with these very qualities has passed away from other buddha-fields and been reborn here? The Blessed One replied: "It could be so, Subhūti. A bodhisattva mahāsattva who, having attended upon, questioned, and interrogated other Buddhas, Blessed Ones, in other buddha-fields, should be known as one endowed with these very qualities."
Furthermore, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who has passed away from among the Tuṣita devas and has been reborn here should also be known as being endowed with these very same qualities—
by whom the bodhisattva mahāsattva Maitreya was attended upon, questioned, interrogated, and cross-examined concerning this perfection of wisdom.
He, too, should be known as being endowed with these very same qualities.
Furthermore, Subhūti, it may be that this profound perfection of wisdom has been heard by a bodhisattva mahāsattva from the past,
yet it has not been fully questioned.
Not having been questioned or interrogated [about it],
when this profound perfection of wisdom is being taught, there arises in him, who has been reborn among humans once again, a state of doubt and a state of hesitation.
Subhūti, it should be understood that when there is a lack of confidence in the mind,
this bodhisattva was likewise of a nature that did not inquire in the past.
For what reason? Because,
while this profound perfection of wisdom is being taught, there arises a state of hesitation and a state of sluggishness.
There is a lack of dejection in the mind.
Furthermore, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva by whom this profound perfection of wisdom has been heard even in the past,
and who has attended upon it, questioned it, inquired about it, and interrogated it—
whether for one day, or two, or three, or four, or five days—
His faith is temporary at first,
and it may be withdrawn; yet, through inquiry, it becomes once more incapable of being withdrawn.
For what reason?
It is because, Subhūti, it happens thus: by one who has not previously inquired about this perfection of wisdom, nor questioned it thoroughly...
It has not been thoroughly questioned,
nor has it been followed;
for a certain period of time, his inclination persists toward hearing this profound perfection of wisdom.
For a certain period, no desire arises;
yet he is once again uplifted and sinks down,
and his mind becomes unsteady.
And he becomes like a tuft of cotton wool;
this bodhisattva should be known as one who has recently set out in the vehicle.
Having come by means of a new vehicle, that bodhisattva will abandon that faith, that clarity, and that zeal.
That is to say, he will not embrace, follow, or attend upon this profound perfection of wisdom.
For him, one of two states is to be expected: either the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha.
Subhūti, it is just as if a ship traveling upon the great ocean were to break apart, and those on board do not seize a piece of wood or a plank.

Or if they do not cling to a dead body, it should be understood that these people, without even reaching the further shore, will perish in the water. However, Subhūti, those who, when a ship at sea has broken apart, take hold of a log or a plank—
Or if they take hold of a dead body,
Subhūti, it should be known that these will not die in the water;
they will cross over to the far shore in safety and without obstacle.

"Just as grains that are unbroken and undamaged will remain on dry land, even so, Subhūti, it should be known that a bodhisattva who possesses merely a measure of faith, merely a measure of serene confidence, merely a measure of affection, and merely a measure of aspiration, yet does not take hold of the perfection of wisdom, will fall into despondency midway along the path."
"Without even reaching omniscience, they will remain at the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who possess faith and possess patience—
There is interest, there is desire, there is vigor.
There is heedfulness, there is resolute conviction, and there is the superior intention.
There is renunciation,
there is reverence, and there is affection.
There is joy, there is serene confidence, and there is affection.
There exists an unshakable persistence in their commitment to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
and they take hold of the perfection of wisdom.
Thus, for them, that is faith, that is patience, that is inclination, that is desire, that is vigor, that is heedfulness, and that is resolute confidence.

Such is their resolute intention, such their renunciation, such their reverence, such their joy, such their gladness, such their serene faith, and such their love for the sake of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
and having attained the perfection of wisdom, they shall abide in omniscience.
Subhūti, it is just as if a woman or a man were to carry water in an unbaked clay jar;
Subhūti, you should know that this jar will not last long, but will soon break.
"It will dissolve.
For what reason?
Because that jar is as yet unripened.
"He will indeed reach the culmination of the stages.

In the same way, Subhūti, although a bodhisattva possesses faith, possesses patience, possesses inclination, possesses desire, possesses vigor, possesses diligence, possesses resolute conviction, possesses high resolve, and possesses renunciation;
There is reverence, there is affection, there is joy, and there is serene confidence.
There is love and there is the non-abandonment of the burden for the sake of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
yet he remains unaided by the perfection of wisdom and by skill in means.
Subhūti, it should be understood that this bodhisattva will fall into despondency midway on the path.
And what, Subhūti, is the despondency of a bodhisattva midway on the path? It is either the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha.
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a woman or a man with a well-baked jar were to go from a river, or a lake, or a pond, or a well, or from other such reservoirs of water...
If he were to carry water,
Subhūti, it should be known that as he carries that water, "this jar will reach the house safely and without obstacle."
For what reason?
Because it is just as a jar that is thoroughly matured.
In the same way, Subhūti, for whichever bodhisattva there is faith, there is patience, there is delight, and there is aspiration, [he is like that jar].
There is vigor, there is heedfulness, there is resolute conviction, and there is the high resolve.
There is renunciation,
there is reverence, there is affection, and there is joy.
There is serene confidence, there is affection, and there is the quality of not casting off the burden in order to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
and that [aspiration] is embraced by the perfection of wisdom and by skillful means.
Subhūti, it should be understood that this bodhisattva mahāsattva will not fall into despondency midway on the journey;

uninjured and unharmed, he will stand firm in omniscience. Subhūti, it is just as if a man of poor wisdom were to launch upon the water a seafaring ship that has not been caulked, nor prepared for its voyage, which has been tied up for a long time, and into which cargo has already been loaded.
If he were to board it when it was fully loaded and oppressed by a heavy burden,
Subhūti, it should be known that this boat will have such a nature: namely, it will sink in the water with its cargo still unlanded.
"By one [load] his merchandise will be lost, and by the other that ship will be wrecked.
Thus, that caravan leader, unskilled in means, through his faulty wisdom will come to be possessed of a great loss of wealth.
"And he will be deprived of a great mine of jewels.
In the same way, Subhūti, although a bodhisattva possesses faith, possesses patience, possesses inclination, and possesses zeal, [he may still fall away].
There is vigor, there is heedfulness, there is resolute conviction, and there is the superior intention.
There is renunciation,
there is reverence, and there is affection.
There is joy,
there is serene confidence, there is affection, and there is the refusal to lay down the burden in order to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
And if he is devoid of both the perfection of wisdom and skill in means,
Subhūti, it should be known that this bodhisattva, without having reached the jewel-mine of omniscience, will fall away midway and will come to despair.
He will be deprived of his own great interest,
and he will be deprived of the great jewel-mass of the welfare of others;
that is to say, because he has been deprived of the great jewel-mine of omniscience.
Furthermore, Subhūti, what is the bodhisattva’s despondency midway along the path?
It is, namely, the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha.
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a wise caravan leader, having had a sea-going ship well-fastened together, [were to set out upon the ocean].
Having polished it until it is well-refined, having made it well-prepared, having lowered it into the water, having loaded the cargo,
having filled it, and having balanced it, one would travel by means of a suitable wind toward the desired direction in due order; thus, that is called "the vehicle."
Subhūti, it should be understood that this boat will not sink in the water;
this boat will reach that destination which is to be reached by it.
Furthermore, this caravan leader will be joined with great gain, namely, with worldly jewels.

In the same way, Subhūti, for whichever bodhisattva mahāsattva there is faith, there is patience, there is liking, there is desire, there is vigor, there is heedfulness, there is resolute conviction, and there is high resolve.
There is renunciation,
there is reverence, there is affection, and there is joy.
There is serene confidence, there is affection, and there is the refusal to cast off the burden for the sake of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

And he, being embraced by the perfection of wisdom and not separated from skill in means— Subhūti, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva will not collapse midway on the path, nor will he fall into despondency.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva will stand firm in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, it is thus: this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses faith.
There is patience, there is interest, and there is aspiration.
There is vigor, there is heedfulness, there is resolute conviction, and there is the high resolve.
There is renunciation, there is reverence, there is joy.
There is joy, there is clarity, there is affection.
There is an unflagging persistence in order to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And these qualities of his, being embraced by the perfection of wisdom and not separated from skill in means, will not lead to the level of a śrāvaka nor to the level of a pratyekabuddha;
rather, they lead toward omniscience.

Therefore, these dharmas have been brought face-to-face and set forth so that they will lead to his full awakening to this unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Subhūti, it is just as if there were a certain man who was aged, old, advanced in years, being two hundred years of age by birth,
and in his body some disease were to arise— whether from wind, or from bile, or from phlegm, or from a combination of the humors.
"What do you think, Subhūti? Would that man, being unsupported, be able to rise from his bed?
Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "But if, Subhūti, that man were to rise from his bed,"
And yet, he is not even capable of walking a distance of half a krośa. Wasted by that old age and that disease, even if he were to rise from his bed,
that man would still be incapable of proceeding.
In the same way, Subhūti, although a bodhisattva possesses faith, possesses patience, and possesses inclination,
There is zeal, there is energy, and there is heedfulness.
There is resolute conviction, there is noble intention, and there is relinquishment.
There is reverence, there is affection, there is joy.
There is love and there is the non-abandonment of the burden for the sake of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
yet he remains unassisted by the perfection of wisdom and is devoid of skill in means.
Even though he has set out to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nevertheless,
Subhūti, it should be understood that this bodhisattva will collapse midway on the path and will fall into despondency.
Namely, that he will abide on either the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha.
For what reason?
Because he is not sustained by the perfection of wisdom and is devoid of skill in means.
Subhūti, it is just as if there were a man who was aged, elderly, and decrepit, being a hundred and twenty years old by birth;
some kind of disease might arise in his body— whether from wind, bile, phlegm, or a combination of them— and he would rise from his bed.

Then two strong men, supporting him from the left and right sides by firmly grasping his middle as it was already supported, would take hold of him well and say this: "Go, O man, wherever you wish and for as long as you wish to go;
you are well-supported by us."
There will be no fear of falling for you on the way until you have reached that destination where you must go.
In the same way, Subhūti, for whichever bodhisattva mahāsattva there is faith, there is patience, there is inclination, and there is aspiration, [he will not fall back].
There is vigor, there is heedfulness, and there is resolute conviction.
There is resolute intention,
there is relinquishment,
and there is reverence.
There is joy, there is gladness, there is serenity.
There is love and there is the non-abandonment of the burden in order to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
and he is sustained by the perfection of wisdom and is endowed with skill in means.
Subhūti, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva will not perish midway,
nor will he fall into despondency;
this bodhisattva mahāsattva is capable of reaching that state, namely, the state of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The fourteenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Similes," in the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom.
(Vaidya 146) Chapter Fifteen: The Chapter on the Gods.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how should a beginner bodhisattva mahāsattva abide in the perfection of wisdom? How..."

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "In this regard, Subhūti, a beginner bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom should serve, revere, and attend upon spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) who will instruct and advise him in the perfection of wisdom."
And those who shall teach him the meaning of the perfection of wisdom, Subhūti, should be known as the good friends of that bodhisattva mahāsattva.
And they shall teach him the meaning of the perfection of wisdom in this way: "Come, son of good family, apply yourself to the perfection of giving."

In this way, apply yourself to the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom. Whatever gift you give, noble son,
dedicate it all toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And you, son of good family, do not grasp at unexcelled perfect enlightenment by way of form;
likewise, do not [grasp it] by way of feeling, perception, or mental formations.
And you, son of good family, do not grasp at unexcelled perfect enlightenment by way of consciousness.
For what reason?
Because, noble son, omniscience is not to be grasped.
Thus, noble son, whatever morality you maintain... [and so forth] ...whatever patience you accomplish, noble son, [all that is for the sake of omniscience].
Whatever vigor you exert, noble son; whatever meditative concentration you enter, noble son; whatever mastery you cultivate in wisdom, noble son—
Dedicate all of that toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
And you, noble son, do not grasp at unexcelled, perfect enlightenment by way of form;
likewise, do not [grasp it] by way of feeling, perception, or mental formations.
And you, son of good family, do not grasp at unexcelled, perfect enlightenment from the standpoint of consciousness.
Why is that?
Because omniscience, son of good family, is beyond grasping.
"And do not, son of good family, harbor a longing for the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha.
In this way, Subhūti, a beginner bodhisattva mahāsattva should be gradually introduced to the perfection of wisdom by spiritual friends.
Subhūti said: "O Blessed One, the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, who have set out to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, are doers of what is difficult,
having relied upon such a form of giving."
such morality,
such patience,
and such vigor;
Having attained such meditative concentration and such wisdom, although they have mastery over parinirvāṇa, they do not wish to enter parinirvāṇa. Rather,

observing the realm of sentient beings who are most afflicted by suffering, they desire to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and thus they do not tremble before cyclic existence.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "So it is, Subhūti; so it is.

Subhūti, those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who have set out for the welfare of the world, who have set out for the happiness of the world, and who have set out out of compassion for the world, are doers of what is difficult."
We shall become a protection for the world, we shall become a refuge for the world, we shall become a sanctuary for the world.
We shall become the ultimate refuge for the world; we shall become an island for the world;
we shall become light for the world.
"We shall become leaders of the world;
having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, we shall become the refuge of the world"—
with such thoughts, they exert vigor toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

And how, Subhūti, do bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, become a protection for the world? Subhūti, from whatever sufferings belonging to the realm of saṃsāra there are for the world, from those [they protect it].
They protect; they strive for the abandonment of those sufferings;
they arouse vigor.
For in this way, Subhūti, bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, become a protection for the world.

And how, Subhūti, do Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, become a refuge for the world? Subhūti, those beings who are subject to birth, subject to aging, subject to sickness, subject to death, and subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair—
they liberate all those beings from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
In this way, Subhūti, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, become a refuge for the world.
And how, Subhūti, do Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, become a shelter for the world?
It is because, Subhūti, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas teach the Dharma to sentient beings so that they may be free from attachment.
"In this way, Subhūti, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, they become a refuge for the world.
Subhūti asked: "How, Blessed One, does there come to be non-attachment?
The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, it is that which is the non-connection with form."
That is the non-adherence to form;
that which is non-adherence to form is the lack of connection with form.
That which is the non-connection of form is the non-arising and non-ceasing of form;
that which is the non-arising and non-ceasing of form—
That is the non-adherence to form;
that which is the non-adherence to form is the non-connection with form.
This is the non-attachment to form;
likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Subhūti, that which is the non-connection of consciousness—
That is the non-attachment to consciousness.
That which is non-attachment to consciousness is the non-connection with consciousness.
That which is the non-connection of consciousness is the non-arising and non-ceasing of consciousness;
that which is the non-arising and non-ceasing of consciousness—
That is the non-adherence of consciousness.
That which is the non-adherence of consciousness is the non-connection of consciousness; this is the non-adherence of consciousness.
For it is thus, Subhūti, that through the vision and knowledge that all phenomena are unattached and unbound, there comes about non-attachment.
It is thus, Subhūti, that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, become a refuge for the world.
And how, Subhūti, do Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, become a final resort for the world?
Subhūti, that which is the limit of form is not form;
and as the limit is, so is form.
The same applies to feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Subhūti, that which is the further shore of consciousness is not consciousness;
and as is the further shore, Subhūti, so is consciousness; and as is form, Subhūti...
In the same way, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the further shore, as are all phenomena.
Subhūti said: "If, Blessed One, it is as with form..."
In this way, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the further shore, and likewise all phenomena are the further shore.
Indeed, Blessed One, have all phenomena been fully awakened to by the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas?
For what reason is that so?
"For indeed, Blessed One, there is no conceptual construction whatsoever here.
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Subhūti; so it is.
That which is the 'far shore'—in that, there is no conceptual construction whatsoever."
Subhūti, because they are non-conceptual, all dharmas have indeed been fully awakened to by Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, Subhūti, this is also supremely difficult for Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas: that they contemplate all dharmas in such a manner.

They do not realize [them], nor do they become discouraged; rather, they reflect: "In this way these dharmas are to be fully awakened to by us, and having thus fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, we shall teach and proclaim these dharmas."
For it is thus, Subhūti, that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, become the ultimate refuge for the world.
And how, Subhūti, do Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, become islands for the world?
Subhūti, it is just as those places which are surrounded by water, whether in rivers or in the great oceans, are called "islands.
In the same way, Subhūti, form is delimited by the prior and subsequent limits.
In the same way, Subhūti, feeling, perception, and mental formations are so;
likewise, consciousness is delimited by its prior and subsequent limits.
By this delimitation, Subhūti, all phenomena are delimited by their prior and subsequent limits.
And that which, Subhūti, is the discernment of all dharmas— this is peaceful, this is sublime.
This is final nirvana; this is as it truly is; this is non-erroneous.
In this way, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, become islands for the world.
And how, Subhūti, do bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, become lights for the world?
Here, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment...

For a long time, beings have been enveloped by the veil of the eggshell of ignorance and overwhelmed by darkness; [the Bodhisattvas], illuminating them with wisdom, dispel all the blinding darkness of nescience.
It is in this way, Subhūti, that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, become lights for the world.
And how, Subhūti, do bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, become leaders of the world?

Here, Subhūti, bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, teach the Dharma for the sake of the non-arising and non-ceasing of the intrinsic nature of form;
likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
They teach the Dharma for the sake of the non-arising and non-ceasing of consciousness by its very nature;
they teach the Dharma for the sake of the non-arising and non-ceasing of the dharmas of ordinary persons by their very nature;
and they teach the Dharma for the sake of the non-arising and non-ceasing of the dharmas of the śrāvakas by their very nature.
They teach the Dharma for the sake of the non-arising and non-ceasing of the nature of the dharmas of the Pratyekabuddhas;
they teach the Dharma for the sake of the non-arising and non-ceasing of the nature of the dharmas of the Bodhisattvas;
