and they teach the Dharma for the sake of the non-arising and non-ceasing of the nature of the dharmas of the Buddhas.
They teach the Dharma for the sake of the non-arising and non-ceasing of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
In this way, Subhūti, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they become leaders of the world.
And how, Subhūti, do Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, become the refuge of the world?
In this regard, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, teach the Dharma to the world, saying: "Form has the nature of space.
Likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations;
they teach the Dharma, saying: "Consciousness has the nature of space."
In the same way, Subhūti, all phenomena have the nature of space; they have no coming, no going, and are equal to space.

Just as space has no coming, no going, is unmade, unmodified, unconditioned, non-abiding, non-stationary, non-fixed, unarisen, and unceasing—so too, Subhūti, all phenomena have no coming, no going, are unmade, unmodified, unconditioned, non-abiding, non-stationary, non-fixed, unarisen, and unceasing. Because they are like space, they are free from conceptual construction.
For what reason? Subhūti, that which is the emptiness of form neither comes nor goes.
In the same way, it is with feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Subhūti, that which is the emptiness of consciousness neither comes nor goes.
In the same way, Subhūti, the emptiness of all phenomena neither comes nor goes.
Why is that?
For, Subhūti, all dharmas have emptiness as their destination;
they do not transcend that destination.
For, Subhūti, all dharmas have the signless as their destination.
They do not transcend that destination,
Subhūti, for all dharmas have the wishless as their destination;
they do not transcend that destination.
For, Subhūti, all dharmas have a nature that is without volitional construction;
they do not transcend that nature.
For all phenomena, Subhūti, have non-arising as their destination;
they do not deviate from that destination.
For all phenomena, Subhūti, have non-birth as their destination.
They do not transcend that state.
For, Subhūti, all dharmas have non-existence as their state;
they do not transcend that state.
For, Subhūti, all phenomena have the nature of a dream;
they do not transcend that nature.
For, Subhūti, all phenomena have the nature of a self.
They do not transcend that course;
for, Subhūti, all dharmas have an infinite course,
and they do not transcend that course.
For, Subhūti, all dharmas have peace as their destination;
they do not deviate from that destination.
For, Subhūti, all dharmas have nirvāṇa as their destination.
They do not transcend that state; for, Subhūti, all dharmas have a state from which there is no turning back,
and they do not transcend that state.
For all dharmas, Subhūti, are without coming; they do not transcend that state of non-coming. For all dharmas, Subhūti, are without going.
They do not transcend that state;
for, Subhūti, all phenomena have an immovable state,
and they do not transcend that state.
For, Subhūti, all phenomena have form as their destination;
they do not transcend that destination.
The same applies to feeling, perception, and mental formations.
For, Subhūti, all dharmas have consciousness as their destination;
they do not transcend that destination.
For, Subhūti, all dharmas have the state of an Arhat, the state of a Pratyekabuddha, and Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Enlightenment as their destination.
They do not transcend that destination.
Therefore, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, they teach the Dharma, saying: "All phenomena have space as their destination.
In this way, Subhūti, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, become the destination for the world.
Subhūti said: "Lord, who will understand this profound perfection of wisdom?

The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have practiced in the presence of former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas, and who have ripened their roots of merit—those bodhisattvas, Subhūti, should be known as the ones who will understand this profound perfection of wisdom."
Subhūti said: "Blessed One, what will be the nature of those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who shall understand this profound perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas will have a nature that is secluded and fit for discipline."
Those who shall understand this profound perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti said: "Blessed One, will those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas have such a destiny alone?
Having fully awakened to this very destiny, will they teach this very destiny to sentient beings?
Will they thus become the refuge for sentient beings?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "So it is, Subhūti; so it is.
Subhūti, those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, will have exactly such a destination.
Having fully awakened to this very destination, they will teach this very destination to sentient beings."
In this way, they will become the refuge for sentient beings.
For it is thus, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, will become the refuge for immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings.

Subhūti said: "O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is a doer of what is difficult, he by whom this armor has been donned with the thought: 'I shall bring immeasurable and incalculable beings to final nirvāṇa.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "So it is, Subhūti; so it is.
Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is a doer of what is difficult, he by whom this armor has been donned with the thought: 'I shall bring immeasurable and incalculable beings to final nirvāṇa.'"
Furthermore, Subhūti,
this armor of the bodhisattva mahāsattva who is clad in the great armor is not bound to form, nor is it bound for the sake of form;
likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
It is not connected with consciousness, nor is it connected for the sake of consciousness;
it is not connected with the level of the śrāvaka, nor is it connected for the sake of the level of the śrāvaka;
it is not connected with the level of the pratyekabuddha, nor is it connected for the sake of the level of the pratyekabuddha.
Nor is it connected to the stage of a Buddha, nor is it connected for the sake of the stage of a Buddha.
Why is that?
Subhūti, this armor of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has donned the great armor is, indeed, unconnected with all dharmas.
Subhūti said: "Blessed One, for this bodhisattva mahāsattva who is thus clad in the great armor and who courses in such profound perfection of wisdom, three things are not to be expected.
What are these three?"
Namely, the level of a śrāvaka, or the level of a pratyekabuddha, or the level of a buddha.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, perceiving what purpose do you say this: 'Of this bodhisattva mahāsattva who has donned such a great armor'?"
For one who courses in such profound *prajñāpāramitā*, three states are not to be expected.
Which three? Namely, the level of a *śrāvaka*, the level of a *pratyekabuddha*, or the level of a Buddha.

Subhūti, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that for this bodhisattva mahāsattva who is thus clad in such great armor and who courses in such profound perfection of wisdom, there could be the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha; rather,
only the level of a Buddha is to be expected for him, since he has donned this armor for the sake of all sentient beings.
Subhūti said: "O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is profound;
it is not to be cultivated by anyone, for no one has ever cultivated it."
Neither does anyone cultivate it, nor will anyone cultivate it,
nor is there anything to be cultivated.
It should not be cultivated anywhere.
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, in the perfection of wisdom, no dharma whatsoever is fully established.
“O Blessed One, this cultivation of space is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
O Blessed One, this cultivation of all phenomena is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
O Blessed One, this cultivation of non-attachment is indeed the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.”
“O Blessed One, this cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is an infinite cultivation;
O Blessed One, this cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is a non-existent cultivation;
O Blessed One, this cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is a cultivation of non-appropriation.”
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "So it is, Subhūti; so it is.

For, Subhūti, by dwelling in the dwelling of this profound perfection of wisdom, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be examined as one who is irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment—how indeed, Subhūti, is a bodhisattva..."

The Mahāsattva does not form an attachment to this profound perfection of wisdom. Does he not become attached to the speech or the counsel of others? Does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva not proceed by relying on the faith of another?

"Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when this profound perfection of wisdom is being taught, not shrink back, not cower, not turn his back, not tremble, not be terrified, and not fall into terror; does he not hesitate, does he not doubt, and does he not falter, but rather plunges into it, gains faith in it, and rejoices in the seeing and hearing of the perfection of wisdom?"
Subhūti, it should be known that this person has also inquired about the perfection of wisdom in the past.
Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, when the profound perfection of wisdom is being taught, he does not tremble, does not become terrified, and does not fall into fear.

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, when this profound perfection of wisdom is being taught, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not tremble, is not terrified, and does not fall into terror, by what mode, Blessed One, has that perfection of wisdom been investigated by him?
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is by means of a mental continuum inclined toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) that the perfection of wisdom has been investigated by that bodhisattva mahāsattva."
Subhūti asked: "How, Blessed One, is the mental continuum directed toward omniscience?

The Blessed One replied: "By means of a continuum inclined toward space, Subhūti; by means of a continuum sloping toward space, Subhūti; by means of a continuum leaning toward space, Subhūti, the mental continuum is directed toward omniscience.
Furthermore, Subhūti, that which is the directing of the mental continuum toward omniscience—"
This, Subhūti, is that investigation.
Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, omniscience is indeed immeasurable.
For all-knowledge, Subhūti, is immeasurable.
That which, Subhūti, is immeasurable and infinite is not form, not feeling, not perception, not mental formations, not consciousness; it is not attainment, not realization, and not achievement.

There is no path, no fruit of the path, no gnosis, and no consciousness; there is no arising and no destruction, no production and no passing away, no cessation, no cultivation, and no non-cultivation;
it is not made by anyone, it does not come from anywhere, it does not go anywhere, it does not abide in any location, nor does it abide in any particular place.
Rather, it is reckoned as "immeasurable and measureless.
Due to the immeasurability of space, there is the immeasurability of omniscience;
and that which is immeasurability—
It cannot be fully realized by anyone;

it is not [realized] by means of form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations, nor consciousness; nor by the perfection of generosity, nor the perfection of ethical discipline, nor the perfection of patience, nor the perfection of vigor, nor the perfection of meditative concentration, nor the perfection of wisdom.
It is possible to fully awaken to it.
For what reason? Because, Subhūti, form itself is omniscience.
In the same way, Subhūti, feeling itself, perception itself, mental formations themselves,
and consciousness itself are indeed omniscience; for the perfection of giving itself, Subhūti, is indeed omniscience.

For it is precisely the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom, Subhūti, that is omniscience.

Then indeed Śakra, the lord of the gods, together with the sons of the gods belonging to the realm of desire, and Brahmā Sahāpati, together with the sons of the gods belonging to the realm of form, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and stood to one side.

Standing to one side, Śakra, the lord of the gods, together with the sons of the gods of the realm of desire, and Brahmā Sahāpati, together with the sons of the gods of the realm of form, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
—Profound, O Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom; difficult to fathom, O Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom;
difficult to see, O Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom.
“Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to understand.

It was with this very purpose in view that the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened One— immediately upon awakening to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment while seated at the seat of awakening— allowed his mind to incline toward a lack of exertion rather than toward teaching the Dharma.”

When this had been said, the Blessed One addressed Śakra, the lord of the gods, the sons of the gods of the desire realm, Brahmā Sahāpati, and the sons of the gods of the form realm: "So it is, O sons of the gods;
so it is!
Indeed, O sons of the gods, this perfection of wisdom is profound."
O sons of the gods, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to fathom;
O sons of the gods, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to see;
O sons of the gods, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to realize.

Perceiving this very purpose, as soon as the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, had awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and was seated at the seat of awakening, his mind inclined toward a lack of exertion rather than toward teaching the Dharma, thinking: "Alas, this Dharma I have awakened to is profound!"
Wherein no one has awakened, no one will awaken, and no one is awakening—
this is the profundity of the Dharma.
Through the profundity of space, this Dharma is profound.
"This Dharma is profound because of the profundity of the self;
this Dharma is profound because of the non-coming of all dharmas;
this Dharma is profound because of the non-going of all dharmas—thus have I fully awakened to it."

When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, the sons of the gods belonging to the realm of desire, Brahmā Sahāpati, and the sons of the gods belonging to the realm of form, said this to the Blessed One: "It is wonderful, Blessed One!
It is marvelous, Sugata!
This Dharma that is being taught is contrary to the entire world."
And for the sake of favoring all phenomena, O Blessed One, this Dharma is taught;
yet the world proceeds by means of grasping.
The fifteenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Gods," in the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom.
(Vaidya 153) Chapter Sixteen: Suchness.
Then the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, indeed, this Dharma that is being taught is the non-apprehension of all dharmas."

“Blessed One, this Dharma is not obstructed anywhere. Indeed, Blessed One, this Dharma has the characteristic of non-obstruction because, through its equality with space, no state whatsoever is apprehended.
Indeed, Blessed One, this Dharma has the characteristic of being peerless because it is without a second.”
"O Bhagavat, this Dharma is indeed without characteristics, because it is without an adversary;
O Bhagavat, this Dharma is indeed without a footing, because it is unproduced;
O Bhagavat, this Dharma is indeed non-arising, because it is the non-arising in all modes of rebirth."
"Truly, O Blessed One, this Dharma is pathless, because no path whatsoever is to be found."

Then indeed, Śakra, lord of the gods, Brahmā Sahāpati, and those sons of the gods belonging to the realms of desire and form, said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, this elder noble Subhūti has truly been born after the Blessed One! For what reason?"
For indeed, Blessed One, whatever dharma this noble Elder Subhūti teaches,
he teaches that very dharma by taking emptiness as his starting point.

Then the venerable Subhūti addressed Śakra, the lord of the gods, Brahmā Sahāpati, and those sons of the gods belonging to the realms of desire and form, saying: "Sons of the gods, as for what you have said— that this Elder Subhūti is born after the manner of the Tathāgata— "
Because he is unborn, the Elder Subhūti is born after the Tathāgata;
the Elder Subhūti is born after the suchness of the Tathāgata. Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata has neither come nor gone, so too is the Elder Subhūti.
For in this way, Subhūti, the suchness of Subhūti has neither come nor gone;
for in this way, the Elder Subhūti is born after the suchness of the Tathāgata;
from the very beginning, the Elder Subhūti has been born after the suchness of the Tathāgata.
For what reason?
Because that which is the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of all phenomena.
That which is the suchness of all phenomena is the suchness of the Tathāgata;
and that which is the suchness of the Tathāgata is [the suchness of all phenomena].
And that which is the suchness of all phenomena,
that itself is the suchness of the Elder Subhūti;
the Elder Subhūti is born after the manner of that suchness.
Therefore, he is born after the Tathāgata;
and that suchness is non-suchness;
he is born after that suchness.
For in this way, the Elder Subhūti is born after the manner of the Tathāgata;
by that very stability which is the stability of the Tathāgata’s suchness, the Elder Subhūti is born after the manner of the Tathāgata.
Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata is unchanging and immutable,
non-conceptual and free from conceptualization,
so too is the suchness of Subhūti unchanging and immutable.
It is non-conceptual and free from conceptualization.
For in this way, the Elder Subhūti, through that suchness, is unchanging and immutable, non-conceptual and free from conceptualization; he is born after the manner of the Tathāgata.
And just as the suchness of the Tathāgata is unchanging, immutable, non-conceptual, and free from conceptualization, [so too is Subhūti].
It is nowhere obstructed;
likewise, the suchness of all phenomena is unchanging, immutable, non-conceptual, and free from conceptualization,
and it is nowhere obstructed.
For what reason? Because that which is the suchness of the Tathāgata is the same as the suchness of all phenomena.
This suchness is one alone, non-dual, and without division; it is the non-dual suchness.
Suchness is not anywhere, nor does suchness come from anywhere.
It is not the suchness of anything;
because it is not the suchness of anything, that suchness is non-dual, without division, the suchness of non-duality.
For in this way, the Elder Subhūti is born after the Tathāgata by virtue of the uncreated suchness;
and that which is uncreated suchness is never not suchness.
And since that suchness is never not suchness, therefore that suchness is non-dual, without division, the non-dual suchness.
For in this way, the Elder Subhūti is born after the Tathāgata;
just as the suchness of the Tathāgata is non-conceptual and free from conceptualization regarding all things and all dharmas everywhere,
so too the suchness of Subhūti is non-conceptual and free from conceptualization regarding all things and all dharmas everywhere.

In this very way, both the Tathāgata produced by the suchness of the Tathāgata and Subhūti are non-dual; these two are undestroyed and indivisible because no distinction between them can be apprehended.
Thus, the Elder Subhūti is born after the manner of the Tathāgata;
for just as the suchness of the Tathāgata is not other than the suchness of all phenomena, so it is with him.
For in this way, Subhūti, the suchness of Subhūti is not other than the suchness of all dharmas;
that which is not other than the suchness of all dharmas is the suchness of nothing whatsoever.
That very suchness is the suchness of all phenomena;
the Elder Subhūti has approached that suchness by following its non-different suchness.
And herein, no one at all has approached any following whatsoever.
For in this way, the Elder Subhūti has been born after the manner of the Tathāgata:
just as the suchness of the Tathāgata is neither past, nor future, nor present,
so too the suchness of all phenomena is neither past, nor future, nor present.
For in this way, the Elder Subhūti, having conformed to that suchness, is said to have "conformed to the Tathāgata.
Indeed, by conforming to the suchness of the Tathāgata, he has conformed to suchness; by the suchness of the Tathāgata, he has conformed to the suchness of the past.
By the suchness of the past, he has conformed to the suchness of the Tathāgata.
The suchness of the future is followed by the suchness of the Tathāgata;
the suchness of the Tathāgata is followed by the suchness of the future;
the suchness of the present is followed by the suchness of the Tathāgata.
Through the suchness of the present, he has followed the suchness of the Tathāgata;
through the suchness of the Tathāgata, he has followed the suchness of the past, future, and present;
and through the suchness of the past, future, and present, he has followed the suchness of the Tathāgata.
For thus, Subhūti, the suchness of Subhūti and the suchness of the past, future, and present, and the suchness of the Tathāgata—these are non-dual, they are not divided.
Likewise, the suchness of all phenomena and the suchness of Subhūti—these are non-dual, they are not divided.
And that very suchness which belonged to the Blessed One when he was a bodhisattva...
That very suchness belongs to the Blessed One who has awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This is that suchness,
by which suchness a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, receives the designation "Tathāgata."
Furthermore, while this suchness of the Tathāgata was being taught, at that moment this great earth shook, trembled, and quaked in six ways with eighteen great omens.
It shook, it moved, it trembled violently; it quivered, it swayed, it vibrated intensely;
it resounded, it echoed, it reverberated loudly.
It quaked, it quaked violently, it quaked intensely; it roared, it roared loudly, it roared intensely, as the Tathāgata was awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, the Elder Subhūti addressed those sons of the gods: "In this way, O sons of the gods, the Elder Subhūti has been born after the manner of the Tathāgata."

Furthermore, Subhūti the Elder is not born after the manner of form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations, nor consciousness; he is not born after the manner of the fruit of stream-entry, nor the fruit of once-returning, nor the fruit of non-returning, nor the fruit of arhatship; he is not born after the manner of pratyekabuddhahood, nor is he born after the manner of buddhahood.
For what reason?
Because those phenomena do not exist and are not apprehended by which one might be reborn, nor are there those who would be reborn.
For it is in this way that the Elder Subhūti has been born after the Tathāgata.
Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, this practice is profound, namely suchness.
When this was said, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "So it is, Śāriputra, so it is.
This practice, Śāriputra, is profound, namely suchness."
Furthermore, while this teaching on suchness was being expounded, the minds of three hundred bhikṣus were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging;
the dust-free and stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena was purified in five hundred bhikṣuṇīs;
and five thousand sons of gods who had performed prior preparations attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena.
And the minds of sixty bodhisattvas were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging.

Then the venerable Śāriputra, perceiving that the minds of those bodhisattvas were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging, addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, by which the minds of these bodhisattvas are liberated from the outflows through non-clinging?
The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, these bodhisattvas have attended upon five hundred Buddhas."
In every case, they had given gifts, maintained ethical discipline, perfected patience, exerted vigor, and cultivated the meditative absorptions;
yet, these bodhisattvas were indeed not embraced by the perfection of wisdom and were devoid of skill in means.
Moreover, Śāriputra, although these bodhisattvas possessed the path—whether it be emptiness, the practice of the signless, or mental attention directed toward the wishless—
And yet, because they were devoid of skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*), they have realized the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and emerged on the level of the disciples (*śrāvaka-bhūmi*),
not on the level of the Buddhas (*buddha-bhūmi*).

Śāriputra, it is as if, for example, there were a winged bird whose body were a hundred yojanas, or two hundred yojanas, or three hundred yojanas, or four hundred yojanas, or five hundred yojanas in size;
while dwelling among the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, it would think that it must come to Jambūdvīpa.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, that bird might have wings that have not yet grown, or its wings might be withered, or its wings might be severed.
Suppose that bird were to think, "I shall cast myself down from the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa gods and land here in Jambūdvīpa.

Then, as that winged bird is falling from there, while remaining in the midst of the sky and atmosphere, a thought might occur to its mind: "O, would that I could return once more to the Trāyastriṃśa gods!
What do you think, Śāriputra—is that winged bird capable of returning once more to the Trāyastriṃśa gods?
The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Certainly not, Blessed One.

The Blessed One said: "If, however, it were to think: 'Oh, that I might land in Jambūdvīpa unmade and uninjured,' what do you think, Śāriputra—would that bird, the śakuni, land in Jambūdvīpa unmade and uninjured?"

Śāriputra said: "Certainly not, Blessed One. That man, Blessed One, would be ruined and destroyed; having fallen into Jambudvīpa, he would meet death or suffer pain amounting to death. For what reason?"
For it is thus, Blessed One, that this occurs: although he possesses a great physical body, he has no wings, and from on high he falls down.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra: "So it is, Śāriputra; so it is.

Moreover, Śāriputra, even if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated the thought of unexcelled perfect enlightenment, were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, giving gifts and guarding morality..."
One should accomplish patience,
exert vigor,
and [cultivate] the meditative concentrations.
He would enter [into meditative absorption],
and his resolve would be great, and his production of the thought of awakening would be great for the sake of fully awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
If this person were not sustained by the perfection of wisdom and were devoid of skillful means,
they would thus fall to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attends to and retains the ethical discipline, that concentration, that wisdom, that liberation, and that knowledge and vision of liberation of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present, by means of the application of signs.

He does not know and does not see the ethical discipline (*śīla*) of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones; he does not know and does not see their meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), or the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśana*).
Not knowing and not seeing these, he hears the word "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*).
He takes that sound as a sign;
having taken that sound as a sign, he desires to dedicate it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
From this, it should be known: "This one will remain on the level of a śrāvaka or on the level of a pratyekabuddha."
For what reason?
It is because, Śāriputra, it is thus: one who is not sustained by the perfection of wisdom and is devoid of skill in means.
Śāriputra said: "As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken, Blessed One, if a bodhisattva is not sustained by the perfection of wisdom and is devoid of skill in means,
then even if he is endowed with a great accumulation of merit, yet remains separated from spiritual friends,
there is doubt as to whether he will attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Therefore, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should cultivate the perfection of wisdom and should become skilled in means.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra: "So it is, Śāriputra; so it is."
Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva is not sustained by the perfection of wisdom and is devoid of skill in means,
then even though he may be endowed with a great accumulation of merit, he remains bereft of spiritual friends.
He has doubt regarding the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Therefore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should cultivate the perfection of wisdom and should become skilled in means.

Then indeed Śakra, the lord of the gods, together with the sons of the gods belonging to the realm of desire, and Brahmā Sahāpati, together with the sons of the gods belonging to the realm of form, said this to the Blessed One: "Profound, O Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom;
difficult to realize, O Blessed One, is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
“Blessed One, it is extremely difficult to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then the Blessed One addressed those sons of the gods of the desire realm, headed by Śakra, the lord of gods, and those sons of the gods of the form realm, headed by Mahābrahmā, the lord of Sahā:
“It is so, sons of the gods; it is even so.”
"O sons of the gods, this perfection of wisdom is profound.
Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is difficult to realize;

unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is extremely difficult to realize for those who possess poor wisdom, who lack vigor, who have inferior resolve, who are unskilled in means, and who associate with evil friends."
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Regarding what the Blessed One has thus said—that 'unexcelled, perfect enlightenment is difficult to realize;
unexcelled, perfect enlightenment is extremely difficult to realize'—how, Blessed One, is unexcelled, perfect enlightenment difficult to realize?"
Supreme and perfect enlightenment is extremely difficult to realize, yet there is nothing therein that is realized. Why is that?
Because, O Blessed One, all dharmas are empty;
there is no dharma whatsoever that can be fully awakened to as a dharma.
For in this way, O Blessed One, all dharmas are empty.
Blessed One, even that dharma for the sake of abandoning which a dharma is taught does not exist;
likewise, he who would fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment [does not exist].
That which is to be fully awakened to,
that which one would know, and that which is to be known— (Vaidya 157)
"All these phenomena are empty.
By this reasoning as well, Blessed One, it occurs to me that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is easily realized; it is not difficult to realize.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, because it is non-arising, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is difficult to realize."
Subhūti, because it is non-existent, unexcelled perfect enlightenment is difficult to realize;
Subhūti, because it is free from conceptual construction, unexcelled perfect enlightenment is difficult to realize;
Subhūti, because it is not fabricated, unexcelled perfect enlightenment is difficult to realize.
Unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment is extremely difficult to realize.
Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: "Venerable Subhūti, even by this formulation, 'it is empty,' it is difficult to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening;
it is most difficult to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
For what reason?"
For indeed, Venerable Subhūti, it does not occur to space that "I shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
And in this same way, Venerable Subhūti, these dharmas are to be fully awakened to.
Why is that?
"For indeed, Venerable Subhūti, all dharmas are equal to space.

And if, Venerable Subhūti, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment were something that could be fully realized through its own intrinsic nature, then bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā would not turn back from unsurpassed perfect enlightenment."

Therefore, venerable Subhūti, since as many bodhisattvas as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā turn back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, it is understood from this, venerable Subhūti, that unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment is difficult to realize; indeed, unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment is extremely difficult to realize.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, does form turn back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?
Śāriputra replied: "Certainly not, venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said: "Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, is that dharma other than form?"
"Who is it that turns back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?
He replied, "Certainly not, Venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said, "But then, Venerable Śāriputra, does feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness turn back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?"
He said: "No indeed, venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said: "But then, venerable Śāriputra, is that dharma which turns back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment something other than feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?"
He said: "No indeed, venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said: "But then, venerable Śāriputra, does that which is the suchness of form turn back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?"
He said: "No indeed, venerable Subhūti.

Subhūti said: "But then, venerable Śāriputra, is that which is the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, the suchness of mental formations, and the suchness of consciousness [the same as the suchness of form]?"
"Does it turn back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?
He replied, "Certainly not, Venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said, "But then, Venerable Śāriputra, is that dharma other than the suchness of form?"
"Whoever turns back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?
Śāriputra replied, "Certainly not, venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said, "But then, venerable Śāriputra, is there anyone else apart from the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, and the suchness of mental formations?"
"Is there any phenomenon other than the suchness of consciousness that turns back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?
He replied, "Certainly not, Venerable Subhūti."
Subhūti said: "Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, does form fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? He replied: "No indeed, Venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said: "Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, do feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?"
He said: "No indeed, venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said: "But then, venerable Śāriputra, does that dharma exist apart from form?"
"Who is it that awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
He replied, "Certainly not so, venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said, "But then, venerable Śāriputra, is it apart from feeling, perception, and mental formations?"
"Is that phenomenon which fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment anything other than consciousness?
He replied, "Certainly not, Venerable Subhūti."
Subhūti said: "But, venerable Śāriputra, does the suchness of form awaken to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment? He replied: "No indeed, venerable Subhūti.

Subhūti said: "But, venerable Śāriputra, does the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, the suchness of mental formations, or the suchness of consciousness awaken to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment?"
He said: "No indeed, Venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said: "But then, Venerable Śāriputra, is that dharma which awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment anything other than the suchness of form?"
He said: "No indeed, venerable Subhūti.

Subhūti said: "But then, venerable Śāriputra, is that dharma other than the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, the suchness of mental formations, and other than the suchness of consciousness?"
"Who is it that awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
He replied, "Certainly not, Venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said, "But then, Venerable Śāriputra, is form that which is to be awakened to in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
He said: "No indeed, venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said: "But then, venerable Śāriputra, is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness to be awakened to in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?
He said: "No indeed, venerable Subhūti."

Subhūti said: "Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, is that dharma which is to be awakened to in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment other than form? He replied: "Certainly not, venerable Subhūti."

Subhūti said: "Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, is that dharma which is to be awakened to in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment something other than feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness? He replied: "Certainly not, venerable Subhūti."
Subhūti said: "Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, is the suchness of form (rūpa-tathatā) to be awakened to in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? He replied: "Certainly not, venerable Subhūti.

Subhūti said: "Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, is the suchness of feeling (vedanā-tathatā), the suchness of perception (saṃjñā-tathatā), the suchness of mental formations (saṃskāra-tathatā), and the suchness of consciousness (vijñāna-tathatā) to be awakened to in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?"
He said: "No indeed, venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said: "But then, venerable Śāriputra, is that dharma which is to be awakened to in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment something other than the suchness of form?"
He said: "No indeed, venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said: "But then, venerable Śāriputra, is that dharma other than the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, the suchness of mental formations, and the suchness of consciousness?"
"Who is to be awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
He replied, "Certainly not, venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said, "What do you think, venerable Śāriputra? Does suchness turn back from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
He said: "No indeed, venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said: "What do you think, venerable Śāriputra—is there any such dharma within suchness that turns back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?"
He said: "Certainly not, Venerable Subhūti.

Subhūti said: "Then, Venerable Śāriputra, what is that dharma which turns back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—that dharma which stands within that very nature of phenomena (dharmatā) by way of the non-abiding in all dharmas?"
Furthermore, Śāriputra, what is that dharma which is suchness?
Or, venerable Śāriputra, will suchness ever undergo reversal? He replied: "Certainly not, venerable Subhūti."

Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāriputra, since all dharmas are thus unapprehendable in truth and in their established nature, what dharma is there that will turn back from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
When this was said, the venerable Śāriputra [addressed] the venerable [Subhūti].

He said this to Subhūti: "By that very nature of the way of the Dharma which the Venerable Elder Subhūti explains, there is no dharma whatsoever that turns back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, as for these three types of persons belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who have been described by the Tathāgata,"
There is no establishment of these three;
for there is indeed only one vehicle, namely the Buddha-vehicle, the Bodhisattva-vehicle, according to the teaching of the Venerable Subhūti.

Then the venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, does the elder venerable Subhūti not acknowledge even a single bodhisattva— whether one belonging to the vehicle of the disciples, the vehicle of the solitary buddhas, or the Great Vehicle?"
"This Venerable Elder Subhūti should first be questioned.

Then the Venerable Śāriputra said this to the Venerable Subhūti: "But, Venerable Subhūti, do you not acknowledge even a single bodhisattva—whether one belonging to the vehicle of the disciples, the vehicle of the solitary buddhas, or the Great Vehicle?"

Subhūti said: "Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, in that suchness which is the suchness of suchness, do you perceive even a single bodhisattva therein—whether belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the Great Vehicle?
Śāriputra replied: "Certainly not, venerable Subhūti."
"Even suchness itself is not apprehended in three ways, let alone a bodhisattva.
Subhūti said: "But, venerable Śāriputra, is suchness then apprehended even by a single way?"
Śāriputra said: "Indeed not, Venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said: "Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, do you perceive even a single bodhisattva-dharma within suchness? Śāriputra said: "Indeed not, Venerable Subhūti."

Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāriputra, since that dharma of a bodhisattva is thus unapprehendable in terms of reality and its established nature, how can it occur to you to think: 'This one belongs to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, this one belongs to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and this one belongs to the Mahāyāna'?"

Thus, Venerable Śāriputra, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva hears that these [dharmas] are being discerned within suchness as being without distinction, without differentiation, and without variety, and his mind does not shrink back, does not sink down, and does not turn away—
It should be understood that this bodhisattva mahāsattva will go forth to enlightenment.
Then the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!
It is so, Subhūti, it is so.
It occurs to you, Subhūti, just as if by the power of the Tathāgata and through the empowerment of the Buddha that you speak thus."

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having heard that these Bodhisattvas— while being analyzed in terms of suchness— are without distinction, without differentiation, and without any diversity, and his mind does not shrink, does not sink, and does not turn back,
it should be known that this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva will go forth to enlightenment.
Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, by means of which enlightenment will this bodhisattva mahāsattva set forth?
The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will set forth by means of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment abide;
how should he train?
The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should abide with equanimity toward all sentient beings."
One should generate an even mind toward all sentient beings;
one should not take others as objects with a biased mind,
but rather take others as objects with a mind of loving-kindness.
One should relate to others with a mind intent on their welfare; one should relate to others with a virtuous mind;
one should relate to others with a mind in which pride has been subdued.
One should take others as one's object with an unobstructed mind;
one should take others as one's object with a mind free from malice;
one should take others as one's object with a mind free from harm.
Having established the perception of all beings as one's mother, and having established the perception of them as father, son, or daughter, others should be relied upon.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should abide toward all beings and should train thus: "I am the protector of all beings."
One should personally abide in the cessation of all evil;
one should practice giving, guard moral discipline, accomplish patience, exert vigor, attain meditative concentration, master wisdom,
and contemplate dependent origination in both its forward and reverse orders.
He should also be one who encourages others therein, speaks in praise thereof, and gives his approval thereof.

Likewise, having established himself in the truths, up to the entry into the bodhisattva’s certainty and the maturation of sentient beings, he should be one who encourages others therein, speaks in praise thereof, and gives his approval thereof.
For him who thus aspires and trains in this way, unobstructed form—and indeed all things up to the stability of phenomena—will become unobstructed.
The sixteenth chapter, titled "Suchness," in the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom.
(Vaidya 161) Chapter Seventeen: The Characteristics, Signs, and Marks of Irreversibility.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what are the characteristics of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
What are the marks and what are the signs?
Or how, Blessed One, should we know that "this is an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva"?
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, that which is the stage of ordinary persons, that which is the stage of śrāvakas, and that which is the stage of pratyekabuddhas— "
And that which is the stage of a Buddha is called the stage of suchness (*tathatā*).
All these are non-dual, undivided, non-conceptual, and free from conceptualization within suchness; thus they enter into that suchness, that very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Abiding in suchness, one does not conceptualize or discriminate suchness;
in this way, one enters it.
Having entered thus, even upon hearing about suchness as it is, and even after departing from that [teaching], one has no doubt and does not harbor uncertainty.
He does not doubt, nor does he hesitate, thinking "it is not so"; rather, he resolves with conviction and penetrates it, thinking, "This is exactly thus; this is suchness."
He does not engage in idle chatter;
he speaks only words endowed with meaning, never those devoid of meaning,
and he does not look about at what others have done or left undone.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with these aspects, these marks, and these signs should be known as irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva does not look toward the faces of other ascetics or brahmins, thinking: "These venerable ascetics or brahmins know what is to be known."
They behold what is visible;
yet they do not pay homage to other deities,
nor do they offer flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, garments, parasols, banners, bells, or flags to other deities.
Or he considers that a lamp should be given,
and he does not rely upon another deity.
Subhūti, by these modes, these marks, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with them should be held to be irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti, that irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is not reborn in the states of woe,
nor does he assume a female state.
Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva undertakes and abides in the ten paths of wholesome action.
He himself abstains from taking life,
and he also encourages others to abstain from taking life.
He himself abstains from taking what is not given,
and he also encourages others to abstain from taking what is not given;
he himself abstains from sexual misconduct, and...
He also encourages others to abstain from sexual misconduct;
he himself abstains from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence,
and he also encourages others to abstain from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence.
He himself abstains from false speech and also encourages others to abstain from false speech;
he himself abstains from slanderous speech, and...
He also encourages others to abstain from slanderous speech;
he himself abstains from harsh speech and also encourages others to abstain from harsh speech.
He himself abstains from frivolous speech and also encourages others to abstain from frivolous speech;
he himself abstains from covetousness.
He also encourages others to abstain from covetousness;
he himself refrains from ill-will and also encourages others to abstain from ill-will.
He himself abstains from wrong view and also encourages others to abstain from wrong view.
In this way, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva, having undertaken them himself, abides in the ten paths of wholesome action.
Furthermore, he instructs, encourages, inspires, gladdens, establishes, and strengthens others in the ten paths of wholesome action.
Even while in a dream, he does not commit any of the ten paths of wholesome action— whether individually or collectively, in every way and entirely— not even mentally, let alone in deed.
Furthermore, Subhūti, even when in a dream, these ten paths of wholesome action become manifest to that irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
By these modes, by these signs, and by these marks, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with them should be known as irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Moreover, Subhūti, whatever teaching an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva masters, [he masters it with the thought: "I shall master this teaching for the sake of the welfare and happiness of all beings."
And he gives;
with such a mind, he masters that very thing, and he gives, thinking: "For the sake of all sentient beings, I master and give this Dharma."
"For their welfare and happiness;
may it be so!
By this teaching of the Dharma, may the righteous aspirations of all sentient beings be fulfilled."
And he makes that gift of Dharma common to all sentient beings.
Subhūti, by these aspects, these marks, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with them should be understood as irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when profound dharmas are being taught, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva does not hesitate.
He does not harbor doubt, he does not waver, he does not hesitate, and he speaks words that are beneficial.
He speaks with moderation, he speaks with gentleness, and he has little sloth and torpor.
And he becomes free from underlying tendencies;
whether advancing or retreating, he advances or retreats with an undistracted mind.
With mindfulness established, he steps forward; with mindfulness established, he steps back.
He does not lift his foot too slowly from the ground.
He does not place his foot on the ground with a dragging motion;
he lifts it easily and sets it down easily.
He does not lift his foot from the ground hastily, nor does he set his foot down on the ground hastily; rather,
he steps upon the patch of ground only while looking at it.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the robes used by that irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva’s body do not become infested with lice;
he conducts himself with cleanliness and remains free from much illness.
And he has few afflictions;
furthermore, those eighty thousand families of worms that generally arise in the bodies of other sentient beings do not arise at all— in every way and in every respect— within his body.
For what reason?
Because those roots of merit of his have risen above the entire world.
And to the extent that those roots of merit of his increase, to that same extent that bodhisattva mahāsattva acquires purity of body and acquires purity of speech.
And he attains the purification of the mind.
Subhūti asked: "Lord, what then should be understood as the purification of the mind of that bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, it is in accordance with how those roots of merit of that bodhisattva mahāsattva increase."

In that very way, that bodhisattva mahāsattva adopts a state of minimal activity of mind, and he adopts a state of non-deceitfulness of mind, a state of freedom from guile in mind, a state of lack of crookedness in mind, and a state of lack of curvature in mind; and by means of such purity of mind, Subhūti, he transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Subhūti, this should be understood as the purity of mind of that bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with these aspects, these marks, and these signs should be recognized as irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Moreover, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva does not hold gain, honor, or praise in high regard.
He does not become preoccupied with robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, or medicinal requisites for the sick; he does not abound in envy or stinginess;
and he does not falter when profound teachings are being expounded.
He becomes one of steady intellect and of profound intellect,
and he listens to the Dharma from others with due reverence.
Whatever Dharma he hears from others with due respect,
he integrates it all with the perfection of wisdom;
and as for those worldly crafts, arts, and occupations, [he likewise integrates them].
Having relied upon the perfection of wisdom, he brings all those things into harmony with the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
and he does not perceive any phenomenon whatsoever that he does not unite with the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
And he perceives all of that being practiced.
Subhūti, by these characteristics, these marks, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be held to be irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One, having conjured up the eight great hells, [places] therein in each individual great hell...
Having manifested many hundreds of bodhisattvas, many thousands of bodhisattvas, and many hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas,
he would say this to a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva: "Those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have been prophesied by the Tathāgata as non-retrogressive..."
They have been reborn in these great hells;
you too shall likewise fall into such great hells,
since you have been prophesied as one who is irreversible.
Furthermore, you must confess this thought of awakening and relinquish it;
what use have you for Buddhahood?
"In this way you will not be reborn in the hells;
by acting thus, you will go to heaven.
If even upon hearing this, the mind of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is not disturbed, [he is to be known as irreversible].
He does not waver;
he knows thus: "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva should be reborn in the lower realms."
Subhūti, by these modes, these marks, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with them should be recognized as irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One, having approached an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva in the guise of a śramaṇa, will say this: "Relinquish that which you previously heard, that which you previously accepted!"
If you confess in this way,
and if you relinquish in this way, we shall approach you again and again.
That which you have just heard is not the word of the Buddha;
it is a poem composed by a poet.
Furthermore, as for this which I speak, it is spoken by the Buddha; it is the word of the Buddha.
Having heard this, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva is agitated or wavers, it should be understood that this bodhisattva has not been predicted by the Tathāgatas;
he is undetermined.

"A bodhisattva [is one who] has set out for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; he does not abide in the state of irreversibility. Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither shaken nor moved, [he is irreversible].
Even upon hearing these words of Māra, the Evil One, he resorts only to the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā);
he resorts only to non-arising, only to non-ceasing, and only to the absence of volitional construction;
he does not proceed by means of faith in another.
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, an arhat monk whose outflows are exhausted does not proceed by faith in another, but acts through direct perception of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā);
he cannot be led astray by Māra, the Evil One.
In the very same way, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva cannot be crushed by persons belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.
He becomes one whose nature is irreversible;
he is fixed upon the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha, yet he is ultimately destined for perfect enlightenment through omniscience.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is established in the state of irreversibility,
At that time, he becomes one who cannot be led astray by others.
Subhūti, by these modes, these marks, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with them should be held to be irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti, someone might approach an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva and say: "This is merely a wandering in saṃsāra."
"This is not the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Make an end of suffering right here;
you shall no longer experience those sufferings and mental distresses belonging to the realm of saṃsāra."
"Alas! Even this very body of yours here will not come into existence; how much less, then, do you think that you will take up another body?
If, even upon hearing this, he is neither shaken nor moved, [he is a bodhisattva].

Then Māra, the Evil One, will himself say this to him: "Do you wish to see those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, by whom the Blessed Buddhas were attended for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges with robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick; and by whom the holy life was led in the presence of as many Blessed Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges?"

He has attended upon, questioned, and interrogated Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, for the sake of this very Bodhisattva Vehicle— asking how Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, should act and how they should abide— and it was exactly as those Tathāgatas themselves have explained.
Nevertheless, even though they remained thus, practiced thus, and applied themselves to yoga thus, even to this day they have not yet awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Likewise, by remaining in such instruction and admonition and training in such a manner, they did not attain omniscience;
how much less, then, will you attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?

If he is not shaken nor moved even by this, Māra the Evil One will manifest monks right there on that very spot of earth and say to him: "These monks have become Arhats whose outflows are exhausted; they were those who set out for enlightenment."
"In that case, they have attained arhatship and abide in arhatship;
how then could you possibly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Even when this is spoken and thus explained, if the mind of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither shaken nor moved, [he is to be known as irreversible].
This bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be regarded as irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

If, having heard these words on seclusion from another, the mind of this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not fall away from the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and his mind does not turn back, [then he is irreversible].
Nor does any alteration of the mind occur,

and he recognizes all those deeds of Māra for what they are: "Subhūti, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in this way within the perfections should not attain omniscience."

It is impossible, it is out of the question, that Māra the Evil One should find an opportunity against a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in this way, who trains in this way, who is not devoid of such conduct as described by the Tathāgatas, and who dwells with these mental attentions associated with the perfections.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva recognizes the works of Māra,
and having heard from others the words concerning solitude, does not fall away nor does his mind turn back, [he is one who has set out].
And his mind does not waver,
and he recognizes those deeds of Māra for what they are.

Subhūti, by these characteristics, these marks, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with them should be known as irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva does not construct the perception of form,
nor does he give rise to the perception of form. Likewise, he does not [construct] the perception of feeling, the perception of perception, or the perception of mental formations.
He does not construct the perception of consciousness,
nor does he give rise to the perception of consciousness.
For what reason?
For it is thus: an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva has entered the bodhisattva’s certainty through dharmas that are empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*).
He does not apprehend even that dharma, he does not construct it, and he does not produce it.
Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses the patient acceptance of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñānakṣāntika*) is called "irreversible."
Subhūti, by these modes, these marks, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with them should be understood as irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One, approaching in the guise of a monk, will attempt to dissuade the bodhisattva mahāsattva, saying: "This so-called omniscience is equal to space;
this so-called omniscience is non-existent."
This dharma, namely omniscience, does not exist; who here will know it,
and who here will fully awaken to it?
By this, no one will go forth— neither he who would fully awaken, nor that which is to be fully awakened to, nor he who would understand it.
And as for that which is to be known:
in all cases, those phenomena are equal to space;
you are being frustrated in vain.
This is illuminated by the works of Māra, namely: "One should fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
this was not spoken by the Buddha.
That son of good family or daughter of good family should understand it thus, reflect upon it thus, and know it thus: "This is indeed the work of Māra."
Regarding this discernment:
having reflected in this way, one should become firm-minded therein;
one should become unshakable in mind and unassailable in mind.
Subhūti, moreover, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with these aspects, these marks, and these signs should be understood as irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva has turned away from the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and is set toward omniscience.
Desiring it, he enters the first dhyāna.
In that same way, he enters the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
He dwells in these four dhyānas and masters them through repeated practice.
He enters into the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), yet he is not reborn through the power of those absorptions;
rather, he again takes up phenomena belonging to the desire realm as his objects of focus.
Subhūti, this too should be known as a characteristic of the irreversibility of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva does not value his name, does not value fame, renown, or praise, and does not become attached to his name.
He becomes one whose mind is unperturbed,
and he possesses a mind of benevolence toward all sentient beings.
Whether advancing or retreating, he advances with an undistracted mind and retreats with an undistracted mind; indeed,
he advances with mindfulness alone.
Possessing mindfulness, he moves about;
even if he dwells in a household,
he has no excessive attachment to sensual pleasures, nor any intention toward them.
He enjoys sensual pleasures with the very perception of revulsion;
he enjoys sensual pleasures with the very perception of terror.
Subhūti, it is just as if a man who has entered the midst of a wilderness infested with bandits were to take food while maintaining the very perception of terror toward that food.
One who possesses the perception of travel would take food with the thought, "When indeed shall I have passed beyond this wilderness of thieves? Thus perceiving it, he takes food without confidence.
In the same way, Subhūti, those irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas, while dwelling in the midst of a household, whatever sensual pleasures they enjoy, [they do so]...
They enjoy those various sensual pleasures only without desire, without greed, and without attachment;
indeed, they remain without longing for the five strands of sensual pleasure characterized by the agreeable and the pleasant.
While dwelling in the midst of a household, they do not earn their livelihood through either fair or foul means.
They provide their livelihood solely through the Dharma and not even through unrighteousness;
they may face death, but they never inflict injury upon others.
For what reason?
For it was by those true persons, great persons, supreme persons, the most excellent of persons, the beautiful among persons,
bulls among persons, the noble among persons, the heroic among persons, the preeminent among persons, the leaders among persons, the lotuses among persons,
the white lotuses among persons, the thoroughbreds among persons, the elephants among persons, the lions among persons, and the charioteers who subdue persons.
"All sentient beings should be established in supreme happiness.
For it is thus, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattvas dwell in the midst of a household, precisely because they have attained the empowerment of the power of the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by these characteristics, these marks, and these signs, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should be understood as irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Furthermore, Subhūti, the great yakṣa Vajrapāṇi is constantly attached to an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva. He becomes difficult to overcome and cannot be transgressed by either humans or non-humans.
He is difficult for all beings to overcome;
his mind does not become distracted,
nor do his faculties become impaired.
He possesses complete faculties and not incomplete faculties;
he is endowed with the virile faculties of a true man and is not an inferior person.
As for those things which are means of subjugating women—such as mantras, recitations, medicinal herbs, spells, and drugs—[he does not employ them].
He does not employ any of those things at all;
he maintains a pure livelihood and not an improper one,
and he is not disposed toward quarrels or disputes.
He possesses straightforward vision;
he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.
He is endowed with these and other such qualities.
He does not predict regarding a woman or a man, saying, "A son will be born to you," or "A daughter will be born to you.
For him, such faults as these, which consist of being unreliable, do not exist.
Subhūti, by these modes, these characteristics, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with them should be recognized as irreversible from unexcelled,
perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, Subhūti, regarding those modes, those characteristics, and those signs of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva—
by which modes, by which characteristics, and by which signs a bodhisattva is endowed— [he should be known as irreversible].
One should know that such a mahāsattva is irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
I shall teach those aspects, those marks, and those signs.
But what, then, are they?
That is to say: they do not dwell devoted to the practice of application regarding the aggregates, sense bases, elements, and dependent origination;
they do not dwell devoted to the practice of application regarding talk that delights in socializing; they do not dwell devoted to the practice of application regarding talk about kings.
They do not dwell devoted to the practice of talk about thieves, nor do they dwell devoted to the practice of talk about armies, nor do they dwell devoted to the practice of talk about battles.

They do not dwell devoted to the practice of discourse concerning villages, cities, market towns, districts, kingdoms, or royal capitals; they do not dwell devoted to the practice of discourse concerning themselves; nor do they dwell devoted to the practice of discourse concerning ministers or high officials.
They do not dwell devoted to the practice of discourse concerning men, women, or eunuchs;
they do not dwell devoted to the practice of discourse concerning vehicles, gardens, monasteries, palaces, lakes, ponds, pools, lotus-pools, forests, groves, or mountains;
nor do they dwell devoted to the practice of discourse concerning yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, piśācas, kaṭapūtanas, or kumbhāṇḍas.
They do not dwell devoted to the pursuit of talk concerning food, drink, clothing, ornaments, perfumes, garlands, and ointments;
they do not dwell devoted to the pursuit of talk concerning streets, crossroads, junctions, roads, markets, palanquins, and households;
nor do they dwell devoted to the pursuit of talk concerning song, dance, storytelling, actors, dancers, and wandering minstrels.

They do not dwell devoted to the practice and application of talk concerning oceans, rivers, or islands; they do not dwell devoted to the practice and application of talk contrary to the Dharma; they do not dwell devoted to the practice and application of talk that delights ordinary worldlings.
Rather, they dwell devoted to the application and practice of discourse on the perfection of wisdom;
they remain never separated from mental attentions associated with omniscience,
and they do not dwell devoted to the application and practice of discourse concerning quarreling, scolding, strife, and contention.
They desire only the Dharma and not what is contrary to the Dharma;
and they speak in praise of non-differentiation.
They do not speak words that cause division;
they desire friends and do not desire enemies.
They speak in accordance with the Dharma and not contrary to the Dharma;
desiring only to behold the Tathāgata, they long for those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who reside, remain, and maintain themselves in other world-systems.
They generate the aspiration to be reborn in their presence;
desiring that, they are reborn there.
Thus, they remain never separated from the vision of the Tathāgata, the attendance upon the Tathāgata, and the service to the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, Subhūti, irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having passed away from among the gods of the desire realm, or from among the gods of the form realm or the formless realm, are reborn right here in the Middle Country of Jambudvīpa,
where beings are skilled in the arts.
Skilled in poetry,
skilled in mantras,
and skilled in the sciences.
They were experts in the scriptures,
experts in omens,
and experts in the meaning of the Dharma.
Few are reborn in the border regions; for the most part, they are reborn in the Middle Country.
Even those who are reborn in the border regions, [are few].
They too are reborn in great cities;
these qualities are also found in them.

Subhūti, by these characteristics, these marks, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with them should be understood as irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti, it does not occur to an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva to think, "I am irreversible," or "I am not irreversible.
No such doubt arises in him.
And he has no doubt regarding his own stage, nor does he experience any despondency therein.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, a stream-enterer has no longing and no uncertainty regarding the fruit of stream-entry on his own stage.
And he has no doubt regarding his own stage, nor does he experience any sinking back; furthermore,
as soon as various deeds of Māra arise, he recognizes them immediately.
Nor does he fall under the power of the various deeds of Māra as they arise one after another.
Subhūti, it is just as if a man who has committed an act of immediate retribution were never to be separated from that thought of immediate retribution until the moment of his death.
He is unable to dispel or suppress that mind;
rather, that mind continues to follow him even until the time of death.
In the same way, Subhūti, the irreversible mind of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva remains steadfast; it is unshakable upon its own irreversible ground,
and cannot be moved or shaken even by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
He recognizes each and every māra-activity as it arises,
and he does not fall under the power of those māra-activities as they arise.
For him, who is free from doubt and uncertainty regarding his own stage, even after passing through births, neither the mind of a śrāvaka nor the mind of a pratyekabuddha arises.
Even for one who has passed beyond birth, it occurs thus: "I shall not fail;
I shall indeed fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment while remaining established in my own ground.
He becomes one who is no longer led by others.
And he becomes uncrushable in his own stage.
Why is that?
Because he stands with an unassailable mind and is endowed with unassailable knowledge.
Furthermore, if Māra, the Evil One, should approach in the guise of a Buddha and, having approached him, say this: "Realize arhatship right here!
You have not been prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
Those forms, those marks, or those signs do not exist in you,

by which forms, by which marks, or by which signs a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed and fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Or rather, what is it that you are practicing here?

But if, Subhūti, the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva should become otherwise, it should be known that this bodhisattva has not been predicted for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening by previous Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
If, however, he reflects thus: "Ah, this is Māra, the Evil One, who has approached having conjured up the guise of a Buddha," [then he is not led astray].
Whether it be possessed by Māra or created by Māra,
this is not the Tathāgata;
as it was spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, so it is and not otherwise.
If he reflects in this way and attends to it thus:
"Ah, this is Māra the Evil One who, having employed the Buddha's empowerment, desires to alienate me from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment," and if Māra then turns back, [he knows him as such].
Subhūti, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has been predicted for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment by former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva stands upon the irreversible stage of a bodhisattva. Subhūti, if these modes, these marks, and these signs are present in a bodhisattva mahāsattva, [then he is to be known as irreversible].
Subhūti,
it should be understood from these qualities that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has certainly been prophesied by former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas;
this bodhisattva mahāsattva stands firmly on the irreversible stage of a bodhisattva.
For what reason?
Because those aspects, those marks, and those signs that belong to an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva are present in him.

Subhūti, by these modes, these marks, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with them should be known as irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, Subhūti, for the sake of upholding the true Dharma, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva even makes the sacrifice of himself and makes the sacrifice of his life.

Therefore, the bodhisattva mahāsattva who is irreversible exerts supreme effort for the sake of upholding the true Dharma out of love and reverence for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present; and because the Buddhas,
the Blessed Ones, are the Dharma-body, he does so by taking up love and reverence for the Dharma.
He upholds the true Dharma.
This upholding of the true Dharma belongs not only to the past Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, but also to the present Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; it is precisely this same upholding of the true Dharma.

This very same upholding of the true Dharma belongs also to the future Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; I too am included in the number and calculation of those future Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and I too have been prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, for this upholding of the true Dharma is mine as well.
Perceiving this purpose as well, for the sake of upholding the true Dharma, he even effects the sacrifice of himself and the sacrifice of his life,
and he does not falter therein.
Nor does he fall into indolence.
Subhūti, by these modes, these marks, and these signs, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with them should be known as irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
