Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva does not have any doubt when the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, teaches the Dharma.
He does not doubt.
Subhūti said: "Blessed One, is it only when the Tathāgata himself teaches the Dharma that one does not hesitate or doubt, and not when a śrāvaka [teaches]?"
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, even when a śrāvaka teaches the Dharma, one does not hesitate or doubt it.
Why is that?
Because that bodhisattva mahāsattva has attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena."
By means of that, he hears the non-contradictory true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena;
and hearing it, he has no longing and no doubt.
Subhūti, endowed with these qualities, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes irreversible.
Subhūti, these also should be known as the forms, marks, and signs of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
In the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom, this is the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Aspects, Marks, and Signs of Irreversibility."
(Vaidya 170) Chapter Eighteen: Emptiness.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "It is marvelous, Blessed One, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with such great qualities."
“Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with immeasurable qualities;
Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with limitless qualities.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: “So it is, Subhūti; so it is.”
For what reason? Because, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva has attained infinite and boundless knowledge that cannot be taken away by any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
Subhūti said: "Blessed One, you are capable of describing for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges the aspects, marks, and signs of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva;
for this very reason, Blessed One, the most profound points concerning the perfection of wisdom should be indicated to the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is well that you wish to summarize by taking up these most profound points."
"Subhūti, 'profound' is a designation for emptiness;
it is a designation, Subhūti, for the signless, the wishless, the unconditioned, non-arising, non-birth, non-existence, dispassion, cessation, nirvāṇa, and disappearance—
this, namely, 'profound'."
Subhūti said: "Blessed One, is this designation 'profound' an exclusive term for these very dharmas, and not for all dharmas?
The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, this designation 'profound' applies to all dharmas as well. For what reason?"
For form, Subhūti, is profound;
likewise feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness, Subhūti, are profound.
And how, Subhūti, is form profound?
How are feeling, perception, and mental formations?
And how, Subhūti, is consciousness profound?
Subhūti, just as suchness is, so too is form profound;
and the same is true for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Subhūti, just as suchness is, so too is consciousness profound.
In that regard, Subhūti, just as the suchness of form is...
In the same way, form is profound;
as is the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, and the suchness of mental formations.
In that regard, Subhūti, it is just as the suchness of consciousness is.
Likewise, consciousness is profound.
Subhūti, that in which there is no form— this is the profundity of form.
Subhūti, where there is no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness— this is the profundity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Subhūti said: "It is marvelous, Blessed One, how by such a subtle means you have turned one away from form and indicated Nirvāṇa;
and likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and even by such a subtle means you have turned one away from consciousness and indicated Nirvāṇa."

The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, those who will contemplate, weigh, and reflect upon these most profound points associated with the perfection of wisdom—thinking, 'I should abide in accordance with what is instructed in the perfection of wisdom;
I should train in accordance with what is declared in the perfection of wisdom'—"
"In this way I must practice, just as it has been taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

While accomplishing it thus, attending to it thus, examining it thus, applying myself thus, striving thus, and exerting myself thus, if such a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into yoga for even a single day, what kind of karma does he perform in that single day?"

Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, there were a certain man who was prone to passion and prone to discursive thought. That man, being prone to passion and prone to discursive thought, had made an appointment with a woman who was beautiful, lovely, and pleasing to behold. Now, that woman—(Vaidya 171)
She would be taken in marriage by another;
she would not allow herself to go forth from the home. What do you think, Subhūti, with what would that man’s thoughts be associated as they arise?
Subhūti said: "Blessed One, only thoughts associated with women would arise for that man: 'She is coming; she has arrived.
I will do this with her; I will take my pleasure with her.'"
"I shall play in this way;
I shall investigate in this way.
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? At the end of a day, how many thoughts would arise in that man?"
Subhūti said: “Blessed One, many thoughts would arise in that person at the end of a day.

The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, as many thoughts as arise in that person at the end of a day, for so many eons, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cast away, turn his back upon, and bring to an end [the cycle of] saṃsāra.”

Whoever here abides in this perfection of wisdom as it has been commanded, as it has been proclaimed, as it has been taught, as it has been pointed out, and as it has been demonstrated; whoever trains in it, practices it, contemplates it, and applies themselves to its yoga; and whoever avoids those faults by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva turns back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment—[that person shall not fall back].

For in this way, Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva mahāsattva is devoted to the practice of the perfection of wisdom, dwelling by means of this dwelling— namely, through mental attentions associated with the perfection of wisdom— performs in a single day as much work as that.
And if a bodhisattva who is devoid of the perfection of wisdom were to practice giving for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges,
he would still be surpassed by that bodhisattva mahāsattva who applies himself to the yoga of the perfection of wisdom for even a single day.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, giving gifts to those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry,
and likewise giving gifts to once-returners, non-returners, and arhats.
One should establish it;
one should give gifts to and establish them among the pratyekabuddhas;
one should give gifts to and establish them among the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
And [the former] is devoid of the perfection of wisdom.

But that bodhisattva mahāsattva who, for even a single day, applies himself to yoga in the perfection of wisdom exactly as it has been taught, exactly as it has been pointed out, and exactly as it has been explained—
this bodhisattva mahāsattva generates far more merit than that previous bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose a bodhisattva were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, giving gifts and establishing others in them— from those who have entered the stream up to those who are perfectly awakened Buddhas— and were to be one who fulfills the precepts of moral conduct,
yet remains devoid of the perfection of wisdom.
And whichever Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, should arise from that mental attention and teach the Dharma—
Subhūti, this very Bodhisattva Mahāsattva generates far more merit than that previous Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose a bodhisattva were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, giving gifts and establishing them [in the path] among those from stream-enterers up to perfectly awakened buddhas,
and were to be one who fulfills the precepts and is endowed with patience.
And one who is devoid of the perfection of wisdom—
whereas a bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells in the perfection of wisdom, having arisen from that mental attention, should give a gift of Dharma;
this very bodhisattva mahāsattva, Subhūti, generates much more merit than that former bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, giving gifts to those from stream-enterers up to perfectly awakened buddhas; being one who fulfills the precepts and is endowed with patience,
he would, while exerting vigor, apply himself to the meditative concentrations and the dharmas that are the wings of awakening.
And he would be devoid of the perfection of wisdom.
However, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having given such a gift of Dharma, were to dedicate it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
then this bodhisattva mahāsattva, Subhūti, generates far more merit than that former bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having given such a gift of Dharma, dedicates it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the dedication taught in the perfection of wisdom, he generates much more merit than that.

Furthermore, Subhūti, after a bodhisattva mahāsattva has given such a gift of Dharma, he should dedicate it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the dedication described in the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Having dedicated it, however, he should not again apply himself to solitary meditation (*pratisaṃlāna*).
Moreover, Subhūti, suppose there were another bodhisattva mahāsattva who would give only that very gift of Dharma.
But if he were not to apply himself to meditative seclusion (*pratisaṃlāna*),

that bodhisattva mahāsattva would not produce as much merit as a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, while giving such a gift of Dharma, again applies himself to meditative seclusion and, being sustained by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), remains never separated from that seclusion.
By means of the perfection of wisdom,
this bodhisattva mahāsattva generates a much greater amount of merit.

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, since the Blessed One has stated that volitional formation (*abhisaṃskāra*) is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), how then can it be said that one generates a greater amount of merit?
The Blessed One replied: "In this regard, Subhūti, even that meritorious formation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is designated as being empty."
It is described as empty; it is described as hollow;
it is described as pithless.

Moreover, Subhūti, to the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates all phenomena in this way, to that same extent, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is not separated from the perfection of wisdom.
And to the extent, Subhūti, that the bodhisattva mahāsattva is not separated from the perfection of wisdom, [to that same extent...]
In that same way, one generates immeasurable and incalculable merit.
Subhūti said: "Blessed One, what is the difference between the immeasurable (*aprameya*) and the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), or what is their distinction?
The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, 'immeasurable' refers to that wherein all measures cease."
"Subhūti, 'incalculable' means that which cannot be exhausted even by calculation."
Subhūti said: "Blessed One, could there be a way in which form might be immeasurable?
Likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations?
Could there be a way, Blessed One, in which consciousness might be immeasurable?"
The Blessed One said: "As for what Subhūti has said—'O Blessed One, there might be a way in which form could be immeasurable;
likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations;
O Blessed One, there might be a way in which consciousness could be immeasurable'—"
Subhūti, there may be a way in which form itself is immeasurable; likewise, there may be a way in which feeling itself, perception itself, and formations themselves are immeasurable.
Subhūti, there may be a way in which consciousness itself is immeasurable.
Subhūti said: "But of what, O Blessed One, is this a designation, namely 'immeasurable'? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, this is a designation for emptiness;
it is a designation for the signless."
"Subhūti, 'immeasurable' is a designation for the wishless."
Subhūti said: "Blessed One, is 'immeasurable' a designation for emptiness alone?
Blessed One, is 'immeasurable' a designation for the signless alone and the wishless alone, and not for other dharmas?"
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Have I not declared that all phenomena are empty?
Subhūti replied: "Indeed, Blessed One, all phenomena have been declared by the Tathāgata to be empty.
The Blessed One said: "And those which are empty, Subhūti..."
They are also inexhaustible;
and that which is emptiness is also immeasurability.
Therefore, Subhūti, in terms of their actual meaning, no distinction or differentiation whatsoever is found among these dharmas.
These, Subhūti, are merely expressions proclaimed and uttered by the Tathāgata— such as "immeasurable" or "incalculable."
Whether as "inexhaustible," or as "empty," or as "signless."
Or as "wishless," or as "unconditioned," or as "non-arising."
Whether it be called non-arising, or non-existence, or dispassion, or cessation;
Or "nirvāṇa"— Subhūti, this is merely a teaching, an accomplishment, and an exposition proclaimed by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha.

Subhūti said: "It is wonderful, Blessed One, how far-reaching is this reality of all phenomena (dharmatā) taught by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One; yet that reality of all phenomena is inexpressible.
As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken,"
"In the same way, Blessed One, all dharmas are also ineffable.
The Blessed One said, "So it is, Subhūti, so it is.
All dharmas, Subhūti, are indeed ineffable."
For what reason?
Subhūti, that which is the emptiness of all phenomena cannot be expressed in words.
Subhūti said: "But, Blessed One, does there exist any increase or decrease of that meaning which is ineffable?
The Blessed One said: "Not so, Subhūti."

Subhūti said: "If, Blessed One, there is neither increase nor decrease of an ineffable reality, then, Blessed One, there will likewise be neither increase nor decrease of the perfection of generosity;
and so too for the perfection of ethical discipline."
of the perfection of patience as well, of the perfection of vigor as well,
and of the perfection of meditative concentration as well.
"Furthermore, Blessed One, there will be neither increase nor decrease even of the perfection of wisdom.

If, Blessed One, there is neither increase nor decrease of these six perfections, how, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the power of the six perfections as they are increasing?"
"And how does one draw near to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?
Furthermore, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not fulfill the perfections does not draw near to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Subhūti; so it is."
Furthermore, Subhūti, there is indeed no increase or decrease whatsoever to be found in the meaning of the perfections.
Nevertheless, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is skilled in means practices and cultivates the perfection of wisdom, it does not occur to him:
"This perfection of giving is increasing."
"This perfection of generosity is being lost.
However, he further thinks: "This so-called 'perfection of generosity' is merely a name.
While giving that gift, he dedicates those mental attentions, those productions of thought, and those roots of virtue toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
He dedicates in such a way that it is identical to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Furthermore, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, cultivating the perfection of wisdom, and skilled in means, it does not occur to him: "This perfection of ethical discipline is declining."
Moreover, it occurs to him: "This which is called 'perfection of ethical discipline' is merely a name.
Having undertaken and abiding in ethical discipline, he dedicates those mental attentions, those productions of thought, and those roots of virtue toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
he dedicates them in such a way that it accords with unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom and cultivates the perfection of wisdom, being skilled in means, it does not occur to him: "This perfection of patience is diminishing.
Rather, it occurs to him: "This so-called 'perfection of patience' is a mere name."
Accomplishing those mental attentions, those productions of the thought of awakening, and those roots of virtue through patience, he dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening;
he dedicates them in such a way that it accords with unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and cultivates the perfection of wisdom, being skilled in means, it does not occur to him: "This is the perfection of vigor; this perfection of vigor is declining.
Rather, on the contrary, it occurs to him: "This which is called 'the perfection of vigor' is a mere name."
Exerting vigor, he dedicates those mental attentions, those productions of the thought of awakening, and those roots of virtue toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening;
he dedicates them in such a way that they accord with unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and cultivates the perfection of wisdom, being skilled in means, it does not occur to him: "This perfection of meditative concentration is declining.
Rather, it occurs to him: "This so-called 'perfection of meditative concentration' is a mere name."
As he enters into the meditative absorptions, he dedicates those mental attentions, those productions of thought, and those roots of virtue toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
he dedicates them in such a way that it accords with unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom and cultivates the perfection of wisdom, being skilled in means, it does not occur to him: "This perfection of wisdom is diminishing.
On the contrary, it occurs to him: "This which is called 'perfection of wisdom' is a mere name."

Practicing the perfection of wisdom and cultivating the perfection of wisdom, he dedicates those mental attentions, those productions of thought, and those roots of virtue toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
he dedicates them in such a way that it accords with unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "But what, Blessed One, is this unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, this unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is suchness (*tathatā*). And yet, Subhūti, suchness does not increase, nor does it decrease."
Or he may fall away.
However, if the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells frequently and extensively with mental attentions associated with that [perfection], in this way he draws near to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
And by means of those mental attentions, he does not fall away.
In this way, Subhūti, there is neither increase nor decrease of the ineffable reality;
likewise, there is neither increase nor decrease of the perfections.
In this way, Subhūti, there is neither increase nor decrease of all dharmas.
For it is thus, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling with these very kinds of mental attentions, draws near to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The eighteenth chapter, titled "Emptiness," in the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom.
(Vaidya 175) Chapter Nineteen: The Chapter on the Sister Gaṅgadevī.

Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Furthermore, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the first production of the thought of awakening?"
Or rather, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the final production of the thought of awakening?

Blessed One, the prior production of the thought of awakening is not concurrent with the final production of the thought of awakening, and the final production of the thought of awakening is not concurrent with the prior production of the thought of awakening.
“Blessed One, how does the accumulation of the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva come about?

When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: “What do you think, Subhūti? Is that wick burned by the flame of a burning oil lamp at its first incidence, or is it burned by the flame at its final incidence?”
Subhūti said: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
For it is not, Blessed One, that the wick was burned by the flame at its first incidence;
nor yet was the wick burned by the flame without having reached that first incidence."
"Moreover, Blessed One, that wick was not burned by the flame upon its final contact, nor was that wick burned by the flame without reaching its final contact.
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Was that wick burned?"
Subhūti said, “Burnt away, Blessed One; burnt away, Sugata.

The Blessed One said, “In just this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the first production of the thought of awakening alone.”

One does not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without relying on the initial production of the thought of awakening; nor does one awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the final production of the thought of awakening,
nor does one awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without relying on the final production of the thought of awakening.
And he does not awaken through those productions of thought, nor apart from those productions of thought;
yet the bodhisattva mahāsattva does awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti spoke thus to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, this dependent origination is profound.
Indeed, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the first production of the thought of awakening alone;
nor, indeed, does he awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without relying upon the first production of the thought of awakening."
It is not that a bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the final thought-moment alone,
nor is it that he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without having relied upon the final thought-moment;
yet it is not that he awakens apart from those thought-moments, nor elsewhere than in those thought-moments.
And the bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "What do you think, Subhūti, as for that mind which has ceased, will it ever arise again?
Subhūti replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Is that mind which is unarisen subject to cessation?
He replied: "It is subject to cessation, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti, will that which has the nature of cessation actually cease?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti, as for that mind which is unarisen, does it have the nature of cessation?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti, that which is subject to cessation—will that indeed cease?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? As for that mind which has the nature of being neither produced nor ceased, will it ever cease?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti, will that dharma which is by its very nature already ceased in its own-being ever be ceased?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti, will that which is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena ever cease?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti, will it remain just as suchness (*tathatā*) remains?"
He said: "Blessed One, it will abide just as suchness abides.
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? If it were to abide just as suchness abides, would it then not become immutable?"
He said, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "What do you think, Subhūti? Is suchness profound?
He said, "It is profound, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti—is the mind within suchness?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti—is the mind suchness?"
He said, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "What do you think, Subhūti, is the mind something other than suchness?
He said, "Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, do you perceive suchness?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Does he who practices in this way practice in the profound?"
He said: "O Blessed One, he who practices in this manner does not practice anywhere.
Why is that?"
For indeed, those modes of conduct do not arise for him, nor do they manifest.
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom..."
"Where does he course?
He replied, "He courses, Blessed One, in the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
The Blessed One said, "What do you think, Subhūti: does that bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the ultimate truth [course anywhere]?"
“Does he course in signs?
He replied, “Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, “What do you think, Subhūti? Is the sign not yet unmanifested for him?”
He said, "Certainly not, Blessed One.

The Blessed One said, "What do you think, Subhūti? Does a sign (nimitta) become eliminated for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom? Subhūti said, "No, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apply himself in this way: 'How may I, while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, attain here and now the abandonment of signs?'"
If, however, he were to attain it [nirvana] while all the qualities of a Buddha are still incomplete, he would become a śrāvaka.
This, O Blessed One, is the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, namely that—
And he knows that sign— its characteristics and its cause— and he masters the signless.

Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: "Venerable Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while in the midst of a dream, cultivates the three gateways to liberation— emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—
does his perfection of wisdom increase?"
Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāriputra, if it increases through practice during the day, then it likewise increases for one who has entered the state of dream.
Why is that?"

"For it has been said by the Blessed One, Venerable Śāriputra, that dream and day are indeed non-conceptual. If, Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has attained the perfection of wisdom practices the perfection of wisdom day after day,
then through that practice of the perfection of wisdom, even when that bodhisattva mahāsattva has entered the state of sleep, there must be an expansion of the perfection of wisdom."
Śāriputra said: "Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, if a woman or a man, while in a dream, performs an action—whether wholesome or unwholesome—is there an accumulation or a heaping up of that action?
Subhūti replied: "Just as all phenomena have been declared by the Blessed One to be like a dream..."
In that case, there is no accumulation or increase of that karma.

However, Venerable Śāriputra, if that man, having awakened, forms a conceptualization and gives rise to the perception of having killed, then there occurs for him an accumulation or increase of that karma.
And how, venerable Śāriputra, does one who conceptualizes produce the perception of having killed?
If, having committed the taking of life while in a dream, one awakens and conceptualizes thus: "Oh, he has been killed!
Well done, he has been killed!"
Thinking, "He is well-slain," or "He has been slain by me," one thus produces the perception of having killed.

Śāriputra said: "Venerable Subhūti, if that man, having awakened, while conceptualizing, were to produce the perception of having killed, thinking: 'Oh, he is killed! Well done, he is killed! He is thoroughly killed!'"
"Was it killed by me?"—
does that action accumulate or increase for him?
Even the Buddha, the Blessed One, when conceptualizing, gives rise to the perception of destruction.
"Could there be an accumulation or a heaping up of that karma as well?
Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, venerable Śāriputra. And why is that?"
For the Tathāgata has abandoned all conceptual constructions and discursive thoughts.
Venerable Śāriputra, it is just as with space: karma does not arise from various objective referents, nor does the mind arise from various objective referents.
Therefore, venerable Śāriputra, karma arises only with an object, not without an object;
the mind arises only with an object.
It is not without an object.
Venerable Śāriputra, cognition operates with respect to phenomena that are seen, heard, thought, or known.
Among these, certain cognitions grasp at defilement.
A certain kind of cognition grasps purification.
Therefore, venerable Śāriputra, volition arises only with an object, not without an object; action arises only with an object, not without an object.

Śāriputra said: "Venerable Subhūti, since all objective referents (*ālambana*) have been declared by the Blessed One to be secluded (*vivikta*), why then, Venerable Subhūti, does volition (*cetanā*) arise only with an objective referent and not without an objective referent?
Subhūti replied: "Venerable Śāriputra, having made a sign (*nimitta*) and having taken an existing objective referent as its object, volition arises only with an objective referent."
Venerable Śāriputra, volition is also secluded,
and even the sign is secluded; it is not without an object.
In this way, the formative forces conditioned by ignorance are also secluded;
consciousness conditioned by the formative forces is also secluded; and so on, up to old age and death conditioned by birth, which are also secluded.
In the same way, venerable Śāriputra, all objects of perception are secluded;
volition, being secluded from signs, arises by depending upon worldly convention.
Śāriputra said: "Venerable Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while in a dream, gives a gift and dedicates that gift toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment—
how should that dedicated gift be described?"

Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāriputra, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya is present here. He has been prophesied by the Tathāgata for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; he is the witness of this matter with his own body."
"He should be questioned;
he will resolve this matter.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra said this to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya: "Venerable Maitreya, this Elder Subhūti has said: 'I am Maitreya...'"
"The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva will explain this matter;
explain this matter, venerable Ajita!"

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya said this to the Venerable Subhūti: "When the Venerable Subhūti spoke thus— 'This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya will resolve this matter'— is it, then, Venerable Subhūti, that this name 'Maitreya' [exists]?"
Will he resolve this very matter, or will he resolve form,
or feeling, perception, and mental formations?
Now, will consciousness relinquish it, or will color relinquish it, or will shape relinquish it?
Or rather, will that which is the emptiness of form provide the answer?
Likewise, will that which is the [emptiness] of feeling, perception, and mental formations [provide the answer]?
Is that which is the emptiness of consciousness what will answer?
Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, that which is the emptiness of form—
It is not capable of being relinquished;
and so it is with feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Furthermore, Venerable Subhūti, that which is the emptiness of consciousness—
She is not capable of replying.
Furthermore, O Venerable Subhūti, I do not perceive any such phenomenon that could provide a reply.
I do not perceive even that dharma which is to be relinquished;
I do not perceive even that dharma.
I do not perceive even that dharma by which one might make a prediction, nor do I perceive that dharma which has been predicted for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya: "Venerable Maitreya, have these dharmas been realized by you in such a way as you describe them in words?
Maitreya replied: "Venerable Śāriputra, these dharmas have not been realized by me in such a way."
Just as I speak of these things with words, even so, Venerable Śāriputra, I do not know these dharmas, nor do I perceive them.
I do not perceive anything in such a way as that which I speak with speech or that which I think with the mind.
Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, it could not be touched by the body, nor spoken by speech, nor attended to by the mind.
"All phenomena have such a nature because they are without intrinsic nature.

Then, it occurred to the Venerable Śāriputra: "How profound is the wisdom of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya! Indeed, he teaches as one who has practiced the perfection of wisdom for a long time."
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, from where did this thought occur to you: 'Ah, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya is indeed of profound wisdom'?
Do you, Śāriputra, perceive that dharma by virtue of which one is designated as an Arhat?
Śāriputra said: "Certainly not, Blessed One."

The Blessed One said: "In the same way, Śāriputra, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, it does not occur to him: 'This dharma has been prophesied for unexcelled perfect enlightenment;
this dharma will be prophesied for unexcelled perfect enlightenment;
this dharma is being prophesied for unexcelled perfect enlightenment.'"
"This dharma will realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Practicing in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom;
coursing thus, he is not terrified.
He is not terrified,
nor does he fall into terror;
because he has attained the empowerment of strength, he applies himself to yoga with the thought, "I shall not fail to attain perfect awakening."
If he courses in this way,
he courses in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has entered a wilderness infested with predatory beasts should not be terrified,
should not be frightened, and should not fall into a state of panic.
For what reason?
Because that bodhisattva mahāsattva must relinquish everything for the sake of all sentient beings. He should generate this thought: "Even if predatory beasts were to devour me,"
May that gift be given to them alone;
thus my perfection of generosity will be fulfilled,
and my unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment will draw near.
And I shall act in such a way that,
when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, beings belonging to the animal realm will not be perceived at all, in any way, by any means, or anywhere within my buddha-field.
And they will possess the enjoyment and utilization of divine pleasures.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has entered the midst of a wilderness infested with robbers should not be terrified,
should not be frightened, and should not fall into a state of terror.
For what reason?
Because Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, are indeed those who delight in the skillful relinquishment of all their possessions.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must be one who has renounced the body and abandoned all personal requisites and utensils.
He should generate this thought: "If sentient beings were to take away all my requisites and utensils, let that very gift be given to them."
If some were to deprive me of life, I should not give rise to malice, anger, or resentment toward them;
nor should I commit any offense against them by body, speech, or mind.
And at that time, my perfection of generosity, my perfection of ethical discipline, and my perfection of patience will reach fulfillment;
furthermore, my unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment will draw near.
I shall act in such a way that—

And I shall practice in such a way that, when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, even the wildernesses of thieves in that buddha-field will, in every respect, entirely and in all ways, neither exist nor be perceived.
And thus I shall strive for the purification of the Buddha-field,

so that when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, all these and other defects in that Buddha-field will, in every way and in every respect, no longer exist and will not even be perceived.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has entered the midst of a waterless wilderness should not be afraid, should not be terrified, and should not fall into a state of panic.
Why is that?
Because bodhisattva mahāsattvas possess dharmas that are unafraid and undaunted.
And he should generate this thought: "I must train for the sake of cutting off all craving in all sentient beings.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be afraid, nor should he be terrified.
One should not fall into terror,
thinking: "If I should die of thirst, my rebirth will take place in the world of hungry ghosts (preta)."

Furthermore, one should indeed generate a mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings, thinking: "Alas! These beings have little merit, since such waterless deserts are known to exist for them in this world.
I shall act in such a way that [this shall no longer be so]."
I shall practice in such a way that,
when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, in that buddha-field there will be no waterless deserts whatsoever, in any way or at all, nor will they even be known to exist.
And so, I shall engage all sentient beings in meritorious deeds, so that they may become recipients of water endowed with the eight qualities;
and likewise, for the sake of all sentient beings, I shall undertake firm vigor.
"In such a way that, at that time, my perfection of vigor shall reach fulfillment."
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has entered the midst of a wilderness of hunger should not be afraid, should not be terrified, and should not fall into a state of terror.
Moreover, he should arm himself with this armor: "I shall exert such firm vigor and I shall purify my own buddha-field in such a way that..."
"May it be that when I have realized unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, such wildernesses of hunger shall not be perceived at all, in any way, or in any manner whatsoever in that Buddha-field;
may those beings there be happy, possessed of happiness, and endowed with every form of bliss."
And I shall act in such a way that whatever intention those beings may have, whatever they may desire in their minds, [that very thing shall be fulfilled].
That very thing will manifest; just as, for example, among the Trāyastriṃśa gods everything arises by means of the mind alone,
so too for those beings everything will manifest by means of the mind alone,
and everything will arise through the mind.
In that way, I shall exert firm vigor so that the righteous aspirations of those beings will reach fulfillment,
and so that all beings will have no lack of the necessities of life.
"It shall be so in every way, everywhere, and at all times;
and thus I shall exert myself for the sake of purifying my own mind for the benefit of all sentient beings,
so that at that time the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā) will reach fulfillment for me."
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has entered the wilderness of illness should not be afraid, should not be terrified, and should not fall into terror.
He should examine, reflect upon, and weigh this matter in this way: "There is no dharma here whatsoever that is afflicted by illness, nor is there any dharma whatsoever that is called 'illness'."
In this way, emptiness should be contemplated by him;
he should not be startled, nor terrified, nor fall into a state of terror.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not give rise to the thought, "I shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening after a long time," nor should he be startled or terrified.
One should not fall into terror.
Why is that? Because whatever is a moment of mind, [is...]
This very limit, which is unprecedented, is indeed no-limit. Thus,

that bodhisattva mahāsattva should not conceive the thought that "this unprecedented limit is vast and long," for this unprecedented limit, which is no-limit, is conjoined with a single moment of mind.

In this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be afraid, should not be terrified, and should not fall into terror at the thought, "I shall realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment only after a long time. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not afraid and not terrified by these and other fearsome and terrifying things— whether seen, heard, thought, or known— it should be understood, Śāriputra, that this son of good family or daughter of good family is capable of realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And so, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should don the great armor, thinking: "I shall act in such a way,
and I shall exert such firm vigor,

that when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, there will be no diseases whatsoever for all sentient beings in that buddha-field, in every respect, in every way, and entirely."
They shall not be known [as such].
I shall act in such a way that I become one who speaks according to what the Tathāgatas have said and acts according to what they have said.
And thus I shall practice mastery in the perfection of wisdom for the sake of all sentient beings, so that at that time the perfection of wisdom itself will reach fulfillment for me as well.
Then, indeed, a certain woman who was present and seated in that assembly rose from her seat, draped her upper robe over one shoulder, placed her right knee upon the ground,
and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, in this matter I shall not be terrified."
"I shall not be terrified,
nor shall I fall into fear;
and being unafraid and undaunted, I shall teach the Dharma to all sentient beings."
Then, at that time, the Blessed One manifested a golden smile.

Its light pervaded infinite and boundless world-systems, rose as far as the Brahma-world, and then, returning once more, circumambulated the Blessed One three times to the right and vanished into the very crown of the Blessed One’s head.

Immediately upon the manifestation of that smile by the Blessed One, that woman took golden flowers and scattered and showered them over the Blessed One; then those golden flowers remained suspended in the sky, unattached, in the firmament.

Then, indeed, the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"What, O Blessed One, is the cause?"
"What is the cause, what is the condition, for manifesting this smile?
Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or without condition.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, this sister Gaṅgadevā, in the future..."

"A Tathāgata named Dhvanisuvarṇapuṣpa will arise in the world, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans; he will appear as a Buddha, a Blessed One, in the world."

"In the aeon called Tārakopama, she will fully awaken to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Ānanda, this sister Gaṅgadevā, having turned away from her female state and attained a male state, will pass away from here and be reborn in the world-system Abhirati, the buddha-field of the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened One Akṣobhya."
Having been reborn there, she will practice the holy life in the presence of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha.
When she passes away from there, she will travel from buddha-field to buddha-field, never being separated from the sight of the Tathāgatas.
From those buddha-fields as well, she will continue to travel to other buddha-fields.
He will pass from one place to another wherever he may be, never separated from the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
Ānanda, it is just as if a universal monarch were to move from palace to palace;
throughout his entire life, he would not touch the surface of the earth with the soles of his feet.
Just as she would pass away without her feet ever touching the surface of the earth during the state of death, even so, Ānanda, will this sister Gaṅgadevā pass away;
and there she shall never be separated from the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, until she fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

Then, this thought occurred to the Venerable Ānanda: "Those who will be bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, in the presence of that Tathāgata Akṣobhya, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha—this should be understood as a true assembly of Tathāgatas.
Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind such a reflection in the mind of the Venerable Ānanda, said this to the Venerable Ānanda: "It is so, Ānanda; it is even so."
Those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice the holy life in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya have crossed over the mire;
Ānanda, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas should be known as having reached the full accomplishment of awakening.
Furthermore, Ānanda, the community of disciples of that Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Suvarṇapuṣpa will not be limited by measure.
Why is that?
Because, Ānanda, there will be so many disciples there that they cannot be measured.
Rather, they will be reckoned as immeasurable and incalculable.

Furthermore, Ānanda, at that time and in that era, in that buddha-field there will be no wildernesses of predatory beasts, nor wildernesses of thieves, nor wildernesses of water, nor wildernesses of disease, nor wildernesses of famine.
Ānanda, these and other such desolate wildernesses will, in that buddha-field, not exist at all in any way whatsoever, nor will they even be known.
Furthermore, Ānanda, for the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Suvarṇapuṣpa, [there will be] the unsurpassed...
For one who has fully awakened to perfect enlightenment, such terrifying and fearsome wildernesses as these will at that time no longer exist in any way whatsoever,
nor will they be perceived.

When this had been said, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, in the presence of which Tathāgata did this sister Gaṅgadevā plant the root of merit consisting of the first production of the thought of unsurpassed [enlightenment]?

When this had been said, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, this sister Gaṅgadevā planted the root of merit consisting of the first production of the thought."
And it was dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
That Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara was also strewn with golden flowers by me while I was aspiring for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
When I scattered five blue lotuses over the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, [he prophesied my future attainment].
And I attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of all phenomena;
therefore, I was prophesied by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment:
"Young man, in a future time you shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni."
"One who is perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
Then, upon hearing this prediction for me, this sister conceived this thought: "O, would that I too might be so predicted for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment as this young brahmin!"
She has been prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

And thus, Ānanda, this sister planted the root of merit consisting of the first production of the thought of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara.

When this had been said, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, this sister Gaṅgadevā has indeed performed her preparatory work; she has reached the limit and has been prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

When this had been said, the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Ānanda: "So it is, Ānanda, so it is! It is just as you say: this sister Gaṅgadevā has indeed performed her preparatory work; she has reached the limit and has been prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
The nineteenth chapter, titled "Gaṅgadevī Bhaginī," in the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.
(Vaidya 183) Chapter Twenty: The Examination of Skill in Means.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom achieve mastery in emptiness?"
"How, then, should the concentration on emptiness be attained?
The Blessed One said: "In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should contemplate that form is empty;
likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations."
One should contemplate that consciousness is empty.

And it should be contemplated in such a way—with an undistracted continuity of mind—that while contemplating, one does not perceive that true nature (dharmatā) as "form" by means of that very true nature. Not perceiving that true nature, one should not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).

When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Regarding what the Blessed One has thus said—that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not realize emptiness—how, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in that samādhi not realize emptiness?
The Blessed One replied: "Because, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects."
He does not reflect, "I shall realize [it]," nor does he reflect, "It is to be realized"; rather,
he reflects, "I shall master it."
He reflects: "This is the time for mastery; this is not the time for direct realization.
While still in a state of non-concentration, he fixes his mind upon the object of focus, thinking: "In this way, the perfection of wisdom will be fully grasped by me."
And it is not yet directly realized;
meanwhile, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not fall away from the factors conducive to enlightenment,
nor does he bring about the destruction of the outflows.
And herein he achieves mastery: at whatever time a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells by means of the gate of liberation that is the concentration on emptiness,
at that time the bodhisattva mahāsattva should also dwell by means of the concentration on the signless.
And yet, the signless should not be realized.
Why is that?
Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is thus endowed with the qualities of roots of goodness already ascended [to maturity] thinks: "This is the time for ripening."
He reflects, "This is not the time for direct realization," and being sustained by the perfection of wisdom, he does not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, there were a certain man who was most heroic.
He shall be endowed with supreme vigor,
he shall be firmly established,
and he shall be handsome.
He would be gracious, most beautiful to behold,
and endowed with many virtues.
He would be endowed with supreme qualities;
he would be endowed with qualities such as supreme sovereignty, ethical discipline, learning, and renunciation;
and he would be wise.
He would be capable of speech,
endowed with eloquence,
and endowed with correct practice.
He should be one who knows the proper time, he should be one who knows the proper place, and he should be one who knows the proper occasion.
He would have attained the supreme mastery in archery and weaponry, he would possess many weapons and shields, and he would be most skillful in all the arts.
Through being perfectly accomplished, he shall become one who has reached the ultimate mastery in all fields of craft;
he shall be possessed of mindfulness and possessed of intelligence.
He would be possessed of skillful means,
he would be possessed of fortitude,
and he would be possessed of moral conduct.
He shall be proficient in all treatises,
he shall have friends, and he shall possess wealth.
He shall be strong, he shall have no deficient limbs,
and his sense faculties shall be complete.
He shall be endowed with all necessary provisions and be dear and pleasing to many people;
whatever task he may undertake, it shall be successful.
In every such situation, he would be capable of overcoming all difficulties,
he would conduct himself with right method,
and in all circumstances, he would obtain great profit.
Being endowed with that great gain, he should share it with many people; he should honor what is worthy of honor and revere what is worthy of reverence.
One should honor what is to be honored, and one should worship what is to be worshipped.
What do you think, Subhūti? Would that person, on that account, not become even more exceedingly joyful?
"And he would be joyful, and he would be filled with gladness and happiness?
Subhūti replied, "So it is, Blessed One."
"So it is, Sugata.

The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Subhūti, that man, endowed with such great prosperity, having taken his parents, children, and wife, might set out for a vast, desolate wilderness due to a combination of certain circumstances—a place of great terror."
Terrifying and hair-raising for the foolish, he enters there and addresses those parents, children, and wives with words of fearlessness: "Do not fear!
Do not fear!"
"I shall quickly lead you out from this great, terrifying, and fearsome wilderness and forest track by a secure and safe path;
I shall swiftly set you free.
Yet, Subhūti, in that very wilderness and forest track, many adversaries and many enemies would have confronted that man.

What do you think, Subhūti? Would that heroic man— endowed with firm vigor and strength, wise, very affectionate, compassionate, steadfast, and possessed of a great accumulation of provisions— consider it right to abandon those parents, children, and wife, and withdraw himself alone from that great, terrifying, and fearsome wilderness of the forest when his adversaries and enemies have risen up against him?
Subhūti said: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
And why is that?
Because, Blessed One, that man has not abandoned his mother, father, children, or wife."
There is both an internal and an external powerful provision.

In that forest wilderness, there are many other adversaries and enemies of those [enemies], who are even more heroic, possess even stronger weapons, and are more noble; they stand guard and protect them.

Those adversaries and enemies of his, looking for a weak point and seeking an opportunity to strike, shall find no such opening. Therefore, Blessed One, that capable man is able— unwounded and unhurt— to lead his mother, father, children, wife,
and himself safely and securely out of that great, terrifying, and formidable wilderness.
until he has reached a village, or a city, or a town.

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "It is just so, Subhūti. A bodhisattva mahāsattva, compassionate for the welfare of all beings, dwelling in loving-kindness, dwelling in compassion, dwelling in sympathetic joy, and dwelling in equanimity—being sustained by skill in means and the perfection of wisdom, and having dedicated his roots of virtue through a dedication authorized by the Buddhas—"
Furthermore, although he enters the gateways of concentration and liberation— namely emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—
he does not personally realize the limit of reality,
that is to say, the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha.
For what reason?
Because he has the most powerful and most firm supporters,
namely, the perfection of wisdom and skill in means.
Because he has not abandoned all sentient beings,
he is thus capable of awakening to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment in safety and well-being.
Subhūti, at the time when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having taken a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings as his object, binds them with supreme loving-kindness—

In this interval, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, having transcended the faction of the afflictions and the faction of Māra, and having transcended the level of the śrāvakas and the level of the pratyekabuddhas, abides in that samādhi; yet, without having attained the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), he achieves complete mastery in emptiness, the supreme perfection.
Subhūti, at whatever time the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells by means of the gate of liberation that is the samādhi of emptiness,
In the meantime, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not yet dwell in the signless concentration (*ānimitta-samādhi*),
nor has he realized this signless concentration.
Subhūti, it is just as if a winged bird were to move through the sky, in the mid-air.
He does not fall to the ground,
nor does he remain supported by anything;
he dwells in the very midst of the sky, in open space.
And even there he is not dependent and not established.
In just this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells by means of the dwelling in emptiness and masters emptiness.
He dwells by means of the signless dwelling,
he masters the signless,
and he dwells by means of the wishless dwelling.
He masters the wishless state,
yet he does not fall into emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness while the Buddha-qualities remain incomplete.
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, there were a powerful master of archery who was well-trained and thoroughly perfected in the science of archery.
He should shoot an arrow upward;
having shot an arrow upward, he should, with other arrows, intercept and ward off that arrow before it falls to the ground.
One should not allow that previous arrow to fall to the ground through its succession of arrows;
that arrow would not fall to the ground as long as one does not desire: "Oh, alas! Let this arrow fall to the ground!"

In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom and sustained by skill in means does not directly realize that ultimate limit of reality as long as those roots of merit have not matured and fully ripened for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
When those roots of merit have matured and fully ripened for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, [then he realizes it].
Then he realizes that supreme limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing and cultivating the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) should thus contemplate the profound nature of these phenomena, yet he must not realize it [prematurely].
When this had been said, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows: "O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is a doer of what is difficult;
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is a doer of what is supremely difficult, he who courses in emptiness."
He dwells in emptiness and enters the concentration of emptiness,
yet he does not realize the limit of reality.
“O Blessed One, this is most wonderful;
O Sugata, this is supremely wonderful.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: “So it is, Subhūti; so it is.”
The bodhisattva mahāsattva is a doer of what is difficult;
the bodhisattva mahāsattva is a doer of what is supremely difficult, who courses in emptiness and dwells in emptiness.
He enters the meditative absorption of emptiness,
yet he does not personally realize the limit of reality.
Why is that?
For it is thus, Subhūti: all sentient beings have not been abandoned by the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
He possesses such specific aspirations as these: "I must liberate all these sentient beings.
When the bodhisattva mahāsattva generates the thought, "All sentient beings have not been abandoned by me," [he acts accordingly].
Thinking, "I must liberate these beings," he brings forth the emptiness gateway to concentration and liberation,
and he brings forth the signlessness gateway to concentration and liberation.

When he brings forth the wishless concentration as a door to liberation, then it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with skillful means; he will not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) in the interim while the buddha-qualities remain incomplete.
Why is that?
For indeed, his skill in means provides protection for him;
and that very production of the thought of awakening consists in his not abandoning any sentient beings.
Thus, endowed with this production of the thought of awakening and with skill in means, he does not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) in the interim.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates these profound states,
or desires to contemplate them— namely, the emptiness gate of liberation, the signlessness gate of liberation, [and the wishlessness gate of liberation]— (Vaidya 186)
The wishless (*apraṇihita*) is a gate of liberation consisting of meditative concentration;
by means of it, one should thus direct the mind: "For a long time these beings have wandered in the realm of objective apprehension through the perception of a 'being.
For the sake of abandoning the view of objective apprehension in those beings who possess such views, I shall, having fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, teach the Dharma."
Having reflected thus, he enters the concentration on emptiness, the gateway to liberation,
yet he does not realize the limit of reality;
he enters the concentration on the signless, the gateway to liberation.
And he does not realize the limit of reality;
he enters the wishless gate of liberation, which is meditative concentration, yet he does not realize the limit of reality.
Thus, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with this production of the thought of awakening and this skill in means does not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) in the interim,
nor does he fall away from the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (maitrī-samādhi), nor from the meditative absorptions of compassion, sympathetic joy, or equanimity. Why is that?
For a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is embraced by skill in means increases all the more in pure qualities;
his faculties, such as faith and the rest, become sharper, and he attains the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path.
Furthermore, Subhūti, it occurs to a bodhisattva mahāsattva: "For a long time these beings have wandered in the apprehension of phenomena through the notion of a dharma.
For the sake of abandoning the view of apprehension in those who hold the view of apprehension, I shall, having awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, teach the Dharma.
Endowed with this production of the thought of awakening and his previous skill in means, he enters the emptiness concentration, which is a door to liberation.
Yet he does not realize the limit of reality,
nor does he fall away from the meditative absorptions of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. For what reason?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva embraced by skillful means increases all the more in pure qualities;
his faculties, such as faith and the rest, become sharper,
and he attains the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path.

Furthermore, Subhūti, it occurs to a bodhisattva mahāsattva: "For a long time these beings have wandered in signs by means of the perception of signs. For the sake of abandoning their perception of signs, I shall, having awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, teach the Dharma.
For the sake of sentient beings, he enters the signless concentration, which is a gateway to liberation.
Endowed with this production of the thought of awakening and with his former skill in means, he enters the signless concentration, the gateway to liberation,
yet he does not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Nor does he fall away from loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, or from any meditative concentration.
For what reason?
Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is embraced by skill in means increases all the more in pure qualities;
furthermore, his faculties, such as faith and the rest, become sharper.
One attains the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path.

Furthermore, Subhūti, it occurs to a bodhisattva mahāsattva: "For a long time these beings have been perverted by the notion of permanence, the notion of pleasure, the notion of self, and the notion of purity.
I shall act in such a way that, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, [I may eliminate] the notion of permanence and the notion of pleasure..."
I shall teach the Dharma for the sake of abandoning the notion of a self, the notion of purity, and perversion—[teaching that] "all this is impermanent, it is not permanent;
all this is suffering, it is not happiness;
all this is non-self, it is not possessed of a self."
"All this is impure; this is not pure.

Endowed with this production of the thought of awakening and sustained by his previous skill in means and the perfection of wisdom, he does not realize the limit of reality midway while the Buddha-qualities are as yet incomplete.
Thus, having attained and dwelling in the wishless concentration, which is a gateway to liberation, he does not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi),
nor does he fall away from loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, or equanimity.
For what reason?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva, being embraced by skill in means, increases all the more in wholesome qualities;
moreover, his faculties, such as faith and the rest, become sharper.
He attains the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path.
For any bodhisattva mahāsattva, Subhūti, who generates this thought: "These beings, indeed, have for a long time practiced in apprehension, and even now they practice in apprehension."

Those who have previously practiced with the perception of signs continue even now to practice with the perception of signs; those who have previously practiced in perversion continue even now to practice in perversion;
those who have previously practiced with the perception of a composite whole continue even now to practice with the perception of a composite whole.
Having practiced in false perceptions, they still practice in false perceptions even now;
having practiced in wrong views, they still practice in wrong views even now.
I shall act in such a way that all these faults of theirs will cease to exist in every respect, in every way, and entirely.
"They shall not be known.
In this way, he attends to all sentient beings;
and thus the bodhisattva mahāsattva, endowed with this mental attention of mindfulness and this production of the thought of awakening, [proceeds].

Endowed with skill in means and sustained by the perfection of wisdom, he thus contemplates the true nature (*dharmatā*) of these profound phenomena— whether from the perspective of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, lack of formative activity,
non-arising, non-birth, or non-existence.
Subhūti, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with such knowledge should fall into the state of non-conditioning or dwell together with the triple world.
This possibility does not exist.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should be questioned by another bodhisattva mahāsattva as follows: "Of which dharmas must mastery be achieved?
And what kinds of mental states must be brought forth?"
Those mental states which a bodhisattva mahāsattva brings forth, while not actualizing emptiness, not actualizing the signless,
and not actualizing the wishless.
He does not realize the unconditioned, he does not realize non-arising, and he does not realize non-birth.
He does not realize non-existence, yet he cultivates the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being thus questioned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva, answers in this way: "Only emptiness should be brought to mind by a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should attend to the mind upon the signless alone, the wishless alone, the unconditioned alone, non-arising alone, non-birth alone, and non-existence alone;
provided that he does not fail to demonstrate the production of the thought of never abandoning all sentient beings,
or fails to explain skill in means."

Subhūti, it should be understood that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not been predicted by those previous Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as being irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is that?
For he does not indicate, nor does he manifest that unique quality of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
He does not demonstrate it,
he does not understand it,
and when questioned, he does not explain it.
He does not relinquish it, nor does he cause him to enter that stage,
which is the stage of the irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Subhūti said: "Could there be, Blessed One, another way by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva would become irreversible? The Blessed One said: "There could be, Subhūti, such a way by which that bodhisattva mahāsattva would become irreversible:
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having heard this perfection of wisdom or even without having heard it, should practice in this manner."

One should respond thus: "A bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as irreversible. Subhūti said: "In that case, Blessed One, many practice for the sake of awakening, but few are those who respond in this way."
The Blessed One said: "For it is thus, Subhūti, that those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have been prophesied for the stage of knowledge that is irreversible are few.
But as for those who will be prophesied, they will answer in this way."
Those various bodhisattva mahāsattvas should be known as those who have cultivated roots of virtue with fervor;
those various bodhisattva mahāsattvas are incapable of being led astray by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, even while in a dream, contemplates that all phenomena are like a dream, [he is to be known as such].
And yet he does not realize it;
Subhūti, this too should be known as a characteristic of the irreversible nature of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, even when in a dream, a bodhisattva mahāsattva has no longing for or a mind that finds praise in the level of a śrāvaka, the level of a pratyekabuddha, or the triple world— Subhūti, this too should be known as a characteristic of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, even in his dreams, a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the Tathāgata, the Arhat, seated in the midst of an assembly of many hundreds, many thousands, up to many hundreds of thousands of koṭī-niyutas, within a circular pavilion, surrounded by the community of monks and honored by the community of bodhisattvas, teaching the Dharma.
He perceives himself as a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Subhūti, this too should be known as a mark of irreversibility of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, even while in a dream, a bodhisattva mahāsattva rises into the air and teaches the Dharma to sentient beings;
he perceives that fathom-wide radiance and manifests those monks.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva, even while in a dream, perceives those who, having gone to other directions and other world-systems, perform the work of a Buddha and teach the Dharma."
Subhūti, this too should be known as a mark of irreversibility for an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, even when in the midst of a dream, is not startled, does not tremble,
and does not fall into terror.
Whether during a destruction of a village, a city, a town, a district, or a kingdom; or when a fire is raging;
or upon seeing wild beasts or other species of small animals; or when the severing of one's head is imminent;
or having encountered various other great terrors, horrors, sufferings, and dejections.
Furthermore, having seen the great terrors and fearsome sufferings of other beings as well, no fear or terror arises within him;

he does not tremble, he does not become terrified, nor does he fall into a state of panic. Then, having awakened from that dream and immediately upon rising, it occurs to him: "This entire triple world is like a dream."
And thus, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I must teach the Dharma by teaching it correctly.
Subhūti, this too should be known as a characteristic of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva has fallen asleep and sees beings in the hells, this thought occurs to him: "I shall act in such a way that, when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there will be no states of woe whatsoever, in any way or in any manner, in my buddha-field."
Subhūti, this too should be known as a characteristic of the purification from the lower realms of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.

In that regard, Subhūti, how is it to be known that in the buddha-field of this irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva who has awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, all states of woe will not exist in any way, in every respect, and in all things?

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, even while in a dream, sees beings who have gone to the hells, or to the animal realm, or to the realm of hungry ghosts, and regains mindfulness; having regained that mindfulness, he thinks: "I shall act in such a way that when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there will not be any states of woe at all, in any way, in any manner, anywhere in my buddha-field."
In this way, Subhūti, the characteristic of the purification of the miserable states of existence for a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be understood.
This too, Subhūti, should be understood as a characteristic of the non-retrogression of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fallen asleep, finds himself amidst a burning city or a burning village, upon waking from that very dream, he reflects thus: "Those forms, those marks, and those signs which were seen by me while in the state of sleep— "
Those forms, those marks, and those signs by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be known as irreversible—
I possess those forms, those marks, and those signs.
By this truth, by this word of truth, may this burning of the city or the burning of the village that is currently occurring be extinguished!
"May it become cool;
may it go out!
Subhūti, if a village fire or a city fire is extinguished,"
It becomes cool;

it sets. Subhūti, it should be understood that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has been predicted by those former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones as irreversible from unexcelled, perfect awakening.
If it does not become tranquil,
does not become cooled,
and does not go to its cessation,

Subhūti, it should be understood that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not been predicted to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. However, Subhūti, if that conflagration, having passed beyond [the first house], goes from house to house, from street to street, or from one street to another house, and burns them;
It does not become tranquil, it does not become cooled, and it does not set.
Subhūti, it should be understood that this accumulation of karma by that bodhisattva mahāsattva— which leads to the rejection of the Dharma and results in poor wisdom—
is such that this very karma ripens for him even in the present life.
It is precisely because of that rejection of the Dharma that his remaining karma ripens in this manner.
"Subhūti, this is the cause, this is the condition for this bodhisattva mahāsattva’s characteristic of being irreversible.
Subhūti, this bodhisattva mahāsattva also should be understood as irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Furthermore, Subhūti, those aspects, those marks, and those signs by which an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be recognized—
those aspects, those marks, and those signs I shall teach. Therefore, listen well and attend closely.
"Pay attention;
I shall speak to you.
"Very well, Blessed One," the venerable Subhūti replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this: "Subhūti, if some man, woman, boy, or girl were seized or possessed by a non-human being,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should approach them and direct his meditative resolve in this way."
If I have been prophesied for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by those former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones,
