then my resolute intention is pure to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; just as I desire to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
My mental attention toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment is completely pure; my mind as a śrāvaka and my mind as a pratyekabuddha have been removed,
and therefore I must fully awaken to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
"I shall not fail to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; I will indeed attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Furthermore, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who currently reside, remain, and maintain themselves in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems,"
For those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, there is nothing unknown, unseen, unperceived, unrealized, or not fully awakened to.

Just as those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, knowing my inner resolve— that "I too shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment"— by this truth, by this word of truth, may this woman or man, boy or girl, who has been seized or possessed by a non-human spirit, [be released].

"Let him depart! Subhūti, if that non-human being does not depart even when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva speaks thus, it should be known that this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has not been predicted for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment by those previous Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas."
Furthermore, Subhūti, if that non-human being departs while the bodhisattva mahāsattva is speaking in this way,

then it should be known, Subhūti, that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has been predicted to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by those former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones. Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Examination of Skill in Means," in the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom.
Chapter Twenty-one: On the Deeds of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti, in that regard, a bodhisattva mahāsattva will speak thus: "By this truth, by this word of truth..."
"I have been prophesied for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by those previous Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones;
by that truth, by that word of truth, let this non-human being depart!
In that situation, Subhūti, Māra, the Evil One, will exert himself to make that non-human being depart.
For what reason?

Because Māra, the Evil One, will exert even greater power and more intense energy against that bodhisattva mahāsattva who has long since set out in the vehicle, thinking, "How might this non-human being depart?"
In this way, that non-human being will depart through the influence of Māra;
and it will occur to that bodhisattva mahāsattva: "This non-human being has departed by my own power.
But he will not know: "This non-human being has departed through the power of Māra."
He will become excited by that much alone;

because of that excitement, he will hold other bodhisattva mahāsattvas in contempt, deride them, mock them, revile them, and disparage them, thinking: "I have been prophesied for unexcelled [enlightenment] by those previous Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones."
Regarding "in [the pursuit of] perfect enlightenment":
by that much alone, he will further give rise to pride;
he will produce pride.
He will increase pride, he will fully develop pride,
he will stiffen with pride.
He will support conceit, he will increase conceit, he will further augment conceit.

He will give rise to pride; by that pride— by overweening pride, pride beyond pride, false pride, and conceit— he will distance himself from omniscience and distance himself from the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha.
The self-arisen wisdom,
the wisdom of the omniscient one—
he will distance himself from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Seeing such spiritual friends— bodhisattva mahāsattvas who possess virtuous qualities, noble resolve, and perfected high intention, who are skilled in means, and endowed with the qualities of irreversibility— he will give rise to conceit and, out of contempt, will not serve nor honor such spiritual friends.
He will not attend upon them, nor will he question them;
thus, he will tighten that very bond of Māra.
Two stages are to be expected for him: either the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha.

Thus, Subhūti, by means of this resort to truth, Māra the Evil One [will deceive] a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has recently set out in the vehicle, who has little faith, little learning, and is devoid of a spiritual friend, regarding the perfection of wisdom.
"Subhūti, one who is not taken hold of and lacks skill in means will create an obstacle to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
this too, Subhūti, should be known as a deed of Māra for a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
Furthermore, Subhūti, there will be a work of Māra even by means of the designation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s name.
And how, Subhūti, will there be a work of Māra even by means of the designation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s name?
Here, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One will approach a bodhisattva mahāsattva even by means of the designation of his name and even by means of the empowerment of his name.
Approaching him in one or another guise, he will say this: "You have been predicted for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by those former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
For what reason?
Because this is your name."
This is your mother’s name;
this is your father’s name;
this is your brother’s name.
"This is the name of your sister;
this is the name of your friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations;
and he shall proclaim the names of your maternal and paternal ancestors up to the seventh generation—'In such-and-such a direction you were born.'"
"Born in such-and-such a country, or in such-and-such a village, city, or market town"—
if he is by nature gentle, [he will say this].
He will speak to him thus: "Previously, you were indeed gentle.
If he is by nature of sharp faculties, then he will speak to him thus: "Previously, you were also of sharp faculties."
If he will be a forest-dweller,
if he will be an alms-food eater, or if he will be a wearer of rag-robes;
If he will be one who eats only after the midday meal,
if he will be one who sits at a single sitting, if he will be one who accepts whatever bedding is provided;
If he will be one who wears robes made of discarded rags, if he will be a cemetery-dweller, or if he will be a tree-root dweller;
If he will be one who eats in moderation,
if he will be one who dwells in the open air,
or if he will be one who wears rag-robes;
If he will be one who has few desires, contented, and secluded; if he will be free from the hypocrisy of foot-unguents; and if he will be soft-spoken and of little speech.
Then Māra, the Evil One, will point this out to him by means of various qualities pertaining to the present life, saying: "In the past as well, you were endowed with this and that quality;
you were certainly prophesied for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment on the irreversible stage of a bodhisattva by those former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
For what reason?
For these very qualities of purification (dhutaguṇa) of such a kind exist in him;
certainly, he must have been endowed with these same qualities of purification in the past as well.
Thus, by means of that former designation of a name, that basis of a name, and his present austerity of the qualities of purification, he will give rise to conceit.
It will occur to him: "I have been predicted for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment by those former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, since these qualities are found in me.
And Māra, the Evil One, will say this to him: "You have been predicted as irreversible for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment by the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened One."
For what reason?
Because you possess such ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa) as these.
Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra, the Evil One, will sometimes approach in the guise of a monk.
Sometimes in the guise of a bhikṣuṇī, sometimes in the guise of an upāsaka, and sometimes in the guise of an upāsikā.
Sometimes in the guise of a brahmin, sometimes in the guise of a householder,
and sometimes in the guise of a mother.
Sometimes in the guise of a father,
sometimes in the guise of a brother,
and sometimes in the guise of a sister.
At times he will approach in the guise of a friend, a minister, a kinsman, or a blood relative;

having approached, he will say this: "You have been prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment upon the stage of a Bodhisattva from which there is no turning back by former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas.
For what reason?"
For indeed, such qualities of purification (dhutaguṇa) as these exist in them, which are the very qualities of irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, Subhūti, those qualities of irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas that have been described by me, as well as their forms, marks, and signs, have been described.
Those [qualities] will not belong to him.
Subhūti, other bodhisattva mahāsattvas should understand this: "Alas, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is possessed by Māra.
Why is that?
Those forms, those marks, and those signs which belong to irreversible Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas will not be present in him.
Furthermore, Subhūti, that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva will, by means of this empowerment of a name, give rise to conceit.

Having given rise to conceit, overcome by pride, overcome by arrogance, and overcome by the influence of Māra, he will despise other bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas; he will mock them, deride them, revile them, and disparage them. Subhūti, this too should be understood as a work of Māra for a bodhisattva, mahāsattva, occurring through the influence of names.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize as the work of Māra any prediction based on a name or a designation by name.
And how, Subhūti, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva recognize the work of Māra through a prediction based on a name or a designation by name?
Here, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One, approaching in the guise of a monk, will predict to a bodhisattva mahāsattva in this way:
"When you have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, this shall be your name"—
this is exactly what was followed, reflected upon, and deliberated by that mind, thinking: "O, may such a name as this be mine when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
He will prophesy that very name.

In this regard, a bodhisattva who is of an unwise nature and unskilled in means will think: "Just as I have followed, reflected upon, and deliberated over this name—'Oh, would that this were my name when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment!'"
In this way, that monk has declared it. Thus, whatever name he himself had reflected upon,
and whatever name was uttered by that wicked Māra, or by a deity belonging to the host of Māra who had been conjured up, or by a monk possessed by Māra— [he recognizes them as such].

Having compared those two things— how my production of the thought of awakening arose and how the name was proclaimed by this monk— he will think, "My name accords with the name [given] by those former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones; I have been prophesied for unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening by them."
Subhūti, those modes, signs, and marks that I have described as belonging to irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas will not be present in him.
Devoid of them, he will give rise to conceit on account of this designation by name and this prediction by name.

Having conceived such conceit, he will then look down upon other bodhisattva mahāsattvas, thinking: "I have been prophesied for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, but these others have not been prophesied for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Thus, by means of that pride, excessive pride, pride beyond pride, overweening pride, and false pride, while looking down upon those other bodhisattva mahāsattvas, he will distance himself from omniscience.
He will distance himself from the wisdom of a Buddha.

For one who is not sustained by the perfection of wisdom, who lacks skill in means, who is separated from spiritual friends, and who is embraced by evil friends, one of two grounds is to be expected: either the ground of a śrāvaka or [the ground of a pratyekabuddha].

Or the level of a pratyekabuddha. However, if after wandering and transmigrating for a very long time, he should desire to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment by relying on this very perfection of wisdom, and if he should approach spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), [he will attain it].
And he will frequently visit them;
by that very acquisition of a physical body, he will revile and vomit out those former productions of thought.
He will feel loathing,
he will relinquish it,
and he will confess it.
Nevertheless, the stage of a Buddha will be difficult for him to attain.
Why is that?
Subhūti, it is because the state of mental conceit is a far more serious offense for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Subhūti, it is just as if for a monk belonging to the vehicle of the disciples (śrāvakayānika), there are four root downfalls on the level of a disciple that are grave; by committing any one of these downfalls, he ceases to be a monk, ceases to be a śramaṇa, and ceases to be a son of the Śākya.
This [downfall] is even more serious than those four downfalls.
This arising of a mind of pride— namely, the arising of a great unwholesome thought produced by the disparagement of a bodhisattva mahāsattva under the pretext of his name—
should be understood as a more serious mental offense than those four transgressions.
"Let alone, Subhūti, the four grave root transgressions;
even compared to the five deeds of immediate retribution, Subhūti, this production of the thought [of awakening] is more serious."

This production of the thought of awakening that has arisen accompanied by pride under the pretext of the name of a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be understood as a more serious offense than those five deeds of immediate retribution.
For in this way, Subhūti, even under the pretext of such a name, extremely subtle deeds of Māra will arise.
These should be understood by the bodhisattva mahāsattva;
they should be made known to others,
and having understood them, they should be abandoned.
Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One will approach a bodhisattva mahāsattva with the quality of seclusion and will urge him on and remind him.
And how, Subhūti, will Māra the Evil One approach a bodhisattva mahāsattva with the quality of seclusion and urge him on and remind him?
Here, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One will approach a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Having approached, he will say: "The Tathāgata speaks in praise of solitude; one should dwell in forests, woods, mountain retreats, caves, cemeteries, heaps of straw, and so forth.
But, Subhūti, I do not speak of such solitude for a bodhisattva mahāsattva as this—namely, dwelling in forest hermitages, remote lodgings, and secluded places far from inhabited areas.
Various places such as forest retreats, mountain caves, cremation grounds, heaps of straw, and so forth.

Subhūti said: "But what, Blessed One, is that other solitude of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, if it be the dwelling in forest retreats, remote lodgings, uninhabited places, various secluded spots such as jungle thickets, mountain caves, cemeteries, or heaps of straw,
yet he does not actually reside in them?"
"Furthermore, Blessed One, what is the other kind of solitude for a bodhisattva mahāsattva?

When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is solitary by being free from mental engagements associated with the śrāvakas, and is solitary by being free from mental engagements associated with the pratyekabuddhas,"
In this way, that bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in solitude.

For even while dwelling at the edge of a village, being embraced by the perfection of wisdom and skill in means, he should dwell in the abode of loving-kindness and great compassion toward all sentient beings.
Dwelling in this abode, he indeed dwells in solitude.
Furthermore, Subhūti, this seclusion from mental engagements associated with Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas has been authorized by me for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Dwelling in this seclusion, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva passes his days and nights;
he dwells secluded.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in remote lodgings— such as forest retreats, jungle thickets, mountain caves, cemeteries, or secluded spots— by means of this dwelling,

that bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in solitude. However, Subhūti, as for those remote lodgings in forest retreats, jungle thickets, mountain caves, cemeteries, or secluded spots which Māra, the Evil One, will point out as being solitude:

Because he is mixed with that seclusion by means of mental attentions associated with the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and because he does not apply himself to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), he does not fulfill the knowledge of the omniscient one (sarvajñajñāna).
Thus, dwelling in such a mixed dwelling and dwelling with an unpurified mental attention, his activities of body, speech, and mind will indeed be unpurified.
Being one whose activities of body, speech, and mind are unpurified, he [will disparage] other Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas who dwell in the vicinity of villages...
Dwelling in the abode of wisdom, skillful means, and great compassion, he will look down upon those who dwell with mental orientations associated with Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Even while dwelling in the forest, because his physical, vocal, and mental actions are unpurified, he remains one who dwells in confusion rather than one who dwells in solitude.

While dwelling in the abode of wisdom, skillful means, and great compassion, he lives near a village with completely pure conduct of body, speech, and mind; yet, being secluded from and unmixed with mental orientations associated with the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas,

he disregards those who possess such Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha-associated mental orientations, and thus he will not become an attainer of the meditations, concentrations, attainments, liberations, and superknowledges.
And these [perfections] of his will not reach fulfillment.
Why is that?
Because he is unskilled in means.

Furthermore, Subhūti, even if a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to dwell in forest wildernesses extending for hundreds of yojanas— wildernesses devoid of herds of predatory beasts and birds, free from the roaming of small animals, predators, yakṣas, and rākṣasas, and rid of the terrors, fears, and calamities of robbers and the dangers of the wilderness— and were to remain there for a year, or a hundred years, or a thousand years, or a hundred thousand years, or ten million years, or a hundred million years, or a billion years, or ten billion years;
Whether for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of years, or even longer than that,
they would not understand this seclusion taught by me.
That seclusion by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having set out with resolute intention and being endowed with resolute intention,

dwells— failing to understand that, an unskilled-in-means bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells making the wilderness his supreme goal; and therein, relying on that seclusion, he becomes attached, clinging, obsessed, and fallen into obsession.
"Subhūti, it is not by this much alone that a bodhisattva pleases my mind.
Why is that?
Subhūti, it is because of that seclusion which I have described for bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas."
Dwelling in that solitude, he is not seen in this solitude.
Then Māra, the Evil One, approaches him and, standing in the sky above in the atmosphere, will say: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
This is the solitude of the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, as described by the Tathāgata."
"By this very seclusion, noble son, do you dwell;
in this way you will quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then, departing from that seclusion once again, he went from the forest to the vicinity of a village and [approached] those other bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas.

He will despise those gentle monks who are his fellow practitioners of the holy life, who possess virtuous qualities, who are unmixed with mental orientations associated with the disciples or pratyekabuddhas, and whose bodily, vocal, and mental actions and livelihoods are completely pure.
He will speak thus: "Alas, these venerable ones live in a confused manner!"
"It is not by dwelling in seclusion that these venerable ones dwell; alas, they dwell in a crowded manner,
not dwelling in seclusion."
Those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who dwell in seclusion,
he will accuse of dwelling in confusion and of dwelling in crowded places.
And those who dwell in a crowded manner,
he will approach with a secluded manner of dwelling and will conceive reverence for them therein.
And where one ought to produce reverence,
there he will produce pride.
For what reason?
"I am exhorted by non-human beings; I am reminded by non-human beings.
Subhūti, this is the dwelling in which I dwell."
"Whom dwelling on the outskirts of a village will non-human beings exhort?
Whom dwelling within a village will non-human beings remind?"—
in this way, he will despise persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle.
Subhūti, this person should be known as a caṇḍāla among bodhisattvas,
should be known as a defiler of bodhisattvas, and should be known as a mere counterfeit of a bodhisattva.
He should be known as a counterfeit bodhisattva,
a mere *kāraṇḍava* weed among bodhisattvas,
and a thief in the guise of a śramaṇa.
He is a thief among persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle;
he is a thief of the world with its gods.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a person of such a kind should not be associated with, should not be honored, and should not be attended upon.
For what reason?
Such persons should be known as having fallen into conceit;
and others of such a kind are also few.
They would cause corruption among those who have newly set out upon the Great Vehicle with steadfastness.
Indeed, such persons as these should be known as those whose qualities are impure;
indeed, such persons as these should be known as non-noble.
Indeed, Subhūti, those persons of such a kind should be known as possessing non-noble qualities.
Furthermore, for that bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not abandoned all sentient beings and has not abandoned omniscience, [it is not possible to fall back].

Since unexcelled, perfect enlightenment has not been abandoned by that bodhisattva mahāsattva, who— possessing a resolute intention and desiring to fully awaken to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and wishing to act for the benefit of all sentient beings— should not associate with persons of such a kind.
They are not to be honored, nor are they to be attended upon;
rather, Subhūti, one who has arisen for the sake of all sentient beings [should attend] upon these and others.

Furthermore, one must always maintain a mind of constant vigilance regarding the deeds of Māra; one must have a fearful mind toward teaching the path to all sentient beings who have not yet attained it, while remaining unattached to the three realms.
Even so, one should act with loving-kindness and compassion, generating great compassion and taking up sympathetic concern for those who have correctly entered the practice.
With a mind full of joy toward sentient beings, and being equanimous toward all phenomena by way of the non-apprehensibility of their true nature, one should generate this thought:
"I shall act in such a way that all faults of the works of Māra will, in every respect, in every manner, in every way, everywhere, and at all times, cease to exist."
They will not arise;
if they should arise,
they will immediately pass away.
"I shall train in this way"—
this too should be understood as the courageous exertion of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, undertaken through their own higher knowledge.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize this as the work of Māra, even when it appears as the quality of solitude.
The twenty-first chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Deeds of Māra," in the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom.
(Vaidya 197) Chapter Twenty-Two: On the Spiritual Friend.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Subhūti once more: "In this regard, Subhūti, by a bodhisattva..."

A great being who has set out with resolute intention and desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment must, from the very beginning, serve, honor, and attend upon spiritual friends.
Subhūti asked: "Furthermore, Blessed One, which ones are to be known as the spiritual friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"

"Those spiritual friends whom a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having set out with resolute intention and desiring to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, must from the very beginning serve and honor"— when this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, they are indeed the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones,
as well as those irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are skilled in the conduct of a bodhisattva."
Those who instruct and advise him in the perfections,
and those who teach and explain the perfection of wisdom to him—
Subhūti, these should be known as the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s spiritual friends.
Subhūti, it should be understood that the perfection of wisdom alone is the spiritual friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, all six perfections should be understood as the spiritual friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
indeed, the six perfections themselves are the Teacher.
The six perfections are the path;
the six perfections are the light;
the six perfections are the torch.
The six perfections are illumination;
the six perfections are protection;
the six perfections are refuge.
The six perfections are a shelter; the six perfections are a final resort;
the six perfections are an island.
The six perfections are the mother; the six perfections are the father;
the six perfections lead to knowledge, to awakening, and to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
For what reason?
Because here, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is fully established; that is to say, within the six perfections.
Furthermore, Subhūti, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who, in the past, having awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, have entered final nirvāṇa—
The omniscience of those Buddhas, those Blessed Ones, has also arisen from just this, namely, from the six perfections.
Subhūti, as for those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who will appear in the future time and will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—
The omniscience of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, has likewise arisen from nothing other than these six perfections.

Subhūti, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones who, at present, have fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and remain in immeasurable, incalculable, infinite, and inconceivable world-systems— [their omniscience has also arisen from these six perfections].
They remain, they sustain themselves, and they teach the Dharma.
The omniscience of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, has likewise arisen from these very same six perfections.
Subhūti, I too, as a Tathāgata, Arhat, and perfectly enlightened Buddha, have now fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment through them.
For even my own omniscience, Subhūti, has indeed originated from this very source, namely, from the six perfections.
Why is that?
For, Subhūti, within these six perfections are included the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening,
the four divine abodes,
and the four means of attraction.

Whatever Buddha-dharma there may be— whether it be the knowledge of a Buddha, self-existent knowledge, inconceivable knowledge, incomparable knowledge, immeasurable knowledge, incalculable knowledge, unequaled knowledge, or knowledge equal to the unequaled—
all that is included within the six perfections. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand that the six perfections themselves are their spiritual friends.
The six perfections alone are the Teacher;
the six perfections are the path;
the six perfections are the light.
The six perfections are a torch;
the six perfections are illumination;
the six perfections are protection. (Vaidya 198)
The perfections are the refuge;
the six perfections are the shelter; the six perfections are the ultimate resort.
The six perfections are the island; the six perfections are the mother;
the six perfections are the father.
The six perfections lead to knowledge, to awakening, to omniscience, and to the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the six perfections, he becomes a benefactor even to all sentient beings who have not returned his favor.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in these six perfections must indeed hear, take up, bear in mind, recite, master, promote, teach, explain, proclaim, and study this very perfection of wisdom.
They should be examined in terms of their meaning, their nature, and their method; they should be contemplated, questioned, and interrogated.
Why is that?
Because this perfection of wisdom is the precursor of the six perfections, their leader, their guide, their demonstrator, their instructor, their mother, and their nurse.
For what reason?
Because the five perfections, when separated from the perfection of wisdom, are not known,
nor do they receive the designation "perfection."
"Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain independence from others and wishes to stand in that independence from others should train in this very perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti said: "Blessed One, what is the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom has non-attachment as its characteristic."

Subhūti said: "Could it be, Blessed One, that by the same characteristic of non-attachment through which the perfection of wisdom exists, all dharmas also exist by that very same characteristic of non-attachment?
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Subhūti; so it is."
Subhūti, there may be a way in which, by that very same characteristic of non-attachment through which the perfection of wisdom exists, all dharmas also exist.
For what reason?
For all dharmas, Subhūti, are detached;
for all dharmas, Subhūti, are empty.
Therefore, Subhūti, by that very same characteristic of non-attachment, the perfection of wisdom is detached and empty.
By that very characteristic of non-attachment, all phenomena are secluded and empty.
Subhūti said: "If, Blessed One, all phenomena are secluded and all phenomena are empty,"
"How, Blessed One, is the affliction of sentient beings known?
How, Blessed One, is the purification of sentient beings known?
For, Blessed One, that which is secluded is not afflicted."
"Blessed One, that which is secluded does not become purified;
Blessed One, that which is empty is not defiled, nor does that which is empty become purified."
Moreover, Blessed One, one does not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of that which is secluded or empty.
Furthermore, Blessed One, apart from emptiness, no dharma whatsoever is apprehended, whether it be one who has awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, or the awakening itself.
He will fully awaken, or he is fully awakening;
or how, O Blessed One, are we to understand the meaning of this that has been spoken?
"May the Blessed One teach!
May the Sugata teach!
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "What do you think, Subhūti? Do sentient beings for a long time course in the conceit of 'I' and the conceit of 'mine'?"
Subhūti said: "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
For a long time, sentient beings have wandered in the conceit of 'I' and the possessiveness of 'mine'."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Are 'I-making' and 'mine-making' empty?
Subhūti replied: "They are empty, Blessed One; they are empty, Sugata."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Is it by means of 'I-making' and 'mine-making' that beings wander in saṃsāra?
Subhūti replied: "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata."

"By means of the notion of 'I' and the notion of 'mine,' sentient beings wander in saṃsāra. The Blessed One said: "In this way indeed, Subhūti, the affliction of sentient beings is recognized; it is according to the grasping and the attachment of sentient beings."
Likewise is affliction;
yet herein no one is afflicted.
And just as, Subhūti, there is no grasping and no attachment, so too are "I-making" and "mine-making" not perceived.
In this way indeed, Subhūti, the purification of all sentient beings is perceived.
Just as there is no grasping and no attachment toward sentient beings,
so too is purification;
and herein, no one at all is purified.
"In this way indeed, Subhūti, practicing, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in the perfection of wisdom.
In this way indeed, Subhūti, while all dharmas are secluded and all dharmas are empty, the affliction and purification of sentient beings are discerned.
Subhūti said: "It is wonderful, Blessed One, how it is that while all dharmas are secluded and all dharmas are empty, the affliction and purification of sentient beings are discerned."
And thus, Blessed One, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom.
For practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice in form,
nor in feeling, nor in perception, nor in mental formations.
He does not course in consciousness.
Coursing thus, O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes unassailable by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
Coursing thus, O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva surpasses the conduct of all persons belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas and the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.
And he attains a state that is unsurpassed.
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, Buddhahood, Tathāgatahood, self-become-hood, and omniscience are indeed unsurpassed.

O Blessed One, by dwelling even in this mental engagement associated with the perfection of wisdom, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should pass his days and nights; he will be near to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
and he will quickly awaken to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: “So it is, Subhūti; so it is.
Moving in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva moves in the perfection of wisdom.
For moving in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not move in form.”
He does not course in feeling, nor in perception, nor in mental formations,
nor in consciousness. Subhūti, when he courses in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes invincible to the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva surpasses the conduct of all persons belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas and the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and he attains a state that cannot be surpassed.
Why is that?
For, Subhūti, Buddhahood, Tathāgatahood, Self-Become-hood, and omniscience are indeed unsurpassed.
By dwelling in this very mental engagement associated with the perfection of wisdom, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should pass his days and nights;
he will be close to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And he would swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if all the beings in Jambudvīpa were to simultaneously obtain a human body,
and having obtained a human body, were to conceive the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
Having generated the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, they might remain for as long as life lasts;
remaining for as long as life lasts, they might for the duration of their lives honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate all Tathāgatas;
and likewise, they might give gifts even to all sentient beings.
And they should dedicate that gift toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
What do you think, Subhūti, would those bodhisattva mahāsattvas generate much merit on that account?
Subhūti said: Much, Blessed One.
“Much, Sugata!

The Blessed One said: “Furthermore, Subhūti, that son of good family or daughter of good family who, as a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwells for even a single day with mental engagements associated with the perfection of wisdom, generates far more merit than that.”
For what reason? Because,
Subhūti, to the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells day and night with mental engagements associated with the perfection of wisdom,
to that same extent he becomes worthy of offerings from all sentient beings.
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, other sentient beings do not possess such a mind accompanied by loving-kindness as that which belongs to this bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Setting aside the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, the Tathāgatas are indeed peerless individuals.
For, Subhūti, the Tathāgatas are indeed incomparable;
for, Subhūti, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas are endowed with inconceivable dharmas.
And how, Subhūti, does that son of good family or daughter of good family produce such merit?
It is because, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with such wisdom that, being so endowed, he regards all sentient beings as if they were already standing on the execution ground.
At that time, he becomes embraced by great compassion.

Surveying with his divine eye, he sees immeasurable, incalculable, boundless, and infinite beings who are possessed of actions of immediate retribution, those who have fallen into unfavorable conditions, those who are being afflicted, those shrouded by the net of views, and those who do not attain the path.
He sees others who have reached the opportune moment and sees others who are becoming dispassionate;
at that very moment, a great sense of spiritual urgency arises within him.

And having pervaded all those sentient beings with that great loving-kindness and that great compassion, they bring them to mind, thinking: "I shall become the protector of all these sentient beings; I shall liberate all these sentient beings from all sufferings.
And yet, he does not dwell together with any sign, whether that one or another.

Subhūti, this too is the great light of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva for the sake of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. For, Subhūti, by dwelling in this dwelling, bodhisattva mahāsattvas take upon themselves the state of being worthy of offerings from the entire world,
and they do not turn back from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And for those donors and masters of generosity from whom they consume the requisites of robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal provisions for the sick,
having their minds well-established in this perfection of wisdom,
they purify the gift and the sacrificial offering of those donors and masters of generosity.
And omniscience becomes near for them.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to consume the alms-food of the kingdom not in vain,
who wishes to show the path to all sentient beings, and who wishes to produce a vast illumination for those beings caught in the cycle of existence— [should practice this].
One who desires to liberate all sentient beings from saṃsāra and desires to purify the eyes of all sentient beings should dwell with this mental attention associated with the perfection of wisdom.
If one wishes to dwell with this mental attention, [one should do so].
Therefore, mental attentions associated with the perfection of wisdom should be cultivated.
Why is that?
For whoever considers these mental attentions as those to be cultivated—
That alone shall be his mental attention;
no opportunity should be given to other mental attentions that are devoid of the perfection of wisdom.
He should act in such a way that he passes his days and nights with mental attentions associated with the perfection of wisdom.

Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a certain man who possesses knowledge of precious gems and is an expert in the varieties of precious gems were to obtain a great precious gem that he had never obtained before; having obtained that great precious gem, he would be endowed with a great and sublime joy and gladness.
Then, that great precious gem of his should be lost once again.
On that account, he would be joined with great suffering and mental distress.

Constantly and continuously, his mental attentions would be directed toward that great jewel: "Alas! I am separated from that great jewel. Indeed, that man would not forget that great jewel, nor its qualities, its kind, or its characteristics, until he had either recovered it or found another of the same quality as that great jewel.
It would be obtained.
In the same way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has fallen away from the great maṇi-jewel of the perfection of wisdom—

just like one who has fallen away from a great maṇi-jewel— yet still possesses the perception of it as a jewel and remains unseparated from the mental attention directed toward the perfection of wisdom.
One should seek it with a mind intent on omniscience that is never separated from mental attention to the perfection of wisdom,
until either that [perfection] or another has been attained; during that time,

one must remain undivided from mental attentions associated with the acquisition of the great jewel of the perfection of wisdom, and mental attentions associated with the acquisition of the great jewel of omniscience.
It must be so.

Subhūti said: "Furthermore, Blessed One, since all dharmas and all mental attentions have been declared by the Blessed One to be devoid of intrinsic nature and empty, how then, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain unseparated from mental attentions associated with the perfection of wisdom and mental attentions associated with omniscience?
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "If, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva brings this to mind: 'All dharmas are secluded by their very nature'..."
"All phenomena are empty by their own nature"—
when he attends to this in such a way, through mental engagements associated with the perfection of wisdom and mental engagements associated with omniscience, he remains never separated from them.
Why is that?
For the perfection of wisdom, Subhūti, is empty;
it neither increases nor decreases.
Subhūti said: "If, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is empty,
and it neither increases nor decreases,
how, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva fully realize awakening through a perfection of wisdom that does not increase?"
"And how does one fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom neither increases nor decreases."
Just as the perfection of wisdom, Subhūti, is empty and neither increases nor decreases,
even so, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is empty.
It neither increases nor decreases;
for, Subhūti, just as the perfection of wisdom is empty, [so too is it].
It neither increases nor decreases;
in the very same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is empty; he neither increases, nor does he decrease.
And he does not fall away from it;
from that, the bodhisattva mahāsattva fully realizes awakening,
and thus he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when this is being spoken, does not tremble, is not terrified, does not fall into terror, and does not become despondent,
it should be known, Subhūti, that this bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom.

Subhūti asked: "But, Blessed One, does the perfection of wisdom course in the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One replied: "No indeed, Subhūti. Subhūti asked: "But, Blessed One, what of that which is the emptiness of the perfection of wisdom?"
“Does she course in the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said, “Not so, Subhūti.
He asked, “But then, Blessed One, apart from the emptiness of the perfection of wisdom, is any dharma at all apprehended?”
"Who practices in the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One replied, "Not so, Subhūti.
Subhūti asked, "But then, Blessed One, does emptiness practice in the perfection of wisdom?"
The Blessed One said, "Not so, Subhūti.
Subhūti asked, "But then, Blessed One, is any dharma whatsoever apprehended within emptiness that practices the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said, "Not so, Subhūti."
He asked: "But, Blessed One, does emptiness course in emptiness?
The Blessed One said: "Not so, Subhūti.
He asked: "But, Blessed One, does form course in the perfection of wisdom?"
The Blessed One said, "Not so, Subhūti.
He asked, "But then, Blessed One, do feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness practice in the perfection of wisdom?"
The Blessed One said, "Not so, Subhūti.
He asked, "But then, Blessed One, is that dharma which practices the perfection of wisdom perceived as something other than form?"
The Blessed One said: "Not so, Subhūti.
He asked: "But then, Blessed One, is that dharma perceived as something other than feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?"
“Who is it that practices in the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said, “Not so, Subhūti.
Subhūti asked, “But how then, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice in the perfection of wisdom?”
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Furthermore, Subhūti, do you perceive that dharma which practices the perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, do you perceive that perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices?"
He said, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "What do you think, Subhūti? Do you perceive that dharma which is non-apprehendable?"
"Is that very same dharma which has arisen, will arise, or is arising, or which has ceased, will cease, or is ceasing?
He replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is in this way that the patience regarding non-arising phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva takes such a form.
And, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with such patience is prophesied for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Subhūti, this is the path of fearlessness (vaiśāradya-pratipad) of the Tathāgata, which a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices."

Practicing in this way, striving in this way, and exerting oneself in this way, it is impossible that one should not attain unsurpassed Buddha-knowledge, the knowledge of the omniscient, and the knowledge of the Great Caravan Leader.
Subhūti said: "Blessed One, is that which is the non-arising nature of all dharmas predicted for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?
The Blessed One said: "Not so, Subhūti."
Subhūti said: "How, then, O Blessed One, does there come to be a prediction (vyākaraṇa) for this dharma regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Do you perceive that dharma for which there comes to be a prediction regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?
Subhūti said: "Certainly not, Blessed One."
“O Blessed One, I do not perceive that dharma which has been predicted, will be predicted, or is being predicted for unexcelled perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, O Blessed One, I do not perceive that dharma which fully awakens.”
Whether it be the dharma that is to be fully awakened to, or the dharma by which one awakens to it—
why is that so?

"O Blessed One, since all dharmas are non-apprehendable, it does not occur to me that 'this dharma is fully awakened to,' or 'this dharma is to be fully awakened to,' or 'one awakens to it by means of this dharma.'"
In the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom, this is the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Spiritual Friend."
(Vaidya 203) Chapter Twenty-Three: Śakra.
Now at that time, Śakra, the lord of the gods, had gathered and was seated in that very assembly.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: "Profound, O Blessed One, is this perfection of wisdom!
Indeed, O Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is difficult to see and difficult to realize.
When this had been said, the Blessed One said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "So it is, Kauśika; so it is."
"O Kauśika, this perfection of wisdom is profound;
indeed, O Kauśika, this perfection of wisdom is difficult to see and difficult to realize.
This perfection of wisdom is profound because of the profundity of space."
"Because it is secluded, this perfection of wisdom is difficult to see;
because it is empty, it is difficult to realize.

When this was said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, those beings who [will encounter] this profound [perfection of wisdom] will not be endowed with inferior roots of virtue."
"They will hear the *prajñāpāramitā*;
and having heard it, they will take it up, retain it, recite it, master it, set it in motion, teach it, explain it, proclaim it, study it, and write it down.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "So it is, Kauśika; so it is."

Kauśika, those beings who shall hear this profound perfection of wisdom, and having heard it, shall take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, set it in motion, teach it, explain it, proclaim it, study it, and write it down, will not be endowed with inferior roots of merit.
Kauśika, suppose all the beings in Jambūdvīpa were to be endowed with the ten paths of wholesome action;
what do you think, Kauśika, would those beings generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family produces even more merit than that."

Kauśika, compared to this mass of merit belonging to one who hears this *prajñāpāramitā*, and having heard it, takes it up, bears it in mind, recites it, masters it, sets it in motion, teaches it, explains it, proclaims it, studies it, and writes it down— compared to this, the mass of merit consisting of the morality of all those beings living in Jambudvīpa in the past does not approach even a hundredth part.

It does not approach even a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-ten-millionth part, nor a thousand-ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-koṭī-niyuta part.
It does not admit of any calculation, any fraction, any counting, any comparison, any likeness, any resemblance, or any proportion whatsoever.
By whatever root of merit that son of good family or daughter of good family is endowed,
who shall hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*,
and having heard it, shall take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, set it in motion, teach it, explain it, proclaim it, study it, and write it down.

Then, indeed, a certain monk said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "O Kauśika, you have been surpassed by that son of good family or daughter of good family who shall hear this profound perfection of wisdom;
and having heard it, shall take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, set it in motion, teach it, explain it, proclaim it, study it, and write it down."

When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, spoke thus to that bhikṣu: "Noble one, by the mere arising of a single thought, I have been surpassed by that son of good family or daughter of good family;
how much more so for one who shall hear this profound perfection of wisdom, and having heard it, shall take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, and set it in motion?"
He will teach it, instruct in it, recite it, study it, and write it down.

How much more so for those who, having heard it, take it up, bear it in mind, read it, master it, set it in motion, teach it, instruct in it, recite it, and write it down, and then train for the sake of suchness and practice for the sake of suchness?
They will apply themselves to the yoga for the sake of suchness;
those bodhisattva mahāsattvas will proceed surpassing the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
Not only will they proceed surpassing the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, [but...]
Those bodhisattva mahāsattvas will surpass all those who are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and perfectly awakened buddhas;
they will not only surpass the stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas, but will surpass them as they proceed.
Those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are great masters of generosity but lack the perfection of wisdom and skill in means—all of them these bodhisattva mahāsattvas will surpass as they proceed.
They will not only surpass those bodhisattvas who are great masters of generosity; [they will surpass all others as well].
Furthermore, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who possess perfectly pure ethical discipline— endowed with a mass of morality that is unbroken,

flawless, unblemished, complete, pure, and untarnished— even they will all be surpassed by these bodhisattva mahāsattvas as they proceed, provided they are devoid of the perfection of wisdom and skill in means.
Not only will they surpass those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are endowed with a mass of ethical discipline that is unbroken, flawless, unstained, complete, perfectly pure, and untarnished;

they will also surpass all those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, though perfected in patience and tranquility, possess minds free from resentment—even such that they do not give rise to a thought of malice even toward a burnt pillar—and yet remain devoid of the perfection of wisdom and skillful means.
All these bodhisattva mahāsattvas will surpass them as they proceed.
These Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas will proceed surpassing not only those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who are endowed with patience, endowed with tranquility, and possess unimpeded minds;

they will also proceed surpassing all those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who have initiated vigor, who do not cast off their burden, who are not indolent, and whose physical, vocal, and mental activities are not slackened, yet who are devoid of the perfection of wisdom and skill in means.
These Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas will proceed surpassing them all.

These Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas will not only surpass those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who have initiated vigor, who do not cast off their burden, who are not indolent, and whose physical, vocal, and mental activities are not slack;

they will also surpass all those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who delight in meditation, who rejoice in meditation, who possess the power of meditation, who are endowed with the strength of meditation, who are established in meditation, and who have mastery over meditation, yet who are devoid of the perfection of wisdom and skill in means.
These Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas will surpass them all.

For when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in the perfection of wisdom as it has been described, he surpasses the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, as well as all those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who lack skill in means;
moreover, he remains unsurpassed by them.
For what reason?
Because whichever bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in the perfection of wisdom as it has been taught, follows after the perfection of wisdom,
This bodhisattva mahāsattva stands for the non-interruption of the lineage of the omniscient ones;
this bodhisattva mahāsattva will not distance himself from the Tathāgatas;
and this bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in this manner, will before long go to the seat of awakening.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in this way, will rescue beings who are sinking in the mire of the afflictions.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in this way, trains in the training of a bodhisattva; he does not train in the training of a śrāvaka.
He does not train in the training of a pratyekabuddha.

And when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains thus in the perfection of wisdom, the four great kings, the world-protectors, will approach him and say: "O son of good family, train quickly in this conduct of a bodhisattva."
"Train yourself briefly:
these four bowls are for you to receive when you have sat at the seat of enlightenment and attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way within the perfection of wisdom as it has been described, not only will the four great world-protecting kings think that they should approach him, but...
O Blessed One, I too shall approach that bodhisattva mahāsattva;
what need is there to mention other sons of the gods?
That bodhisattva mahāsattva will also be constantly held in the mindful regard of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Thus, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, whatever worldly sufferings there may be— whether caused by the aggression of others or otherwise—

they shall not arise for him in any way, in any manner, or in any respect whatsoever. Lord, this too is a quality pertaining to the present life for that bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Then, this thought occurred to the Venerable Ānanda: "Is this Śakra, the lord of the gods, speaking by means of his own inspired eloquence, or rather through the power of the Buddha?

Then, through the power of the Buddha, Śakra, the lord of the gods, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the mind of the Venerable Ānanda, said this to the Venerable Ānanda: "It is through the power of the Buddha."
"This, Ānanda, should be understood as the empowerment of the Buddha; this too, Ānanda, should be understood as the empowerment of the Buddha,
for I am not capable, Ānanda, of speaking concerning the bodhisattva mahāsattvas."
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "It is so, Ānanda, it is so, just as Śakra, the lord of the gods, has spoken.
This is the power of the Tathāgata."
This is the empowerment of the Tathāgata, that it was spoken by Śakra, the lord of the gods.
The twenty-third chapter, titled "Śakra," in the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom.
(Vaidya 206) Chapter Twenty-Four: On Conceit.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda once more: "Furthermore, Ānanda, at whatever time a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom..."
When one applies oneself to the yoga of the perfection of wisdom and cultivates the perfection of wisdom,
Ānanda, at that time, as for the Māras, the evil ones, who exist within this triple-thousand great-thousand world system—

They all become filled with doubt: "Will this bodhisattva mahāsattva realize the limit of reality midway on the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha, or will he fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Furthermore, Ānanda, at that time, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the dwelling of the perfection of wisdom, the Māras, the evil ones, become pierced by the arrow of grief.
Furthermore, Ānanda, at whatever time a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom,
applies himself to the yoga of the perfection of wisdom, and cultivates the perfection of wisdom,
At that time, the Māras, the Evil Ones, bring about harassment for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva;
they produce fear and hurl down meteors in every direction.

They display conflagrations of the quarters, thinking: "Perhaps this bodhisattva mahāsattva might become discouraged or experience horripilation, whereby even a single thought-moment of his regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment might perish.
In that regard, Ānanda, Māra the Evil One does not approach every bodhisattva mahāsattva with the intention of causing harm.
Nevertheless, he approaches some, while he does not approach others.
Ānanda said: "Blessed One, what kind of bodhisattva mahāsattva does Māra, the Evil One, approach with the intention of causing harm?

The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, that bodhisattva mahāsattva by whom no mind of resolute faith has been produced toward the Perfection of Wisdom while it was being spoken in the past—to such a bodhisattva mahāsattva, Ānanda, Māra, the Evil One, approaches with the intention of causing harm."
And one finds an opportunity for his downfall.
Furthermore, Ānanda, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while this profound perfection of wisdom is being taught, falls into doubt and conceives a hesitation,
thinking, "This might be the perfection of wisdom, or it might not be so," [he is far from it].
Ānanda, Māra the Evil One also approaches this bodhisattva mahāsattva with the intention of causing harm,
and he finds an opportunity to do so.

Furthermore, Ānanda, any bodhisattva mahāsattva who is deprived of virtuous friends and is taken hold of by evil friends does not hear the very deep points when the perfection of wisdom is being taught.
Not hearing, he does not know;
not knowing, he does not inquire: "How should the perfection of wisdom be cultivated?
Ānanda, Māra the Evil One approaches this bodhisattva mahāsattva with the intention of causing him harm.
And he finds an opportunity for his entry.
Furthermore, Ānanda, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes attached to one who upholds the true Dharma, thinking: "This person is my companion;
he does not abandon me in any matter," [while] thinking:
"I have many other bodhisattva mahāsattvas as my companions as well."
Furthermore, they did not fulfill my intention; however,
I have now found a suitable companion who will fulfill my intention.
Ānanda, Māra the Evil One also approaches this bodhisattva mahāsattva with the intention of causing harm,
and he gains an opportunity to do so.
Furthermore, Ānanda, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while this profound perfection of wisdom is being taught, should say to another bodhisattva: "How profound indeed is this perfection of wisdom!
What is the use of your hearing it?"
"For this is not consistent with what has been spoken by the Tathāgata in other sūtras;
I too do not find any profound flavor in it. What is the use of your hearing or writing this?"
In this way, he also alienates other bodhisattva mahāsattvas. Ānanda, Māra the Evil One approaches even this bodhisattva mahāsattva with the intention of causing harm,
and he finds an opportunity to gain entry into him.

Furthermore, Ānanda, at whatever time a bodhisattva mahāsattva disparages other bodhisattvas, thinking: "I dwell in the dwelling of seclusion, whereas others do not dwell in the dwelling of seclusion;
the dwelling of seclusion does not exist for others."
At that time, Ānanda, Māra the Evil One becomes satisfied, elated, joyful, glad, and filled with happiness and cheerfulness;
he becomes thrilled, his heart is gladdened, and he is filled with joy and rapture.
Why is that?
"This [person] keeps unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment at a distance."

Furthermore, Ānanda, at whatever time a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s name is mentioned, or his clan is mentioned, or his ascetic virtues (*dhutaguṇa*) are proclaimed, he— by that much alone— despises other bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are disciplined and possessed of virtuous qualities,
even though those very qualities do not exist in him.
Those qualities which belong to irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom—
those modes, those marks, and those signs— are not found in him.
Since those qualities of irreversibility are not present, he gives rise to affliction.
That is to say, he exalts himself and disparages others, thinking: "These people are not seen to possess those qualities in which I am seen to possess them."
In that regard, it occurs to the wicked Māras: "The abodes of Māra will not be empty;
they will become overcrowded.
The great hells, the animal realms, the domains of the hungry ghosts, and the hosts of asuras will become overcrowded."
And furthermore, Māra the Evil One will exert his influence such that those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have engaged in this way will be overcome by gain and honor,
and their words will become persuasive.
Because their words will be authoritative, they will cause many people to accept them;
and that great multitude of people will consider what they say worthy of being heard and worthy of being believed.
Having seen and heard them, those people will follow their example.
Imitating what they have seen and heard, they will not train for the sake of suchness,
they will not practice for the sake of suchness,
and they will not apply themselves to yoga for the sake of suchness.
Thus, by not training in suchness, not practicing in suchness, and not applying themselves to yoga in suchness, they will increase their afflictions.
In this way, with a perverted continuum of mind, whatever action they undertake— whether by body, speech, or mind— all that will lead to what is undesirable, unlovely, unpleasant, and disagreeable.
In this way, those great hells will become overcrowded, as will the animal realm, the domain of hungry ghosts, and the hosts of asuras;
and the abodes of Māra will also become overcrowded.
Ānanda, seeing this purpose as well, Māra the Evil One becomes satisfied, elated, joyful, glad, and filled with a sense of pleasure and happiness.

Furthermore, Ānanda, at whatever time a bodhisattva mahāsattva quarrels, disputes, contends with, reviles, abuses, becomes malicious toward, or gives rise to ill will against a person belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas—
on that occasion...
At that time, it occurs to Māra, the Evil One: "Alas, this son of good family will distance himself from omniscience;

he will remain far removed from omniscience," if a person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle quarrels, disputes, contends with, reviles, scolds, becomes malicious toward, or gives rise to ill-will against another person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle.
In that situation, Māra the Evil One becomes even more satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and cheer;
and he thinks to himself: "Both of these bodhisattvas will remain far from omniscience."

Furthermore, Ānanda, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has received a prophecy should quarrel, dispute, contend with, revile, abuse, harbor malice toward, or give rise to ill will against another bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not yet received a prophecy,
and should cause that person's mind to become hostile;
That bodhisattva mahāsattva must don the armor for as many eons as there were moments of generating the thought of awakening,
provided that he has not abandoned omniscience.

When this had been said, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, is there some way of escape from those productions of thought, or must that bodhisattva mahāsattva necessarily don the armor for all that many eons?

The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, I have taught the Dharma with a way of escape for persons belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and the vehicle of the bodhisattvas."

In this regard, Ānanda, if a person belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle, having quarreled, disputed, contended, reviled, abused, and become malicious toward another person belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle,
gives rise to ill-will and does not confess it, nor practices restraint for the future, [he increases his own demerit].
"He carries the latent tendency and dwells bound by the latent tendency; Ānanda, I do not speak of the escape for such a person."
Ānanda, that person must necessarily don the armor once again for exactly that many eons.

Furthermore, Ānanda, if a person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, after having quarreled, disputed, contended, reviled, abused, and become malicious toward another person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle,
then confesses [the fault] and practices restraint for the future, [he shall not fall back].
And he generates this thought: "I, who ought to dispel, reconcile, and pacify the quarrels, disputes, and conflicts of all sentient beings—yet here I am, myself engaged in dispute!
My gains are ill-gotten, not well-gotten."
I, who engage in conversation with those who speak,
am one who ought to serve as a bridge for all sentient beings; yet I address others even with the word "you."
"I must not utter even this: a harsh or abrasive retort.
Like one who is dull-witted, like one who is mute as a sheep, I should remain so amidst quarrels, disputes, and conflicts."
When hearing ill-spoken words, harsh arrivals, and unpleasant speech being uttered by others, one should not allow the mind to become resentful;
nor should one think toward others, "This is not good for me," or "This is not fitting for me."
That I perceive a fault in another—
this too is not fitting for me, that I should consider even the faults of others as something worth hearing.
For what reason?
Because I must not disturb my resolute intention,
by which I am to bring happiness to all sentient beings through every means of providing comfort.
And having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, they are to be led to final nirvana;
yet I would harbor ill will,
whereas I ought not to harbor ill will even toward others who have wronged me.
"I shall not fall into agitation;
this must not be done by me. I must exert myself with firm valor."
"And even if my life were being cut short, I should not give way to agitation,
nor should I knit my brows upon my face. Regarding this, Ānanda—
I declare this to be the deliverance of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

And thus, Ānanda, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide even toward those persons belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas in such a way that he is not disturbed in the presence of any sentient being whatsoever.
In this very same way, one should abide toward all sentient beings.
And how, Ānanda, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide toward other persons belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle?
Just as, Ānanda, [one would abide] toward the Teacher.
One should abide with this thought: "These bodhisattva mahāsattvas are my teachers.
Indeed, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas of mine have mounted the single vehicle;
indeed, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas of mine have mounted the single path.
"Ah, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas of mine are indeed of identical intention; ah, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas of mine have set out upon the same path!
It is in this very [Dharma] that they must train."
In this regard, I must train myself;
and just as they must train,
so too must I train.
If, however, any among them should dwell in a state of distraction,
I shall not dwell in a state of distraction;
but if they should dwell in a state free from distraction through mental engagements associated with omniscience, [then I shall do likewise].
I, too, should train in this way. Ānanda, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva training thus in omniscience, there shall be no obstacle to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
and he will swiftly awaken to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The twenty-fourth chapter, titled "Pride," in the Noble Eight Thousand Line Prajñāpāramitā.
(Vaidya 210) Chapter Twenty-Five: Training.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "In what, O Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva train when he trains in omniscience?"
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in exhaustion, he trains in omniscience;
likewise, he trains in non-arising, in non-cessation, in non-birth, in non-existence, in solitude, in dispassion, in space, and in the realm of phenomena."
"If, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in nirvāṇa, he trains in omniscience.
Subhūti asked: "For what reason, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while training in cessation, train in omniscience?"
"In this way, by training in non-arising, non-cessation, non-birth, non-existence, solitude, dispassion, space, the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and nirvāṇa, does one train in omniscience?

When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, as for what you say: 'For what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by training in exhaustion, train in omniscience; and likewise, by training in non-arising, non-cessation, non-birth, non-existence, solitude, dispassion, space, the realm of phenomena, and nirvāṇa, train in omniscience? [Tell me that]."
"What do you think, Subhūti? Does that suchness of the Tathāgata—by which suchness a Tathāgata is designated as 'Tathāgata'—ever undergo diminution?
Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One."
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, exhaustion does not exhaust;
for, Blessed One, exhaustion is indeed inexhaustible.

The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? As for that suchness of the Tathāgata, by which suchness a Tathāgata is designated as 'Tathāgata'—does it arise or cease, is it born or does it come into being, does it pass away or is it differentiated, does it become impassioned or dispassionate, or does it become like space or become a phenomenon?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Is that suchness of the Tathāgata—by which suchness a Tathāgata is designated as 'Tathāgata'"—does that ever pass into extinction?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this way trains with the thought, 'Suchness does not perish.
Training in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in omniscience;
training in this way, he trains in the perfection of wisdom."
He trains in the stage of a Buddha; he trains in the powers; he trains in the grounds of self-confidence.
He trains in all the qualities of a Buddha;
he trains in the knowledge of omniscience.
Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva will attain the perfection of all trainings.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this way cannot be overcome by Māra, nor by the assembly of Māra, nor by the deities belonging to the host of Māra.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this way will quickly attain the state of irreversibility.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this way will quickly sit at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa).
Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in his own proper range.
Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the qualities that act as protectors;
he trains in great loving-kindness.
He trains in great compassion, he trains in great sympathetic joy,
and he trains in great equanimity.
Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains for the turning of the wheel of Dharma in its three revolutions and twelve aspects.
Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains with the thought, "I shall not diminish the entire realm.
Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains for the non-interruption of the lineage of the Tathāgatas.
Training in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains with the thought, "I shall open the door to the realm of the deathless.
Subhūti, this sublime training cannot be mastered by one who is an inferior being.
For it is not possible for one of little strength to train in this training.
Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, they are the very essence of all sentient beings.
For those, Subhūti, who train in this training desire to be protectors of all sentient beings;
they desire to attain the state of being preeminent above all sentient beings.
Those who train here in this way— Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training thus is not reborn in the hells,
nor is he reborn in the animal realms.
One is not reborn in the realms of hungry ghosts,
nor is one reborn among the bodies of asuras,
nor is one reborn in the borderlands.
He is not reborn in the families of outcastes, nor is he reborn in the families of fowlers, nor is he reborn in the families of hunters, fishermen, or sheep-butchers.
Nor is he reborn in other such families that are of low birth or that engage in lowly occupations.
Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not become blind,
nor does he become deaf.
He does not become one-eyed;
he does not become crippled;
he does not become hunchbacked.
He does not become one with a withered arm,
he does not become lame, and he does not become crippled.
He does not become dull-witted,
he does not become fickle, and he does not become restless.
He is not deformed, he does not have missing limbs, and he does not have impaired limbs.
He does not have deformed limbs, he does not become weak, and he does not become ill-favored in complexion.
He does not have a deformed body, he does not have deficient sense faculties, and he does not have impaired sense faculties.
He possesses sense faculties that are complete in all their aspects and is endowed with a beautiful voice.
Subhūti, when training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not take life.
He does not take what is not given, he does not engage in sexual misconduct,
and he does not speak falsehoods.
He does not engage in divisive speech,
he does not engage in harsh speech,
and he does not engage in frivolous chatter.
He does not become covetous, he does not become malevolent in mind,
and he does not hold wrong views.
He does not maintain his livelihood through wrong means of living.
Training in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not reborn among the long-lived gods,
nor does he become one who embraces immoral conduct.
He does not grasp at non-existent phenomena,
nor is he reborn through the power of meditative attainments.
Why is that?
For he possesses skill in means, and it is through being endowed with that skill in means that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not reborn among the long-lived gods.
Furthermore, Subhūti, what is this skill in means of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?
It is precisely this perfection of wisdom.

And thus he applies himself to skill in means in such a way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, endowed with another kind of skill in means, enters into the meditative absorptions and yet is not reborn through the power of those absorptions.
Training in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the purification of the powers, attains the purification of the grounds of self-confidence,
and attains the purification of all the qualities of a buddha.
He attains that.

The Venerable Subhūti said: "Blessed One, since all phenomena are thus pure by nature, of which phenomenon, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain the purity of powers, and of which does he attain the purity of intrepidities?"
"He attains the complete purity of all the qualities of a Buddha;
he reaches that state.
