When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "So it is, Subhūti, so it is."
For what reason? Subhūti, all dharmas are indeed pure by their very nature.
Thus, Subhūti, regarding all dharmas that are pure by nature, the non-despondency and non-dejection of a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in the perfection of wisdom—
This, Subhūti, is that perfection of wisdom.
Thus, Subhūti, because foolish common people do not know and do not see these dharmas, they do not know and do not see the true nature of dharmas.
Subhūti, it is for the sake of those beings that bodhisattvas mahāsattvas exert themselves and arouse their vigor, thinking: "We shall cause these ignorant beings to know."
"We shall see sentient beings who do not see thus"— in this training they train.
Training in this training, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas attain the powers and attain the fearlessnesses.
They attain all the qualities of a Buddha.
Subhūti, when training in this way, bodhisattva mahāsattvas understand, as they truly are, the movements, activities, and fluctuations of the minds of other beings and other individuals.
Understanding them as they truly are, they reach the further shore of the knowledge of the mental conduct of others.
Subhūti, it is just as if there were few places on this great earth that are free of stones,
where gold, silver, or precious metals are produced;
rather, there are far more places on this great earth [that are not so].

Just as there are saline wastes, arid lands, and places filled with various kinds of grass, stalks, and thorns, even so, Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who exist within the assembly of beings and who train in this training for omniscience— that is, the training in the perfection of wisdom— are few in number.
Furthermore, among the multitude of beings existing within the realm of sentient beings, those who train in the discipline of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are indeed more numerous.
Furthermore, Subhūti, it is just as if there were only a few beings found among the class of beings who,
having undertaken it, engage in the karma that leads to the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch; whereas, on the contrary, there are far more beings found among the class of beings [who do not].

Just so, Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who exist within the assembly of beings and have set out upon this path— namely, the path of the perfection of wisdom— are few in number, compared to those who engage in and persist in actions that lead to the status of a local king.
"We shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Now, among the multitude of beings in the realm of sentient beings, there are far more who have set out upon the path of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, Subhūti, it is just as if there were few beings found among the class of beings who,
having undertaken the karma conducive to becoming Śakra, continue to practice it; whereas, on the contrary, far more numerous are those beings found among the class of beings [who do not].
Just so,
Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who exist within the assembly of beings and who, having undertaken the practice, abide in this training of the perfection of wisdom are few indeed.
Furthermore, among the multitude of beings, there are indeed more bodhisattva mahāsattvas who train in the training of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, Subhūti, it is just as if there were only a few beings found among the classes of beings who,
having undertaken it, abide in karma conducive to rebirth in the Brahma world; whereas, on the contrary, far more numerous are those beings found among the classes of beings [who do not].
Just so, Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who exist within the assembly of beings and have undertaken the conduct that leads to rebirth among the retinue of Brahmā are few;
even fewer still are those who are irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti, among the multitude of beings, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who turn back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment are far more numerous;
therefore, Subhūti, those beings who [do not turn back] are few indeed within the multitude of beings.
Subhūti, even among those few beings who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there are fewer still who practice in accordance with suchness.
Subhūti, even among those very few who practice for the sake of suchness, there are fewer still who apply themselves to the yoga of the perfection of wisdom.

Subhūti, even among those very few who apply themselves to the yoga of the perfection of wisdom, there are the rarest of the rare Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who are irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to be counted among those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are irreversible— the very least among the fewest— should train in this very perfection of wisdom and apply himself to its practice.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way in the perfection of wisdom, a mind accompanied by stubbornness does not arise, a mind accompanied by doubt does not arise,
and a mind accompanied by envy or avarice does not arise.
A mind accompanied by immorality does not arise;
a mind accompanied by malice does not arise;
a mind accompanied by laziness does not arise.
A mind accompanied by distraction does not arise,
nor does a mind accompanied by faulty wisdom arise.
It is in this way, Subhūti, that all the perfections are encompassed by a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in the perfection of wisdom.
All the perfections are grasped;
all the perfections are followed;
all the perfections are included within it.
Subhūti, just as, for example, the sixty-two types of views are contained within the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),

even so, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), all the perfections are contained within it. Subhūti, just as, for example, when a person’s life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is active, all the other faculties are contained within it.
In the same way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in the perfection of wisdom, all wholesome dharmas are included within it.

Just as, Subhūti, when a person's life-faculty has ceased, all their other faculties cease, even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in the perfection of wisdom, when ignorance has ceased, all unwholesome dharmas cease.
And all the other perfections are included and encompassed within it.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to embrace all the perfections should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Training in the perfection of wisdom, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains for the sake of preeminence among all sentient beings.
For what reason?
Because it is the foremost of merits.
What do you think, Subhūti, as for all the sentient beings included within the enumeration of beings in the trichiliocosm—would they be numerous?
"Would they not indeed be many?
Subhūti replied, "Blessed One, the beings in Jambudvīpa alone are already numerous;
what need is there to mention those beings who exist in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system?"

The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, suppose a single bodhisattva mahāsattva were to remain for as long as his life lasts, providing all those sentient beings with robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
What do you think, Subhūti, would that bodhisattva mahāsattva generate a great deal of merit on that account?
Subhūti replied: "A great deal, Blessed One."
“Much, Sugata!

The Blessed One said: “Therefore, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva generates much more merit on that account than [the former], who would cultivate this perfection of wisdom even for as little as the snap of a finger.”
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is of such great benefit to a bodhisattva mahāsattva, as it brings about unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment—
By one who desires to attain the unsurpassed state for all sentient beings; by one who desires to become a protector for all sentient beings who are without a protector;

by one who desires to reach the domain of the Buddhas; by one who desires to follow the bull-like leadership of the Buddhas; by one who desires to sport the sport of the Buddhas; by one who desires to roar the lion’s roar of the Buddhas; and by one who desires to attain the perfection of the Buddhas within the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system—
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to engage in discourse on the Dharma within the world-system should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in the perfection of wisdom, I do not perceive any such excellence that has not been mastered by him.
Subhūti asked: "But, Blessed One, has even the excellence of the śrāvaka been trained in by that bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, even the excellence of the śrāvaka has indeed been trained in by that bodhisattva mahāsattva.
However, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train thinking, 'I shall abide in the excellence of the śrāvaka.'"
He does not train with the thought, "I shall attain the perfection of a śrāvaka.
Subhūti, he also knows those who are the hosts of śrāvakas.
And he does not abide therein;
he investigates in this way and does not oppose it, training himself with the thought: "I too must teach and reveal these qualities of the śrāvakas."

Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes worthy of offerings from the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva surpasses all other recipients of offerings associated with the disciples and associated with the pratyekabuddhas,
and omniscience draws near to him.

Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abandon [the practice]; he courses in the perfection of wisdom and is never separated from the perfection of wisdom through his dwelling in the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in this way should be known as one whose nature is non-retrogression, one characterized by non-retrogression.
He distances himself from the level of the śrāvaka and the level of the pratyekabuddha,
and draws near to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
If, however, he should think, "This is that perfection of wisdom; it will bring forth this omniscience," and perceives it in this way,
he is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not even perceive that perfection of wisdom, thinking, "This is that perfection of wisdom," or "This perfection of wisdom will bring about omniscience. In this way, too, he does not perceive it.
He does not perceive [them].
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, he practices in the perfection of wisdom.
The twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Training," in the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom.
(Vaidya 215) Chapter Twenty-Six: The Illusion-like.
Then, it occurred to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Even while merely practicing, this bodhisattva mahāsattva surpasses all sentient beings."
How much more so when he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment!
Great is the gain for those beings;
well-lived indeed is the life of those beings.
Those whose minds incline toward omniscience are already rare;
how much more so those who have generated the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment!
Those beings who are the essence of beings and who will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment are truly objects of longing.

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, having miraculously created māndārava flowers and formed a handful of those flowers, scattered them over the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, and spoke these words: "Those persons belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who have resolved their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, thinking: 'We shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
and having fully awakened, we shall establish all sentient beings—who are being carried away by the great ocean of saṃsāra—safely upon the further shore.'"
May their desired and intended aspirations be fulfilled;
may these very productions of the thought of awakening lead to the complete fulfillment of these very qualities of a Buddha,
and may they lead to the complete fulfillment of these very qualities associated with omniscience.
May they be for the fulfillment of these very self-existent dharmas;
may they be for the fulfillment of these very unassailable dharmas.
O Blessed One, not even a single thought arises in me [to the contrary].

"As for those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, though endowed with great compassion, would turn back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment— Blessed One, not even a single thought arises in me that those persons belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle, who have set out to fully awaken to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, would ever turn back from it."
Thus, perceiving these sufferings of sentient beings belonging to the realm of saṃsāra, they will, for the most part, generate the aspiration for unexcelled perfect enlightenment.
Why is that?
Because, through that great compassion, desiring their welfare and desiring their benefit, they are compassionate toward the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
Those who are endowed with such mental resolves as these think: "Since we have ourselves crossed over, let us help beings cross over;
since we are liberated, let us liberate them;
since we are comforted, let us comfort them."
"May we cause those who have entered final nirvāṇa to attain final nirvāṇa"— it is with such productions of the thought of awakening that they dwell.
Blessed One, whoever rejoices in the productions of the thought of awakening of those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have first set out in the vehicle, [attains great merit].
He rejoices in the non-retrogressive nature of those who are non-retrogressive,
and he also rejoices in the one-birth-bound nature of those Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas who are bound to only one more birth.
Blessed One, how much greater merit does that son of good family or daughter of good family produce?

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Furthermore, Kauśika, it might indeed be possible to grasp the measure of Sumeru, the king of mountains, by weighing it with the tip of a blade of grass;

but it is not at all possible, Kauśika, to grasp the measure of the merit of that son of good family or daughter of good family, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, who has generated a thought accompanied by sympathetic joy.
Furthermore, Kauśika, it might indeed be possible to grasp the measure of a world-system of four great continents by weighing it with the tip of a blade of grass."
But, Kauśika, it is not possible to grasp the measure of merit of that production of the thought accompanied by rejoicing.
Indeed, Kauśika, it might be possible to grasp the measure of a thousandfold world-system of the Cūḍika type when weighed on the tip of a hair,
but it is not possible, Kauśika, to grasp the measure of merit of that production of the thought accompanied by rejoicing.
Furthermore, Kauśika, it might indeed be possible to grasp the measure of a medium two-thousandfold world-system when weighed on the tip of a hair;
but, Kauśika, it is not at all possible to grasp the measure of the merit of that production of the thought of awakening accompanied by sympathetic joy.
Furthermore, Kauśika, it might indeed be possible to measure the extent of a great trichiliocosm world-system by weighing it on the tip of a hair;

but it is not at all possible, Kauśika, to grasp the measure of the merit of that son of good family or daughter of good family, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, who has generated a thought accompanied by sympathetic joy.

When this had been said, Śakra, lord of the gods, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, those beings should be known as being under the influence of Māra who do not hear that the merit of the production of a thought accompanied by rejoicing is thus immeasurable— [the merit] of bodhisattva mahāsattvas from the first production of the thought of awakening until they have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
They do not know,
they do not see,
and they do not attend to that rejoicing.
"Blessed One, those beings will belong to the faction of Māra who do not rejoice in these productions of the thought of awakening of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
And, Blessed One, those beings will have passed away from the abodes of Māra."
Those who do not rejoice in these productions of the thought of awakening belonging to those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas—
for what reason? Because,
Blessed One, these productions of the thought of awakening have been brought forth by them as the destruction of Māra’s realm.
By those who have dedicated these productions of the thought of awakening toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, or who have rejoiced in these productions of the thought;
O Blessed One, those productions of the thought of those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, should be rejoiced in.
Those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have generated the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
and for whom, O Blessed One, the Tathāgata has not been forsaken,
nor has the Dharma been forsaken.
The Saṅgha has not been forsaken;
those sons of good family and daughters of good family should rejoice in these productions of the thought of awakening.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "So it is, Kauśika, so it is!
For those, Kauśika, for whom the Tathāgata has not been forsaken and the Dharma has not been forsaken..."
The Saṅgha has not been forsaken;
those sons of good family and daughters of good family should rejoice in these productions of the thought [of awakening].

Kauśika, by whichever sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the vehicle of the Bodhisattvas, or the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, or the vehicle of the Śrāvakas, these productions of the thought have been rejoiced in...
They will quickly please the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas, and will not displease them.
When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: "So it is, Blessed One."

"So it is, Sugata! Those sons of good family or daughters of good family— whether belonging to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the vehicle of the śrāvakas— who rejoice in these productions of the thought of awakening,
will quickly please the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the perfectly awakened ones."
They shall not become disenchanted.
Thus, wherever they may be reborn through those roots of merit arising from the production of thought accompanied by sympathetic joy,
there they shall be honored.
They will be treated with respect by their teachers, they will be honored,
and they will be venerated.
They will be honored and they will be revered;
and they shall not see unpleasant forms.
And they shall not smell unpleasant odors,
nor shall they consume unpleasant tastes.
They shall not touch unpleasant tactile objects,
nor should their rebirth in the states of woe be expected;
rather, their rebirth in heaven should be expected.
For what reason?

Because those sons of good family or daughters of good family have rejoiced in the roots of merit of immeasurable and incalculable beings that bring happiness to all sentient beings; and, O Blessed One, they have likewise generated the aspiration for enlightenment on behalf of those who belong to the Bodhisattva vehicle.

Those productions of the thought of awakening by those persons have been rejoiced in; as those productions of the thought of awakening increase, they will become the nourishers of unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening.
They too, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, will lead immeasurable and incalculable beings to final nirvāṇa.
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Kauśika; so it is."
It is through the very power of the Tathāgata that you have spoken these words.
Kauśika, by whatever son of good family or daughter of good family those productions of thought of persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle have been rejoiced in,
by this method, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family [has performed a great deed] for those persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle.
By rejoicing in those productions of the thought of awakening, the roots of goodness of immeasurable and incalculable beings become rejoiced in, planted, and brought to fulfillment.
Subhūti said: "And how, Blessed One, does a mind that is like an illusion realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "What do you think, Subhūti? Do you perceive a mind that is like an illusion?
Subhūti said: "Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Do you perceive illusion?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
I do not, Blessed One, perceive a mind that is like an illusion, nor do I perceive illusion itself."

The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? Since you do not perceive an illusion, nor a mind that is like an illusion, do you then perceive any dharma apart from the illusion or the mind that is like an illusion which awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One."

"Blessed One, apart from illusion or a mind that is like an illusion, I do not perceive any dharma whatsoever that fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Therefore, Blessed One, since I do not perceive any such dharma apart from illusion or a mind like an illusion, what dharma could I teach as being 'existent' or 'non-existent'?"
And that phenomenon which is utterly secluded does not approach [the notion] that it exists or that it does not exist;
even that phenomenon which is by its very nature utterly secluded [does not do so].
He does not fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is that?
Because, Blessed One, a non-existent dharma does not fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Therefore, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is absolutely secluded;
and that dharma which is absolutely secluded is not a dharma to be cultivated.
Nor does it bring about or carry away any dharma whatsoever.
How, O Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having relied upon the utterly secluded perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
For even unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, O Blessed One, is utterly secluded.
“Blessed One, since even the perfection of wisdom is utterly secluded,
and even unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is utterly secluded,
how then, Blessed One, is that which is secluded fully awakened to by means of that which is secluded?”
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!
It is so, Subhūti; it is just so.
Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is absolutely secluded."
Supreme perfect enlightenment is indeed utterly secluded.
Subhūti, it is precisely because the perfection of wisdom is utterly secluded that supreme perfect enlightenment, which is itself utterly secluded, is fully awakened to.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives the perfection of wisdom as being ultimately secluded,
that would not be the perfection of wisdom.
It is precisely by relying on the perfection of wisdom in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Nor, Subhūti, does one awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by relying on the perfection of wisdom;
nor does one awaken to solitude through solitude.
And yet, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And one does not attain full awakening without relying upon the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti said: "As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in a profound meaning.
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Subhūti; so it is."
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the profound meaning;
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the profound meaning is a doer of what is difficult.
And he does not personally realize that goal, namely, the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha.
Subhūti said: "As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken, Blessed One, no bodhisattva mahāsattva is a doer of anything difficult.
Why is that?"
For in this way, Blessed One, that very dharma which would realize is not apprehended;
that dharma which is realized is also not apprehended; and that dharma by which one would realize is likewise not apprehended.
If, Blessed One, when this is being spoken, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not sink, does not become cowed, does not shrink back, and does not turn his back, [he is to be known as irreversible].
He is not afraid, he is not terrified, and he does not fall into terror;
he courses in the perfection of wisdom.
If he does not even perceive that "I am coursing," [then he truly courses].
If one practices in the perfection of wisdom,
and does not perceive even this thought— "Unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is near to me"— then one practices in the perfection of wisdom.
If it does not even occur to him, "The stage of the Śrāvaka or the stage of the Pratyekabuddha has been left far behind by me," then he courses in the perfection of wisdom.
Lord, it is just as, for example, it does not occur to space: "I am near to anyone."
Or for someone it is far.
Why is that?
Blessed One, because space is non-conceptual.

In the same way, Blessed One, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, it does not occur to him: "Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is near to me; the level of the śrāvakas and the level of the pratyekabuddhas are far from me.
Why is that?
Because, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is free from conceptual construction.
It is just as, Blessed One, a person created by magic does not think: "The magician is near to me, but that other assembly of people who have gathered is far from me."
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, an illusory person is devoid of conceptual construction.
In the same way, Blessed One, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, it does not occur to him: "Unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is near to me."
"The stage of the śrāvaka and the stage of the pratyekabuddha are far from me.
For what reason?
Blessed One, it is because the perfection of wisdom is free from conceptual construction.

It is just as if, Blessed One, a reflection does not think: "That object by which this reflection arises is near to me, whereas those who have not approached it—whether in a mirror or in a vessel of water—are far from me.
For what reason?
“Because, Blessed One, an appearance is non-conceptual.

In the same way, Blessed One, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, it does not occur: ‘Unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is near to me; the level of the śrāvakas and the level of the pratyekabuddhas are far from me.’”
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is non-conceptual.
Just as, Blessed One, for a Tathāgata there exists no one who is either dear or not dear, so it is with the perfection of wisdom.
For what reason?
Because the Tathāgata has abandoned all conceptual constructions and discriminations;
in the very same way, Blessed One, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, nothing whatsoever exists that is either dear or not dear.
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is free from conceptual construction.
For just as the Tathāgata has abandoned all conceptualization and discrimination, so too is the perfection of wisdom.
In the same way, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is also free from all conceptualization and discursive thought.

Just as, Blessed One, a magical creation produced by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, does not have the thought: "The stage of the Śrāvaka and the stage of the Pratyekabuddha are far from me."
"Unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment is near to me. For what reason? Because, Blessed One, that which is emanated is without conceptual construction.

In the same way, Blessed One, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, it does not occur to him: "The stage of the śrāvaka and the stage of the pratyekabuddha are far from me; unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening is near to me.
Why is that?

It is precisely because the perfection of wisdom, Blessed One, is non-conceptual. Just as, Blessed One, a magical creation performs whatever task it was created for, so too does the perfection of wisdom.
And that emanation is free from conceptual construction.
Why is that?
Precisely because the emanation is devoid of conceptual construction.
In the same way, Blessed One, for whatever purpose a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates this perfection of wisdom,
he accomplishes that purpose,
and yet that perfection of wisdom is non-conceptual.
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is indeed non-conceptual.
It is just as if, Blessed One, a skilled carpenter or a carpenter’s apprentice were to fashion a wooden woman or a wooden man, equipped with mechanical devices.
It performs that very task for the sake of which it was made;
yet that assembly of wood is itself devoid of conceptual construction.
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, the collection of wood is itself without conceptual construction.
In the same way, Blessed One, for whatever purpose a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates this perfection of wisdom, [he does so without conceptualization].
And it performs that function,
yet that perfection of wisdom is non-conceptual.
Why is that?
"O Blessed One, it is precisely because this perfection of wisdom is non-conceptual."
The twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Simile of an Illusion," in the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom.
(Vaidya 220) Chapter Twenty-Seven: The Chapter on the Essence.
Then, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: "O venerable Subhūti, this bodhisattva mahāsattva indeed courses in the essence!"
"He who courses in the perfection of wisdom.

When this was said, the venerable Subhūti said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "O venerable Śāriputra, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom courses, indeed, in the essence!"

Then, indeed, it occurred to many thousands of sons of the gods belonging to the realm of desire: "Those beings who have generated and brought forth the resolve for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and who now course in this profound perfection of wisdom, are worthy of homage."
Practicing in this way, they do not realize the limit of reality— that is, neither the level of a śrāvaka nor the level of a pratyekabuddha.
By this method as well, it should be understood that bodhisattva mahāsattvas are performers of what is difficult to do.
Those who course in the true nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena, yet do not realize that true nature— then indeed,
the Venerable Subhūti, by means of his own mind, [perceived] those many thousands of gods of the desire realm...
Knowing their mental reflections, he addressed those many thousands of gods of the desire realm:
"O gods, it is not difficult for those bodhisattva mahāsattvas that they do not realize that limit of reality."
But this, O sons of gods, is indeed difficult and most difficult for those bodhisattva mahāsattvas:
that they don the armor, thinking, "We shall bring immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite beings to final nirvāṇa," even though those beings do not exist at all in reality.
Being non-existent, they are not apprehended,
because of the solitude of sentient beings;
likewise, those to be trained do not exist at all.

And thus, O sons of the gods, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have set out to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment with the thought, "We shall discipline sentient beings," would be like one who thinks that space is to be disciplined if they think that sentient beings are to be disciplined.
Why is that?
For, O sons of the gods, by the solitude of space, the solitude of sentient beings is to be understood.
By this method, O sons of the gods, bodhisattvas mahāsattvas are doers of what is difficult, who don the armor for the sake of sentient beings who do not exist and are not to be apprehended.
O sons of the gods, he who would think that the armor should be donned for the sake of sentient beings should not think that it is to be known as being together with space.
And this very armor has been donned by the bodhisattva mahāsattva for the sake of sentient beings.
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, has taught that there is the absolute non-apprehension of sentient beings.
That [non-apprehension] is to be understood precisely through the solitude of sentient beings,
and the solitude of sentient beings is to be understood through the solitude of those to be trained.

If, O sons of the gods, when this is being spoken, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not become despondent, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
For by the solitude of sentient beings, the solitude of form should be understood;
likewise, by the solitude of sentient beings, the solitude of feeling, perception, and mental formations should be understood;
and by the solitude of sentient beings, the solitude of consciousness should be understood.
In this way, up to the point that through the solitude of sentient beings, the solitude of all phenomena is to be understood.
Thus, O sons of the gods, the solitude of all phenomena is to be seen.
Thus, O sons of the gods, when the solitude of all phenomena is being spoken of, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not become despondent.
Since he does not sink down,
he therefore courses in the perfection of wisdom.

Then the Blessed One, though already knowing, said this to the venerable Subhūti: "For what reason, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva not become despondent when the solitude of all dharmas is thus being taught?
Subhūti replied:
“Because of its solitude, Blessed One, it does not despond.
For this reason, Blessed One, when the solitude of all dharmas is being taught, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not despond;
nor, Blessed One, does any dharma whatsoever despond.”
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, no dharma whatsoever is found that could sink down.
"Even that dharma, O Blessed One, by which any dharma might be discouraged, is not to be apprehended.
The Blessed One said, "So it is, Subhūti; so it is."

Moreover, Subhūti, if, while this is being spoken, taught, explained, and thus instructed, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not sink, does not despair, does not become cowed, does not shrink back, and does not turn his mind away;
He does not become dejected, he is not startled, he is not terrified, and he does not fall into terror;
thus he courses in the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti said: "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in this way,"
He courses in the perfection of wisdom.
As a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in this way, the gods with Indra, with Brahmā, with Prajāpati, and with Īśāna, together with hosts of men and women, pay homage from afar with palms joined.

The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is not only the gods with Indra, with Brahmā, with Prajāpati, and with Īśāna, together with hosts of men and women, who [pay homage] to a bodhisattva mahāsattva coursing in this way."

From afar, with palms joined in reverence, they pay homage; and those, Subhūti, who are the gods of the Brahma-realm— the Brahmapurohitas, the Brahmapārṣadyas, the Mahābrahmans, the Parīttābhas, the Apramāṇābhas, the Ābhāsvaras, the Parīttaśubhas, the Apramāṇaśubhas, the Śubhakṛtsnas, the Anabhrakas, and the Puṇyaprasavas— [also do so].
The Bṛhatphala, Asaṃjñisattva, Abṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha gods— Subhūti, even they pay homage to that bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in this very perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who at present reside, stay, and maintain themselves in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems [also pay homage].
Those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, also behold with their Buddha-eye the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who courses thus in the perfection of wisdom;
and they, Subhūti, favor and attend upon that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, are sustained and taken into consideration by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones— those bodhisattva mahāsattvas, Subhūti, should be held to be irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; and no obstacles shall arise for them, whether from Māra or from any other source.
For what reason?
Subhūti, if all the beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system were to become Māras, the Evil Ones;
And each evil Māra conjures up just as many Māra-armies;

yet, Subhūti, those evil Māras are not capable of creating an obstacle for that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is attended by the Buddhas and who courses in the perfection of wisdom regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti, let alone all the wicked Māras in this trichiliocosm;
even if, Subhūti, as many beings as there are in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges were each to become a wicked Māra, they would all be such.
And each evil Māra conjures up just as many Māra-armies;

yet, Subhūti, those evil Māras are not capable of creating an obstacle for that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is attended by the Buddhas and who courses in the perfection of wisdom regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, endowed with two qualities, a bodhisattva mahāsattva at that time becomes invincible to Māra the Evil One or to the deities belonging to Māra’s host.
With which two?
Namely, all sentient beings are not abandoned by him.
And all phenomena have been viewed by him through their emptiness.
Subhūti, endowed with these two qualities, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes invincible to Māras, evil ones, or deities belonging to the host of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti, endowed with another two qualities, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes invincible to Māras, evil ones, or deities belonging to the host of Māra.
By which two?
Namely, that he acts in accordance with what he says,
and that he is taken into account by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with these two qualities becomes invincible to Māras, the Evil Ones, or to the deities belonging to the host of Māra.
Subhūti, as a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, even the gods will think they should approach him;
and having approached, they will think they should question him.
They will think that he should be questioned, they will think that he should be attended upon,
and they will increase his enthusiasm, saying: "O son of good family, you will quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Therefore, son of good family, dwell in this very dwelling, namely, the dwelling of the perfection of wisdom.
For what reason?
Because by dwelling in this very dwelling, son of good family, you will become a protector for those beings who are without a protector.
You will be a protector for beings who are without protection;
you will be a refuge for beings who are without refuge; you will be a sanctuary for beings who are without a sanctuary.
You will be a refuge for beings who have no refuge; you will be an island for beings who have no island;
you will be a light for beings who are blind.
"You shall be a guide for beings who lack a guide; you shall be a destination for beings who have no destination;
you shall be a path-finder and a refuge for beings who have lost their way and have no resort."
In this way, those sons of the gods will increase the enthusiasm of that bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Why is that?

Subhūti, it is because for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells in this dwelling of the perfection of wisdom, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who reside in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems—

They remain and sustain themselves, surrounded by the community of monks and preceded by a host of bodhisattvas; and for that bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses and dwells in the perfection of wisdom and is endowed with such qualities— namely, the qualities of dwelling in the perfection of wisdom— [they do so].

The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach the Dharma while proclaiming the name, the lineage, the power, and the physical form of that bodhisattva mahāsattva, and they utter inspired utterances concerning him. Subhūti, it is just as I am doing now with respect to the bodhisattva mahāsattva Ratnaketu.
I teach the Dharma while proclaiming the name, the lineage, the power, the complexion, and the form of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śikhin;
and I utter inspired utterances concerning other Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas who are now leading the holy life in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya.

In the same way, Subhūti, those Buddhas, Blessed Ones who at present here in my buddha-field proclaim the Dharma while praising the names, lineages, strengths, complexions, and forms of those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas who practice the holy life and dwell in this dwelling of the perfection of wisdom— [they do so] in such a manner.
And they utter an inspired utterance.

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, do all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach the Dharma and utter inspired utterances by way of proclaiming the names, lineages, powers, complexions, and forms of all Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas?"
The Blessed One said: "Not so, Subhūti.
It is not the case, Subhūti, that all those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are proclaiming the names, lineages, powers, complexions, and forms of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas while teaching the Dharma."

They teach the Dharma and utter inspired exhortations; however, Subhūti, it is those irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are free from all attachments that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, praise by proclaiming their names, their lineage, their strength, their complexion, and their form, while teaching the Dharma.
And they utter an inspired utterance.

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, setting aside those irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas, are there other bodhisattva mahāsattvas besides them whom those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach the Dharma while proclaiming their names, their clans, their strength, their complexion, and their forms, and who utter inspired utterances concerning them?"
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, there are persons belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who possess the power of the counteractive forces, setting aside those irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas,
for whom those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, while teaching the Dharma, proclaim their names, clans, powers, colors, and forms, and utter inspired utterances."
Who, then, are they?
They are those who, at present, while appearing to train in the conduct of a bodhisattva, practice the bodhisattva path under the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha;
appearing to train, they dwell [in that state].
Subhūti, these persons belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle— excluding those irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas—
are those for whom the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, while teaching the Dharma, proclaim their names, their lineage, their power, their complexion, and their form.
And they utter an inspired utterance.
Subhūti, those who, emulating the conduct of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Ratnaketu, practice the bodhisattva conduct and dwell while training in it, [they too shall do so].
Subhūti, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas as well— excluding those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are irreversible—
are those for whom those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, while teaching the Dharma, proclaim their names, their clans, their powers, their complexions, and their forms.
And they utter inspired utterances.
Furthermore, Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, have conviction that all phenomena are non-arising,
yet have not yet attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena;
they have conviction that all phenomena are peaceful.
Furthermore, they have not yet entered into the attainment of mastery that is irreversible regarding all dharmas.

Subhūti, even while those bodhisattva mahāsattvas dwell in this dwelling, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach the Dharma by proclaiming their names, their lineages, their powers, their complexions, and their forms.
And they utter inspired utterances.
Furthermore, Subhūti, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who teach the Dharma while proclaiming the names, lineages, powers, complexions, and forms of those Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas—
And they utter inspired utterances;
for them, the stage of the śrāvaka and the stage of the pratyekabuddha have been abandoned;
only the stage of a Buddha is to be expected for them.
They, too, shall be predicted to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
For what reason? Because, Subhūti, for those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who thus course in the perfection of wisdom, those Buddhas...
The Blessed Ones, proclaiming their names, clans, powers, complexions, and forms, teach the Dharma and utter inspired utterances;
they too shall abide in the state of irreversibility.
Furthermore, Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, upon hearing this profound perfection of wisdom being taught, will have faith in it,
will not be sluggish, and will not doubt;
They will not doubt;

having resolved with the conviction that "it is exactly as it has been spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One," they will listen to it in detail, and they will produce this thought: (Vaidya 224)
Thinking, "May we hear this Perfection of Wisdom in detail from the presence of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One," they will,
having heard this very Perfection of Wisdom from those persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who practice the holy life in his Buddha-field, develop resolute faith in it.
They too, having faith in this perfection of wisdom, will believe in it exactly as it was spoken by the Tathāgata; and believing in it thus, they will stand in the state of non-retrogression.
Thus, Subhūti, I say that even the hearing of the perfection of wisdom is of great benefit.
How much more so for those who will have faith in it, and having had faith, will abide in suchness and practice for the sake of suchness?
Having stood for the sake of suchness and having practiced for the sake of suchness, they abide in suchness;
abiding in suchness, they teach the Dharma for the sake of omniscience.
Subhūti said: "Blessed One, since no dharma whatsoever other than suchness is apprehended, then, Blessed One, what dharma will abide in suchness?
Or who is this that will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
"Or who indeed will teach this Dharma?

When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, as for what you have said—that when no dharma whatsoever other than suchness is apprehended, then, Blessed One, what dharma is there that will abide in suchness?"
"Who will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Or who will teach this Dharma?
Subhūti, no dharma whatsoever is apprehended apart from suchness.
Subhūti, since even suchness itself is not apprehended, what need is there to mention one who will abide in suchness— that dharma which shall abide in suchness?
Subhūti, it is not suchness that awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
nor, Subhūti, is there any dharma whatsoever to be apprehended that has awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
He will fully awaken, or he is fully awakening;
yet, Subhūti, suchness does not teach the Dharma.
Even that dharma which might be taught, Subhūti, is not apprehended.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said this to the Blessed One: "Profound, O Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom!
Difficult is the task performed by those Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, who desire to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
For what reason? Because,
Blessed One, there is no dharma whatsoever that abides in suchness,
nor is there any dharma that fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Nor does anyone teach any dharma;
and herein they do not falter,
nor do they have any doubt.
Nor do they act with delay.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Kauśika, as for what you say— that Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, are doers of what is difficult,
since they do not experience hesitation or confusion when these profound dharmas are being taught."
"Kauśika, since all dharmas are empty, who here could have any hesitation or confusion?
Śakra said: "Whatever the noble Subhūti teaches, he teaches it starting from emptiness."
And it does not cling anywhere;
just as, for example, an arrow shot into the air does not cling anywhere,
even so the Dharma teaching of the noble Subhūti does not cling anywhere.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, in speaking thus and teaching thus concerning the Elder Subhūti, am I one who speaks the words of the Tathāgata and speaks the Dharma?
And in explaining the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, do I explain it correctly?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Kauśika, as for what you have spoken— 'It is even so, Kauśika, it is even so'—
by speaking thus and teaching thus, you are one who speaks according to the words of the Tathāgata and one who speaks according to the Dharma."
And you explain the secondary dharma in accordance with the primary dharma.
For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, whatever indeed occurs to the mind of the Elder Subhūti, [that he explains].
Whatever appears, Kauśika, it appears starting from emptiness.
For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, the Elder Subhūti does not even perceive the perfection of wisdom.
One does not apprehend [them]; how much less so one who practices the perfection of wisdom?
One does not even apprehend awakening itself.
How much more so for one who will fully awaken to enlightenment?
One does not even perceive omniscience itself;
how much less so for one who will attain omniscience?
He does not even perceive suchness itself; how much less, then, will he perceive one who will become a Tathāgata?
He does not even perceive non-arising itself.
How much more so for one who will realize non-arising?
One does not even perceive a bodhisattva; how much less so one who will fully awaken to enlightenment?
He does not even perceive the powers themselves;
how much less so one who will possess the powers?
He does not even perceive the grounds of self-confidence itself.
How much less, then, could there be one who is fearless?
Since one does not even perceive the Dharma itself, how much less could there be one who will teach the Dharma?
"Kauśika, it is indeed by dwelling in the seclusion of all dharmas and by dwelling in the non-apprehension of all dharmas that the Elder Subhūti dwells.

Furthermore, Kauśika, this dwelling of the Elder Subhūti— in which all dharmas are secluded and all dharmas are not apprehended— does not approach even a hundredth part of the dwelling of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses and dwells in the perfection of wisdom."

It does not approach even a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-ten-millionth part, nor a thousand-ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-koṭī-niyuta-part. It does not admit of any calculation, fraction, reckoning, comparison, analogy, resemblance, or even a point of reference.
Kauśika, setting aside the dwelling of the Tathāgata, this dwelling of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses and dwells in the perfection of wisdom surpasses all other dwellings.
Kauśika, this is declared to be the foremost of all those dwellings.
He is called the most excellent, he is called the eldest, he is called the best.
It is called excellent, it is called sublime, it is called supreme.
It is called the unsurpassed, it is called the peerless, it is called the unequaled.
He is called "the peerless one.
This dwelling of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses and dwells in the perfection of wisdom surpasses all the dwellings of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Therefore, Kausika, one who wishes to attain the foremost position among all beings, who wishes to attain the most excellent position, the eldest position, the best position, the most distinguished position, the sublime position, the highest position, the unsurpassed position, the peerless position, and the incomparable position— [should train in this perfection of wisdom].

Kauśika, a son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to attain the state of equality with the unequaled should dwell in this dwelling, which is the dwelling of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, as they course and dwell in the perfection of wisdom.
The twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Essence," in the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom.
(Vaidya 226) Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Strewing of Flowers.

Now at that time, a certain son of the gods, together with many sons of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, took hold of Māndārava and Mahāmāndārava flowers and approached the place where the Blessed One was.
At that very time, six hundred bhikṣus were assembled and seated in that same assembly.
They rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, placed their right knees upon the ground, and extended their joined palms toward the Blessed One.
Through the power of the Buddha, those hands joined by those bhikṣus became filled with māndārava and mahāmāndārava flowers.
They scattered, showered, and strewed those *māndārava* and great *māndārava* flowers over the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
And they spoke these words: "O Blessed One, we shall practice this perfection of wisdom;
O Blessed One, we shall dwell by means of this unsurpassed dwelling in the perfection of wisdom."
Then, at that time, the Blessed One manifested a smile.

Now, this is the natural law of the Blessed Buddhas: whenever they manifest a smile, rays of light of various colors and many hues issue forth from the Blessed One’s mouth—namely, blue, yellow, red, white, madder-red, crystal-colored, silver-colored, and gold-colored.

Having emerged, they illuminated infinite and boundless world-systems with their radiance, ascended as far as the Brahma-world, and then, returning once more, circumambulated the Blessed One three times and vanished into the crown of the Blessed One’s head.

Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not manifest a smile without cause or condition."
“Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for manifesting this smile?

When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, these six hundred monks will, in a future time, during the aeon known as Tārakopama, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
And having attained perfect enlightenment, he will teach the Dharma to sentient beings;
and all [those Buddhas] will have a single name, namely, Avakīrṇakusuma.
They will appear in the world as Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and Teachers.
Furthermore, Ānanda, for all those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas named Avakīrṇakusuma, the community of disciples will be equal;

and for all those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas named Avakīrṇakusuma, the measure of their lifespan will be exactly the same—twenty thousand kalpas. And the teaching of each one of them shall be widespread, attaining great expansion among gods and humans.
And the True Dharma of all of them alike shall endure for exactly twenty thousand eons each;
and from whichever villages, towns, market-towns, districts, kingdoms, or royal capitals they shall go forth, [they will do so].
Having gone forth, wherever they shall turn the wheel of Dharma, and having turned it, wherever they shall dwell, and from wherever and into whatever place they shall enter;
And by whichever way and from whichever place they shall go forth, there, in those very places, as they enter, go forth, and dwell, showers of five-colored flowers will fall.
Therefore, Ānanda, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who wish to dwell in the supreme dwelling should dwell in the dwelling of the perfection of wisdom.
One should dwell;
Ānanda, those who wish to dwell in the dwelling of the Tathāgata should dwell in the dwelling of the perfection of wisdom.
For whatever bodhisattva mahāsattvas, Ānanda, shall practice in the perfection of wisdom, [they shall do so].
One should reach the conclusion that these beings must have passed away from among humans;
or, having been reborn here, they must have passed away from the Tuṣita heaven and been reborn among humans.
Why is that?
For it is thus: this Perfection of Wisdom will circulate extensively among humans and among the Tuṣita gods.
Furthermore, Ānanda, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who shall practice in this Perfection of Wisdom should be known as being looked upon by the Tathāgatas.
Those who shall take up this perfection of wisdom, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, propagate it, teach it, explain it, set it forth, study it, and at the very least, write it down.

Having taken it up, retained it, recited it, mastered it, set it in motion, taught it, explained it, pointed it out, studied it, and even having written it down, they will instruct, exhort, demonstrate, inspire, encourage, and gladden the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas.
Ānanda, it should be known that those bodhisattva mahāsattvas have planted roots of merit under the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
It is not only in the presence of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas that they have planted roots of merit in order to train here in the perfection of wisdom;
indeed, Ānanda, there is no doubt that those roots of merit have been planted by those bodhisattva mahāsattvas under the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Those who train here in this perfection of wisdom and do not fall into terror,
and those, Ānanda, who will take up this perfection of wisdom, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, propagate it, teach it, explain it, and expound it—
They will study it, they will write it down,

and they will follow it according to its meaning, its dharma, and its method; Ānanda, you should reach the conclusion that those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, have actually stood in the presence of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
And those who do not revile this perfection of wisdom, do not oppose it, and do not become incensed against it.
They do not withdraw it, they do not prohibit it,
and they do not reject it.
They will not think that it should be rejected;
Ānanda, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas should also be known as having performed services for previous Victors.
Furthermore, Ānanda, although a bodhisattva mahāsattva has planted roots of merit in the presence of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas,
it will not yield its fruit for the sake of the state of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha,
provided that the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not fail his vow regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Moreover, Ānanda, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who has practiced the perfection of wisdom should generally be grateful.

Therefore, Ānanda, I entrust and re-entrust this perfection of wisdom to you, so that it may be taken up, retained, recited, mastered, promulgated, and preserved for a long time through the assembly of its syllables.
So that this [teaching] might not disappear:
Ānanda, if you were to take up all those teachings of the Dharma that I have taught to you in person— setting aside the Perfection of Wisdom— and then were to let them be lost again;
If you were to abandon it again or cause it to be forgotten,
Ānanda, you would not have committed such an offense against me as this.
However, Ānanda, if you were to destroy even a single word or a portion of a word associated with the perfection of wisdom, [that would be a far greater offense].
If you were to cast it aside or cause it to be forgotten,
by that alone, Ānanda, you would have committed an offense against me.
And you would not have pleased my mind.
Furthermore, Ānanda, if you were to take up the perfection of wisdom and then again destroy it, or again abandon it, [you would not have pleased my mind].
If you cause me to be forgotten, I would not have been honored, revered, esteemed, worshiped, venerated, or respected by you.

Moreover, Ānanda, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who are past, future, and present— even they, Ānanda, have not been honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, adored, or venerated by you. Yet, if you, Ānanda, having taken up the perfection of wisdom, were again to lose it, [the fault would be yours].
If you were to cast it away again or cause it to be forgotten,
by that alone, Ānanda, you would have offended me.
And you have not pleased my mind.
Why is that?

Ānanda, this has been said by the Tathāgata: "The perfection of wisdom is the mother, the progenitor, the birther of the past, future, and present Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly awakened ones; it is the source of omniscience."
"Bringer [of benefit]," [he said].
"Therefore, Ānanda, I entrust and hand over to you this perfection of wisdom, so that it may not disappear."
This perfection of wisdom, Ānanda, should be taken up; this perfection of wisdom, Ānanda, should be retained;
this perfection of wisdom, Ānanda, should be recited.
Ānanda, this perfection of wisdom is to be mastered; Ānanda, this perfection of wisdom is to be set in motion;
Ānanda, this perfection of wisdom is to be taught.
This perfection of wisdom, Ānanda, must be taught; this perfection of wisdom, Ānanda, must be recited;
this perfection of wisdom, Ānanda, must be studied.
"This Perfection of Wisdom, Ānanda, must be written down; this Perfection of Wisdom, Ānanda, must be cultivated.
This Perfection of Wisdom, Ānanda, must be well-attended to by you, well-retained, thoroughly mastered, and well-proclaimed."
It should be grasped with well-articulated syllables, words, and phonemes, and it should be properly explained.
Why is that?
Because, Ānanda, it is the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present; it is by taking that *dharmatā* as the authoritative standard.

Ānanda, just as you consider that which should be done, given, or attended to— whether out of a desire for welfare, out of love, out of respect, out of goodness, or for the sake of living in comfort— toward me, the Tathāgata, who am currently staying,
existing, and maintaining myself, even so, Ānanda, should this Perfection of Wisdom be taken up, retained, recited, and mastered by you.
It should be set in motion, taught, explained, recited, studied, written down, cultivated, honored, revered, respected, worshipped,
venerated, and esteemed— with that desire for welfare, with that affection, with that reverence, and because of its possession of such qualities.
In this way, Ānanda, you have honored me and those bodhisattva mahāsattvas;
and love, faith, and reverence have been generated toward the Blessed Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Ānanda, if I, the Tathāgata, am dear to you, pleasing to you, and not to be abandoned, then, Ānanda, let this Perfection of Wisdom be dear to you, pleasing to you, and not to be abandoned,
so that not even a single word of it may be lost to you.
So that it may not disappear. Ānanda, were I to speak at great length concerning the entrustment of the *prajñāpāramitā*, I might speak for an eon, or the remainder of an eon,
or a hundred eons, or a thousand eons, or a hundred thousand eons, or ten million eons, or a hundred ten-million eons.
Or for a thousand koṭis of kalpas, or a hundred thousand koṭis of kalpas, or even beyond that.
In brief, Ānanda, just as I am your teacher, so too is the perfection of wisdom your teacher.
Just as those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present are the teachers of the world with its gods, humans, and asuras,
so too is the perfection of wisdom the teacher of the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Therefore, Ānanda, the perfection of wisdom is immeasurable.
With an immeasurable entrustment, I entrust and re-entrust this perfection of wisdom to you for the benefit and happiness of the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
Ānanda, it is for one who has not forsaken the Tathāgata and has not forsaken the Dharma.
The Saṅgha has not been forsaken;
the enlightenment of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present, has not been forsaken;
may his perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) likewise remain unforsaken.
This is our instruction: Ānanda,

whoever should take up this perfection of wisdom, bear it in mind, master it, recite it, learn it, propagate it, teach it, explain it, point it out, study it, write it down, and cultivate it— by him the enlightenment of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, future, and present, will be upheld.
For whoever, Ānanda, upholds this Perfection of Wisdom while it is being lost,
by him the enlightenment of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present, is upheld. Why is that?
For, Ānanda, the enlightenment of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is born from the perfection of wisdom.
Moreover, Ānanda, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones who existed in the past—
of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones as well, the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment was likewise born solely from the perfection of wisdom.

Ānanda, those [Tathāgatas] who will appear in the future as Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones— even for those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, Ānanda, their unsurpassed perfect enlightenment will likewise be born from the perfection of wisdom alone.
And Ānanda, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones who currently exist, abide, and maintain themselves in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems— [for them too, it is so].
Ānanda, for those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones as well, supreme perfect enlightenment was born precisely from the perfection of wisdom.

Therefore, Ānanda, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to supreme perfect enlightenment and who desires to train in the six perfections should hear, take up, and retain this very perfection of wisdom.
It should be recited, mastered, promulgated, taught, explained, pointed out, studied, and written down.
One should train in this very perfection of wisdom and apply oneself to its practice.
For what reason?

For this, Ānanda, is the perfection of wisdom, the mother, the progenitor, the begetter of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. Whatever bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, Ānanda, have trained in the six perfections and have emerged, will emerge, or are emerging in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, [it is all due to her].
Ānanda, all of them have trained in the six perfections by relying on the perfection of wisdom;
they too have all emerged in the six perfections by relying on this very perfection of wisdom.
For what reason?
For it is from the perfection of wisdom, Ānanda, that all the perfections are born; they become the bringers of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Therefore, Ānanda, I entrust and hand over this perfection of wisdom to you again and yet again, even a second and a third time, so that it may not disappear.
For this, Ānanda, is the inexhaustible treasury of the Dharma of the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the perfectly awakened ones, namely, the perfection of wisdom.
And why is that?

For whatever Dharma, Ānanda, has been taught by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, to sentient beings throughout the past, beginningless cycle of existence— all of that has come from this very treasury of Dharma,
namely, from the Perfection of Wisdom.
Ānanda, those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who in the future time, having awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment within the immeasurable cycle of existence, will teach the Dharma to sentient beings—
they too, those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, [will do so] from this very treasury of Dharma,
namely, from the perfection of wisdom.

Ānanda, those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who at present abide, remain, and maintain themselves in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems, and who teach the Dharma— they too, Ānanda, have their manifestation from this very treasury of Dharma.
Namely, from the perfection of wisdom.
Therefore, Ānanda, this inexhaustible treasury of Dharma is the treasury of the perfection of wisdom.
If you, Ānanda, were to teach the Dharma on the level of the Śrāvakas to persons belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle, [you would produce much merit].

And even if, during that teaching of the Dharma, all the beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system were to personally realize arhatship, nevertheless, by you, my disciple, who teaches the Dharma by following the turning of the wheel of Dharma,
the duty of a disciple would not have been fulfilled; yet, Ānanda, if you [were to teach] even a single [verse] for a bodhisattva mahāsattva...

If you were to teach and fully illuminate even a single dharma connected with the perfection of wisdom, I would be more gratified by you as a disciple for thus teaching the Dharma in accordance with my turning of the wheel of Dharma, than by that previous teaching of the Dharma through which you caused all sentient beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system to attain arhatship.

“Ānanda, what do you think: is that mass of merit—consisting of the basis of meritorious action through giving, the basis of meritorious action through ethical discipline, and the basis of meritorious action through cultivation—which belongs to those Arhats, indeed great? Ānanda replied:
“Much, Blessed One! Much, Sugata!
The Blessed One said:

“Then, Ānanda, that person belonging to the vehicle of the disciples (śrāvakayānika) produces much more merit who teaches the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to bodhisattvas, the great beings (mahāsattvas). Even more than that, Ānanda, he produces much more merit who is a bodhisattva, a great being, teaching the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom to another bodhisattva, a great being.”
Let it remain, Ānanda, even for a single day; let it remain, Ānanda, even for a single morning meal; let it remain, Ānanda, even for a single morning meal as it has been taught.
"Let it remain, Ānanda, for even a single nālikā, or even for the duration of a single nālikā;
let it remain, Ānanda, for the duration of a single nālikā, or even for a single muhūrta; let it remain, Ānanda, for a single muhūrta, or even for a single lava."
Ānanda,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for even a single moment, or even for the duration of a single instant, teaches to another bodhisattva mahāsattva a Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom, he generates far more merit than that.
For this, Ānanda,
is the gift of Dharma of that bodhisattva mahāsattva which surpasses the roots of merit of all persons belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
In this way, Ānanda,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with such roots of merit— while attending to these roots of merit in this manner— it is impossible, Ānanda, it is out of the question that such a bodhisattva mahāsattva should turn back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This possibility does not exist.”

Then, at that time, the Blessed One performed such a miraculous feat (*ṛddhyabhisaṃskāra*) by means of which miraculous feat all those four assemblies— the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, as well as gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans,
and non-humans— all of them, through the power of the Buddha, [beheld] the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
They saw him surrounded by the community of monks and preceded by a host of bodhisattvas,

teaching the Dharma in an ocean-like, profound, and unshakeable assembly; he was encircled and honored by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas endowed with inconceivable qualities, as well as by all the arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who were free from afflictions, self-mastered, and possessed of minds perfectly liberated.

[They were] those with well-liberated wisdom, noble thoroughbreds, great elephants, who had accomplished what was to be done, performed their duties, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, exhausted the fetters of existence, whose minds were rightly liberated through perfect knowledge, and who had reached the supreme perfection of mastery over all states of mind.
Then the Blessed One withdrew that miraculous manifestation once again.
When the Blessed One had withdrawn that miraculous manifestation, the Blessed One Akṣobhya, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, was no longer visible,
nor were all those bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
Those great śrāvakas and that buddha-field no longer came within the range of vision of those four classes— the gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas— nor of humans and non-humans.
For what reason was this?
For that miraculous feat had been withdrawn by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened Buddha;
consequently, none of them appeared before the eyes of any of those others anymore.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "In this way, Ānanda, all phenomena do not even come into the range of vision; they do not come into the range of what is dharma or non-dharma;
nor do they perceive what is dharma or non-dharma."
They do not know dharma or non-dharma. Why is that?
For all phenomena, Ānanda, are indeed without a knower and without a seer.
They are not capable of performing any function.
For what reason?
Because, Ānanda, all phenomena are devoid of agency and are ungraspable, due to the lack of agency in space.
For all phenomena, Ānanda, are inconceivable, being like an illusory person.
For all phenomena, Ānanda, are without an experiencer, by virtue of their non-existence. Practicing in this way, Ānanda, bodhisattva mahāsattvas course in the perfection of wisdom.
They do not adhere to any dharma whatsoever.
Ānanda, training in this way, bodhisattva mahāsattvas train in the perfection of wisdom.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain great awakening—the supreme perfection of all training—must train in the perfection of wisdom.
For what reason?
Because, Ānanda, this training is declared to be the foremost of all trainings;
it is declared to be the most excellent.
She is called the eldest, she is called the most excellent, she is called the most preeminent.
It is called sublime; it is called supreme;
it is called unsurpassed.
It is called unsurpassed; it is called peerless;
it is called equal to the unequaled.
Bringing benefit to all the world, bringing happiness to all the world, acting as a protector for those without protection, authorized by the Buddhas, and praised by the Buddhas—
having trained in this perfection of wisdom, Ānanda, and having stood firm in this training, the Tathāgatas, Arhats,
and Perfectly Enlightened Ones could lift up this great trichiliocosm world-system with a single big toe and set it down again.
And it would not occur to those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, that "this trichiliocosm has been lifted up" or "it has been set down.
Why is that?
Because the perfection of wisdom is endowed with immeasurable and incalculable qualities.

Ānanda, having trained in this training of the perfection of wisdom, the Buddha Bhagavāns have attained non-attachment regarding all phenomena of the past, future, and present. Ānanda, whatever trainings there may be in the past, future, or present time, among them all, Ānanda, this very training of the perfection of wisdom is declared to be the foremost.
It is called the most excellent, it is called the eldest, it is called the best.
It is called excellent, it is called sublime, it is called supreme.
It is declared to be unsurpassed, it is declared to be peerless, it is declared to be unequaled.
It is called "the peerless to the peerless.
For, Ānanda, the perfection of wisdom is immeasurable;
for, Ānanda, the perfection of wisdom is inexhaustible.
For the perfection of wisdom, Ānanda, is indeed infinite.
Why is that? Precisely because it is non-existent.

Of the perfection of wisdom. For, Ānanda, he who would think that a measure, an exhaustion, or a limit of the perfection of wisdom should be grasped, would indeed think that a measure, an exhaustion, or a limit of space should be grasped.
For what reason?
Because, Ānanda, the perfection of wisdom is immeasurable;
because, Ānanda, the perfection of wisdom is inexhaustible.

For the perfection of wisdom, Ānanda, is indeed limitless. I have not, Ānanda, declared a measure, an exhaustion, or a limit for the perfection of wisdom. Indeed, Ānanda, the sets of names, phrases, and syllables are bound by measure.
This perfection of wisdom, Ānanda, is not bound by measure.
Why is that?
Because, Ānanda, the collection of names, the collection of phrases, and the collection of syllables are not the perfection of wisdom.
For this perfection of wisdom, Ānanda, is not something that can be measured;
indeed, Ānanda, the perfection of wisdom is immeasurable.
Ānanda said: "For what reason, Blessed One, has the Blessed One not declared a measure for the perfection of wisdom?

The Blessed One replied: "Because it is inexhaustible, Ānanda, the Tathāgata does not indicate a measure for the perfection of wisdom. Because it is secluded, Ānanda, no measure for the perfection of wisdom has been declared by the Tathāgata."
For indeed, Ānanda, even the state of seclusion of a dharma that is secluded is not apprehended; how much less, then, will there be a measure for it?
Thus, Ānanda, because it is immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom is measureless and limitless.
