Ānanda, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who appeared in the past were also manifested from this very perfection of wisdom.
And yet, Ānanda, this perfection of wisdom is neither exhausted nor completely exhausted.

Ānanda, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who will appear in the future time, they too, Ānanda, will be manifested from this very Perfection of Wisdom. And yet, Ānanda, this Perfection of Wisdom will neither be exhausted nor completely depleted.
Moreover, Ānanda, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones who now reside, remain, and maintain themselves in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems—
they too, Ānanda, are manifested from this very perfection of wisdom. And yet, Ānanda, this perfection of wisdom is neither exhausted nor completely exhausted.

I too, Ānanda, am now the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. It is from this very Prajñāpāramitā, Ānanda, that my manifestation has come forth. And yet, Ānanda, this Prajñāpāramitā is neither exhausted nor completely depleted.
For what reason? Because,
Ānanda, he who would think that the perfection of wisdom is something to be exhausted would be thinking that space is something to be exhausted.
Therefore, Ānanda, this perfection of wisdom is indeed inexhaustible.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the venerable Subhūti: "Profound is this matter spoken by the Tathāgata;
what if I were to question the Tathāgata regarding this matter?
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Is the perfection of wisdom, Blessed One, inexhaustible?"
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is indeed inexhaustible; that is to say, because space is inexhaustible and because all phenomena are non-arising.
Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by way of the inexhaustibility of form."
In the same way, Subhūti, feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness should be brought forth by a bodhisattva mahāsattva through their inexhaustibility;
indeed, Subhūti, it is in this manner that the perfection of wisdom should be brought forth by a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom through the inexhaustibility of ignorance;
likewise, through the inexhaustibility of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, and birth.

Subhūti, by means of the inexhaustibility of aging and death, and by means of the inexhaustibility of sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s contemplation of dependent origination, which is free from the two extremes.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates in this way, he contemplates dependent origination as being without beginning, end, or middle. Subhūti, this is the unique quality of a bodhisattva mahāsattva seated at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa),
namely, that he thus contemplates dependent origination.
Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who contemplates in this way, there is the attainment of the knowledge of omniscience through dependent origination.

Subhūti, whichever bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom through this inexhaustible accomplishment, contemplates dependent origination, he will not abide on the level of a śrāvaka nor on the level of a pratyekabuddha.

Nevertheless, Subhūti, they will abide in omniscience. As for those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who turn back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, if they do not rely upon these mental engagements and this skill in means, they do not know: "How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom [proceed] by way of inexhaustible accomplishment?"
The perfection of wisdom is to be brought forth;
and how, through the bringing forth of the inexhaustible, should dependent origination be observed within the perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have turned back or are turning back [from enlightenment]...

And those who have turned back, are turning back, or will turn back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment— all of them did so, do so, or will so without resorting to this skill in means. Subhūti, as for those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have not turned back, are not turning back, and will not turn back—
All of them, having relied upon this perfection of wisdom, have not turned back, do not turn back, and will not turn back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus, by means of an inexhaustible accomplishment, the perfection of wisdom should be accomplished by a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom;
and in this way, through an inexhaustible accomplishment, dependent origination should be contemplated within the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus contemplates dependent origination, he does not perceive any dharma arising without a cause;
nor does he perceive any dharma as permanent, stable, eternal, or of an unchanging nature;
nor does he perceive any dharma as an agent or an experiencer.
Subhūti, this is the contemplation of dependent origination for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices this perfection of wisdom by means of its inexhaustible accomplishment.

Subhūti, at the time when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, accomplishing the perfection of wisdom through its inexhaustible accomplishment, contemplates dependent origination— at that time, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive form.
He does not perceive feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations, nor consciousness;
he does not perceive ignorance.

In this way, one does not perceive volitional formations, nor consciousness, nor name-and-form, nor the six sense bases, nor contact, nor feeling, nor craving, nor clinging, nor existence, nor birth, nor aging and death, nor sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. One does not perceive, "This is a buddha-field."
He does not perceive another buddha-field;
nor does he perceive that phenomenon by which one might perceive this or another buddha-field.
This, Subhūti, is the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas.
At the time, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, at that time Māra the Evil One becomes pierced by the dart of supreme sorrow.
Subhūti, it is just as if a man, when his mother and father have passed away, were pierced by the dart of supreme sorrow;
even so, Subhūti, at the time when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, at that time Māra the Evil One is pierced by the dart of supreme sorrow.
Subhūti said: "Blessed One, is it only a single Māra, the Evil One, who becomes pierced by the dart of supreme sorrow; or rather, are many Māras, the Evil Ones, pierced by the dart of supreme sorrow;
or indeed, are all those Māras, the Evil Ones, who exist within the triple-thousand great-thousand world-system, pierced by the dart of supreme sorrow at that time?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, at the time when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the dwelling of the perfection of wisdom,
at that time all the Māras, the evil ones, within the triple-thousand great-thousand world-system become pierced by the dart of supreme sorrow and find no pleasure in their respective seats."

For what reason? Subhūti, because when this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells by means of dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, the world with its gods, humans, and asuras finds no opportunity to seize him,
nor does it find a foothold.
In this regard, Subhūti, if someone were to seize this person and either harass them or turn them back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
therefore a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment should practice the perfection of wisdom.
Why is that?
Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of giving reaches the fulfillment of its cultivation;
likewise, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration reach the fulfillment of their cultivation.
Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, all six perfections reach the fulfillment of their cultivation.
And all skillful means reach fulfillment through cultivation for that bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom; whatever deeds of Māra may arise,
he will recognize them all as they are arising.
Knowing this, he will relinquish it.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to master all skillful means should practice the perfection of wisdom and cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, at the time when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom and brings forth the perfection of wisdom,
at that time, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not [perceive] those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who reside, stay, and maintain themselves in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems.
They should be brought to mind;
for even their omniscience has issued forth from this very source, namely, the perfection of wisdom.
Having reflected thus, that bodhisattva mahāsattva should again produce this thought: "I too shall attain those dharmas which were attained by those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones."
Thus,

Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should produce and bring forth these productions of the thought [of awakening] at the end of each day, even if only for as long as the snap of a finger.
And furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva who perceives objective referents were to give gifts for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges,
this very bodhisattva mahāsattva who, at the end of a single day, brings forth this perfection of wisdom, generates much more merit than that bodhisattva mahāsattva who perceives objective referents.
Even for as long as the snap of a finger,
this bodhisattva mahāsattva will abide in the state of non-retrogression;
that bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as being sustained by the Tathāgata’s attention.
If one practicing this perfection of wisdom generates these productions of the thought [of awakening] even for as long as a day passes, or even for as little as the snap of a finger,
how much more so for one whose productions of the thought would continue throughout the entire day?
Subhūti, what destiny should be expected for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is sustained by the attention of the Tathāgata?
Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva sustained by the attention of the Tathāgata, no other destiny is to be expected except for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
moreover, such a person is incapable of being reborn in the lower realms.
Rebirth in heaven alone is to be expected for him;
even there he will not be separated from the Tathāgatas,
and he will be reborn in those buddha-fields that are not devoid of Tathāgatas.
And he will bring sentient beings to maturity.
Subhūti, these too are the qualities and these too are the benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom.
For one who brings forth the perfection of wisdom and generates these thoughts of awakening— even if only for as long as the snap of a finger—
how much more so for one whose thoughts of awakening should persist throughout the day?
Subhūti, it is just as with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gandhahastin, who is currently leading the holy life in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya.
The twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Scattered Flowers," in the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom.
(Vaidya 235) Chapter Twenty-nine: The Chapter on Following.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should follow the perfection of wisdom in this way: the perfection of wisdom should be followed by way of non-attachment to all dharmas.
The perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the non-differentiation of all phenomena;
the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the non-arising of all phenomena;
the perfection of wisdom is to be understood as the equality of all phenomena in their lack of transformation.
The perfection of wisdom is to be followed by way of understanding through wisdom that all phenomena are without self and are mere representations;
and the perfection of wisdom is to be followed by way of understanding that all phenomena are expressed merely as names and merely as conventional designations;
and yet this conventional designation is nowhere, from nothing, and is no conventional designation at all.
The perfection of wisdom is to be followed as the fact that all phenomena are beyond conventional discourse, beyond verbal expression, unspoken, and unuttered.
The perfection of wisdom is to be followed through the immeasurability of all phenomena; the perfection of wisdom is to be followed through the immeasurability of form.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom is to be followed by way of the immeasurability of feeling, the immeasurability of perception, the immeasurability of mental formations, and the immeasurability of consciousness;
the perfection of wisdom is to be followed by way of the signlessness of all phenomena.
The perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the penetration of all phenomena;
the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the natural purity of all phenomena;
the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the ineffability of all phenomena.
The perfection of wisdom is to be followed by way of the equality of abandonment, because all phenomena are non-ceasing;
the perfection of wisdom is to be followed by way of the equality of suchness, because all phenomena have attained nirvāṇa;
all phenomena do not come.
They do not go, because they are unknowing, unborn, and absolutely unborn; thus should the perfection of wisdom be followed.
The perfection of wisdom should be followed by way of not perceiving a self or another.
The perfection of wisdom is to be followed by understanding that all phenomena are noble arhats, being pure by nature;
the perfection of wisdom is to be followed by understanding that all phenomena have laid down their burden, because no burden is ever imposed upon them;
the perfection of wisdom is to be followed by understanding that all phenomena are neither a location nor a non-location.
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, form is indeed without location and without parts by virtue of its essential nature;
and so too are feeling, perception, and mental formations.

For consciousness, Subhūti, is without location and without parts by virtue of its natural essence, because it is the cooling cessation of all phenomena; thus should the perfection of wisdom be understood.
The perfection of wisdom should be understood through non-attachment and non-detachment;
the perfection of wisdom should be understood through being neither attached nor detached.
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, form, by its very essence and intrinsic nature, neither becomes impassioned nor dispassionate;
and the same is true for feeling, perception, and mental formations.

For consciousness, Subhūti, does not become attached nor does it become detached by way of its own-being or its true nature, because it is pure by nature; thus should the perfection of wisdom be followed. All phenomena are unattached, being free from attachment and non-attachment; thus should the perfection of wisdom be followed.
Awakening consists in the awakening to all phenomena through the knowledge of a Buddha; thus should the perfection of wisdom be followed.
The perfection of wisdom is to be followed by way of the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness of all dharmas;
the perfection of wisdom is to be followed by way of all dharmas being preceded by the medicine of loving-kindness;
the perfection of wisdom is to be followed by way of all dharmas abiding in loving-kindness, abiding in compassion, abiding in sympathetic joy, and abiding in equanimity.

The perfection of wisdom is to be understood as all phenomena having become *brahma* by virtue of the non-arising of faults—that is, the non-arising of all faults. The perfection of wisdom is to be understood as the wishlessness and the unimpededness of all phenomena.
The limitlessness of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the limitlessness of the ocean.
The boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom should be understood through the boundlessness of space;
the multicolored variety of the perfection of wisdom should be understood through the multicolored variety of Mount Meru;
and the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom should be understood through the boundlessness of form.
It should be understood in this way:
feeling, perception, and mental formations [should be understood].
Through the boundlessness of consciousness, the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom should be understood.
The boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the boundless illumination of the orb of the sun’s rays;
the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the boundlessness of all sounds;
the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the boundlessness of the complete attainment of all the qualities of a Buddha.
The boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the boundlessness of the accumulations of merit and knowledge of the realm of all sentient beings;
the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the boundlessness of the earth element;

likewise, the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the boundlessness of the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
The immeasurability of the perfection of wisdom should be understood through the immeasurability of the accumulation of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas;
the immeasurability of the perfection of wisdom should be understood through the immeasurability of the accumulation of all dharmas;
and the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom should be understood through the attainment of the boundlessness of the meditative concentrations on all dharmas.
The boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom should be understood through the boundlessness of all buddha-qualities;
the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom should be understood through the boundlessness of all phenomena;
the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom should be understood through the boundlessness of emptiness.
The boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom should be understood through the boundlessness of mind and mental factors;
the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom should be understood through the boundlessness of the conduct of the mind;
and the immeasurability of the perfection of wisdom should be understood through the immeasurability of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena.
The roar of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the roaring of the lion’s roar;
the indestructibility of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the indestructibility of all phenomena.
Why is that?
For form, Subhūti, is like the ocean;
likewise are feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness, Subhūti, like the ocean.
For form is equal to space;
likewise are feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness equal to space.
Form is like a variegated Meru;
likewise are feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness like a variegated Meru.
Form is equal to the infinite;
likewise are feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness equal to the infinite.
Form is equal to the arising of rays from the solar disk;
likewise are feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Consciousness is equal to the arising of rays from the solar disk.
Form is equal to the infinity of all sounds;
likewise are feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness equal to the infinity of all sounds.
Form is equal to the boundless realm of all sentient beings;
likewise are feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness equal to the boundless realm of all sentient beings.
Form is equal to the boundless attainment of all the qualities of a Buddha;
likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness— the consciousness is equal to the boundless attainment of all the qualities of a Buddha.
Form is equal to the limitless accumulation of merit and wisdom of the realm of all sentient beings;
likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness— the consciousness is equal to the limitless accumulation of merit and wisdom of the realm of all sentient beings.
Form is equal to earth;
likewise are feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness equal to earth.
Form is like water;
likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness are like water.
Form is equal to fire;
likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness are equal to fire.
Form is equal to wind;
likewise are feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness equal to wind.
Form is equal to space;
likewise are feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness equal to space.
Form is equal to consciousness;
likewise are feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Consciousness is equal to consciousness.
Form is devoid of the accumulation of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas;
likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
consciousness is devoid of the accumulation of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.
Form is devoid of the accumulation of all phenomena;
likewise are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
consciousness is devoid of the accumulation of all phenomena.
Form is equal to the boundlessness of the samādhi of all dharmas;
likewise are feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness equal to the boundlessness of the samādhi of all dharmas.
Form is departure;
the intrinsic nature of form, the suchness of form, are the Buddha-dharmas.
The same applies to feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Consciousness is departure;
the intrinsic nature of consciousness, the suchness of consciousness, are the Buddha-dharmas.
Form is the infinite dharmic nature of all dharmas.
In this way, feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness are the infinite dharmic nature of all phenomena;
form is empty, the infinite dharmic nature.
In this way, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty; they are the nature of phenomena that is without limit.
Form is the boundlessness of mind and mental factors.
In the same way, feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness are the boundlessness of mind and mental factors;
form is the arising of the movements of the mind.
In the same way, feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness are the arising of mental conduct;
form is wholesome or unwholesome.
This continues until non-apprehension;
likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness, whether wholesome or unwholesome.
Up to non-apprehension:
form is equal to the lion’s roar;
likewise are feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Consciousness is like the lion’s roar;
form is unshakable;
and so too are feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Consciousness is unshakable.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should follow the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, when this bodhisattva mahāsattva follows this perfection of wisdom in this way—
investigating it, entering into it, awakening to it, reflecting upon it, weighing it, examining it, and cultivating it with mental attentions free from all deceit and guile,
and with mental attentions free from all conceit— then...
with mental orientations free from self-exaltation,
with mental orientations free from all laziness,
and with mental orientations free from disparaging others;
by means of mental attentions free from the notion of a self, mental attentions free from the notion of a sentient being,
and mental attentions free from gain, honor, and praise;
by means of mental attentions free from the five hindrances,
by means of mental attentions free from envy and avarice,
and by means of mental attentions free from all worldly bustle;
Then, the fulfillment of all qualities will not be difficult for him to attain, nor will the fulfillment of the unsurpassed Buddha-qualities of a Buddha-field be difficult.
The twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Following," in the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom.
(Vaidya 238) Chapter Thirty: Sadāprarudita.
Furthermore, Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom should be sought in this manner:
"Just as this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita formerly searched for it, he is now practicing the holy life in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Bhīṣmagarjitanirghoṣasvara.
When this was said, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how did the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita search for this Perfection of Wisdom?"

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita was formerly seeking the perfection of wisdom, he sought it while being indifferent to his body, regardless of his life, and independent of gain, honor, and fame."
While he was searching for the perfection of wisdom, having gone into the forest, he heard a voice from the sky: "Go, noble son, toward the eastern direction;
there you will hear the perfection of wisdom.
Go in such a manner," [and so forth].
Just as you do not give rise to the mental preoccupation with physical fatigue, nor do you give rise to the mental preoccupation with sloth and torpor,
nor do you give rise to the mental preoccupation with food.
You do not give rise to the mental application of water,
you do not give rise to the mental application of night, and you do not give rise to the mental application of day.
Do not give rise to the mental application of cold, nor do you give rise to the mental application of heat;
do not direct the mind toward anything at all, whether internally or externally.
And do not go, noble son, looking to the left,
nor to the right, nor to the east.
Not to the west, not to the north, nor upwards.
Do not look down, nor look toward the intermediate directions as you go;
and so, noble son, proceed.
Just as you do not waver from the self, nor from the view of a real body; just as you do not waver from form, nor from feeling, nor from perception, nor from mental formations;
In such a way that you do not waver from consciousness; for whoever wavers from this,
they fall away.
From what does he deviate?
He deviates from the qualities of a Buddha (buddhadharma).
Whoever deviates from the qualities of a Buddha...
He wanders in saṃsāra;
he who wanders in saṃsāra does not course in the perfection of wisdom.
He does not attain the perfection of wisdom.
When this had been said, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita spoke thus to that voice: "I shall indeed do so.
For what reason?
Because I desire to bring light to all sentient beings and desire to fully realize the qualities of a Buddha."
When this had been said, that voice spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita: "Excellent, excellent, noble son Sadāprarudita!"

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita again heard a voice, and he heard this: "O son of good family, having produced resolute conviction regarding all dharmas as being empty, signless, and wishless, you must seek the perfection of wisdom.
You must remain free from signs, free from the conception of existence, and free from the view of a sentient being."
Noble son, you must avoid evil friends;
you must serve, revere, and attend upon virtuous friends—
those who teach the Dharma that all phenomena are empty, signless, wishless, unarisen, unborn, unceasing, and non-existent.

"Noble son, practicing in this way, before long you will hear the perfection of wisdom, either as it has come down in a book or as it resides in the person of a monk who is a preacher of the Dharma. And from whichever noble son you hear the perfection of wisdom, you should conceive of him as the Teacher himself. You should be grateful and appreciative, thinking: 'This is my spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), from whom I hear this perfection of wisdom.'"
Hearing which, I shall very quickly become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and I shall draw near to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
"I shall be reborn in Buddha-fields that are not devoid of Tathāgatas; I shall avoid the unfavorable conditions and fulfill the perfection of favorable conditions."
Noble son, weighing these benefits, you should conceive the perception of the Teacher toward the Dharma-preaching monk.
Noble son, you should not follow the Dharma-preaching monk with a mental continuum associated with worldly material gain;
rather, seeking the Dharma and out of reverence for the Dharma, you should follow the Dharma-preaching monk.
Furthermore, you must recognize the works of Māra.

For there is, noble son, an evil Māra who provides a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is a Dharma-preacher with forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles in order that he may serve, enjoy, and attend upon them; yet, having mastered those [sensual objects], he serves, enjoys, and attends upon them through skillful means.
And in that regard, noble son, you should not give rise to a mind of lack of faith toward the Dharma-preaching monk;
rather, you should give rise to this thought: "I do not know that skill in means which he understands."
By means of this discipline of sentient beings, and for the sake of gathering the roots of virtue of sentient beings, he practices, pursues, and attends to these dharmas.
Indeed, no attachment or objective support whatsoever exists for bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
And at that very moment, noble son, you should contemplate the true nature of dharmas.
And what, son of good family, is the true principle of all phenomena?
It is this: that all phenomena are neither defiled nor purified. For what reason?
For all phenomena are empty by their very nature.

All phenomena are indeed devoid of a sentient being, devoid of a life-principle, devoid of a nourisher, devoid of a person, and devoid of a pudgala; they are like an illusion, like a dream, like an echo, and like a reflected image.
Thus, noble son, as you contemplate the true mode of all phenomena and follow the Dharma-preacher, you will before long set forth in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, son of good family, you should attend to another work of Māra:
if, son of good family, the Dharma-preacher discourages a son of good family who seeks the perfection of wisdom and does not attend to him.
In this matter, noble son, you must not offer resistance;
rather, seeking only the Dharma and with reverence for the Dharma, you should follow the monk who preaches the Dharma with an undiscouraged mind.
Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, having received this instruction from that voice, set out toward the eastern direction.
Not long after he had departed, this thought occurred to him: "I did not ask that voice how far I must go.
He remained standing right there on that spot of earth.
There, weeping, wailing, grieving, and lamenting, he thought to himself: "In this very spot of earth, I shall pass one night and day,
or two, or three."
four, or five,
or six,
I shall pass seven days and nights; I will not give rise to the mental preoccupation with physical fatigue,
nor will I give rise to the mental preoccupation with sloth and torpor.
I shall not give rise to the mental preoccupation with food; I shall not give rise to the mental preoccupation with drink; I shall not give rise to the mental preoccupation with night.
I shall not give rise to the mental attention of day; I shall not give rise to the mental attention of cold; I shall not give rise to the mental attention of heat.
"Until I shall hear the Perfection of Wisdom.
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, some man whose only son had died were to become possessed by great suffering and dejection;
because of his grief for that son, no other mental attention would arise in him.
Rather, only the mental attention directed toward his only son proceeded;
in the very same way, Subhūti, at that time no other mental attention whatsoever proceeded in the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita.
But rather, [he thinks]: "When indeed shall I hear that Perfection of Wisdom?"
Then, Subhūti, as the bodhisattva mahāsattva Sadāprarudita was thus longing, the form of a Tathāgata stood before him and gave his approval, saying: "Excellent, excellent, noble son,
you who speak these words!"

For it was in this very way, noble son, that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past, while formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, sought the perfection of wisdom, just as you seek it now. Therefore, noble son, continuing with this very vigor, this very enthusiasm, this very purposefulness, and this very desire, go toward the eastern direction.
"Noble son, five hundred yojanas from here there is a city named Gandhavatī, made of the seven precious gems,
surrounded by seven walls,
and encircled by seven moats and seven rows of palm trees."
It was twelve yojanas in length and twelve yojanas in width;

it was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants, and it was pierced through by five hundred market-streets that were as beautiful to behold as variegated paintings.
It was beautifully laid out with roads and thoroughfares for vehicles drawn by yokes, which were not crowded because they were established at intervals by those who were unequaled among equals.
Furthermore, the walls surrounding that city on all sides were made of the seven precious gems;
and upon those walls made of the seven precious gems, massive pinnacles of Jāmbūnada gold rose up.

And upon every turret-top there grew a tree made of the seven precious gems, laden with fruits composed of various and diverse jewels; and from every jeweled tree, a string of gems was suspended reaching to the next jeweled tree. And that entire city was covered by a network of golden bells.
And from that network of tinkling bells, stirred by the wind, there issues forth a sound that is lovely, charming, and delightful— just as, for example,
when a five-fold musical ensemble is performed together in concert by skilled gandharvas, a lovely, charming, and delightful resonance issues forth; even so,
from that network of tinkling bells stirred by the wind, a lovely, charming, and delightful resonance issues forth.
And by that sound, those beings play, rejoice, and enjoy themselves.
All around that city, the moats are filled with water that flows along, full of water that is neither too cold nor too hot.
And upon that water, there are boats made of the seven precious gems, variegated and beautiful, produced through the ripening of the former karma of those very beings.
Upon these, those beings mount and play, rejoice, and enjoy themselves;
and all that water is covered with blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, and great white lotuses,
as well as other most excellent flowers of exquisite fragrance.
There was not a single species of flower in that great trichiliocosm world system that did not exist there.
And all around that city were five hundred parks;
they were all composed of the seven precious gems, variegated and beautiful to behold.
In each garden there were five hundred lotus ponds,
each measuring one *krośa* in extent all around.
In all those lotus ponds grew various, beautiful, and lovely blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses made of the seven precious gems.
By them that water was covered;
and all those blue, red, white, and pink lotuses were as large in circumference as the wheels of a cart, fragrant, blue, blue-colored, blue in appearance, and blue in luster;
yellow, yellow-colored, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster.
They were red— red in color, red in appearance, and red in luster— and white— white in color, white in appearance, and white in luster.
And all those lotus ponds resounded with the cries of swans, cranes, ducks, curlews, and ruddy geese.
And all those parks were without "mine-ness" and without possession;
they were produced through the ripening of the prior karma of those very beings—

beings who, for a long time, had practiced the perfection of wisdom, who followed the wonderful guidance of the Buddhas with attentive hearing and reflection, and who for a long time had been resolved upon profound dharmas.
And there, noble son, in the center of that city of Gandhavatī was the house of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, one yojana in circumference,
variegated and beautiful with the seven precious gems,
and surrounded by seven walls and seven rows of palm trees.
And in that house were four gardens for the enjoyment, use, and pleasure of the household:
a garden named Nityapramudita (Ever-Joyful),
one named Aśoka (Sorrowless), one named Śokavigata (Free from Sorrow), and a garden named Puṣpacitra (Variegated with Flowers).
In each garden there were eight lotus ponds, namely: one named Bhadrā, one named Bhadrottamā,
and one named Nandā.
And one named Nandottamā, and one named Kṣamā,
and one named Kṣamottamā.
They are called "Fixed" and "Unwedded.
Indeed, of those lotus ponds, one side is made of gold, the second side is made of silver, the third side is made of beryl, and the fourth side is made of crystal.
The lower ground is made of karketana stone and is strewn with golden sand;
and in each lotus pond there are eight stairways, adorned with steps made of various and diverse kinds of jewels.
And within every opening between the steps of the staircases, a plantain tree made of Jāmbūnada gold had grown.
And all those lotus ponds had their waters covered with various blue, red, white, and yellow lotuses, and resounded with the cries of swans, cranes, ducks, curlews, and ruddy geese.
And all around those lotus ponds, various beautiful flowering trees had grown.
The flowers of those flowering trees, stirred by the wind, fall into the lotus ponds;
and in all those lotus ponds, the water possesses the fragrance of sandalwood, and is endowed with excellence of color, flavor, and touch.
And there, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, together with his retinue and sixty-eight thousand women, being fully provided with and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure,
played, enjoyed himself, and amused himself; and so too did the other beings who were residents of that city.

Both women and men— all of them constantly joyful— sport, enjoy themselves, and amuse one another in the gardens and by the lotus ponds, fully endowed and provided with the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Furthermore, that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, together with his retinue, sports, enjoys himself, and amuses himself for that length of time.
Then he taught the Perfection of Wisdom during the three times of the day.
Furthermore, those beings who were residents of that city of Gandhavatī also prepared a seat for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata at the center of the city crossroads—
a seat with legs made of gold, or silver, or beryl, or crystal.
Whether it be spread with woolen rugs, or spread with elephant-hide rugs, or provided with a canopy above;
Or there was a spread of Kāśika cloth as a canopy, half a krośa in height;

and above in the sky, they held a canopy of cloth variegated with pearls, well-arranged, joined, and fixed together, wondering, "What is this that stands here? because of its perfectly formed and wonderful ripening.
And on all sides, they scattered and strewed flowers of five colors over that area of earth.
And they perfumed that area of ground with various fragrant incenses,
out of their pure intention for the Dharma and their reverence for the Dharma of that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata;
there, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata sat and taught the Perfection of Wisdom.
In this manner, noble son, through reverence for the Dharma, by relying upon the teachings,
by having faith in what is worthy of faith, and by generating faith, those beings listen to the perfection of wisdom from the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.
There, many hundreds of living beings, many thousands of living beings, and many hundreds of thousands of living beings— both gods and humans— assembled and listened.
Then others among them some recited, some studied it aloud, and some wrote it down.
Some follow by means of wise attention;
all those beings are of a nature not to fall into the lower realms and are irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, noble son, go into the presence of that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.
Then you shall hear the *prajñāpāramitā*.
For he, son of good family, has been your virtuous friend for a long time, one who has shown it to you, encouraged you, inspired you, and gladdened you regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
By him also, son of good family, was the *prajñāpāramitā* sought in this very way in the past.
Just as you are now seeking it, go, noble son; by maintaining focused mental attention day and night, before long you shall hear the Perfection of Wisdom.
Then, having heard this, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita became satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and happiness.
It was just as if a man were pierced by a poisoned arrow and would give rise to no other thought than:
"When indeed shall I find a physician, a remover of arrows, who will extract this arrow from me?"
"Who will liberate me from this suffering?
In this very way, at that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita did not attend to any other phenomenon, but thought instead:
"When indeed shall I see that son of good family who will cause me to hear the Perfection of Wisdom?"
"Having heard my Dharma, they will abandon mental engagements based on apprehension."
Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, remaining on that very spot of earth, heard the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata as he was teaching the perfection of wisdom;
and while hearing it, he produced the perception of non-reliance toward all phenomena.
Many gateways to meditative concentration became manifest before him,
such as the concentration called "Contemplation of the Intrinsic Nature of All Phenomena" and the concentration called "Non-apprehension of the Intrinsic Nature of All Phenomena."

The samādhi called "the emergence of the knowledge of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena," the samādhi called "the non-differentiation of all phenomena," and the samādhi called "the vision of the immutability of all phenomena."

The concentration named "Illuminator of All Phenomena," the concentration named "Attained to the Darkness of All Phenomena," and the concentration named "Destroyer of Knowledge Regarding All Phenomena."
The concentration named "Shaking Off All Phenomena," the concentration named "Non-apprehension of All Phenomena," and the concentration named "Strewn with Flowers."
The samādhi called "the manifestation of the self-nature of all phenomena," the samādhi called "free from illusion," and the samādhi called "the manifestation of reflections in a mirror-disk."
The samādhi called "the production of the sounds of all sentient beings," the samādhi called "approached by dust," and the samādhi called "causing all sentient beings to rejoice."
The concentration called "following skill in the voices of all sentient beings," the concentration called "the production of various sounds, words,
and syllables," and the concentration called "unimpeded."
The concentration called non-activity by nature;
the concentration called attainment of unobstructed liberation;
the concentration called approached by kings.
The concentration named "the manifestation of the syllables of the etymological definition of names";
the concentration named "insight into all phenomena";
the concentration named "gone beyond the domain of all phenomena."
The concentration named "the unobstructed limit of all phenomena," the concentration named "resembling space," and the concentration named "like a diamond."
The concentration named King of Proximity,
the concentration named Peerless King,
and the concentration named Attainment of Victory.
The samādhi called the irreversible eye;
the samādhi called fixed in the realm of phenomena;
the samādhi called emerged from the realm of phenomena.
The concentration named Bestower of Consolation;
the concentration named Lion’s Roar.
The concentration named "Overpowering All Sentient Beings," the concentration named "Free from Dust," and the concentration named "Unafflicted."
The samādhi named Padmavyūha;
the samādhi named Kāṅkṣocchedana;
the samādhi named Sarvasārānugata.
The concentration named "Surpassing All Phenomena";
the concentration named "Attaining the Superknowledges, Powers, and Grounds of Self-confidence";
the concentration named "Piercing Through All Phenomena."
The samādhi called the Seal of the Non-existence of All Phenomena;
the samādhi called the Ocean of the Non-existence of All Phenomena;
the samādhi called the Vision of the Indistinguishability of All Phenomena.
The concentration named "Free from the Thicket of All Views," the concentration named "Attained to Darkness," and the concentration named "Departed from the Signs of All Phenomena."
The concentration named "Liberated from All Attachment," the concentration named "Departed from All Laziness," and the concentration named "Illuminator of the Profound Dharma."
The samādhi called Merukalpa; the samādhi called Asaṃhārya; the samādhi called Māramaṇḍalavidhvaṃsanakara.
The concentration named "unattached to the three worlds," the concentration named "issuance of rays," and the concentration named "vision of the Tathāgata."
There is a samādhi called "Beholding All Tathāgatas.

Abiding in these samādhis, he beheld in the worlds of the ten directions immeasurable and incalculable Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as they were proclaiming this very Perfection of Wisdom to the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas.
And those Tathāgatas gave their approval and prepared seats for him,
saying: "O son of good family, when we too were formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, we likewise sought the perfection of wisdom in this very way."
And while they were searching, these very same samādhis were attained by them, which you have now attained;
and having attained these samādhis, they became those who had reached the ultimate goal.
Established in the perfection of wisdom and in the irreversible qualities of a Buddha,

we, while observing the nature and intrinsic essence of these very samādhis, do not perceive any such phenomenon that either enters into or emerges from meditative absorption, nor any that would practice for the sake of awakening.
Or whoever might fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment— this, noble son, is the perfection of wisdom,
which is the absence of conceit regarding any dharma whatsoever.
By us, abiding in a state of non-conceptualization, this very golden color of the body has been attained,
as well as the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics.
And there is the radiance extending one fathom;
and the inconceivable, unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha and the insight of a Buddha,
as well as the unsurpassed meditative absorption of a Buddha.

And you have attained the perfection of the qualities of all the Buddha-dharmas, a perfection of qualities whose measure even the Tathāgatas themselves cannot grasp, nor can they demonstrate its limit—
how much less so the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas? Therefore, noble son, you should produce even greater reverence for these very dharmas, with a sense of purpose and a desire for them.

For a noble son who is earnest and zealous, O noble son, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is not difficult to attain. Furthermore, you must generate intense reverence toward spiritual friends and show them love.
And you should cultivate faith;
for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who are sustained by spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) very quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita said this to those Tathāgatas: "Who is our spiritual friend?
They said this to him: "Noble son, for a long time you have been ripened and sustained by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
He has been trained in the perfection of wisdom, in skillful means, and in the qualities of a Buddha.
O son of good family, he is your protector and your spiritual friend;
therefore, out of gratitude and a sense of indebtedness, you should honor him and remember what he has done for you.

If you, son of good family, were to serve the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata for one eon, or two eons, or three eons, or a hundred eons, or a thousand eons, or a hundred thousand eons, or even longer than that, carrying him on your head like a bundle of rags while providing him with every comfort for the sake of all sentient beings;

"O son of good family, even if you were to offer all the forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles that exist within the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system to that son of good family, you would still not have repaid his kindness."
For what reason?
It is because, noble son, through the power of that noble son, you have come to obtain such concentrations as these;
and through hearing the perfection of wisdom and skill in means, you have come to obtain the perfection of wisdom.
Then those Tathāgatas, having comforted the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, vanished.
That son of good family emerged from those meditative absorptions, and upon emerging, this thought occurred to him: "Where have those Tathāgatas gone?"
"Where are those Tathāgatas?
Not seeing those Tathāgatas, he fell into great longing and anxiety.

This thought occurred to him: "The noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata has attained the dhāraṇīs and possesses the five superknowledges; having performed services for previous Victors, he is my protector and my spiritual friend."
And for a long time he has acted for my benefit; what if I were now to approach and go up to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata and ask him this matter: "From where have those Tathāgatas come?"
Or where have those Tathāgatas gone?
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita conceived love, serene faith, esteem, and reverence for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata;
having established these, he reflected thus: "With what kind of honorific service indeed should I approach that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata?
For I am poor."
And I do not possess any such thing as clothing, or jewels, or gold, or gems, or pearls, or beryl,
or conch-shell, or stone, or coral, or silver, or flowers, or incense, or perfumes, or garlands, or ointments, or powders, or robes, or parasols, or banners, or bells, or flags.
With what might I honor and revere the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata?
It would not be fitting for me simply to approach the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata in this manner.
I am poor,
and neither joy nor gladness arises within me.

Then, indeed, as the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita proceeded with such qualities and reflections of reverence, he eventually reached a certain city. While he was in the midst of the marketplace there, this thought occurred to him: "What if I were to sell this body of mine and, with that price, perform an act of honor for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata?"

For a long night indeed, thousands of my own bodies have been broken, wasted away, ceased, and sold; again and again, throughout immeasurable saṃsāra, immeasurable sufferings of hell have been experienced by me for the sake of sensual desires, with sensual desires as their cause— but never for the sake of such teachings, nor for the sake of honoring such beings as these.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, having gone into the midst of the marketplace, caused his voice to be heard and uttered this cry: "Who needs a man?
Who needs a man?"
"Who wishes to buy a man? he asked.

Then, indeed, this thought occurred to Māra, the Evil One: "If this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, out of his love for the Dharma, sells himself and performs an act of honor for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata," (Vaidya 245)

He will inquire about the perfection of wisdom and skill in means: "How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, quickly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening? How will he then reach the state of one whose learning is like an ocean, and how will he become invincible to Māra or to the deities belonging to Māra’s host?"
He will attain the perfection of all qualities and will there act for the benefit of many sentient beings;
he will lead them beyond my domain, as well as others, after having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
"What if I were to create an obstacle for him? he thought.
Then indeed Māra, the Evil One, so bewildered those brahmins and householders that they did not hear the cry of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita: "Who needs a man?
Who needs a man?"
"Who wishes to buy a man? Then, when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita could not find a buyer for himself,
he went to a solitary place and wept.
He shed tears and spoke thus:
"Alas! What a misfortune for us that we do not even find a buyer for our own bodies—so that, by selling our bodies, we might honor the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata!"

Then, indeed, this thought occurred to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Suppose I were to test the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita— whether or not this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita has truly set out with a resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) regarding the relinquishment of his own body out of a desire for the Dharma."
Then Śakra, lord of the gods, having manifested himself in the guise of a young brahmin, approached the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita.
Having approached him, he said this to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita: "Noble son, why do you stand here with such a dejected mind, your heart full of longing, shedding tears?"
Sadāprarudita said to him: "Young man, I desire to sell myself, yet I do not find a buyer for this body.
Śakra, in the form of the young man, asked: "For what purpose, noble son, do you desire to sell yourself?"

Sadāprarudita said to him: "Young man, out of a desire for the Dharma, I wish to sell this body of mine to perform an offering to the Dharma, desiring to honor the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.
Yet, I do not find a buyer for this body."
Then this thought occurred to me: "Alas, how very little merit I possess, that I cannot even find a buyer for this body, by selling which I might make an offering to the Perfection of Wisdom!"
"I wish to honor the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.
Then the young brahmin said this to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita: "Indeed, noble son, I have no need for a man;
rather, my father must perform a sacrifice."
"In that regard, I have need of a man's heart, his blood, and his marrow.
Will you give these to me for a price?"

Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita: "I have gained a supreme gain; I know that my person has been perfected in the perfection of wisdom, in skillful means, and in the qualities of a Buddha, since I have found this young man as a buyer for my heart, blood, and marrow."
With a joyful mind, a wholesome mind, and an exultant mind, he said this to that young man: "I shall give you, young man, whatever it is that you require for the sake of your own body.
He said to him: "Noble son, what price shall I give you?
He said to him: "Young man, give me that which you have renounced."
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita took a sharp weapon and, having pierced his right arm, let the blood flow out.
Having pierced his right thigh and stripped it of its flesh, he approached the base of a wall to break the bone.
At that time, a certain daughter of a merchant was situated on the upper floor of a palace.
She saw the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita having pierced his arm and let the blood flow, having made his thigh fleshless, and approaching the base of a wall to break his bone.
This thought occurred to her: "Why indeed does this son of good family inflict such torture upon himself? What if I were to approach this son of good family and question him?"
Then the merchant’s daughter approached the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita.
Having approached him, she said this to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita: "Noble son, why indeed do you subject yourself to such a practice that takes away your own life?
And what will you do with this blood, and with these bones and marrow?"
Sadāprarudita said: "O girl, having sold this to this young brahmin, I shall worship the Perfection of Wisdom and honor the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata."

Then that merchant’s daughter said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita: "Noble son, what kind of class of qualities or distinction of qualities will arise for you from this, such that you desire to honor that noble son by selling your own heart, blood, bones, and marrow?
He said to that girl: "Girl, that noble son will teach us the perfection of wisdom and skill in means."
And therein we shall train;
training therein, we shall become a refuge for all sentient beings.
Having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, we shall obtain a body of golden color.

We shall obtain the thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty minor characteristics, the fathom-wide aura, the continuous rays of light, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity,
as well as the four grounds of self-confidence.
And we shall attain the four analytical knowledges,
the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha,
and the five superknowledges.
And inconceivable purity of ethical discipline, inconceivable purity of meditative concentration,
and inconceivable purity of wisdom.
We shall attain the ten powers of a Tathāgata;
we shall manifestly awaken to unsurpassed Buddha-knowledge;
and we shall obtain the unsurpassed jewel of the Dharma.
And by means of which we shall make a distribution among all sentient beings.
Then the merchant’s daughter said this to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita: "It is marvelous, noble son, how sublime and excellent these dharmas you have proclaimed!

Noble son, for the sake of even a single dharma of such a kind, one should be willing to sacrifice bodies as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges throughout kalpas; how much more so for the sake of many!"
In this way, these sublime and excellent dharmas have been proclaimed by you, such that they are pleasing to me as well and are acceptable to me.
Furthermore, O son of good family, whatever purpose you may have to accomplish—

I shall give you that very thing— be it gold, or jewels, or pearls, or silver, or lapis lazuli, or musāragalva, or red coral, or crystal, or flowers, or incense, or perfumes, or garlands, or ointments,
or powders, or garments, or parasols, or banners, or bells, or flags, or lamps.
Therefore, you shall pay honor to that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata; do not undergo such hardship for yourself alone. We too shall go along with you.
"Where the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata is,
we too shall plant roots of merit together with you, namely for the sake of attaining such dharmas as these."
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, having made his disguise as a young brahmin disappear, appeared before the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita in his own form and said this to him:
"Excellent, excellent, noble son! It is well that you possess such a firm commitment."
And it was by means of such a seeking of the Dharma that the former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones,
while formerly practicing the conduct of a Bodhisattva, inquired about the perfection of wisdom and skill in means, and thereby fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
And the jewel of the Dharma has been obtained;
therefore, noble son, I have no need for my heart,
nor for my blood.
"Not for the sake of the bones or the marrow; rather, I have come here specifically desiring to test you.
Choose a boon, noble son."
"What kind of boon shall I grant you?
He said to her, "O Śakra, give me the unsurpassed qualities of a Buddha. The Lord of Devas said, "In this matter, noble son, I have no jurisdiction."
"But as for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, they possess mastery in this domain.
Choose another boon," [Śakra] said.
Sadāprarudita replied, "O Lord of Gods, do not be concerned about this matter regarding the perfection of my own body."
O Lord of Devas, I myself shall perform an act of truth (satyādhiṣṭhāna) here;
by that truth, through which I have been prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment as irreversible by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones,
and who am known by them through my guileless resolute intention—
"O Lord of Gods, by this truth, by this word of truth, may this body of mine become as it was before.

Then, at that very instant, at that very moment, at that very second, through the power of the Buddhas and through the purity of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita’s intention, his body became established just as it had been before.
He was healthy and free from affliction.
Then indeed Śakra, the lord of the gods, and Māra the Evil One, being rendered speechless and unable to provide a further rejoinder to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, vanished right there.
Then that merchant’s daughter said this to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita: "Come, son of good family;
go to where our residence is."
"I will cause that wealth to be given to you from the presence of your parents, by means of which you shall worship that Perfection of Wisdom and honor that noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata."
That is to say, out of a desire for the Dharma.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, together with that merchant’s daughter, went toward her own home;
having arrived, he stood at the gateway.
Then that merchant’s daughter, having entered her own residence, said this to her mother and father:
"Mother, Father, give me gold, bullion, jewels, gems, garments, flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, and flags;
and provide various kinds of divine musical instruments."
"Let me also go together with these five hundred maidens who were given to you by you as my attendants;
I too shall go along with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita to the presence of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata for the sake of honoring him,
and he will teach the Dharma to us."
"By means of that, we shall attain the qualities of a Buddha.
Then, the mother and father of that girl said this to her: "But who, girl, is this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Sadāprarudita, and where does he currently reside?"
The girl said: "This son of good family is standing right here at the threshold of our house.

And this son of good family has set out with a resolute intention to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—that is to say, desiring to liberate immeasurable sentient beings from the sufferings of saṃsāra."
Desiring to honor the Perfection of Wisdom by selling himself out of a longing for all dharmas,
and desiring to pay homage to the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.
And he could not find anyone to purchase that body.
Not finding anyone, he remained there distressed, dejected, brooding, with a sorrowful mind, shedding tears.

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, having manifested in the form of a young brahmin, said to him: "Noble son, why do you remain here distressed, dejected, brooding, with a sorrowful mind, shedding tears?"
He said to him, "I desire to sell myself,
yet I cannot find a buyer. Śakra, in the form of a young brahmin, said to him, "For what purpose, noble son, do you desire to sell yourself?"
Sadāprarudita said: "I shall worship the Perfection of Wisdom and I shall honor the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, namely out of a desire for the Dharma;
for the qualities of a Buddha are dependent upon that."
Śakra, in the form of a young brahmin, said to him: "I have no need for you, noble son.
However, my father is about to perform a sacrifice, and for that he requires the heart, blood, bones, and marrow of a man."
Then this son of good family, with an undaunted mind, said, "I shall give.

Taking a sharp weapon, he pierced his own arm and let the blood flow; he then stripped the flesh from his thigh and approached the base of a wall to break the bone. Standing to one side, he thought, "Having broken the bone, I shall give the marrow."
And from atop the palace roof, I saw this son of good family with blood flowing from his body.
This thought occurred to me: "Why indeed does this man inflict such treatment upon himself?
Having approached him, I said to him: "For what purpose, son of good family, have you thus disfigured your own body, causing blood to flow from yourself?"
Then he said this to me: "O girl, I shall give the blood, heart, bone, and marrow of this young brahmin.
For what reason?
Because I possess no other wealth whatsoever."
"I am poor," he said.
To him I spoke thus: "What, then, will you do with that wealth?
He replied to me: "I shall worship the Perfection of Wisdom."
"And I shall honor that noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, namely out of a desire for the Dharma.
Then I said to him, "Noble son, what kind of category of qualities or what specific excellence of qualities will you gain from that?
Thereupon, he described and revealed to me the inconceivable qualities of the Buddhas.
"I shall obtain from him such immeasurable Buddha-qualities as these. Upon hearing of those inconceivable qualities of a Buddha, a greater joy and rapture arose within me.
And this thought occurred to me: "How marvelous! This son of good family is a performer of exceedingly difficult deeds and is so intensely devoted to the Dharma."
This son of good family, who is able to endure such a source of pain for his own body, truly renounces himself out of a desire for the Dharma. Why, then, should we not honor the Dharma?
"In such circumstances as these, one should not make a vow, thinking, 'We possess abundant and extensive wealth.
Therefore, I said this to that son of good family: 'Do not, O son of good family, inflict such a deed upon yourself that would take your life!'"
"I shall cause you to be given a vast amount of wealth for whatever purpose you have.
With that, you shall honor and revere that noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.
I too shall go together with you to where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata is."
"I too shall perform worship for that son of good family;
we too shall accomplish such dharmas as these—namely, the unsurpassed Buddha-dharmas which have been proclaimed by you.
Therefore, mother and father, grant me your permission."
"And grant me a very great mass of wealth,
so that I may go together with this very son of good family and honor the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata."

Then, indeed, her parents said this to that girl: "It is wonderful how you describe the state of this son of good family as so difficult to perform; those qualities of yours are entirely inconceivable, distinguished above all the world, and bringers of happiness to all sentient beings."
"O girl, since this son of good family is thus striving for such a difficult task on their behalf, we two grant you our permission;
make room for us as well."
Therefore, let us two also go together with you to see, pay homage to, attend upon, and honor that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.
Then, indeed, that merchant’s daughter, having learned that her mother and father were setting out for the sake of honoring and revering the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata,
said this to them: "Mother, Father, do exactly as you say."
"I shall not create any obstacle for anyone's side of wholesome virtue.
Having said this, the merchant’s daughter set out to honor and pay respect to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.
Then that merchant’s daughter had five hundred chariots adorned,
and she also had those five hundred maidens adorned.

Having adorned them, she took flowers of various colors and kinds, as well as garments of various hues, and flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, and flags.

Having taken various jewels and diverse flowers made of various jewels, and having taken abundant solid food, soft food, and delicacies, he mounted a single chariot together with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, along with those five hundred chariots occupied by the five hundred maidens.
Surrounded and escorted by a great retinue, with her parents at their head, she set out toward the eastern direction.

As the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita proceeded by stages, he saw from afar that city of Gandhavatī— wondrous and beautiful to behold, composed of the seven precious gems, and encircled by walls made of the seven precious gems.
It was surrounded by seven archways, seven moats, and seven rows of palm trees; it was twelve yojanas in width and twelve yojanas in length— prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food,
and teeming with many people and inhabitants— and it was pierced through by five hundred market-streets that were as beautiful to behold as variegated paintings.
It was well-paved with level surfaces where people, draft animals, and vehicles could pass without jolting,

and at the center of the city crossroads, he saw the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata seated upon the Dharma-throne, surrounded and honored by an assembly of many hundreds, many thousands, and many hundreds of thousands, as he taught the Dharma.
From the very moment he saw him, he attained such happiness as that of a monk who has entered the first dhyāna with one-pointed attention.
Having seen him, this thought occurred to him: "It would not be fitting for me to approach the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata while still mounted on my chariot."
"What if I were to descend from the chariot?
He then descended from the chariot,
and those five hundred maidens, together with the merchant's daughter, also descended from their chariots.

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, surrounded and escorted by five hundred maidens headed by the merchant’s daughter, approached the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata with an immeasurable array of offerings.

Furthermore, at that time, for the sake of the perfection of wisdom, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata had a gabled pavilion constructed made of the seven precious gems, adorned with red sandalwood and draped with nets of pearls;
in the four corners of the gabled pavilion, precious jewels were placed.
There were those which performed the function of lamps,
and four incense burners made of precious materials were suspended in the four directions.
There, pure black aloe-wood was being burned as incense for the purpose of making offerings to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
In the center of that gabled hall, a couch made of the seven precious gems had been prepared,
and a casket made of four kinds of jewels was fashioned.
Therein, the Perfection of Wisdom was deposited, written upon golden plates with melted lapis lazuli;
and that gabled hall was adorned with various multicolored silk banners hanging down.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, together with the five hundred maidens headed by the merchant’s daughter, beheld that gabled pavilion adorned with an immeasurable array of offerings;
and there he saw many thousands of deities.

He heard Śakra, the lord of the gods, scattering, showering, and strewing that peaked pavilion with divine māndārava flowers, divine sandalwood powder, divine gold dust, and divine silver dust, while divine musical instruments were being played. Having seen and heard this, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods:

"For what purpose, O Lord of Devas, do you, together with many thousands of deities, scatter, strew, and shower this jewel-encrusted gabled chamber with divine māndārava flowers, divine sandalwood powders, divine gold powders, and divine silver powders?"
"And why are these divine musical instruments being played by the gods in the sky above?
When this was said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita: "Do you not know, noble son?
For this is that Perfection of Wisdom, the mother and guide of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas."
"Wherein training, the bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, swiftly attain all the qualities of a Buddha that follow upon the perfections, as well as the knowledge of all aspects.

When this had been said, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Sadāprarudita said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Kauśika, where is that perfection of wisdom which is the mother and the guide of the bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas?"

Śakra said: "Noble son, this [teaching] has been written upon golden plates with melted lapis lazuli by the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata inside this peaked pavilion; having sealed it with seven seals, it has been placed there.
It is not easy for us to show it to you."

Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, together with the five hundred maidens headed by the merchant’s daughter— all gathered as one company— took those flowers he had obtained, as well as the flower-garlands, robes, jewels, incense, perfumes, wreaths, ointments, powders, monastic garments, parasols, banners, bells, and flags, and the flowers made of gold and silver.
They made offerings to the Perfection of Wisdom and set aside various portions from it, namely for the sake of honoring the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.

Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, together with those five hundred maidens headed by the merchant’s daughter, first honored the Perfection of Wisdom with flowers, incense, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, and flags, as well as with flowers made of gold and silver and with divine musical instruments; and then [he approached] where the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata was.

The Mahāsattva approached the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata and scattered, showered, and strewed him with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, and flags, as well as sandalwood powder and flowers made of gold and silver; he also played divine musical instruments, doing so solely for the sake of honoring the Dharma.
Then, indeed, those flowers settled above the head of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Dharmodgata as a pavilion of flowers.
And those flowers of various colors, including flowers made of gold and silver, remained suspended in the air like a canopy.
Those robes and garments of fine cloth also came to rest in the air like a pavilion made of various jewels.

When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita and those five hundred maidens, headed by the merchant’s daughter, saw this miraculous display of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*) of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, they thought to themselves: "How wonderful! This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata possesses such great supernatural power, such great majesty, and such great splendor!"
If such a display of supernatural power and transformation belongs even to this son of good family while he is merely practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva,
what need is there to mention when he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?

Then indeed, those five hundred maidens, led by the merchant’s daughter, having conceived a longing for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, all together with one accord and through their resolute intention (adhyāśaya), generated the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
And they spoke thus: "By this root of merit, may we become Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in a future time.
And while practicing the conduct of a Bodhisattva, may we become recipients of those very same dharmas that this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata has obtained."
In this very way, we shall honor and revere the Perfection of Wisdom, just as this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata honors and reveres it;
and we shall proclaim it to many people, just as this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata proclaims it.
And in this very way, may we be endowed with the perfection of wisdom and skill in means,
and may we be fully perfected, just as this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata is endowed with the perfection of wisdom and skill in means and is fully perfected.

Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, together with those five hundred maidens headed by the merchant’s daughter, having worshipped the Perfection of Wisdom and having honored the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata,
bowed their heads at the feet of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata and stood to one side with reverence.
Waiting expectantly, they stood with their palms joined in reverence.

Standing to one side, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata: "O son of good family, while I was searching for the perfection of wisdom here in the wilderness, I heard a voice."
"Go, son of good family, to the eastern direction; there you will hear the Perfection of Wisdom.
Having heard that voice correctly, I set out toward the eastern direction.
Then this thought occurred to me: "I have indeed heard that voice correctly,
yet I did not question that voice as to how far I must go, or from whom I shall hear or obtain the Perfection of Wisdom."
Great dejection came over me;
because of that dejection, I fell into a state of intense longing and burning anguish.
Right there on that spot of earth, I spent seven days and nights in a state of longing.

I do not give rise to the thought of seeking food; rather, I direct my mind solely toward the perfection of wisdom, wondering: "How much further must I go, and from where shall I obtain the perfection of wisdom for the sake of hearing it?"
"And I did not question that voice.
Thereupon, an image of the Tathāgata appeared before me and said to me: "Go, noble son; five hundred yojanas from here, you will reach a city named Gandhavatī by following the path in due order."
"There you will see the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata teaching and elucidating the Perfection of Wisdom.
Then, I was filled with a great and sublime joy and gladness. Pervaded by that very same great and sublime joy and gladness, I did not move from that spot on the earth.
And as you were teaching the Prajñāpāramitā, I heard it;
while I was listening, many gateways to meditative concentration appeared to me.
