Abiding therein, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, dwelling in the world-systems of the ten directions, comforted me.
And they give their approval, saying: "Excellent, excellent, noble son!
These samādhis are born from the perfection of wisdom;
abiding in them, we have brought all the qualities of a Buddha to full completion."
Those Tathāgatas, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened me thoroughly and well, vanished.
I then arose from that samādhi, and this thought occurred to me: "From where indeed have those Tathāgatas come?"
"Or where have those Tathāgatas gone?

Then this thought occurred to me: "The noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata has attained the dhāraṇīs, possesses the five superknowledges, has performed his duties under previous Victors, has planted roots of merit, and is well-trained in the perfection of wisdom and in skillful means."
"He will investigate this matter for me exactly as it is—
where those Tathāgatas came from and where those Tathāgatas went.
Having heard the voice of that manifestation of the Tathāgata, I set out toward the eastern direction just as I had been instructed.
As I was approaching from afar, I saw the Noble One teaching the Dharma.
Upon seeing him, such bliss arose within me as that which arises for a monk who has attained the first dhyāna and possesses one-pointed attention.
Therefore, son of good family, I ask you: from where have those Tathāgatas come, and where have those Tathāgatas gone?
Son of good family, explain to me the coming and going of those Tathāgatas.
May we know the coming and going of those Tathāgatas,
and may we never be separated from the vision of the Tathāgatas.
The thirtieth chapter, titled "Sadāprarudita," in the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom.
(Vaidya 253) Chapter Thirty-one: Dharmodgata.
When this had been said, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita: "Indeed, noble son, Tathāgatas do not come from anywhere."
or go;
for suchness is indeed unshakable,
and that which is suchness—
He is the Tathāgata.
For, noble son, non-arising neither comes nor goes;
and that which is non-arising—
He is the Tathāgata.
For, noble son, neither coming nor going is perceived in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). And that which is the limit of reality—
That is the Tathāgata.
For, noble son, neither the coming nor the going of emptiness is perceived;
and that which is emptiness—
He is the Tathāgata.
For, noble son, neither coming nor going is perceived in suchness;
and that which is suchness—
That is the Tathāgata.
For, noble son, neither the coming nor the going of dispassion is perceived;
and that which is dispassion—
That is the Tathāgata.
For, noble son, neither the coming nor the going of cessation is perceived;
and that which is cessation—
That is the Tathāgata.
For, noble son, neither coming nor going is perceived in the realm of space;
and that which is the realm of space—
He is the Tathāgata. For, noble son, the Tathāgata does not exist apart from these dharmas. And that which is the suchness (tathatā) of these very dharmas, noble son, [is the Tathāgata].
That which is the suchness of all phenomena and that which is the suchness of the Tathāgata— this suchness is one and the same.
Noble son, there is no duality in suchness;
this suchness, noble son, is one alone.
Suchness is neither two nor three.
Noble son, suchness transcends all calculation because it is non-existent.
Noble son, it is just as if a man, scorched by the summer heat in the last month of summer, were to see a shimmering mirage at the time of midday and run toward it,
thinking, "I shall drink water here."
"I shall drink water that is not there.
What do you think, noble son, from where does this water come, or where does that water go—
does it go to the eastern great ocean, or the southern, the western, or the northern?"
Sadāprarudita said: "No, noble son, water does not exist in a mirage.
How, then, could its coming or going be perceived?
Furthermore, noble son, that man, scorched by the summer heat, being of a foolish and unwise nature, perceives water where there is no water upon seeing a mirage."
Furthermore, water does not exist there by way of its own intrinsic nature.
Dharmodgata said: "It is so, noble son; it is just so.
In the same way, noble son, those who are attached to the Tathāgata either by means of his form or by means of his voice,"
They conceptualize the coming and going of the Tathāgata;
and those who conceptualize the coming and going of the Tathāgata should all be called people of a foolish nature and people of poor wisdom.
It is just as if that very person were to produce the perception of water where there is no water.
Why is that? Because a Tathāgata is not to be seen by means of the form-body (rūpakāya).
The Tathāgatas are the Dharma-body.
Furthermore, noble son, the nature of phenomena neither comes nor goes.
In the very same way, noble son, there is no coming or going of the Tathāgatas.
Noble son, it is just as, for example, there is no coming or going of an elephant corps, a cavalry corps, a chariot corps, or an infantry corps created by a magician;
in the very same way, noble son, there is no coming or going of the Tathāgatas.
Noble son, it is just as, for example, a man who has fallen asleep might see a single Tathāgata within his dream.
Whether two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, or even more than that, upon waking, he would not see even a single Tathāgata.
"What do you think, noble son, from where have those Tathāgatas come, or where have those Tathāgatas gone?
Sadāprarudita replied, "Furthermore, noble son, in a dream, the perfection of any dharma whatsoever is not perceived."
"For false speech was indeed like a dream.
Dharmodgata said, "In just this way, noble son, all phenomena have been declared by the Blessed One to be like dreams.
Noble son, those who do not understand, as they truly are, all phenomena taught by the Tathāgata to be like dreams—"
Having become attached to those Tathāgatas either by way of their name-body or their form-body, they conceptualize the coming or going of the Tathāgatas.
Indeed, those who do not understand the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and who conceptualize the coming or going of the Tathāgatas are all of a foolish nature— mere worldlings (pṛthagjana).
All of them have gone, are going, and will go into the saṃsāra of the six realms;
all of them are far from the perfection of wisdom.
All those are far from the qualities of a Buddha.

However, noble son, those who understand, as they truly are, all phenomena as being like a dream— just as the Tathāgata has taught that "all phenomena are like a dream"— do not conceptualize the coming or going of any phenomenon whatsoever.
Whether it be arising or cessation;
and those who do not conceptualize the coming or going of any dharma,
nor its arising or cessation.
They understand the Tathāgata through the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
And those who understand the Tathāgata through the nature of phenomena do not conceptualize the coming or going of the Tathāgatas.
And those who understand such a nature of phenomena (dharmatā) of the Tathāgata,
they move close to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
and they move within the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
And those disciples of the Blessed One consume the alms of the nation not in vain;
they are worthy of offerings from the world.
It is just as if, noble son, the jewels in the great ocean do not come from the eastern direction.
Not from the south, not from the west, nor from the north.
They do not come from the intermediate directions, nor from below, nor from above, nor from any place or direction whatsoever;
rather, it is by depending upon the roots of virtue of sentient beings that jewels arise in the great ocean.
Yet, they do not arise without a cause.
They are dependent upon causes, conditions, and reasons, being dependently originated;
and as they cease, those jewels do not migrate anywhere in the world of the ten directions.
Nevertheless, it is when certain conditions exist that those jewels are manifested.
Just as those jewels do not manifest when their conditions are absent,
even so, noble son, the perfection of the bodies of those Tathāgatas has not come from anywhere in the worlds of the ten directions,
nor does it go anywhere in the worlds of the ten directions.
Furthermore, the body of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is not without cause;
it is perfected through former conduct, dependent upon causes and conditions, arisen from causal factors, and produced from the ripening of prior karma.
It does not exist anywhere in the world of the ten directions.
Moreover, noble son, when those conditions exist, the manifestation of the body occurs;
when those conditions do not exist, the manifestation of the body is not perceived.
It is just as, for example, noble son, when the sound of a lute arises, it does not come from anywhere.
Even when ceasing, it does not go anywhere,
nor does it transmigrate anywhere; rather,
depending upon the totality of causes and conditions, it arises, being dependent on causes and dependent on conditions.

It is just as, for example, depending on a hollow body, depending on a hide, depending on strings, depending on a neck-staff, depending on bridges, depending on a plectrum, and depending on the exertion of a person skilled therein, this sound of a lute emerges— dependent upon causes and dependent upon conditions.
And that sound does not issue from the hollow body,

nor from the hide, nor from the strings, nor from the neck-staff, nor from the bridges, nor from the plectrum, nor from the effort of the person playing it; rather, indeed, the sound is designated through the conjunction of all these factors.
Even as it ceases, sound does not go anywhere.

In the same way, noble son, the manifestation of the body of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is dependent on causes, dependent on conditions, and perfected through the application of manifold roots of merit.
Yet, the manifestation of the Buddha-body does not arise from a single cause, nor from a single condition, nor from a single root of merit.
Nor is it causeless;
having arisen from the assembly of many causes and conditions, it does not come from anywhere.
When the assembly of causes and conditions is absent, it does not go anywhere.
In this way, son of good family, you should perceive the coming and going of those Tathāgatas; furthermore,
son of good family, you should understand that this very same nature of phenomena (dharmatā) applies to all phenomena as well.
Since, noble son, you will thus clearly understand that both the Tathāgatas and all phenomena are unarisen and unceasing, you will become fixed in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
you will practice with certainty in the perfection of wisdom and in skillful means.
Furthermore, while this teaching on the non-coming and non-going of the Tathāgatas was being spoken, a great earthquake occurred;
and the entire trichiliocosm shook, trembled, and quaked in six ways with twelve great omens;
it moved, vibrated, and surged.
It quivers, it quivers intensely, it quivers all over; it resounds, it resounds intensely, it resounds all over;
it trembles, it trembles intensely, it trembles all over.
He roared, roared aloud, and roared intensely;
all the abodes of Māra were shaken and rendered dimmed.
Whatever grasses, shrubs, medicinal herbs, and forest trees there were in the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, they too were stirred.
They all bowed down toward where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata was;
they scattered out-of-season flowers,
and from above, from the sky, a great rain of flowers fell.

Śakra, the lord of the gods, and the four great kings scattered and showered divine sandalwood powder and divine flowers over the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata; and they spoke these words: "Excellent, excellent, noble son!"

"By your power, noble son, we have today heard this discourse being taught, which has arisen from the ultimate truth and is contrary to the entire world; it is a groundless terrain for all beings who are established in the view of a self-identity and who are deeply attached to all false views."

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita said this to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata: "What, noble son, is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of this great earthquake in the world?
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata replied: "Noble son, it is because of this teaching on the non-coming and non-going of the Tathāgatas."
As you were questioning and I was explaining, eight thousand living beings attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
eighty million living beings conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
and sixty-four thousand living beings attained the pure, stainless, and dustless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.

Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita was endowed with a most sublime joy and gladness, thinking: "It is a supreme gain for me, a most fortunate attainment, that while I am inquiring about this Perfection of Wisdom and this teaching on the non-coming and non-going of the Tathāgatas, the welfare of so many beings has been accomplished.
May this very merit be sufficient for us toward the full realization of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
Furthermore, no further doubt arises in me regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
without a shadow of a doubt, I shall become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Endowed with that very joy and rapture, he rose into the air to the height of seven palm trees, and at the height of seven palm trees—
Remaining there, he thought to himself: "By what means may I now, while standing in the air, pay honor to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata?
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, seeing the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita standing there and knowing his thought with his own mind, [offered] to him divine *māndārava* flowers.
He offered flowers and spoke thus: "O son of good family, with these divine flowers, pay honor to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata."
"Indeed, noble son, we must honor your benefactor.
For by your power, noble son, the welfare of many thousands of living beings has been accomplished today.
Noble son, such beings as these are difficult to find."
Those who, for the sake of all sentient beings, are able to bear the great burden for immeasurable and incalculable eons, just as you have borne it.

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, having taken Māndārava flowers from Śakra, the lord of the gods, scattered them, showered them, and strewed them over the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.
And he covered the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata with his own body, and spoke these words: "Noble son, from this day forward, I offer myself to you for the sake of service and attendance.
Having thus offered himself, he stood before the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata with his palms joined in reverence.
Then that merchant’s daughter and those five hundred maidens said this to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita: "O son of good family, we too give ourselves to you;
by this root of merit, may we also become attainers of these very same dharmas, and together with you, may we repeatedly honor and revere the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the Bodhisattvas."
"And may we become close to you indeed.

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita said this to the merchant’s daughter and those five hundred maidens: "If you, maidens, will follow my resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) and surrender yourselves to me with that same resolute intention, [I shall take you as my attendants]."
"In this way, I shall accept you.
The maidens said, "We shall comply with your intention and your resolute purpose;
we offer ourselves to you to be used according to your will."

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, having adorned those five hundred maidens headed by the merchant’s daughter with all kinds of ornaments, and having likewise decorated those five hundred chariots, offered them all to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata for the purpose of attending upon and serving him.
"Noble son, I give these attendants of mine to you, and I also give these five hundred chariots for your use."
Then Śakra, lord of the gods, gave his approval to that son of good family, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
Bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, must be those who renounce all their possessions.
And by means of such a mind of renunciation, a bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
And by thus making offerings to the Dharma-preachers, it is possible to hear the perfection of wisdom and skill in means.

Furthermore, O son of good family, those former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, while formerly practicing the conduct of a Bodhisattva, likewise established themselves in such renunciation and thereby fully realized unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, [having relied upon] the perfection of wisdom and skill in means.
And by those who are making inquiries.

Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, for the sake of fulfilling the roots of virtue of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, accepted those five hundred maidens headed by the merchant’s daughter and the five hundred chariots;
having accepted them, he gave them back to that very son of good family, Sadāprarudita.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata rose from his seat and entered his own home, and it was the time for the sun to set.

Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita: "It would not be proper or fitting for me, having come here out of love for the Dharma, to sit down or to prepare a bed."
"What if I were to pass the time by remaining in only two postures— standing and walking—
until the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata emerges from his own house for the purpose of proclaiming the Dharma?"
Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata remained for seven years entirely absorbed in a single samādhi;
he dwelt through immeasurable and incalculable thousands of bodhisattva-samādhis born from the perfection of wisdom and skill in means.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita also, for seven years, passed the time in only two modes of conduct and did not allow sloth or torpor to overcome him.
For seven years, he gave rise to thoughts of desire,
yet he did not give rise to thoughts of ill will or thoughts of cruelty;
he did not give rise to craving for flavors nor to mental agitation.
"But when indeed will the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata arise from this samādhi,
so that we may prepare a Dharma-seat for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, upon which this son of good family might sit and teach the Dharma?"

And he thought: "We shall thoroughly sprinkle and sweep that spot of earth and scatter it with various flowers, at that place on the earth where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata will fully proclaim the Perfection of Wisdom and skill in means.
Those five hundred maidens, headed by the merchant’s daughter, [also followed] the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita.
Training themselves after the Mahāsattva, they passed their time by means of only two modes of conduct, all their activities following his example.

Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita heard a divine voice saying: "On the seventh day from now, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata will emerge from this samādhi; having emerged, he will sit in the middle of the city and teach the Dharma.
Then, having heard that divine voice, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita was filled with joy.
Exultant, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and cheerfulness, he cleansed that spot of earth together with five hundred maidens headed by the merchant’s daughter,
and he prepared a Dharma throne made of the seven precious gems.
He removed his own upper robe from his body and spread it over that seat.

Then those maidens each removed their own upper robes from their bodies and spread five hundred upper robes upon that seat, thinking, "The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata will sit upon this seat and teach the Dharma."

Thus, having spread the Dharma-throne for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, all those maidens became satisfied, elated, joyful, and delighted, and a sense of gladness and happiness arose within them.

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, desiring to sprinkle that area of ground, could not find any water anywhere with which he might sprinkle that area of ground, even though he searched all around.
Just as if the Evil Māra had caused all that water to vanish, thinking:
"Perhaps the mind of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, not obtaining water, might become weary,
and experience pain and dejection."
Or else there might be a transformation of the mind by which this root of merit would disappear, or the offerings would not shine forth.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita: "What if I were to pierce my own body and sprinkle this region of earth with my blood?
For what reason?
Because this region of earth is full of rising dust."

"Let not the cloud of dust fall from this spot of earth upon the body of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata. What indeed could I do with this physical form, which is necessarily subject to disintegration? It would be better for me that this body [should perish]."
May it perish through such an action,
but not by an action that is devoid of efficacy.
Furthermore, for the sake of sensual desire and with sensual desire as its cause, thousands of my own bodies have been repeatedly shattered as I wandered again and again through saṃsāra.
But not for the sake of upholding the true Dharma in such circumstances;
rather, if they should split,
let them split in such circumstances as these.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, having reflected thus, took a sharp weapon and pierced his own body all over, drenching that entire area of ground with his own blood.
Those five hundred maidens, headed by the merchant’s daughter, [also followed] the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita...
Following the example of the Mahāsattva, they all took up sharp weapons, pierced their own bodies,
and drenched that entire area of ground with their respective blood;
yet there was no change of heart in the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, nor in any of those maidens.
Where that Māra, the Evil One, might find an opportunity to create an obstacle to their roots of merit.

Then, indeed, this thought occurred to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "How wonderful it is that this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita is so devoted to the Dharma, so firm in his undertaking, and so armored with the great armor; he is indifferent toward his body, his life, and his possessions, having set out with a resolute intention for the attainment of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
Namely: "Having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, I shall liberate all sentient beings, immeasurable in number, from the sufferings of saṃsāra.
Then Śakra, lord of the gods, transformed all that blood-water into divine sandalwood water;
and from all sides around that region of earth there arose an inconceivable and most sublime fragrance, which was the full essence of that divine sandalwood water.
Its fragrance wafts for a hundred yojanas.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
Excellent is your inconceivable vigor, son of good family; excellent is your unsurpassed love for the Dharma and your quest for the Dharma."
Noble son, it was by means of such a resolute intention, such vigor, and such a longing for the Dharma that those former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones fully realized unexcelled,
perfect enlightenment.

Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita: "I have prepared the Dharma-seat for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, and this spot of earth has been well-sprinkled and well-swept;
but from where indeed shall I obtain flowers?"
"By means of which I might strew this region of the earth with flowers, and scatter them over the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata as he sits upon the Dharma-throne teaching the Dharma?
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita: "O son of good family, accept these divine Māndārava flowers."
"With these, scatter flowers over this region of the earth,
and shower them upon the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata as he sits upon the Dharma-throne teaching the Dharma.
He then presented to him a thousand celestial *khārīs* of divine *māndārava* flowers.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, having taken those flowers, scattered some of them over that spot of ground so that it was strewn with flowers,
and with other flowers he showered the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata.
Then, at the end of seven years, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata arose from that samādhi, approached the Dharma-throne,
and sat down upon the seat that had been prepared;
surrounded and honored by an assembly of many hundreds of thousands, he taught the Perfection of Wisdom.

Then, at the very moment he saw the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita attained such bliss as that experienced by a monk who has entered the first dhyāna with one-pointed attention.

In this regard, this is the teaching on the perfection of wisdom of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata: namely, that through the equality of all phenomena, there is the equality of the perfection of wisdom.
Through the solitude of all phenomena, there is the solitude of the perfection of wisdom;
through the immovability of all phenomena, there is the immovability of the perfection of wisdom;
through the non-conceit of all phenomena, there is the non-conceit of the perfection of wisdom.
Because all phenomena are unimpeded, the perfection of wisdom is unimpeded;
because all phenomena have a single flavor, the perfection of wisdom has a single flavor;
because all phenomena are limitless, the perfection of wisdom is limitless.
Through the non-arising of all phenomena, there is the non-arising of the perfection of wisdom; through the non-ceasing of all phenomena, there is the non-ceasing of the perfection of wisdom;
through the boundlessness of space, there is the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom.
Because the ocean is boundless, the perfection of wisdom is boundless; because Mount Meru is variegated, the perfection of wisdom is variegated;
because space is non-conceptual, the perfection of wisdom is non-conceptual.
Due to the boundlessness of form, there is the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom;
likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Due to the boundlessness of consciousness, there is the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom.
The boundlessness of the earth element is the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom.
Likewise, through the boundlessness of the water element, the fire element, the wind element, and the space element, there is the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom.
Through the boundlessness of the consciousness element, there is the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom.
Through the equality of phenomena that are like a diamond, there is the equality of the perfection of wisdom;
through the non-differentiation of all phenomena, there is the non-differentiation of the perfection of wisdom;
through the non-apprehension of all phenomena, there is the non-apprehension of the perfection of wisdom.
Through the sameness of the non-manifestation of all dharmas, there is the sameness of the non-manifestation of the perfection of wisdom;
through the immobility of all dharmas, there is the immobility of the perfection of wisdom;
through the inconceivability of all dharmas, the inconceivability of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood.
Then, while the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita remained seated in that very manner, at that moment there arose for him the king of samādhis called "The Equality of All Dharmas.
From that [arose] the samādhi called "Seclusion from All Dharmas" and the samādhi called "Immovability of All Dharmas."

And there is the concentration called "non-conceptualization of all phenomena," the concentration called "unfaltering regarding all phenomena," and the concentration called "the single flavor of all phenomena."
The concentration named "the boundlessness of all phenomena," the concentration named "the non-arising of all phenomena," and the concentration named "the non-ceasing of all phenomena."
And there is the samādhi called "Boundless as Space," the samādhi called "Boundless as the Ocean," and the samādhi called "Variegated as Mount Meru."
And there is the samādhi called "Incomparable as the Sky," and the samādhi called "Limitless Form.
Likewise for feeling, perception, and mental formations.

There is a samādhi called "Infinite Consciousness," a samādhi called "Infinite Earth Element," and likewise samādhis called "Infinite Water Element," "Infinite Fire Element," "Infinite Wind Element," and "Infinite Space Element."

There is the concentration called "the boundlessness of the element of consciousness," the concentration called "diamond-like," and the concentration called "the non-differentiation of all phenomena."

And there is the samādhi called "non-apprehension of all phenomena," the samādhi called "the equality of the non-conceptualization of all phenomena," and the samādhi called "the motionlessness of all phenomena."
And there is the samādhi called "The Inconceivability of All Dharmas.
With this as the foremost, six million samādhi-gates were attained by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita.
The thirty-first chapter, titled "Dharmodgata," in the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom.

(Vaidya 260) Chapter Thirty-Two: The Entrustment. Subhūti, as soon as the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita had attained those six million gateways to samādhi, [he beheld] in the eastern direction...
In the southern, western, and northern directions,

in the intermediate directions, below, and above— in all ten directions, throughout world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, each being a great trichiliocosm— he beheld Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, surrounded by assemblies of monks.
They were preceded by the qualities of bodhisattvas, speaking this very perfection of wisdom through these same methods, these same names, and these same syllables—
just as I, at present, in this very triple-thousand great-thousand world-system, teach the Dharma surrounded by a community of monks and preceded by a host of bodhisattvas.
By these very methods, by these very names, and by these very syllables, I speak this very Perfection of Wisdom.
He became endowed with inconceivable erudition and the state of being an ocean of learning;
and in all his births, he was never separated from the Buddhas.
Wherever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, were present in person, there he was reborn;
and he was never separated from the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
Even when he has entered into a dream,
all unfortunate states are avoided by him,
and the perfection of the opportune moment is attained.

Then, indeed, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Therefore, Ānanda, by this method as well, it should be understood thus: 'This perfection of wisdom is the bringer of the knowledge of omniscience for the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas.'"
Therefore, Ānanda, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who desire to attain the knowledge of omniscience should practice this perfection of wisdom;
they should hear, take up, bear in mind, recite, master, propagate, teach, explain, instruct, study, and write down this perfection of wisdom.
Having had it well-written in a great volume with very clear letters through the empowerment of the Tathāgata,

one should honor it, revere it, respect it, worship it, adore it, and venerate it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, musical instruments, garments, parasols, banners, bells, and with rows of lamps all around.
And with many kinds of offerings.
This, Ānanda, is our instruction to you.
For what reason?
For herein, in this perfection of wisdom, the accomplishment of the knowledge of omniscience will occur.
What do you think, Ānanda—is the Tathāgata your teacher?
Ānanda said: He is my teacher, Blessed One.
"The Sugata is my teacher.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, the Tathāgata is your teacher.
You have attended upon me, Ānanda, with friendly bodily action that is pleasing to the mind."
With loving verbal action that is pleasing, and with loving mental action that is pleasing.

Therefore, Ānanda, just as you have now shown love, faith, and reverence toward me while I am currently staying, existing, and maintaining this physical form, [so should you act toward the Tathāgata after my passing].
In the same way, Ānanda, after my passing, you must act toward this perfection of wisdom.
A second time and a third time, Ānanda, I entrust and hand over to you this perfection of wisdom,
so that it may not disappear.
Just as there would be no other man for you in this [woman],
so, Ānanda, it should be understood that as long as this perfection of wisdom circulates in the world, for that long the Tathāgata remains.
It should be understood that the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for that long.
Ānanda, it should be understood that those beings are never separated from the vision of the Buddha, the hearing of the Dharma, and the service of the Saṅgha;
Ānanda, those beings should be understood as being in the very presence of the Tathāgata.
Those who shall hear this Prajñāpāramitā, take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, propagate it, teach it, explain it, proclaim it, study it, write it down, honor it, and revere it—
They will honor, worship, revere, and venerate [it] with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, bells, and flags,
as well as with rows of lamps all around and with many kinds of offerings.
The Blessed One spoke thus, and with joyful minds,

the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas headed by Maitreya, the Venerable Subhūti, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Ānanda, Śakra the lord of the gods, and the world with its gods, humans, asuras, garuḍas, and gandharvas rejoiced.
They rejoiced in what was spoken by the Blessed One.
The thirty-second chapter, titled "Entrustment," in the Noble Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom.

And thus concludes this *Bhagavatī Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, the mother of all Tathāgatas, the mother of Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas; the seal of the Dharma, the torch of the Dharma, the hub of the Dharma, the drum of the Dharma, the guide of the Dharma, the treasury of the jewels of the Dharma, the inexhaustible Dharma, the inconceivable and marvelous garland of stars that reveals [reality], honored by the world of gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, and the cause of all happiness.
Having correctly taken up the Perfection of Wisdom, mastered it, retained it, and set it in motion, may those who always seek the goal dwell in this.
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; thus speaks the Great Śramaṇa.
This is the religious gift of Lakṣmīdhara, son of Saurāja, a supreme lay devotee and follower of the most excellent Mahāyāna.
Whatever merit is herein, may it, placing the teachers, preceptors, mother, and father foremost, be for the attainment of unsurpassed knowledge by the entire mass of sentient beings.
